replies:
+---------------

Here's my bibliography for ECC:

	- Lin & Costello, "Error Control Coding: Fundamentals and
	  Applications" (Prentice-Hall)
	- Peterson & Weldon, "Error Correcting Codes" (MIT Press)
	- Blahut, "Theory and Practice of Error Control Codes" (Addison-Wesley)
	- Berlekamp, "Algebraic Coding Theory" (Aegean Park Press)

But for beginners, good books are:

	- Hamming, "Coding and Information Theory" (Prentice-Hall)
	- Arazi, "A Commonsense Approach to the Theory of Error-Correcting

correction. Lin & Costello is a pretty good cross-section, and has some

on pp.525-531 they discuss the particularly simple single-error correcting
shortened (174,171) R-S code over GF(256) used in the IBM 3370 disk. [You
can also use it in the unshortened (255,252) form.] This R-S code can easily

subject: How many different chess games can be played
q: Does a chess game always end, and how many different chess games can be played? Is the number finite?
ref: It's finite. The number of positions is finite, and a third repetition of a position ends the game as a draw. A hard upper bound is 64!/32! * 8^5, about 58 zeros, and transpositions and pawn limits cut it down. Hardly a stupid question, but think a bit.
replies:
The number off chess games is definitely finite.
This is because the number of chess positions is finite and the same
position cannot occur 3 times or the game ends in a draw.

I havent seen this number calculated but a definite maximum is:
64! / 32! * 8^5 (The 8^5 is the promotion factor). This gives us something
with 58 zeros (HUUUGE...).
This number has to be reduced because of transpositions and because all
pawns cannot reach every square.

I have tried it to no avail.  I think any time you are over the

It seems that once you have gone over the speed limit or committed
something illegal, anytime you are near a cop, they will pull you
over even if they didn't see you commit the act.

In the city I don't worry about them when I hear the siren because

 2. If you pass the cop in the far left of the left lane (far away

subject: empty but 2K resource forks?
q: My HyperCard stacks have resource forks that ResEdit reports as empty but take up about 2K each. How do I remove the whole resource fork?
ref: An emptied fork still holds an empty resource map of around 256 bytes, which rounds up to sector size. It's harmless apart from wasted space. To remove it, SetEOF the resource fork to zero with Fedit or an MPW tool. ResEdit won't do it, naturally.
replies:
If a stack has ever had a resource in it, but is now empty, the resource
fork still contains an empty resource map to the tune of 256 or so
bytes.  This will occupy a larger amount on disk depending upon the
sector size of your particular hard/floppy disk.

There is no problem with having an empty resource fork other than the
wasted space on the disk.

You can remove the resource fork of a file by doing a SetEOF of the file
(the resource fork of the file that is) to zero.  This can be done
interactively with Fedit or you can write an MPW Tool, or whatever.
Unfortunately ResEdit itself does not offer this feature.

Early versions of HyperCard liked to open empty resource forks which is
another cause of this problem, but later versions shouldn't do this.

Dan Allen
Apple Computer

subject: 69 Bug Idle problem
q: My 69 VW Bug 1500 with a 30 PICT carb idles erratically when warm. It almost stalls, hunts, then settles high, and adjusting mixture and volume screws doesn't help. What should I try besides a new carb?
ref: Sounds like a vacuum leak, often at the butterfly shaft or base gasket. With the engine warm and idling, spray carb cleaner sparingly around the shafts and gaskets. If idle changes a lot, that's your leak. Don't drench the intake throats. Swapping carbs first is amateur hour.
replies:
Unfortunately, what this sounds like is a vacuum leak, and
many times these will happen around the butterfly valve shaft.
It could also be possible to have one around the base gasket,
in which case you are lucky.  To find out if you have a vacuum
leak, go out and get a can of carb cleaner (the kind meant to
be sprayed into the throat while the engine is running).
Run the car until it is fully warmed up.  While idling,
use the plastic tube on the can and sparingly spray carb cleaner
at the butterfly shafts, the base gaskets and any other places
which may have openings into the carbs.  If the idle speeds up
or slows down considerably, then this is a very good sign
of a vacuum leak.  Be careful of spraying so much around
that it is getting sucked in over the top through the throats
of the air intake.  This will cause it to change idle speed,
but not be indicative of a vacuum leak.

subject: Hypersonic Transport
q: Is hypersonic transport, skipping supersonic and going via space as a shuttle spinoff, really on the horizon, or is it science fiction?
ref: Pretty much science fiction. Airlines and manufacturers concluded the problems and costs are out of proportion to the benefits: new fuel storage, revamped air-traffic control, gates for still-hot aircraft, and the aircraft itself. Supersonic research goes up to around Mach 4, but nobody takes hypersonic airliners seriously. Your guest lecturers need to get out more.
replies:
Pretty much so.  Both the airlines and the aircraft manufacturers have
concluded that hypersonic speeds do not appear to be worthwhile at present.
Not that the higher speed would not be useful, but the problems and costs
are out of proportion to the benefits.  Problems include things like new
fuel storage systems, radically revamped air-traffic control, special
gate facilities for still-hot aircraft, etc., quite apart from the
costs of the aircraft itself.  There is active research on supersonics,
up to circa Mach 4, but nobody is taking hypersonic or ballistic airliners
very seriously right now.

subject: Beware formating HD floppies in DSDD drives
q: Why does an HD floppy formatted as 400K or 800K in a DSDD Mac drive get rejected as unrecognized when I put it in an HD drive like the SE/30 or IIcx?
ref: Because HD media isn't built for 800K tracking. The old drive's wider tracks leave gaps and the test format isn't fully overwritten, so the newer drive reads good 800K data plus garbage between tracks. Blame Sony's standard, not Apple. Use the right disks, for crying out loud.
replies:
You are assuming that this is the way that "Apple" engineered it, and that
is not the case. You are dealing with two entirely different types of
floppies from HD to 800K. HD diskettes are formulated to be more sensative
to the lower voltages that the FDHD drives use in the HD mode. When you
format and use an HD diskette as an 800 or 400K disk, the FDHD cannot

subject: DPaint II brushes to C
q: I'm converting small low-res IFF brush files from DPaint II into C source with the GI program, but every file gives the same data and the color map is wrong. Did the brush file format change from DPaint I to DPaint II?
ref: DPaint II brushes add CRNG color-cycling chunks that DPaint I ones lack. A correctly written IFF reader just skips chunks it doesn't understand, so GI is wrongly assuming chunk order and position. Try ILBMDump from the IFF disk, though it only dumps image data, not the colormap. Sloppy code.
replies:
gi makes a whole lot of unwarrented assumptions about the way a brush
file looks.  It sounds, from the symptoms, like DPaint II has added
some additional chunks to the beginning of the files, and this would
cause gi to lose it in a big way.  When I get my hands on DPaint II, I
would be pleased to modify gi so that it'll work with DPaint II
brushes as well as the originals (I've been thinking about slicking it
up anyhow, so wotthehell...).  If and when this happens, I'll be sure
and post it.

I checked out brush files from both DPaint and DPaint II.  DPaint II
brushes contain CRNG (color cycling) chunks, DPaint brushes do not.
This should not bother a correctly written IFF reader because that's
what IFF is all about.  IFF readers are supposed to just skip chunks
they don't care about or don't understand.

   It sounds like GI is not doing this, but rather is making assumptions
about the order and position of the chunks it is interested in.

   The IFF disk contains a utility called ILBMDump which converts a brush
to a C source file.  But it only writes out source for the image data,
not for the colormap.  The source is provided and could be modified to
handle additional chunks.

subject: Random permutation algorithm
q: A paper says the fastest imperative algorithm for a random permutation takes O(n) time. Given n random integers in 1..n, there are n^n inputs but only n! outputs, and n! doesn't divide n^n. Am I misreading the problem?
ref: You're misreading it. There's only one input, the given sequence of length n, and you generate a uniformly random permutation of it. Duplicates are irrelevant. Loop i from 1 to n, pick j randomly from i to n, exchange a(i) and a(j). Done.
replies:
You are misreading the question.  There is only one input, namely
the given sequence of length n.  The problem is that you are given a
sequence of integers a1 ... an.  Generate a uniformly random permutation of
that sequence.  From the statement of the problem there may be duplicates
in the sequence, but that is irrelevant.  The imperative algorithm runs as
follows:

	for i from [1...n] sequentially chosen
	  select j from [i...n] randomly
	  exchange a(i),a(j)
	  end loop

ref: Because that is what gave us the procedural interpretation of Prolog, which made it usable as a programming language at all. Breadth-first can need exponentially more memory, making it infeasible on real problems. Iterative deepening is trivial in Prolog if you want the safety. Think before asking.

When you come right down to it, the answer is "because THAT is what
gave us the procedural interpretation of Prolog in the first place",
that is precisely the thing that made Prolog usable as a programming
language.

I don't know any programming language in which it is impossible to find
logically equivalent programs which are behaviourally different (at least
in the sense of taking greately different amounts of time and/or space).
(Yes, I do know about lazy functional languages.  They're the ones I had
in mind where it's easy to find gross cost differences between equivalent
programs.)

Breadth-first search can require EXPONENTIALLY more memory than
depth-first search, to the point that breadth-first search on non-trivial
problems is almost always completely infeasible.  We are talking about
ENORMOUS differences here.

Prolog (see "The Craft of Prolog" plug plug), which gives you the safety

subject: news
q: I want a VHF/UHF antenna for my scanner. How would I feed several vertical antennas cut for different frequencies with one coaxial cable, and what impedance would it be?
ref: Just use a discone. Simple, no gain, flat from 30 to 1000 MHz, ugly too. Combining separate antennas needs combiners, matching networks and filters, and without them you throw away half your signal at each junction. You really don't want to do this.
replies:
Just use a discone. Simple, elegant, no gain, flat from 30 to 1000 Mhz.
Ugly too.

To feed several separate antennas you'll need power combiners, matching
networks, and bandpass and band-reject filters. You don't really want to do
this. Since the antennas are for different frequencies, simple combining
networks won't do. Without filters all the antennas will contribute some
signal at each frequency. This will lead to some mighty weird patterns.
Also without proper filters you'll be throwing away half your signal at
each combining point. You may wind up with less than the unity gain of
the discone even though all your individual antennas have gain. Doing this
right can be expensive and tedious. You *really* don't want to do this.

Gary KE4ZV

I think what you want is a ground plane antenna (one vertical element,
and the other element consisting of 4 or more horizontal or slightly
drooping radials).  Then just use two or more vertical elements connected
in parallel.  At any given frequency, the impedance of the one that is
resonant will be *much* lower than that of the others in parallel with it.

  The radials should be at least as long as the longest vertical element.

  Note also that any antenna of this type will also resonate at 3 and
  5 times the frequency it is cut for. This combined with the generally
  non-critical nature of receiving antennas, might let you get by with
  *one* vertical element.

subject: Does XENIX have sockets? Also, software availability.
q: Does XENIX support sockets? If not, what does it use for interprocess communication? And where can I find XENIX software vendors?
ref: No, Xenix doesn't have sockets as such. It does IPC with message queues, where you can tag messages with a type, plus semaphores and shared memory in both Xenix and AT&T versions. Pipes work as always. A TCP/IP kit may add a socket library. Read the manuals.
replies:
No, Xenix does not support sockets as such and I don't think
AT&T Unix does either.  Xenix does support IPC though, using
different routes.

The most common and closest to sockets, is messaging, which is
a "stream" connecting 1 or more processes together. So you can have
1 process send something, and have 3 other ones receiving (like
sockets, once a message is "received", it is deleted from the queue).

Unlike sockets though, you can attach a message type (that you define)
to each message, so that a process which goes to read the message
queue, can receive the first message of a certain type (the type
may be its PID number or something).  Messaging also supports
normal permissions -- owner,group,other (read/write) -- for the queues
providing some security.

Xenix also has semaphores (Xenix version and AT&T) as well as
shared memory (again, Xenix & AT&T versions).

I'm redisigning the "talk" program that was posted a while back from
pipes to messages.

We are running SCO xenix; like you, we have a need for IPC.
In our case we use the message passing operations msg_send, msg_receive,
etc.  As far as pipes go, they look just like they always have.

In our case, we also have the "socket library" that comes with the
TCP/IP protocol software we use for our ethernet.  This came with
the Micom/Interlan ethernet kit.  It includes such system calls
as bind, which mentions sockets in the man page.

subject: Video Attributes
q: How do I get bold, reverse and underline strings on the screen of an IBM PC? What escape sequences do I use?
ref: Use ANSI escape sequences. Put device=ansi.sys in config.sys, and it should be on your DOS disk. Then ESC[ followed by attribute numbers and m sets the attributes: 0 normal, 1 bold, 4 underline on mono, 5 blink, 7 reverse. Read the manual.
replies:
ASSUMPTION: using MS-DOS

A PC uses ANSI escape sequences to print underlined, blinking , etc
characters.  First you must have device=ansi.sys in your config.sys
file and of course have ansi.sys available.  ANSI.SYS should be on
your MS-DOS diskette.  The following is an incomplete set of ANSI
sequence's :

	ESC code sequence		Function
	-----------------		--------

Erase Functions:

	ESC[2J				Clear screen and home cursor

	ESC[K				clear to end of line

Set graphics rendition:

	ESC[#;#;...;#m			Set display attributes where # is

					0 for normal display

					1 for bold on

					4 underline (mono only)

					5 blink on

					8 invisible

					30 black foreground

					31 red foreground

					32 green foreground

					33 yellow foreground

					34 blue foreground

					35 magenta foreground

					36 cyan foreground

subject: An Obvious Security Problem?
q: Couldn't a bad guy on a gateway between two nodes monitor TCP/IP traffic for Telnet connections and capture the login names and passwords?
ref: Yes. With a LAN sniffer you can read the whole Ethernet cable, since all networking schemes assume physical security of the media. The fix is to encrypt the comm line, or better, end-to-end. Welcome to networking, newbie.
replies:
I am a complete novice at matters relating to networking and haven't
    read the Telnet RFC so I may be missing something obvious.

No question is unworthy of asking.

    Assume the following network organization:

    A <------------------> M <------------------> Z

    (Node M is actually one or more gateways.) Couldn't a bad guy
    on   M   monitor   the  TCP/IP  traffic  looking  for  Telnet
    connections and then follow through  the  exchange  of  login
    names  and  passwords,  thereby  capturing  a  node/login and
    password pair? (I realize that  the  path  from  A  to  Z  is
    dynamic and that this might not always be possible.)

Yes.  In fact if one has a LAN sniffer one can  read  the  entire
traffic  on  the  EtherNet  Cable.  All networking schemes assume
physical secuirty of the communications media.

The DoD people have a solution: encrypt the comm-line.  There  is
a  secure  version  on  the  Internet  that does just that.  Even
better is to use end-to-end en

subject: Smail 2.5 and Domain Addressing
q: Can Smail 2.5 be set up so mail for anything like xxx.cynic.uucp is tried via uux to xxx!user and bounced if unknown, instead of going back to my smarthost? Is that even a good strategy?
ref: Smail 3.1 can strip a list of domain names before looking up the host, which does this automatically. With 2.5 you must keep the exact names in your paths file, but merge uuname output with your own name to build it. And yes, treating x.y.z as z!y!x is sensible.
replies:
Smail 3.1 can be given a list of domain names to remove before searching
for a hostname so you can get this behaviour pretty much automatically.
With Smail 2.5, you would probably have to maintain the exact names
in your paths file.  It shouldn't be too hard to merge the output
of 'uuname' and your own name to produce the list you need in the
paths file.

I think so.  It should always be possible to route uucp mail as though

what it is supposed to mean but once you get to a machine where this
interpretation makes sense, it doesn't matter.  Usually, though,
you wouldn't get this kind of address unless your neighbors are
putting it in their From: header lines and they shouldn't be doing
that without your approval.

subject: SYSV R4.0 High speed UUCP
q: My SysV R4 uucico to uunet over a V.32/V.42bis modem dies with alarm errors. How should flow control be set up?
ref: It's flow control, as usual. Turn xon/xoff off on both modem and computer, and RTS/CTS on. With g-protocol, modem error correction should be OFF, since it can interfere with g's own software error correction. Lost packets cause those alarms. Every week, this one.
replies:
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

  Does the new FAS have streams support? I had al older one which
didn't, and I didn't even look at the new one yet.

With high speed modems it is most important to have flow control set up
properly. Any lost or corrupted packets cause alarms. Depending
on what protocol you are using you need the following flow control:

Protocol Used           Modem       	   		Computer
--------------------------------------------------------------------
g-protocol		xon/xoff OFF			xon/xoff OFF
			RTS/CTS  ON			RTS/CTS  ON
			Error Correction OFF

f-protocol		xon/xoff OFF			xon/xoff OFF
			RTS/CTS  ON			RTS/CTS  ON
			Error Correction ON

Modem Error Correction sometime interferes with the g-protocol (which
uses software error correction) and should be OFF.

subject: Domain across phone line and SLIP
q: Can we run Domain across a SLIP phone line so engineers can work from home on an Apollo, and what could such a user do?
ref: Stop thinking of it as Domain across SLIP. You get the standard IP services, telnet, ftp and so on. Domain protocols expect low round-trip times and want 56kb or faster links, not slow phone lines.
replies:
The standard IP services -- telnet, ftp, etc.

You really shouldn't think of this as "Domain across SLIP".  SLIP
specifically refers to a way of doing point-to-point IP links over
(typically slow speed) serial lines.  Domain can run over point-to-point
links, but the target is high speed links to connect bridges (Domain
routers) to pass traffic between between high speed LANs (ethers or rings).
We require that the links be fairly high speed since the Domain protocols
expect low round-trip times.  (I don't know what the "advertised" minimum
speed link is, but it's certainly 56kb or higher.)  It has not been a
goal to make Domain protocols run across slow-speed links.  Thus, while
you could in principle put nodes at home, you'd need to spend a lot of
money to get them connected.

offers.  For example, if you access Domain files via NFS, you'll lose
things like type information.  Further, I don't know whether people

subject: Something similar to netstat ... but quicker.
q: Netstat is slow when I use it to see who is remotely fingering my machine. Is there a quicker way?
ref: Use the -n flag. It's slow because netstat does a DNS lookup on every address, possibly contacting far-away nameservers. One test took 2 seconds with -n and 56 without. You can look up the interesting hosts afterwards. RTFM.
replies:
Often "netstat" runs slow because of the cost of translating IP host
addresses to names, via the domain name system.   This is especially
true if the host names are from "far away", since it means you might
have to contact a foreign nameserver for each one.

You can get around this by giving the "-n" flag to netstat.  I ran
netstat on gatekeeper.dec.com, which has a lot of non-local connections,
and timed it:
    with -n:	     0.6u 0.3s 0:02 46% 89+173k 23+1io 0pf+0
    without -n:	    14.7u 1.2s 0:56 28% 91+233k 33+2io 0pf+0w
Kind of dramatic, no?

Of course, you won't know the names of the hosts or services, but
you can look them up afterwards when you find the particular line that
interests you.

This is even more useful with "netstat -r", which tries to look up
lots of network names and usually fails.  On gatekeeper.dec.com:
    with -n:	   1.7u 1.2s 0:08 36% 91+184k 0+1io 0pf+0w
    without -n:	   I got bored and gave up after more than 8 minutes.

subject: Ilford XP-1 B&W
q: What are the pros and cons of Ilford XP-1 film compared with conventional B&W film?
ref: Pros: any colour-neg lab can develop it, it's a chromogenic film, and it's usable from ASA 200 to about 3200 with grain getting smaller at higher speeds. Cons: contrast and definition are far worse, and you get weird equidensity areas. For speed, use TMax P-3200; the rest is a matter of taste.
replies:
Pros (if any): you can drop this film off for development at any place that does
colour neg processing as it is essentially a monochrome colour neg film (they
call it a chromogenic B&W film); sensitivity is no issue from ASA 200 to
approx 3200 (or so), with grain getting _smaller_ at higher speeds. No real
need to push process either.

Cons (in my opinion): contrast and especially definition of this film are
far worse than "normal" B&W film. I always used to get lots of equidensity
areas on my negs, which gives your prints a very wierd look. I stopped using
XP-1 a long time ago. If you want the speed, go Kodak TMax P-3200, if you want
a good quality standard film go TMax 400 (OK I'll admit, my advice is biased,
and a lot at that). If you want the possibility of C41 development, you're
stuck with XP-1

subject: Security problem: user not at console starting X
q: Anyone can rlogin to a machine with X and run startx, kicking off the person already at the console. Why is this possible and how do I prevent it?
ref: It's possible because the permissions on the frame buffer, keyboard and mouse devices are wrong. Tie their ownership to the console user in /etc/fbtab; see man 5 fbtab. Better, run XDM. You can also make startx exit unless tty is /dev/console.
replies:
The startx script says "Site administrators are STRONGLY urged to write nicer
versions," so I did.  When we started to have this problem I added the
following to the begining of startx:

if ( "`tty`" != "/dev/console" ) then
	exit
endif

At least something similar to this.  I also moved xinit out of the normal
users' path and put it in /usr/lib/X11/xinit.  Therefore, I also modified the
line near the bottom of startx to the absolute path for xinit.

I ran into a problem when I applied a new patch to X and reinstalled X.  I
forgot to reinstall my modified version of startx.  It seemed that many of our
users put startx in their .login.  Many of these people login remotely and we
had problems again. So I modified startx again with:

if ( "`tty`" != "/dev/console" ) then
	echo "Please run startx from the console not from" `tty`
	echo `whoami` "ran startx from a tty other than console" | root
	echo "Please run startx from the console not from" `tty` | mail `whoami`
	sleep 10
	exit 1
endif

Environment: X11R4 on SunOS 4.0.3, X11R5 on SunOS 4.1.1

   Anyone can log into (e.g. `rlogin' to) a machine equipped with X
   windows and type startx (or indeed X), and away they go.
   [...]
   So, Why is this possible and How can I prevent it from happening ???

It is possible because the permissions on the frame buffer/keyboard/
mouse devices are incorrect.  You can tie the ownership of these files
to the user who is logged in at the console by editing /etc/fbtab;
see `man 5 fbtab'.

A better solution would be to run XDM.  The problem is that you can't
easily switch between window systems (X11R5, OpenWindows, SunView).

subject: Slowest Amiga
q: My Lucas/Frances combo on my A500 is flaky. It crashes after a few hours, and CPU_Speed shows nonsense. I've got fans blowing and thought it was heat. Any help?
ref: Probably not heat, but noise. The RAM controller sits on top of the A500 RAM chips and doesn't like them. Cut a roughly 4 inch square of copper clad board, tape one side, and put it under the controller with the taped side toward the Frances board. Solder wires from its edges to ground points. It never crashes now.
replies:
After putting my lucas/frances in my 500, I found lots of flakey behavior too.
It also crashed after running awhile.  I thought that it was heat too.  What
it really seems to have been was noise.  It seems the ram controller resides
on top of the a500 ram chips, and the former doesn't like the latter.  I did
the following fix:

1) cut a small square of copper clad board (about 4" sq).
2) insulate one side with electrical tape
3) place the copper board under the controller chip and neighboring circuitry
   with the taped side towards the frances board
4) solder small lengths of wires from the edges of copper board to ground
   points on the frances board.

Anyway, sorry to be so simplistic, but the above fix worked wonderously for me.
My machine used to crash constantly.  Now it never does!

Hope this helps.

-Vince

subject: 2.88 meg floppy drives
q: Why are the 2.88 meg floppy drives so expensive, and can they use standard high density floppies?
ref: No. The 2.88Mb disk needs a special formulation, nothing like the current HD stuff, and a better substrate that costs more. Until prices fall, use 1.44M high density media, which costs less than half as much. You swap more, so deal with it.
replies:
According to some research into the new 2.88Mb floppy (which is currently
only made by Toshiba), it required a special formulation, that is NOTHING
like the current HD formula.  The 2.88Mb floppy is 4Mb unformatted (so where
did all that space go?) and has twice as many sectors/track as teh 1.44Mb
HD disks, otherwise it is the same.

The reason for the price is that they must use, again, a better substrate,

subject: Car stereo; good sound but feels wrong
q: After listening to my new rear car speakers a while, my ears feel tired and pressurized. The highs seem too strong and the midrange weak. What causes it, and can an equalizer fix it?
ref: Ear fatigue is common with overly bright speakers. Turn down the treble for a few days and see. If that works, cut the highs to the rear speakers only, since you want good highs up front. A capacitor shunt might do it.
replies:
I believe 'ear fatigue' is a common occurance with speakers that are
overly bright.  I would try simply turning down the treble control
(assuming no equalizer) for a few days to see if that solves your problem.
If that works, you may want to think about somehow reducing hi-end
output from the rear speakers without affecting the front speakers
(generally, you want decent high-frequency response up front, to 'pull
the image forward').  Can this be done by shunting the rear speakers
with a capacitor of appropriate value?

subject: Fonts and freeing memory
q: My Amiga C program loads a font with OpenDiskFont(), uses SetFont(), and later calls CloseFont(), but I lose 3k-4k of memory on every run. Is there a bug in the font functions, or am I doing something wrong?
ref: You're not doing anything wrong, so stop worrying. The system frees the font memory on its own when memory gets low. If you must have it back now, request an impossibly large AllocMem(), which flushes unused resources. I wouldn't, since reloading the font costs time.
replies:
Well, you don't need to worry about it.  When the system gets low on memory,
it will automagically free the memory that is used for the font.

Now, if you _really_ want to get that memory back immediately, you can
request an impossibly large amount of memory with AllocMem().  This will
flush all unused resources from memory.  (This is one of the main reasons
that the documents keep telling you to close everything you open, so it
can keep track).

But again, I recommend that you avoid doing this.  After all, if your
program (on another one) needs this font again, it will save time if
it doesn't have to reload it.

BTW, try "loadwb -debug" sometime and look for the invisible menu to
the right of 'special'.  See 'flushlibs'?  Don't try "Debug" unless you
have a terminal connected to your serial port.

Richard Addison

subject: Need Info: Red eye problem
q: I took pictures at a wedding under lots of video lights and many came out with red eye. How do I avoid red eye?
ref: The video lights had nothing to do with it. Red-eye is the flash lighting the back of the eyeball, caused by the flash being too close to the lens axis, and it worsens with distance. Use a flash or bracket that puts it farther from the lens.
replies:
The video lights had absolutely nothing to do with the red-eye problem.

Red-eye is caused by the flash illuminating the interior surface of
the subject's eyeball and that surface being visible in the photograph.
It is the result of the axis of the flash being too close to the axis
of the camera lens.  The effect becomes more pronounced as distance
from the camera is increased.

To solve the problem, use a flash (or a flash bracket) that places the
flash further from the lens.

subject: Video Blackjack
q: Is video blackjack worth playing? Many machines seem to offer a 2:1 blackjack payoff and surrender, and how can you tell when the shuffle happens?
ref: Read the machine properly: it says 2 FOR 1, which is just 1:1. A true 2:1 payoff would give you about a 2% edge. If it doesn't say when it shuffles, assume it shuffles after every hand. Wishful thinking isn't a strategy.
replies:
I have never seen a video BJ machine with 2:1 BJ payoff.  If you read
them carefully, they usually say 2 *FOR* 1 payoff, which is equivalent
to 1:1.  A true 2:1 payoff would give the player about a 2% edge, unless
they have some silly rules like letting the machine win all ties.

Machines that offer both surrender and insurance will usually let you
surrender before the machine checks for dealer BJ.  This gives you
early insurance when the dealer shows an ace.  These machines have
less than a 2% edge.

If the machine doesn't say when it is shuffling, you can assume that it
shuffles after each hand.

subject: Postscript in Xenix 2.3.4?

ref: Yes, though PostScript is just ASCII, so the dumb interface script already printed it. What 2.3.4 adds is a PostScript banner page, a filter turning ASCII text into PostScript, and landscape and side-by-side printing (land2). Marketing made it sound grander than it is.
replies:
Since PostScript is basically ASCII text, the ``dumb'' interface script
will work fine with PostScript.  I've used the hpjet interface, hardcoding
the option '-o raw' into it so as to not have the interface script change
the PostScript text.
As I understand it, printing a PostScript file to a PostScript printer
is virtually transparent to the spooler.

1) a postscript banner page

   function.

   side by side mode (land2), which puts two normal pages in smaller
   type side by side on one landscape page.

Tim Ruckle

subject: Mac II D/A resolution
q: How can the Mac II deliver CD-quality audio with only 8 bits of D/A resolution?
ref: It doesn't. The one DAC in the Mac II sound chip is 8 bits, multiplexed for stereo, and can sample at 22 or 44.1 kHz. It sounds very good, but it's not strictly CD quality, which needs 14 to 16 bits. Marketing, sigh.
replies:
It doesn't.  It samples at 44.1KHz, but the sampling word is 8bit instead
of 14 or 16.  The S/N is around 40 to 50db.  Noisy...
  For the poop on the II, read this months BYTE.

Ed, old buddy, the Amiga D/A's are 8-bit *linear* with a 6-bit volume
control.  You can view this as floating point if you wish, but it's
quite different from the exponential converters used on some "noise
generator" class chips.

The Mac II can manage a 44KHz sample rate, but it can't handle the
14-16 bits normally considered as CD quality.

The Amiga is nominally limited 8 bits, with a 28.8 KHz, but by playing
games with the multiple channels and volume controls you can get another
bit or two and get some rather impressive dynamic range.  If you are
willing to dedicate the processor to sound generation you can directly
drive the sound channels to achieve >> 44KHz sampling rates.  (a little
snip-snip on the low-pass filter helps here).

Still, 16-bit resolution at 44KHz would be nice, but one has to comtemplate
the noise floor in the personal computer environment, especially when using
on-chip converters.

I haven't seen/heard the Mac-II yet, but I have seen Bob Hoover demonstrating
h

The one DAC in the Mac II sound chip is only 8 bits; it is time multiplexed
via a S/H for two channel (stereo) operation.  The sample rate can be either
Macintosh compatible at 22.26kHz, or CD compatible at 44.1 kHz.  The sound
quality is 'very good', but it is not strictly 'CD quality', because of the
lower resolution of the DAC.  However, you won't believe how good only 8 bits
can sound until you hear it in person.

subject: TCP connection failure detection
q: My TCP client sends a message to a TCP server that has crashed, and send() returns no error. Is this normal? It only errors after I reset the server.
ref: Perfectly normal. send() just buffers the data and returns before anything is acked, so the client hasn't noticed the server is dead. It retries several times, gives up eventually, and only then do later send()s fail. Kill just the process and the kernel tells you at once. Sigh.
replies:
In many TCPs, the data you send() is bufferred in the client and the send()
call returns before the data has been sent and acknowledged. So, you get
no error from the send() because your client has not yet discovered that
there is a problem with the server.  It only makes that discovery after
it has tried sending the client's data several times.

The client will eventually decide that the server is not going to answer.
Any send()s you do after that point will get error returns.
In addition, it may be possible to get some kind of asynchronous notification
from the kernel as soon as TCP discovers the problem.
The details depend on your particular implementation.

If you kill the server process without crashing the server host, then
the server's kernel notifies the client TCP right away that something is dead.
The client then doesn't have to work to discover this fact.
Obviously, if the entire server machine dies, no such notice is possible.

subject: How do I abort an asynchronous PBControl? (ADSP driver)
q: How do I abort an asynchronous PBControl on the ADSP driver? KillIO is too severe because it aborts all ADSP activity, and I just want to cancel one connection's I/O, such as for a timeout.
ref: Use dspReset, which clears all activity on a given connection and resynchronises it without touching other connections. Or turn it around: poll with dspStatus and only call dspRead once the data has arrived. Likewise check free buffer space before writing. Then there's nothing to abort.
replies:
Two ideas come to mind.  dspReset will clear all activity on a given
connection and resynchronise the connection.  This won't affect any
other connection.

Another idea is that instead of issuing either a dspRead or dspWrite
then waiting for completion, you would sort of turn this around.

Take the read example.  Use dspStatus to see how much data has arrived
and don't make the dspRead call until you know it will complete successfully.
This way you can "abort" at any time since you aren't waiting around
for a dspRead to complete.

Likewise, the write example would check for enough free buffer space
to know that the write will complete right away.

There are a few restrictions with this scheme.  Your messages must
fit into your buffers, and I'm if you are using eom's the read example
gets more complicated.  But it can provide a very clean abort mechanism
without messing with trying to get ADSP to do it for you.

subject: TeX pk fonts to sfp

ref: Not as such, but use the batch download option of Jetroff 2.5 or later. Printing one character downloads the entire font; redirect that with -d- and strip the positioning commands and trigger character, and you have a softfont file. Untested, mind you, but it makes sense.
replies:
According to recent advice from Rick Richardson, author of JetRoff, the
easiest way to achieve this is to use the batch download option to Jetroff 2.5
or later.

This switch is designed to make JetRoff compatible with not-fully-compatible
laser printers which are unable to do the incremental downloading supported
by HP laser printers.

In effect, with this switch, printing a single character in a given font
causes the entire font to be downloaded to the printer. You can then take this
output (by redirecting it using the -d- option and shell output redirection)
and strip off extraneous material (i.e. positioning commands at the beginning,
the actual command printing the trigger character at the end). The resulting
file should be a HP SoftFont compatible file.

I have not tried this myself, but it makes sense :-).

Wolf

subject: SR-71 Maximum performance
q: Did the calculation of the SR-71's maximum speed take into account the airframe elongation, about a foot, from aerodynamic heating?
ref: Yes, in effect. Even if the length grows a foot with the span fixed, the Mach cone vertex angle changes by under half a degree, so Mach number moves only in the second decimal, about 17 knots TAS. Measurement error in the drawings is bigger. Not worth fussing over.
replies:
Larry Smith posted calculations based on the Mach No. required to
create an oblique shock from fully retracted inlet spikes that would
just enter the inlet.

I posted calculations based on the speeds necessary to create conical
bow shocks that would touch different parts of the airframe, the lower
limits being set by the inlet spikes/nacelles and the wingtips.

I assumed that the span would increase by the same percentage as the
length, which would have no effect on my calculations. Even if the
span stayed the same, and the length increased by one foot, the vertex
angle of the Mach cone would only change by less than half a degree,
and the Mach No. (reciprocal of sine of half the vertex angle) changes only in
the 2nd decimal (about 17 knots difference in TAS):

cone angle= 36 degrees. Mach No. = 1/sin18  = 3.24

My measurements (done on a 3" long plan and side elevation views of
the Blackbird in a book) and assumptions (limiting shock positions)
probably have more error.

Gopal

subject: How do you view slides?
q: I'm starting to use slides but I don't want to buy a slide projector. What other options are there for viewing them? What does everyone else use?
ref: Plenty of cheap ways. Use a light box, say an 8 x 10 piece of opal glass, or look through a spare 50-mm camera lens. Or hold a slide up toward white paper lit by a lamp, so the paper acts as a light table. Buying a projector is the lazy option anyway.
replies:
Buy the slide projector; don't be so cheap!  I use a light box I made
using an 8 x 10 inch piece of opal glass.  But I make 120 slides, and I
have to crop them for mounting.  You don't.

I use a 50-mm camera lens. Originally I used the lens of my camera.
Over the years I've acquired a couple of junked lenses (bad diaphragms,
etc.) that I now use as slide viewers. One of them is a genuine
Meyer Domiplan (East Germany's cheapest!).

Well, I have a really cheap and simple way to view slides. So cheap that a
college student can afford it and so simple that even an engineer-in-training
(like me) can figure it out.

For this method you will need the appropriate materials. They are:
	1) A piece of white typing paper
	2) A lamp
	3) Your slide

Hold the white paper in such a way that the light from the lamp shines
onto it. Now hold the slide between the paper and your eye, without holding
it between the lamp and the paper. It looks something like this:

               O --- Lamp
            \
     Paper -- \            |    (O) Your eye
                \         Slide

The idea is that the paper performs the same function as a light table. This
works especially well if you are nearsighted (I am) B-). If your close-up
vision ain't so good, you can use the same tecnique with a magnifying glass
between the slide and your eye.

subject: Advice Wanted: How to USE a 60 MB Tape Backup for 386 Xenix 2.3.1
q: How do I use a 60 MB tape cartridge drive on 386 Xenix 2.3.1? dd only got me 20 to 35 MB onto the tape.
ref: Stop using dd. Use cpio from the directory to back up: find . -print piped to cpio -ocduvmC 10240 -O/dev/rct0 -K60000. The -K tells it the tape size and it prompts for a new tape at the end. Adjust -K for the tape type, and RTFM.
replies:
Try:

place yourself in the directory that you want backed up

find . -print | cpio -ocduvmC 10240 -O/dev/rct0 -K60000

This will tell cpio that you have a 60 meg tape and it should go to the end.
If you have more than 60 meg to backup then cpio will prompt you for a new tape.

The tape sizes:

DC600A		60 meg
DC600XTD	60 meg
DC6150		150 meg
DC6250		250 meg

Adjust your -K option for the correct tape size.
To read your tape back in drop the -o and -K commands and change the -O
to a -I.

subject: VLT trouble with Kermit uploads
q: Uploading files from VLT using XPRKermit to a Sun in server mode, the files arrive named like "VD0:xxxx" with the source directory in the name. Is this a bug, or do I need "Convert Filenames" on?
ref: Expected behavior, not a bug. "Convert Filename" does more than lowercase: it strips leading path information and reduces the name to least-common-denominator form. With it off, the literal Amiga name goes out. Use VLT's Change Directory command (right-amiga-D) before sending.
replies:
This is, unfortunately, expected.  The "Convert Filename" switch
does much more than lower-case the name:  it actually strips off
all leading path information and reduces the name to a least-common
denominator form, in accord with standard Kermit procedure.
With "Convert Filename" off, the literal Amiga filename is sent
to the receiving system.

I'm open to easy-to-implement suggestions for improving this.

If you use the Change Directory command (right-amiga-D) of VLT
before sending, this won't happen.

Steve Walton, XPR Kermit co-author and maintainer

subject: Why aren't spins required for flight training?

subject: Pakistani Brain Virus
q: What useful information is there about the Pakistani Brain virus? We seem to have some of it running around here.
ref: CHKDSK will show it, reporting 3K of bad sectors. The volume label may read (c) Brain. It lives in the boot sector and in sectors it marks bad, infects at bootup even if you boot a non-system disk, and only hits 360K disks. Doesn't seem malicious. Basic stuff.
replies:
Our experience of the Brain virus is that it can be located by CHKDSK, which
reports 3K of bad sectors, normally 5K is the minimum. Depending on the state
of the disk, it will have a volume label (c) Brain. It resides in the boot
sector and elsewhere (in sectors it marks as bad), and it spreads by infecting
a machine at bootup time, even if you first boot with a non system disk. It
will then copy itself onto every disk that uses that machine. It will only
reside on 360K disks, and does not seem to be malicious as far as we can tell.
We have only seen version 9. There are innoculation programs written in the
U.K., details on request.

subject: TC2.0 bugfree ?
q: Is Turbo C 2.0 bug-free? It generates code that increments the pointer after both references in the expression i = (*cp++ << 8) + *cp++.
ref: Not a bug. K&R say the increment may happen any time between use and the next sequence point, so order of evaluation within an expression is undefined. Even lint warns about it. i++ + i++ + i++ has three legal results. Learn C before blaming the compiler.
replies:
[ statement in about TC2.0 being bug free, context of a subroutine ]

I can't find it in my copy of K&R, but I think that they (and most
C compilers I have seen) indicate that ++'ing the same variable multiple
times in a single expression is undefined.  Hence, this statement cannot
really be used as an example of a TC bug.

NO FLAMES PLEASE!!!  I would like any ANSI X3J11'ers or TC hacks or anyone
who can find documentation one way or the other to respond in a reasonable
manner.

*** Omitted code showing that "cp" gets incremented twice at end of
        generate code instead of after each reference ***

Sorry, this isn't a bug.  The order of evaluation of the ++ operators in
an expression is not guaranteed.  As evidence, this is what lint has to
say about the above code fragment:

	Script started on Fri Jan 20 09:21:51 1989
	1: lint foo.c
	foo.c(6): warning: cp evaluation order undefined
	foo.c(6): warning: i set but not used in function sub
	sub defined( foo.c(3) ), but never used
	2: ^D
	script done on Fri Jan 20 09:22:04 1989

Nevertheless, Turbo C likes to make noises about practically everything else,
I wonder they don't issue warnings about this?

[fragment omitted]

That is not a bug.  K&R explicitly state that the compiler may do the
increment any time between the value's use and the next sequence point
(comma, end of statement, etc.).  You cannot rely on order-of-execution
within an expression, since the compiler is free to rearrange things as
it sees fit.  The code fragment

	i = 4 ;
	printf("%d",i++ + i++ + i++) ;

has three legal results:
	12
	14
	15
depending on how many of the increments are deferred until after the
additions.

  1 RES\            28 PHI2 (out)

  5 A0              24 D1
  6 A1              23 D2

  8 A3              21 D4
  9 A4              20 D5
 10 A5              19 D6

subject: 3270 bisynch question
q: Is an RVI followed by a status sense response of "DEVICE BUSY" a legal response to a host device selection on 3270 bisynch? If the device is busy when the host selects it, should it use a WACK instead?
ref: Use WACK. Per the notes in the manual, a device with only Busy or only Device End should not send an RVI at all. Busy alone gets a WACK; Device End alone gets an ACK 0. RTFM, page 4.21 in mine.
replies:
The manual actually notes that WACK is the legal response
   according to Notes 2 and 3.

   Actually, as long as the ABSOLUTE NEXT outbound sequence to
   the device (after the RVI) is an EOT, then an Specific Poll,
   this is an error.

   Note 2 of the BSC Selection Addressing diagram specifically
   states that the device has pending status....EXCLUDING either
   Device End or Busy.   In other words, a device with ONLY Busy
   or Device End should NOT issue an RVI.

   If the status is only Device End, the device should send an
   ACK 0, reset it's DE status internally, and take the
   following command.

   If the status is Busy (which would obviously be exclusive of
   Device End), the device should return a WACK.

   As noted, if the ONLY status is Busy, the WACK is the proper
   response.   (Page 4.21 in my version of the Desc,
   Manual....but these haven't changed since the older 3271...)

subject: APL for Parallel Algorithms

make it very difficult to access those concepts.  I always find it interesting
how many papers on parallel languages footnote APL without really taking
anything from APL (Steele's C* comes first to my mind, but there are others).

subject: create remote process
q: Running crp -on B -me from node A fails with "no rights to server mailbox" on SR10.1. What causes the crp devices in /dev to get screwed up?
ref: On SR10.1, using any option other than -me, such as -login, or forgetting -me, corrupts the crp device. Doing it as root also locks the /dev/crp* protections so only root can touch them. Fix the rights or re-run mkdev, and don't crp as root. Later releases fixed it, I believe.
replies:
The only explanation I have gotten is that it happens when you are logged in
as root and do a "cpr -on B -me" to another machine.  Take a look at the
protections on the /dev/crp* files on the machine.  They should be wide open
but after root gets a hold of them they get set so that only root can do
anything with them.  The strange thing is that root can't crp on either after
this has happened.  Instead of running /etc/mkdev you could also just change
the rights of the /dev/crp* files.  The way to avoid the problem is to avoid
doing a "crp -on B -me" when logged in as root.  If you do this check the
protections of the crp files of machine B after disconnecting.

One bug with SR10.1 is that if any option other than the -me option is used,
such as -login username (or even if -me is accidentally omitted), the crp
device will be corrupted.  It is known and has, I believe, been corrected in
later versions of Domain/OS.

subject: Must main return a value?
q: Is int main(void) { return; } strictly conforming? I can't find a requirement in the Standard that main must return a value.
ref: No. Section 2.1.2.2.3 says that if main executes a return specifying no value, the termination status returned to the host environment is undefined. That's undefined behavior. Read the Standard more carefully; it's right there.
replies:
Yep.  The construct you used, 'int main (...' declares main to be a
function which returns an int.  You have declared it as returning a
value, and then not returned a value of the type specified.  Speaking
pedantically, that's a prima facie violation.

In practice, since return from main() generally throws you out of your
C-program environment, and back into your native operating system
environment, whether or not it makes any difference depends on your
OS.  Many OSes expect progs to return status codes -- especially progs
which have been declared to return status codes.  If you don't return
one, the results will be OS-dependent but can range the full gamut from
unpleasantly surprising to unpleasantly mysterious.

If you're really unlucky, your failure to return the value you promised
won't make any difference at all -- until next year, when you've got to
move the prog to another OS platform and have forgotten what you did.

For the effect of the program to be defined, the main function must return
a value.  It does seem strange that the compiler is required to issue a
diagnostic for a return statement with a value in a void function, but not
for the opposite mistake.

OK, if you don't want your program to send a small nuclear device at your car,
the main function must return a value.  (2.1.2.2 neither allows nor disallows
this extreme an effect; 3.6.6.4 allows it.)

You must be -- 2.1.2.2.3 states explicitly "If the main function executes a
return that specifies no value, the termination status returned to the host
environment is undefined."  That meets the condition for causing undefined
behavior on at least two counts.

subject: LocalTalk v. AppleTalk
q: What is the distinction between LocalTalk and AppleTalk?
ref: AppleTalk is the protocol suite. LocalTalk is the physical cabling and link layer, the hardware built into Macs, and AppleTalk also runs over EtherTalk and TokenTalk. Old docs used AppleTalk for both, which is why people mix them up. Learn the terms.
replies:
AppleTalk refers to the whole protocol suite.

LocalTalk refers to the built in hardware found in all Macs.

AppleTalk runs on top of LocalTalk Link Access Protocol when you use
the LocalTalk hardware as well as EtherTalk LAP (for Ethernet)
and TokenTalk LAP (for Token Ring).

Of course, this is current usage.  In old AppleTalk documentation
they never use the word LocalTalk, but rather use AppleTalk to refer
to both the protocol suite and the hardware.  Once other hardware
became available for running AppleTalk, the old fuzzy names didn't
work.

AppleTalk is the protocol.  LocalTalk is the physical cabling, this
includes phonenet.

Mike.

"AppleTalk" is the name of the protocol suite. "LocalTalk" is the name
of the cable that plugs into your Mac - really LocalTalk is an ISO
Data Link Layer thingdroid.

Likewise EtherTalk is what you have when it is running over Ethernet
physical cable, and TokenTalk is...

Lots of people (me included) get unjustly annoyed if you use the wrong
term. If you want to know the whole box and die, get "Inside AppleTalk
Second Edition" - nice light bedtime reading.

know what else to say).

subject: Booting MS-DOS from Hard Disk
q: I got PC-Ditto II running on my Atari ST with a Syquest hard disk, but it gives a non-system disk error when booting MS-DOS from the hard disk. Any ideas?
ref: The boot program checks both C: and D: for an MS-DOS signature, and if either fails it won't boot. Run pcdfix on both. It doesn't change D: if that's a TOS partition, it just keeps PC-Ditto happy. Annoying, but there it is.
replies:
When I looked into this on PC=Ditto I, it turns out that its boot program
was checking both C: and d: for a Ms/dos signature.  If either failed
it would not boot.  Since little there changed in PC_D II, I suspect its the
same.

The fix then is to use pcdfix on both c: and d: .  This in no way changes
d: if its a TOS partition.  It just makes PC_D happy.

subject: MPW Link Error
q: I'm linking a large application in MPW with a large segment and get 'jump table offset too large (Error 50)', yet the largest jump table offset in my load map is $0120(A5). What's going on?
ref: The error is obtuse, sure. The value being stuffed into the jump table is a signed 16 bit PC-relative offset on the 68000. If any entry point is more than 32K from the start of its CODE segment, it overflows. Shrink your segment.
replies:
I guess that error message is a little too obtuse, especially for an error that
occurs all the time. What the Linker is telling you is that the value
it is trying to stuff into $0120(A5) is too large. On the 68000, PC relative
offsets are signed 16 bit quantities. It is these values that go into the
jump table. It seems that your program is of such a composition that you'd
require a value that is out of this range. This occurs if you have any entry
points that are further away than 32K from the start of your CODE segment.

subject: Orientation during level flight
q: During level flight on a jet like a 757, does the plane fly level or is there always a slight upward nose angle?
ref: Yes, there's a positive deck angle in cruise. It minimizes induced drag at the wing/fuselage junction by keeping the spanwise pressure distribution uniform. Around 4 degrees for an L1011 at full gross weight. The airlines saved millions in fuel. Basic aerodynamics, folks.
replies:
Yes.  They're designed to fly at a positive deck angle
	in order to minimize induced drag at the wing/fuselage
	junction.  The main object is to keep the spanwise pressure
	distribution as uniform as possible.

	One of the artifacts I have in storage is a multi-page
	letter from Lockheed to an airline, TWA I think, explaining
	how many million bucks per year the L1011's deck angle
	would save them in fuel costs.  I don't recall for certain,
	but 4 degrees sounds familiar for an L1011's deck angle
	for cruising at full gross weight, and the airline execs
	at first wanted to know if Lockheed could reduce it.  They
	changed their mind after finding out about the tradeoff
	for bucks spent on glorified kerosene.

Possibly the disk controller is going bad.
Other option is a drop in the power line voltage has caused the disk to
write garbage on itself. If you can, INVOL it and reload.

often when the controller was going bad.

80009 means that the sector being read is not readable.  Usually
you can just add this sector to the badspot list.  The way to do this
is get the node up to the boot shell and look at the lsyserr log.  This

to the badspot list and salvol run on the drive.  In this case you also
will need to find the file that has the badspot and replace that file as
well.  Salvol should give you this information.  This is usually not
sufficient reason to replace the drive.  There is probably one sector
causing all the problems.

What is the exact error message?

You should be able to see the number of processes your
system is configured with in the file /usr/include/sys/kdef.h

"MAXUP" is the max number of processes per user.
"NPROC" is the max number of processes total.

subject: Quitting the Finder under MF
q: Under MultiFinder on a 1Meg Plus, the Finder quit when an app failed to launch, and I was left running PrintMonitor with no Finder. Anybody else seen this?

replies:
Just like any other application, the Finder can crash.  When this happens, the
user is not informed since it is the job of the Finder to do the informing.
When you quit all other apps, a new Finder will automatically be launched.
Until then, you are running "Finder-less".

One more note:  There is nothing in MultiFinder that prevents the Finder from
quitting, there is simply no way for the user to convince the Finder to do so.

-Phil Goldman
Apple Computer

difference, though, since DOS is DOS is DOS ...  However, to overcome

partition 2 cylinders larger than you need, then go back with fdisk to
delete the DOS partition, and re-create it with the correct size starting
at cylinder 2.  I would think this would keep anything from scribbling
on the first two cylinders.

Russ Jorgensen

subject: Looking for a way to gracefully open a file
q: Is there a way to open a text file on an AppleShare server from HyperCard and check for an error if another user already has it open? Is there an XCMD that does this?
ref: No, HyperCard doesn't do that. Write an XCMD, it's a few lines of C or Pascal. Call FSOpen or PBOpen and check the status result. Non-zero means an error, such as the file already being open read/write. Not built in, so quit waiting for Apple.
replies:
An XCMD could be written (very few lines of C or Pascal) that would
open a file.  Such an XCMD would need to call FSOpen or PBOpen or Open
(all variations on a common theme).  All of these calls return a status
result.  If non-zero, then an error (such as the file already being open
read/write) is returned.  Such functionality is NOT build in to
HyperCard.

subject: help with at&t models
q: What's the difference between the AT&T 6300, the 7300, the Unix PC, the 3B1 and the 3B2?
ref: The 6300 is a plain Intel PC clone. The 7300, UnixPX and 3B1 are the same 68010 machine running SysV 5.2. The 3B2 uses AT&T's own WE32000 chips and runs SysV 5.3 or 5.4. None of them are compatible. Honestly, it's not that confusing.
replies:
The 6300 is AT&T's PC clone.  It and newer versions all use
the INTEL 8086 family (ie. 8086, 80286, 80386).
The original was a DOS machine, the newer ones are able to run Unix.

The 7300, UnixPX, and 3b1 are different names for the same machine.
The 7300 was sold with less memory and a smaller disk.
They all use the Motorola 68010 processor,
and run Unix SYS5.2, (ok a slight variant).
The 3b1 (7300) was discontinued before there a second machine was introduced.
It is now an orphan, but one with a captive following.
I have one, it's a great machine.
The unix-pc.* newgroups are devoted to the 3b1.

The 3b2 is an AT&T exclusive.  The different members of the 3b2 line use
AT&T's own WE32000 family of processors, the WE32000, WE32100, and WE32200.
They run SYS5.3 or SYS5.4.

All three are completely different machines.  They are not compatible
with each other in any way.

by Robert Lai and published by Addison Wesley.
  " Caution: DOS function calls are allowed only in processing the

    was reentrant, this would not be true."

This book was written for up to DOS 3.3.  I have always followed this,
but I haven't actually tested it, so your mileage may vary.

subject: Serial port question
q: How do I initialize the Mac serial driver to send at 38400 baud? The constants exist for 57600 and 19200 but not 38400.
ref: A constant of 1 gives about 38,250 baud, per Inside Mac and the Zilog SCC manual. Or use the serial driver control call, csCode 13, with the desired rate and it picks the closest the hardware allows. Read the manual.
replies:
According to IM volumes II & III, and Zilog's SCC manual, a constant of
1 will send at 38,250 baud.  The formula is:

sclk = 1/(3,672,000 / 16)
baud = 1/(2 * (CONSTANT + 2) * sclk)

(0 is 57375, 1 is 38250, 2 is 28688, 3 is 22950, 4 is 19125, ... 380 is 300).

The constant is dropped directly into the SCC's time constant register.

Just looking at the numbers, it looks like they used one of those
drop-a-half-cycle-every-eight-full-cycles (multiply by 15/16) counter
stages to get 3.672 MHz out of a 15.6672 MHz crystal.

+----------------+
! II      CCCCCC !  Jim Cathey
! II  SSSSCC     !  ISC-Bunker Ramo
! II      CC     !  TAF-C8;  Spokane, WA  99220
! IISSSS  CC     !  UUCP: uunet!isc-br!jimc (jimc@isc-br.iscs.com)
! II      CCCCCC !  (509) 927-5757
+----------------+
			"With excitement like this, who is needing enemas?"

There's a control call to the serial driver that will let you give it an
arbitrary speed, and it will set the port to the closest rate that the
hardware will allow, and return the resulting actual baud rate.

	csCode = 13
	csParam = desired baud rate (in), actual baud rate (out).

See IM II-254 for more information.

Amanda Walker <amanda@intercon.com>

I always add the line:

	#define baud38400 1

to the Serial.h file supplied by Apple. I've never understood why, but
for some reason they leave it out of the header file.  I use this baud
rate quite often and have never had any problems.

	Andy Peterman

EOI must be sent.

If it is irq3, could there be anything else using irq3?  Can you switch
it to something else like irq5 (AT)?

Good luck.

-J Baker

ref: You can't have both. Both products want the same type of packets, and two TCP/IP stacks can't share one interface card. Running them together breaks something. Pick one, or look at Beame & Whiteside. Don't expect miracles.
replies:
Sorry, Bill.  Until we can work out some sort of deal with Geoff to
build the PC-NFS client to talk over the UDP/IP found in your LAN
WorkPlace for DOS...  You'll need to settle for one, or the other :-).
You see, both products want to see the same type of packets.

This is along the same lines as the common question about running
two different TCP/IP implementations at the same time...  It can't

subject: REVISED: How do I send e-mail to lots of users at a remote unix site?
q: How can I send one mail message to all the users on another Unix machine over the Internet, without mailing each one separately? Is there a mailing list or a way to have the remote machine distribute it?
ref: Don't. Mail is a lousy broadcast medium, and hundreds of copies will eat disk space in everyone's mailbox. Post to an appropriate newsgroup, use msgs(1) if the machine has it, or ask their sysadmin what medium to use. Admins get cranky about this.
replies:
This sounds like a bad idea.  Electronic mail isn't a good broadcast medium;
if there are lots of users on your destination machine then you're going to
eat up GOBS of disk space with hundreds of copies of your message in
everyone's mailbox.

Is there perhaps an appropriate newsgroup you can post to, or does the
machine have msgs(1), or something like that?  Perhaps you should ask the
system administrator of the destination machine what would be a good medium
for your message.

Someone here once mailed all the users on our local public system, which has
over 800 users.  We, the system administrators, were somewhat upset.  There
are much better ways of doing this sort of thing.

subject: Can an X11R4 client kill an X11R3 server ???
q: Can an X11R4 client, like OpenWindows 2.0 on a Sun, kill an X11R3 server such as an HP X terminal? It blows up after an hour of heavy work, and I get bad atoms messages.
ref: Mostly no. Mixing R4 clients with old R3 servers on HPs and Tek terminals works, except for shape extensions and multi-buffering. The real trouble is R3 window managers with R4 Xt apps, such as tiny xterm windows. Beware those. I can't vouch for your crashing server.
replies:
When we first installed R4 on our Suns and CONVEXen, we still had a few systems running R3 servers. For the most part, we did not see any problems, but
occasionally strange things did happen. Most of the problems seem related to
R3 window managers and not the server. For example, an R4 xterm would not
size properly on an R3 window manager. The xterm window would come up
8x4 or some random, tiny size.

Right now we use several old R3 servers on HPs and old Tek X terminals.
Everything works ok, except for shape extensions and multi-buffering.
Beware R3 window managers and R4 Xt applications.

Martin Streicher
Manager, Graphics and Windowing Software Development Group
Software Environments Product Department
CONVEX Computer Corporation
Richardson, TX

subject: libg++ and c++ question
q: I built libg++ on NeXT 2.1 and compiled hello.cc with cc++ -I... -L... -lg++ hello.cc, but ld reports undefined symbols _cout and _sputs__9streambufPCc. What am I doing wrong?
ref: Put -L/LocalLibrary -lg++ at the end of the command line. The linker only pulls in functions from a library that are already referenced, so a library listed before your source files links nothing. Link order, kid. Learn it.
replies:
I tried to make it by typing:

       cc++ -I/LocalLibrary/g++-include -L/LocalLibrary -lg++ hello.cc

   and this is what I get:

   /bin/ld: Undefined symbols:
   _cout
   _sputs__9streambufPCc

   Can anyone please tell me what I am doing wrong?

Try putting -L/LocalLibrary -lg++ at the end of the line.  Only the
functions in the library that you actually call are linked.  If you
put the libraries before the file, the linker won't link anything.

-Mike

A common mistake, which I suspect you might have, is to put "noauto" in

#

subject: What is the format of .forward files that sendmail can use?
q: What format can a .forward file take for sendmail? I want to forward special mail, like NeXTmail faxes, to different people depending on type, or print it.
ref: Each line is a comma-separated list of addresses: local usernames, E-mail addresses, files, or commands starting with a pipe. A backslash before a username stops further alias expansion. A .forward alone can't sort mail, so pipe it through a sorting program. And read aliases(5), this is a sendmail question.
replies:
(Note the cross-post and followup-to.  This is a sendmail question, not a
wizardly Unix question.)

Each line in the .forward file is a comma-separated list of addresses.  The
addresses can be any address that can appear in the aliases file; there should
be an aliases(5) man page on your system to document that.  There are four
types of addresses, basically -- local usernames (e.g. "phayes"), E-mail
addresses (e.g. jik@cats.ucsc.edu), files (e.g. /usr/home/phayes/mail.log),
and commands (e.g. |/usr/home/phayes/bin/process-mail).  Also, a username
quoted with a backslash prevents further alias expansion, so you can use
"\phayes" in your .forward to force a copy of the message to be placed into
your local mailbox, despite the .forward file.

You are not going to be able to use a .forward file on its own to do the mail
sorting you describe.  Instead, you are going to have to pipe the mail through
some sort of program to do the sorting.  For example, you might use the
"deliver" or "procmai

subject: Ada tasking with Mach
q: Where can I find out about Ada tasking on the Mach operating system?
ref: Talk to Encore, who have a Verdix Ada compiler modified to implement Ada tasks with threads. TRW has plain Ada bindings to the Mach system calls, but they don't promise to play nice with tasking. Pick the right tool.
replies:
Encore Computer has a version of the Verdix Ada compiler (VADS) which
I understand has been modified to use threads to implement Ada tasks.
I don't know if it's a product, though.

We (TRW) also have a set of Ada interfaces which allow access to all
the Mach system calls (they're available for free if you sign our
non-disclosure license).  However, they are not guaranteed to interact
properly with Ada tasking, because they're simply bindings to the Mach
system calls, and not a reimplementation of the run time system (as
Encore did).

to use other Mach features (like using ports & messages), use our
interfaces.

--Jeremy

The MINIX operating system is a Unix 7th Edition clone, that is currently

subject: What do you use to remove Paragraph Returns from your Text?
q: What do you use on a Mac to remove the Return characters from the end of every line in a paragraph of downloaded text? Is there an easy utility or a PD/shareware app?
ref: No utility needed, three search-and-replace passes do it. Change double returns to a unique temporary string, delete all the single returns, then change the temporary string back to double returns. Word does it fine, or use Emacs. It's not rocket science.
replies:
As a long-time Word victim I used to do a trio of search and replace
operations, first translating pairs of carriage-returns (CR) into a
hopefully unique string, then replacing all remaining CR's with a space,
then finally replacing the unique string with a CR to give me back my
paragraphs.  Had it down to a fine art, at least for small docs.

Now I use Emacs at both ends, Gnu on the UNIX machines and micro-Emacs
on the Mac, and remove the CR whichever end I remember I need to do it.
Micro-Emacs came over the net a few months ago (version 3.8).

Works for me.

Robert_S

I use MS-Word 3.01 to perform this function. It really is quite simple,
it only requires three 'search&replace' sequences (oh yes, a specific
utility would be better... but then again.. ;)

What you want is to remove all the returns at the end of the lines.
But removing all returns would also remove paragraph formatting. So what
you do first is to change all _double_ returns (at the end of a paragraph)
to a temporary code (like two asterisks: **). This is achieved with:

Find: ^13^13 (you actually type the carret in the dialog box)
Replace with: ** (or whatever unique code you like)

Now it's time to remove all _single_ returns (at the end of each line)

Find: ^13 (again, also type the carret)
Replace with: <zilch>

And now turn the temporary code back into double returns:

Find: **
Replace with: ^13^13

That's it.

        Paul Molenaar

	"Just checking the walls"
		- Basil Fawlty -

subject: SPECmarks....

ref: It comes from an industry consortium of workstation vendors, a composite of 10 tests, harder to cheat than Dhrystone MIPS. It leans toward floating point, so Intel made an integer version, I Spec. A 25 MHz Compaq 486 gets 8.7 SPECmark, 12.9 I Spec.

floating-pt. performance vs. integer performance, so Intel branched off
and created the I Spec or Integer Specmark.

then call CloseWindow.  If the window is not yours, just pass the
window pointer to CloseNDAbyWinPtr.

subject: Error in using Mail
q: Whenever I mail or forward a news article from ANU News to an account on another node, I get an error activating transport IN and IN_MAILSHR.EXE file not found. Local mail and VMS Mail work fine. What's wrong?
ref: Look in your news_address.cnf for an entry like *@* gateway::in%"\001@\002". The IN% transport is typically PMDF, and you evidently don't have PMDF, so it's invalid. Change it to your real transport. If you only send to DECnet nodes, drop the in% and the quotes.
replies:
You probably have an entry in the file news_address.cnf something similar to
what follows:

                *@*       gateway::in%"\001@\002"

the transport "IN%" typically is PMDF.  Your error message indicates that you
probably don't have PMDF, therefore this is invalid.  You need to determine
what your valid transport is and change the entry to that in your
NEWS_ADDRESS.CNF file.  If you are only sending to DECnet nodes, try removing
the in% and "'s altogether.

subject: backslash-newline inside C++ comments?
q: Is a backslash-newline inside a C++ // comment legal in ANSI C++? In ANSI C the backslash-newline pairs are removed before comments are handled, so it seems like it should be.
ref: Yes, it's legal. The Annotated C++ Reference Manual lists the same translation phases as ANSI C: backslash-newline gets deleted, then comments become white space, so the next line joins the comment. Why anyone would want it, I couldn't tell you. Sigh.
replies:
According to ELLIS, Margaret A., STROUSTRUP, Bjarne, "The Annotated C++
Reference Manual", pp 370ff, [Chapter 16, section 1]:

	1.  If needed, new-line characters are introduced to replace
	    system-dependent end-of-line indicators and any other
	    necessary system-dependent character set translations
	    are done.  Trigraph sequences are replaced by their single
	    character equivalents.
	2.  Each pair of backshash character \ immediately followed by
	    a new-line is deleted, with the effect that the next source
	    line is appended to the line that contained the sequence.
	3.  The source text is decomposed into preprocessing tokens and
	    sequences of white space.  A single white space replaces
	    each comment.  A source file may not end with a partial
	    token or comment.
	...

So, yeah,

		// This is a comment \
		   though a rather useless one.

is a legal comment.  God help me if I know why you'd ever want to *use*
such a construction...

subject: Domain Ring and NFS
q: We have Apollos on a Domain Ring and Suns on the same site, but they can't talk since NFS isn't on both. What are the advantages of running NFS on an Apollo network?
ref: The obvious one: Suns and Apollos can finally share files. You can mount the entire ring through a single server, which keeps fstab small. The catch is mount points are typed files, so you can't mount remote filesystems on remote directories and you lose hierarchy. Newer NFS fixes bugs.
replies:
Well, the obvious (and compelling) advantage is that Suns and Apollos
will be able to share files if you run NFS on your ring...

	There's good news and bad news about Apollo NFS.  The good news is
that it lets you mount the entire ring through a single server:

		/etc/mount -t nfs foo:// /nfs/apollo

will mount an entire Domain internet (as seen by //foo) on /nfs/apollo on a
Sun.  You then use node names below that.  This helps keep /etc/fstab and/or
your automount map within bounds, although it may not work well with estabished
naming conventions.

	The bad news is that since mount points are typed files (nfs_gate),
you can't mount remote filesystems on remote directories (like you can on Suns
and other native UNIX boxes), so you lose the filesystem hierarchy on remote
mounts.  All of our mount points for a given host are in a flat namespace.

	It looks like they've fixed a lot of bugs at NFS 2.1, so I'm not sure
what the other bad news is at present.  It's worth trying.

subject: Disk Data Transfer Question
q: On my AT&T 3600 (Olivetti M24) with a Seagate ST251-1 and WD controller, I need interleave 5 and get about 100K/s, while 4.77MHz XTs run interleave 3 at 170K/s. Why?
ref: You've been had. The M24 or AT&T 6300 has an 8MHz 8086, but the bus runs at 4MHz, not 4.77, so it's slower than a real PC. Interleave 4 works well; 3 is a dog. Plenty of slow 6300s ship formatted at 3.
replies:
[Has AT&T "3600" (think you mean 6300) with ST251-1 and WD1002S-WX1.]
[Use interleave of 5 and gets transfer rate of ~100KB/sec.  True IBM PC']
[use interleave of 3 and get ~170KB/sec.  The PC runs at 4.77MHz and the]
[Olivetti (what he actually has and which is the same thing as an AT&T]
[6300) runs at 8MHz.]

Frank,  You've been had.  The Olivetti M24/AT&T 6300 has an 8086 CPU
running at 8MHz, but I understand that the bus runs at 4MHz (half the
system clock rate) and *NOT* 4.77MHz.  Consequently, your raw data
transfer rate is actually LESS than a real-but-slower IBM PC.  Here
at the Labs, 6300's seem to perform well with an interleave of 4 in
configurations similar to yours, but interleave factor 3 is a dog.
Thus, there a lot of "slow" 6300's around because their hard disks
came preformatted with an interleave factor of 3 and their owners
don't know enough to realize what is wrong.

regards, Larry

packets for the particular net.

 Yes!

problem I have is with the 16bit ISOLan cards in a fast (386SX @16Mhx)
server, where the 3c501's can't keep up and die.

subject: Do flock() locks remain after program termination
q: Do flock() locks go away when a program does an execv() or exit()? The manual pages don't say.
ref: Yes, they should go away. But flock() is outmoded, so use POSIX style locking with fcntl() instead. Also, Ultrix 4.2 NFS has a bug where locks aren't released on close or exit. DEC has a fix, for whatever that's worth.
replies:
yes, they should go away, but

1) Use POSIX style file locking with the fcntl() call;  flock() is outmoded.

2) There is a bug in Ultrix 4.2 NFS where locks are not released when the
file is closed or the process exits.  DEC has a fix available for this bug.

regards,
fletcher

ref: OLIT's XtNlabelImage wants an XImage pointer, not a Pixmap. Use XGetImage to make an XImage from your Pixmap, then give that XImage* to the button as the resource value. Motif habits, tsk.

subject: 1Gbyte file on a 130Mb drive (fsdb)
q: On my Xenix 2.3.3 system, ls and du report a 45Mb accounting file as 1Gbyte, and tar and cpio try to back up the whole gigabyte. fsck only says possible wrong file size. How do I deal with it?
ref: Sounds like a sparse file. Some program seeked a billion bytes in and wrote one byte, so only a sector is allocated and ls reports the last offset. tar and cpio don't detect sparse files and save the zeros. Probably nothing to fix, except maybe the application.
replies:
Could be a sparse file. I'm not sure if Xenix supports sparse files
but on modern unices you can open a file, seek a billion bytes or
so into it and write one byte. Only one sector of data is allocated
(plus some inode sectors). Reading the file returns zeros for the
unwritten sectors. ls reports the offset of the last byte in the file.
Tar, cpio et al traditionally do not detect sparse files
and merrily save a gigabyte of zeros (although I would have expected compress
to work eventually).

I don't think you have anything to fix. Well maybe a bug in the application
that created the file.  Don't know about the fsck message though...

Andy
