subject: Stealth Think C header file attack?
q: Think C 4 can't see my stdio.h or any header file when I try to add it to my project. The .c files show up fine. What am I doing wrong?
ref: You're using Add... on a .h file. You can't add headers, they aren't C source. Just #include them from your code, and read the manual's section on precompiled headers if you want them everywhere. RTFM.
replies:
It sounds to me like you are trying to use the "Add..." selection in the
Project menu to add files to your project.  You cannot add .h files, since they
are not C source (technically).  If you want a C file to include a .h file,
then use #include <file> or #include "file" as is dictated by the location of
the file.  If you want the files transparently included in all your files,
see the section in yout Think C manual on precompiled headers.

Steve Hawley
hawley@adobe.com

subject: tcp-ok mailer
q: Several sendmail.cf files have a mailer called tcp-ok identical to the tcp mailer, with a comment saying it bypasses the uucp to arpa forwarding check. Is that real?
ref: It's not real. They're vestigial leftovers from some older Berkeley sample config. Mailer names are arbitrary; mine is called smtp, and some call it ethernet. Any difference would be in how rule set zero resolves to them. Sigh.
replies:
I posted that thinking that perhaps tcp-ok was some sort of special case
in sendmail.  After further investigation and a couple of responses (thank
you), I've determined that these are just leftovers for some older version
of the configuration files I have.  Those configuration files that define
it either define it just like the "tcp" mailer or only use one of the two.

I figure that it must have been in one of the Berkeley samples sometime,
and made it this far, even though it's now vestigial.

If the mailer definition of "tcp-ok" is the same as "tcp", there is no
reason for them to be different.  The name of the mailers are arbitrary.
For example, "tcp" mailer at our site is called "smtp" but I've seen some
sendmail.cf files call it "ethernet").  The difference might be how they
are resolved in rule set zero (i.e. the include file of the hosts these
mailers can reached might be different).

subject: Question 1 of 3 for assembly language programmers.
q: Can I access DOS command line arguments from assembly language, like argc and argv in C?
ref: Yes, through the PSP. The length byte is at offset 80h and the command line text starts at 81h. Save it at startup, since it's not guaranteed to stay put. For .com programs the PSP is the code segment; for .exe it's in ES and DS. RTFM.
replies:
=>
=>Can I access DOS command line arguments through assembly language?
=>This would be the equivalent to using argc and argv in C.  I would
=>appreciate a short example if possible.

Yes you can. The command line parameters are passed to you through the PSP,
specifically at offset 81 hex. Located at offset 80 hex is a byte which is
the length of the parameter string. The command line is delivered intact:

    If you launched a program:

	    MYPROG -a -b -cde filename

    the PSP would contain this information:

	    Offset	Contents
	    =======	=========================================
	    80h		13h
	    81h-94h	"-a -b -cde filename" (excluding the "'s)

Sorry, I don't have source right here to include. If you have problems,
e-mail a request and I'll try to round up the appropriate code segment..

Good luck....

jim

Yes. Look at offset 80h in the PSP (Program Segment Prefix) segment.
For .com programs PSP is the same as the code segment at start up.
For .exe programs PSP is contained in ES and DS registers at start up.
The information there is not gauranteed throughout the program, so
if you want to use it, you've got to save it somewhere when you start up
your program. DOS also has an function call for parsing a command line
but I don't recall right off what it is.

Dan Floyd
8<D=

subject: Where is /mac/bin/settc?
q: The A/UX manuals say there's a settc command in /mac/bin, but it isn't on my 2.0 system or the install CD-ROM. Where is it?
ref: Documentation mistake. For 2.0 there is no /mac/bin/settc; use /mac/bin/setfile, a superset of settc with the same usage as MPW's SetFile. It sets attributes, creator, dates, icon location and file type. Read the manual's errata next time.
replies:
Oops.  Mistake in the documentation.  For 2.0, there is no /mac/bin/settc.
Instead, use /mac/bin/setfile, which is a superset of settc.  Usage for
setfile is the same as MPW, which is as follows:

SetFile [optionI] fileI
    -a attributes           # attributes (lowercase = 0, uppercase = 1)
    -c creator              # file creator
    -d date                 # creation date (mm/dd/yy [hh:mm[:ss] [AM | PM]])
    -l h,v                  # ICON location (horizontal,vertical)
    -m date                 # modification date (mm/dd/yy [hh:mm[:ss] [AM | PM]])
    -t type                 # file type

    Note: Period (.) represents the current date and time.
    Note: The following attributes may be used with the -a option:
        L   Locked
        V   Invisible
        B   Bundle
        S   System
        I   Inited
        D   Desktop
        M   Shared (can run multiple times)
        A   Always switch launch (if possible)

subject: paragraph blocking
q: How do I get emacs or jove to fill a paper's paragraphs to about 50 columns instead of 72 or 80?
ref: Set the right margin to 50 with M-X set right-margin 50, put the cursor in a paragraph and hit ESC J to run fill-paragraph. Use M-X apropos fill if you want to find these yourself. That online help exists for a reason.
replies:
One great thing about EMACS-like editors is the online and built-in
documentation.  Take JOVE, for instance (since you requested it).
Try:

	M-X apropos fill

And you'll see that there's "fill-region" and "fill-paragraph."
"fill-paragraph" is probably what you want.  (It's normally bound to
M-J.)  Set your right margin to the desired page width;

	M-X set right-margin 50

Set your cursor on a paragraph that you want to fill, and type ESC J
and watch it fill.  It's a great boon to text editing (I've done it
several times typing in this note.)

Note that many editors have fill-paragraph features.  One of the first
macros I wrote for my TED editor (a CP/M teco) was this function.
Want it?  :-)

-mm-

subject: /etc/magic entry for GIF files?
q: How do I write an /etc/magic entry that identifies GIF files as 'GIF image' without printing the version bytes after it?
ref: You can't do it with a wildcard. String matching in file(1) compares exactly the length of the string you give, so your ideal entry just looks for literal 'xxx'. You'd have to hack file(1) itself. Workaround: list the two version numbers Compuserve authorizes, one entry each.
replies:
To quote the man page:

               For string values, the byte string from  the  file
               must  match  the  specified  byte string; the byte
               string from the file which is matched is the  same
               length as the specified byte string.

In other words, your 'ideal' /etc/magic' entry is looking for the character
string 'xxx'.  To fix this problem, one would have to change 'file(1)' to
have some wildcard pattern for strings.  I get around the problem with these
lines:

0       string          GIF             GIF image

These are the only two version numbers currently authorized by Compuserve.

subject: bug in 3b2 console driver?
q: On a 3b2/400 under System V 5.3, printf plus fflush to the console garbles output unless I add an ioctl TCSBRK after the fflush. Is this a 3b2 or System V bug?
ref: Probably neither. printf and fflush just do write(2) calls into the kernel character queue; write is too generic to blame. My guess is Scheme does a later ioctl TCSETA instead of TCSETAW, which mangles or discards pending output. Blame the Scheme software.
replies:
The only thing printf and fflush do is a series of
write(2) system calls to put characters into the kernel
character queue for the device.  Without the fflush the
characters would remain buffered in the user space until
a newline were output.  Write(2) is too generic to blame
for this kind of problem.

It sounds to me like a problem with the Scheme software.
My guess is that a subsequent ioctl() is doing a TCSETA
instead of a TCSETAW; this can cause pending output to
be mangled or discarded.

subject: Long strings in TP
q: What's the best way to implement a long string variable, say 600 characters, in Turbo Pascal?
ref: Depends what you do with it. For little manipulation, use C-style null-terminated strings. For heavy manipulation, use a record with a word length field and a 600-char array. You write the routines yourself, since the TP library has none. Allocate with GetMem and FreeMem.
replies:
Option 1:
	C-like.  Use null-terminated strings.  Flexible but you
	lose all strong typing and Pascal compiler protection.

Option 2:
	Pascal-like.  Use a word for the length counter.  Something
	like

	longstring = record
	     length:word
	     data:array[1..600] of char
	end;

	Advantage: close to Pascal.
	Disadvantages: relatively inflexible, could easily be
	wasteful of memory.

That depends on what you want to do with it.  If you don't need to
know the length, and it doesn't change much, and you don't use nulls in
the strings, probably C-style null terminated strings are best.  Turbo
and Object Professional from TurboPower provide units to handle these, but
they aren't hard to write yourself.

If you want to do a lot of manipulation on the strings, a record with a
length word at the start would probably be best, something like

 type
  longstring =
  record
   length : word;
   chars  : array[1..600] of char;
  end;

Again you'll have to write (or find) routines to do all the usual operations
on these, since the TP library doesn't have them.

If you allocate these in the heap, you can allocate just as much as you need,
and easily deallocate them, using GetMem and FreeMem.

Hope this helps.

subject: Do Amiga libraries support 68000/68881?
q: Do the Amiga IEEE math libraries support a 68000 with a 68881? What address must the 68881 be at, and does the Amiga check for it automatically at boot?
ref: The V1.3 ieee libraries do support 68000 peripheral-style 6888x boards, though 68882 has a bug fixed in the next release. The chip must be autoconfigured and a resource added during binddrivers, so no fixed address. Only a 68020 or better is checked at boot. The docs cover it.
replies:
The V1.3 ieee libraries support the 68000/68881 peripheral style
floating point accelerators such as from Microbotics or from CMI.
However a bug was just found in the 1.3 ieee libraries that prevent
them from working with 68882 chips. This has been fixed and then
next release will support the 68000/68882 combination.

The 6888x must be autoconfiged and an ieee math resource added to
the system during binddrivers. Documentation for this is available.
There is no predetermined address for the 6888x coprocessor chip.

The amiga checks for 6888x only if there is a 68020 or better main
cpu. The ieee libraries themselves check for the existance of
various floating point options when they are first initialized. They
initialize the library vector table to different routines depending
on what is available.

subject: setld on DEC systems
q: setld won't install a software subset from tape on my ULTRIX system. What's the right way to use it, and how do I tell whether the tape is bad?
ref: With -a the order is setld -a device subset, but it's better to let setld do the work with -l, which reads the tape and gives you a menu of what's not installed. If your subset is missing from that menu, you likely have a bad tape. RTFM.
replies:
That's the right order if you want to use -a.  It's best
	to let setld(8) do most of work and use -l.  This will
	see what's on the tape and give you a menu of everything
	not installed.  If the subset you want is still missing
	you might have a bad tape.

	To check, get the subset list and look at it:

		foreach i ( SPACE.1 SPACE.2 SPACE.3 INSTCTRL )
			dd if=/dev/nrmt0h of=$i bs=10k
		end

	Then use tar(1) to look for the XXX.image file in the
	INSTCTRL archive.  It gives the sum(1) information and
	order of the files on the tape.  The subsets start after

subject: connect(2) timeout
q: How can I change the time it takes for connect(2) to time out? The default of 1:15 is too long, setsockopt didn't help, and a SIGALRM handler only works the first time.
ref: The timeout comes from the TCP keep-alive timers in the BSD kernel, set in netinet/tcp_timer.h. You can change the kernel variable tcp_keepintvl with adb, for example tcp_keepintvl?W 60. Numbers vary between releases, so go read your own source.
replies:
When connect() is requested, TCP protocol implementation in BSD 4.3-Tahoe
will send a SYN packet and start a keep-alive timer.  Initially, when the
remote machine you're trying to connection to doesn't respond within
75 seconds (TCPTV_KEEP_INIT) with an ACK/SYN (initial phase of the TCP
three-way handshake connection set-up protocol), the keep-alive timer will
start sending a keep-alive packet (<SEQ=SND.UNA-1><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=ACK)>)
every 75 seconds (TCPTV_KEEPINTVL) until it receives a packet from the
other side or upto 8 times (TCPTV_KEEPCNT).   So, 8 * 75 => 600 == 10 minutes
in 4.3 BSD.  The constants in parentheses are defined in netinet/tcp_timer.h.
You can change the global variables "tcp_keepintvl" to change the
kernel's idea of TCPTV_KEEPINTVL using adb on BSD Unix.  As in,

% adb -k -w /vmunix /dev/mem
  tcp_keepintvl?W 60

Note also that these numbers tend to vary in different implementations as
well as in various releases of BSD Unix code itself.  Pre-4.3-tahoe releases
of

subject: Breadth-first search
q: Is there any way of doing a breadth-first search recursively in C?
ref: Why on earth would you want to? Breadth-first isn't a fundamentally recursive process like depth-first. Just make a queue: put the root in, pop a node, append its children to the end, repeat. Recursion buys you nothing.
replies:
[Sorry to post, but mail to the author bounced]

I'm not quite sure why you want to do this recursively. It seems
to me that the most straight-forward approach is to make a queue,
where you put the children of the current node on the end of the
queue, then pop the next node off the front of the queue, etc.
The root node would be the initial element of the queue, of course.
You could make your top-level function recursive, but it seems to
me that you would pass the entire queue every time, so I don't see
that the recursion buys you anything. I guess my point is that
this doesn't seem like a fundamentally recursive process, the way
a depth-first search would be.

Hope that helps; perhaps I am misunderstanding your question?

subject: What's this "sys" window nonsense?
q: On a 3b1 running 3.0, my windows show up as tty "sys" and input to programs like readnews or rn gets lost to the command line. What is this and how do I fix it?
ref: It's a known UNIX PC bug: the window driver sometimes shuts down improperly and /dev/syscon gets unlinked from /dev/window. The kludge is to put ln /dev/syscon /dev/window and ln /dev/systty /dev/window in /etc/rc, with matching major and minor numbers.
replies:
...
Yes, another one of those infamous bugs with the UNIX pc.  It seems
that the window driver improperly shuts down (sometimes).  When this happens
/dev/syscon get's unlinked from /dev/window...  How, who knows?  But the
thing (kludge) you can use to fix this is stick this in your /etc/rc:

ln /dev/syscon /dev/window
ln /dev/systty /dev/window

Make sure the devices look like this (particularly the major minor numbers)...

   0 crw-rw-rw-  3 root    sys       7,  0 Jan  1  1970 /dev/syscon
   0 crw-rw-rw-  3 root    sys       7,  0 Jan  1  1970 /dev/systty
   0 crw-rw-rw-  3 root    sys       7,  0 Jan  1  1970 /dev/window

-Lenny

subject: nVIR infection

replies:
It is always better (and safer) to replace an infected application

subject: cross-compiling with byte-swapped machines
q: I want to cross-compile for 68020 on a little-endian Sequent Symmetry. Does anyone have a 68020 as/ld that works on little-endian machines, or should I add byte-swapping to the tools?
ref: Don't touch the tools. Use the host's natural byte ordering and convert the object files with a conversion program when you transfer them to the m68k. Writing that is far less work than weeding out byte dependencies. Vendors selling m88k cross environments have COFF and a.out converters.
replies:
As someone who has supported m68k cross compilation environments for
several years on a number of different systems, including some with
different byte ordering than the m68k, I would advise making only
minimal changes in the source code of the tools themselves.  Use
the natural byte ordering of the host machine, and convert the
object files with a conversion program when you need to actually
transfer and execute them on an m68k based machine.  Writing the
conversion program will almost certainly be less work than weeding
out all the byte dependencies in the tools.  Conversion tools for
COFF objects and "a.out" objects are available from many vendors
that support m88k cross environments, though this might not be
useful to you if you are trying to work totally with freely
redistributable software.

-Fred

subject: Controlling Dialog Boxes & Button Size in HyperCard
q: In HyperCard, how can I get more than two choices plus Cancel in a sort dialog box, and how do I make newly created buttons smaller and square instead of long and oblong?
ref: The answer command only allows 3 buttons, so build a sort options card instead. Sort is stable, so just run several sorts in a row. For buttons, drag the corner smaller, pick "square" in the button dialog, or hold Option and drag. Read the manual.
replies:
This seems like 2 questions.

I think you can't sort by more than one characteristic per command.  But
HyperCard does a stable sort (I believe that is the proper term), which
means if 2 cards sort identically their relative order is preserved across
the sort.  So you can sort by several characteristics by using several sort
commands.

As for the question of more buttons in a dialog, I think that the answer
command only allows 3 buttons.  If you wanted more options, I think the way
to go is to provide a sort options card that would be used to specify the
sort options.

button to be square.  Rect is a button property that you can get & set.

After creating a "New Button", grab the south east corner with the arrow
cursor and move it north west. This gives you a smaller button. Also, you
can click in the button and from the dialog you then get choose "square".

subject: implementing an interpreter
q: What are the tradeoffs between tagging every object pointer with a type and using an object table index for implementing a Scheme interpreter? Has anyone studied this?
ref: There's a third approach, Big Bag of Pages, where each type is allocated only in certain address ranges so the address gives the type. It makes GC like generation scavenging more complicated, but type checks are cheap. Shebs and Kessler's SIGPLAN 87 paper has a tagging cost study. Go read it.
replies:
A third approach is the Big Bag of Pages (BiBoP) arrangement, in
which objects of various types are each allocated only in certain
ranges of addresses. In this way, an object's type can be
determined by examining its address. This scheme somewhat complicates
an already somewhat complicated gc algorithm if you plan to
use, let us say, generation scavenging, but type determination
is fairly cheap.

Rick, you may find the following reference useful. It includes a cost
study of low/high-bit tagging and pointer spaces.

%A Stan T. Shebs
%A Robert R. Kessler
%T Automatic Design and Implementation of Language Data Types
%J Sigplan 87 Symposium on Interpreters and Interpretive Techniques
%I Association for Computing Machinery
%C St Paul, Minnesota
%P 26-37
%D June 87
%O Published as Sigplan Notices Vol. 22 Number 7, July 87

enjoy.	oz

Teach yourself to solder and then do it yourself. To remove a chip when

subject: File not an object module
q: Amiga binaries from comp.binaries.amiga give me "File not an object module" after I run them through sh and uudecode and move them over via an Atari ST. What's wrong?
ref: Probably the old padded-hunk problem: xmodem pads files to 128-byte boundaries and the Amiga loader sees the last hunk as too long. Look for a CHOP-type utility on old Fish disks. Better, keep the shar and run unshar and uudecode on the Amiga. Same old story.
replies:
Peter,

You really need to tell us EXACTLY the procedure you do to get the file to the
amiga. Do you run it thru /bin/sh on a unix machine? do you run it thru
UUDECODE on a unix machine? Or do you have programs on your amiga that you are
trying? How are you getting the files (ascii or binary at this point?) to your
amiga?

I have a unix machine at work. I grab the files from comp.binaries.amiga and
save them to a file.

1> Then I edit the file to remove the headers (down to and including the --cut
me-- line).

2> /bin/sh file

3> uudecode file

4> go home call up unix machine with Diga! using Xmodem binary mode

5> download file

6> run ZOO and unZOO file on my amiga

7> run file

And that works for me. I have an Amiga 1000, 512K, 2 floppys.

Possibly you are running into the old problem with hunks being padded,
which is the same problem people used to have with doing xmodem
transfers onto the amiga.  There are programs to fix this (called
"CHOP" or something) on old fish disks.  The idea is that xmodem
always filled out the binary to 128 byte boundaries, while the amiga
loader would keep track of how long the hunks were, and notice that
the last hunk was too long.  This caused it to think the file was
screwed up, and it would report the "error".

Other than this you might be having trouble with the way you are doing
the transfers.  You might want to keep the files in shar format and
run an unshar program and a uudecode program on the amiga.  I do this
all the time and it works fine.

-Fred Gilham

subject: Dumb/easy question
q: How does one delete hidden files in DOS?
ref: Hidden files are just files with the Hidden bit set, so use ATTRIB to clear it and then ERASE the thing normally. Or use PC-Tools or Norton, if you've got them. Sigh, read the DOS manual once in a while.
replies:

Un-hidden then delete is from DOS.  But I think that PC-Tools will let
you delete files from within itself (I am not sure here because I have
not used it for a long time).  I do not think that the DOS attribute
command will work here, but who knows.

In DOS, "Hidden" files are nominally protected from normal disk
operations such as DIR, DEL, and the like. These files differ from
"normal" files only in that the "Hidden" bit has been set ON in the
File Attribute part of the directory entry.

     Using something like PC-Tools, you can delete hidden files without
any problems. If you don;t have and/or can't afford such a program or
one like it, you can use the DOS program ATTRIB to alter the file
attribute bits and make it a non-Hidden file and then erase it normally.

subject: Indigo questions
q: Does the Indigo use standard SIMMs, how many sockets does it have, and are CD-ROM or DAT the best devices for loading new system releases?
ref: No, not standard SIMMs. It uses the same ones as the 4D/35, so memory access can be interleaved. The board has 12 sockets, 96 MB max. IRIX 4.0 ships on CD-ROM, and our own CD-ROM and DAT drives carry the audio firmware support. Third-party drives are anyone's guess.
replies:
The Indigo does not use standard SIMMs.  Indigo uses the same SIMMs as
the 4D/35.  This has been done in order to interleave memory access
for increased memory bandwidth.

The motherboard I just looked at has 12 SIMM sockets on it.  The
Indigo supports 96 MB maximum.

CD-ROM for sure.  IRIX 4.0 will be distributed on CD-ROM.  I don't
know if we have plans to release software on DAT.

Don't know, but if you use our CD-ROM and DAT drives you get the
guarantee that their digital audio capabilities will work with Indigo
as well.  Both CD-ROM and DAT drives need special firmware support in
order for Indigo to use them for audio processing (for example, you
can use the Indigo DAT drive to master audio DAT tapes, and play audio
data from a CD-ROM or DAT into the Indigo for processing).

subject: MED 3.11 And Long Samples
q: MED 3.11 loads samples larger than about 200K but they only play for a second or so, with the scopes still running and no sound. Why?
ref: The Amiga audio hardware only plays 64K at a time. To play longer samples, the program has to notice when the first 64K finishes and tell the hardware to play the next chunk. I don't think MED does that, so nothing over 64K plays through. Hardware limits, kid.
replies:
The audio hardware only plays 64K at a time.  To play samples larger than
that, the program must know when the first 64K is finished, and tell the
hardware to play the next 64K.  I don't think MED does this...  If it
doesn't, then no samples >64K will play through to the end.

                                              --Ed.

subject: DECstations 3100 serial port pinout configuraion
q: What are the pinouts to adapt the 6-wire serial port on the DECstation 3100 to a 9-pin or 25-pin RS232?
ref: Per the DECconnect guide, the MMJ pins are 1 RDY OUT, 2 TX+, 3 TX-, 4 RX-, 5 RX+, 6 RDY IN. Jumper 3 and 4 to signal ground, then 2 to 2, 5 to 3, 1 to DTR, 6 to DSR. For a null modem, cross TX+ and RX+. Read the planning guide.
replies:
If it's DECconnect (the clip is offset to one side) then it looks like this
inside:

	RS 232 Specs for DECconnect MMJ

		DTR--- 1
		TD --- 2
		GRD--- 3
		GRD--- 4
		RD --- 5
		DSR--- 6

Obviously, if it's not DECconnect you should ignore this.  Note that
flipping the cable over in the MMJ causes a DTE/DCE flip - clever.

-Andy

This is in the DECconnect System planning and config guide.
The MMJ has
	1. RDY OUT
	2. Transmit +
	3. Transmit -
	4. Receive -
	5. Receive +
	6. RDY IN

To connect to RS232, jumper 3 and 4 together and connect to signal
ground (pin 7), connect 2 - 2, 5 - 3, 1 - 20 (DTR, pin 5 in 9 pin),
and 6 - 6 (DSR).  For null modem, cross the TX + and RX + leads.

subject: run level
q: How can a normal user program running as root reliably detect the current run level, so it only runs in single user mode? Checking whether /etc/utmp is empty seems clumsy.
ref: On System V, use who -r, which reports the current run state. It's the intended way, if not elegant. It can lie, though: on HP-UX, if you interrupt the boot sequence and go straight to single user, the reported state is wrong. Typical.
replies:
With System V, the who command has several options added to it.  One
option reports the current run state.  I'm not sure that I would call this
"elegant", but it does seem to be the intended System V way to obtain the
current run state.  Here is a fragment of a shell script that uses this:
	#! /bin/sh
	set `who -r`
	if [ "$7" = "S" ] ; then
		echo We are in single user mode
		echo I will remount all disk drives
		umount -a
		mount -t hfs -a
	fi

One warning about this.  At least on a HP-UX system, I have seen this fail.
If you get to single user mode via shutdown or init S, then the run state
as reported by who -r is correct.  But if you interrupt to boot-up sequence
and go directly to single user mode, it will be wrong.

Since some versions of TFM get this wrong, here is the output from a who -r:

   .       system boot  May  5 02:49    2    0    S
                                        ^    ^    ^

I hope that this helps.

Paul Hite   PRC Realty Systems  McLean,Va   uunet!prcrs!paul

subject: Does Perl have known memory leaks?
q: Does Perl 4 have known memory leaks? My script just iterates over a big file and runs out of memory on DOS.
ref: A couple of small leaks are fixed in 4.018, one with foreach over null lists and one with local(*FILEHANDLE). To hunt leaks, compile with -DLEAKTEST and run with -D4096. If it isn't a leak, read the Space Efficiency section of Chapter 7.
replies:
A couple of small leaks are fixed in 4.018.  One involved foreach loops
with null lists, and the other involved local(*FILEHANDLE).

You can test for leaks by compiling with -DLEAKTEST, inserting

	warn "New allocations:\n" unless $counter++ % 100;

in the middle of your loop, and running your script with -D4096, which
makes the warn command dump out a list of newly allocated memory.  The
numbers reported correspond to arguments to the New() macro or, in the
700's, the Str_new() macro.

If it's not a leak, look in the Space Efficiency section of Chapter 7.

It would be fun to write a profiler that added up the amount of memory
allocated for each statement.

Larry

subject: FTL -> Science Fantasy
q: Does the FTL idea of a ship generating its own gravity well and falling toward its destination actually work?
ref: No. The ship and the well attract each other but the ship holds the well at a fixed distance, so the forces cancel and nothing moves. Same as standing on Earth, where your legs keep it from pulling you down. Basic physics.
replies:
This can't work buddy. The ship and the gravity well would be trying to attract
each other, trying to meet in the middle, but the ship would be pushing back,
to keep the gravity well at a specific distance. The result: no motion.

You get the same result by standing up on earth. Earth is trying to pull you
down, but you are keeping it at a specific distance (your legs), so there is no
motion.

              long pole       gravity point
     ship--------------------*

the forces cancel out.

subject: Tcl array variables

I'm not sure what you mean here.  There is a procedure in the Tcl source
library included with Extended Tcl, called assign_fields, which will assign
successive elements in a list to named variables, so for example you can
do stuff like:

    assign_fields [split $passwordLine :] user password userID groupID \

"password", and so forth.

If you substituted array references for the variable names, that would work
as-is.  A derivative of assign_fields could be created that took the
array name as a parameter.  One possible implementation...

proc assign_array_fields {list arrayName args} {
    set listIndex -1
    foreach varName $args {
	uplevel 1 "set ${arrayName}($varName) [list [lindex $list [incr listIndex]]]"

For example,
    assign_array_fields "a b c" bar 1 2 3
...will assign a to bar(1), b to bar(2) and c to bar(3)

subject: Regular Expression (vi type) question...

ref: Substitute a literal dot followed by anything but a dot, anchored at end of line, with nothing: s/\.[^.]*$//. Lines without a dot simply don't match, so nothing happens to them. Sigh, no need to assume a dot exists. Use a g/pattern/ prefix if you want to dodge failure errors.
replies:
No need to assume there is a dot:

in english:
    on all lines, substitute a literal dot, followed by anything
    but a dot, only at the end of a line, by nothing.
The substitution happens only on the lines that match.
Works with me (SYSV3.2 vi version 3.9 2/9/83).

{range}s/\.[^.]*$//

To avoid failure problems?

{range}g/\.[^.]*$/s///

subject: Is <math.h> required to declare all the standard math functions?
q: Is <math.h> required to declare all the standard math functions like asin under the ANSI C standard, or do I have to declare them myself?
ref: Yes, they're declared there; the start of the library chapter says so. Some so-called ANSI compilers misdeclare them with long double or extended types, which is non-conforming and its rationale is bogus. The standard reserves other names for extra-precision interfaces. They break hoc, among others.
replies:
Yes; this is explained at the beginning of the library chapter.

It is worth noting that some implementations advertising themselves as
"ANSI C" actually misdeclare the math functions, using "extended" or
"long double" types in these declarations.  Such implementations are
not standard conforming and their rationale for such declarations is
bogus.  The C standard reserves a set of names for such extra-precision
math function interfaces; these should be used for such interfaces, and
the standard interfaces should be declared as required by the standard.
Failure to do so causes problems in some applications, for example "hoc"
from Kernighan and Pike's "The UNIX Programming Environment".  It also
causes problems for code containing its own declarations for these
functions.

subject: Lowly FORTRAN & SANE Question
q: In Absoft FORTRAN or similar compilers on the Mac, when you choose the 68881/68882 option, is SANE bypassed entirely, or does it still use SANE? Does the 96-bit type have more precision?
ref: The choice is made in the Options dialog, and you link the libraries to match. The compiler does everything it can on the FPU, but some things, like string-to-binary conversions, still go through SANE. The 96-bit type has the same precision as 80-bit, plus a padding word of zeros.
replies:
Actually, the choice is made by selecting the appropriate options
from the Options... dialog; the choice of library is made simply to complement
the choice of code generation, so that everything works correctly. The same
holds true for other compilers: choose the code generation, and then link
the libraries to match.

As it turns out the 96-bit data type has the same precision as the 80-bit
data type, but has an extra word of zeros after the exponent "to force
longword alignment and for future expansion", according to the Motorola
manuals.

Generally, the compiler will do everything possible using the FPU, but some
functions (such as string-to-binary conversions) are still done by SANE.

R.

subject: Leaving Mailbox Unchanged?
q: Elm says 'Leaving Mailbox Unchanged' when I quit, yet it knows which messages are new when I come back. How does it do that?
ref: Elm keeps a zero-length file, .elm/last_read_mail, and touches it on a normal exit. It compares that file's date against the date of each message. Quit with x and the time isn't updated. The mailbox itself stays untouched. Not exactly rocket science.
replies:
Elm stores a zero-length file in .elm/last_read_mail.  Elm touches this
file and compares the date on the file with the dates for each piece of
mail.

JB

is used to determine if mail is new.  When you exit elm normally (ie
not with the x command), it updates the time on this file.

subject: Gemini Standard Usages

ref: Not CD-ROM, for pity's sake. CDPATH is a list of directories searched when you type cd with a directory name, as in ksh and bash. With several partitions, cd UTILITY finds it on any drive listed. Any Unix user knows this.
replies:
->I've been working with Gemini off and on for a while now and
->I hope somebody can pass these comments to the programming team.
->It's all regarding the "mupfel.mup" file:
 ...
->Also, I have no idea what they are intending to use the "CDPATH"
->for.  I've never seen it on a Unix system or an OS-9 system and
->I don't know what program would look for it.  Is that supposed to
->be a path for CD Rom applications?

If I recall, CDPATH is the path that mupfel will search when you type
"CD directory".  It's sort of like Norton CD under DOS - you can type "CD
directory" without a partition letter and CD will look on the various paths
specified by CDPATH for that directory name, regardless of which drive it is
on.

I don't use Gemini, but I do know what CDPATH is, from using ksh and
bash.  The CDPATH variable contains a list of directories to scan for
a directory name given to the 'cd' command.  For example, if my CDPATH
is ":/usr:/usr/entropy:/usr/bob/pub/bin/bsd4.3/recreation" then
if I type "cd games" the shell will:

1) cd to ./games if it exists (some shells don't do this if you have a CDPATH)
2) otherwise, cd to /usr/games if it exists
3) otherwise, cd to /usr/entropy/games if it exists
4) otherwise, cd to /usr/bob/pub/bin/bsd4.3/recreation/games if it exists

CDPATH is very useful if you have long paths to very common storage
areas and don't like typing them all the time.

entropy

CDPATH is not for CD Rom applications, it is very handy if you are
using several disk partitions. You can tell gemini where to look
for a directory name when you do a 'cd Directory'. It's also very
handy when you are using a lot of directories.

For example, if you are using the partitions C..F and you have
a directory called 'UTILITY' and is located on drive E:,
CD looks for the directory 'UTILITY' on drive E: only if you have
specified drive E: in CDPATH (CDPATH=C:\;D:\;E:\;F:\).
When you are for example in the directory 'C:\EDITOR\WORDPLUS\DOCS'
and you do a cd UTILITY, gemini will succeed in finding it.
When GEMINI finds it, it also prints the full path of the
directory. Hope you now know where CDPATH is use for.

Geert.

subject: incident meters, what about subject-camera distance?
q: With an incident flash meter, how is subject-to-camera distance accounted for? Given the inverse square law, what happens if I meter at ASA 25, f8 and then move the camera from five feet to ten feet away?
ref: It doesn't matter. Only the distance from the subject to the lights counts. Move back and the light drops by the inverse square, but the image area on the film shrinks by the same square, so light per area stays constant. Basic geometry, people.
replies:
OK: Let us presume you have a 6" square that gives a 4mm image on the film
at 5 feet and you get 16 joules/sec worth of light on the film. This works
out to (tada!) 16joules/(sec (4mm)^2) = 1joule/(sec mm^2)

Let's, now, assume that you move to 10' away.  Simple geometry gives you an
image 1/2 as big (2mm) while inverse-square gives you 1/4 the intensity
(4 joules/sec).

 interestingly enough when you calculate joules/square mm of film, it
comes out to:
	(4joules/sec) / (2mm^2) = 1joule/sec mm

square of the distance, so does the AREA (as opposed to the lineal size)
of the image on the film.  The result is that light per area stays constant.

Distance from subject to camera makes no difference.  Only the distance
of the subject to the lights matters.

			Patrick St. Joseph Teahan Taber

subject: "Pseudo-controls" in Modal Dialogs
q: How do I force a dialog to redraw inside a StillDown() loop in a modal dialog? UpdtDialog() didn't update anything, and I want a pseudo-control's counter to show as it increases.
ref: UpdtDialog needs an update region, and you haven't invalidated anything, so it draws nothing. Just draw directly in your StillDown loop by calling your user item's draw proc. And SetPort to the dialog first, or it draws who knows where. Basics.
replies:
UpdtDialog requires an update region; if you don't specify one, the dialog
manager assumes that the window is completely updated so doesn't draw
anything.   Similarly, re-entering ModalDialog() won't necessarily cause
your window to be redrawn, because you haven't invalidated any of the
contents yet.

The easiest thing to do is to draw directly in your StillDown() loop.
If, for example, your pseudo-control is (still) implemented as a user
item, then you can directly call the itemProc which you've installed
to draw it.  e. g.

   while StillDown do
    begin
     counter:=succ(counter);
     DrawMyCounterItem(theDialog, myCountItem_ID)
    end;

Be sure that your port is set to the dialog (SetPort(theDialog)).
Normally when your user item is called (by the dialog manager),
it can assume that the manager has set the port.  If you call it
directly, this won't necessarily be true unless you do it explicitly.

subject: Whaddya do in ioCompletion routine?
q: What do I do in an ioCompletion routine on the Mac? Which parameter block gets returned by the Device Manager, and how do I access my data with memory moving?
ref: The completion routine gets a pointer to the parameter block of the finished request, in register A0. It runs at interrupt level, so no memory moving and no Toolbox or QuickDraw calls. Stash your own data pointer in an unused field of the block, and don't count on CurrentA5. Read Inside Mac.
replies:
It's best not to use A5 if you can help it.  I prefer to stuff an
unused field of the parameter block with a pointer to some data area
which may be used by the request.  The Mac queue data structures work
well for this, since Enqueue and Dequeue are interrupt-friendly.  To
get at the parameter block, look at register A0 on entry to your
completion routine.

If you must use A5, note that you can't rely on CurrentA5 at the
interrupt level.  You will have to stuff your A5 in the parameter
block, in an unused field.

Completion routines are called when an asynchronous driver request completes
(hence the name).  The completion routine is passed a pointer to the parameter
block from the completing request.  The completion routine is most likely
being called at an interrupt level, so all the rules about not moving memory
apply (i.e., don't call any Toolbox, Quickdraw, etc., routines).

So what does it buy you?  Well, you can modify program variables if you want,
or daisy-chain another request based on whether or not the current request
completed successfully, or...

steve

subject: SetIText -- Does it make a copy?

ref: It copies the string into the item list, so your local can go away safely. That's why a local buffer from NumToString is fine. Pointers to your stack would crash later, and that would be your own fault.
replies:
I believe the answer here is YES.  It does copy the string.  When setting
the text, remember that static and edit text in dialogs are part of the

find myself often writing quick subroutines where the string is a local
to contain a converted number from NumToString, as such if that local
where the only container for that string I would loose it, and possibly
crash later, when the subroutine returned.

subject: Using sigvec & sigcontext
q: In a sigvec handler, how do I use the scp sigcontext pointer? Can I store it and use it later to explicitly restore the context and go back to where I was before the signal?
ref: No. Restoring registers, stack and signal mask atomically only works by returning from the handler. The sigcontext lives on a stack that's gone afterwards, so use it only inside the handler. You can modify the signal mask, PC and status register fields.
replies:
In general, no.  You should do a simulated "return from the interrupt"
to restore the context.  It includes restoring registers (including stack
pointer and program counter), switching stack (if running on sigstack) and
restoring signal mask, all in an atomic operation.  That can be done only
by returning from signal handler.  You can more or less simulate it using
assemby code, but some race condition cannot be avoidable.

No.  The sigcontext points to a position in the stack which will no longer
available after returning from the signal handler.  You can use it
only within the signal handler.  At least you can modify the signal mask,
program couner and status register field of the sigcontext, and they will
take effect upon return from the signal handler.
--------
Hitoshi AIDA (aida@csl.sri.com)
Computer Science Laboratory, SRI International

subject: oversampling
q: Does 8x oversampling give you audibly better sound quality than 4x oversampling, assuming decent speakers?
ref: Definite maybe. Higher oversampling can sound better, or the maker just cheaps out on the analog filter and pockets the difference. The best 8x beats the best 4x, but the best 4x likely beats an average 8x. Go listen and stop asking the net.
replies:
Higher oversampling in and of itself will provide a more accurate
reconstruction of the analog signal given a fixed quality of analog
filter.  However, it can also be used so the manufacturer can cut back
on the quality of the analog filter to save money without sacrificing
the quality of the reconstruction.  So, the higher oversampling *might*
sound better or it *might* mean a higher profit margin for the
manufacturer.  I agree with one of the previous posters on this subject --
just go listen to the alternatives and buy what sounds good to you.

Give you a definite maybe on that one.  8x will (to me at least) sound
better than 4x, IF the two machines you are comparing are otherwise
similar.  However, there's a wide enough range of manufacturers'
implementations (of the player as a whole) that you can't count on it.
The best 8x will sound better than the best 4x.  The average 8x will
sound better than the average 4x.  But the best 4x will probably beat
average 8x's.  There's a lot of overlap.

Go listen, decide for yourself if you can hear a difference.  If you
can, then decide which you prefer.  That's the only realistic practical
answer.

mailing list.  Mail me or <simulator-users-request@cs.rochester.edu> if

broken "psrev" (postscript reverse page order) programs.  Try editing
the file so that the first line is just `%!' instead of `%!PS-Adobe-2.0'.

subject: Sorting with 80x87
q: My Turbo Pascal 4.0 quicksort of 10,000 reals got much slower with {$N+} and an 80287, even though the rest of the program sped up. Why is the sort so slow and how do I fix it?
ref: You're still using REAL. With $N+, each compare and swap converts the 6-byte reals to 8-byte doubles and back, so all that converting kills you. Use SINGLE or DOUBLE instead, or for a quick test, put type Real = Double up front. Basic stuff.
replies:
Are you still using REAL as your data type?   If so, change to either SINGLE
or DOUBLE.  What happens when you use REAL with {$N+} is as follows:

    1)  convert 1st 6 byte real to 8 byte double
    2)  load 8087 with double
    3)  convert 2nd 6 byte real to 8 byte double
    4)  load 8087 with double
    5)  have 8087 to compare function
    6)  *If* swap necessary
        6.1) Pop 8 byte double off 8087
        6.2) convert 8 byte double to 6 byte real
        6.3) Pop 8 byte double off 8087
        6.4) convert 8 byte double to 6 byte real

Needless to say there's a whole lot of converting going on and slowing you down

If you want a quick test just put the following at the begining of your program
(for purposes of readability and maintainabiliy I don't recommend this as a
permanent fix!)

type
  Real = Double;

This will change all your REAL's to DOUBLEs and you should notice a signifigant
speed up.

subject: Clicking on Fields
q: How can a HyperCard script tell which line of a field was clicked, when the field has 3 lines that wrap onto 4 or 5 physical lines on screen? Do we need an XFCN?
ref: No XFCN needed. In HyperCard 2.0 use word 2 of the clickLine in a mouseDown handler. In 1.2.x, unlock the text, click at the clickLoc, then read word 2 of the selectedLine and relock. For unlocked fields, use an idle handler. RTFM.
replies:
Assuming the field is locked, in HyperCard 1.2.2 or 1.2.5:

  on mouseDown
    set the lockText of the target to false
    click at the clickLoc
    get word 2 of the selectedLine -- the line number clicked on
    set the lockText of the target to true
    -- do something with the line number
  end mouseDown

In HyperCard 2.0:

  on mouseDown
    get word 2 of the clickLine -- the number of the line clicked on
    -- do something with the line number
  end mouseDown

If the field is not locked, generally an idle handler at the card level
or higher works best:

  on idle
    global lastLineClicked
    if the selectedLine is lastLineClicked then pass idle -- hasn't changed
    put the selectedLine into lastLineClicked
    if the selectedField is "card field 1" then
      -- do something with the line number -- word 2 of the selectedLine
    end if
  end idle

subject: keeping popups on top
q: How can I force popup dialogs to stay on top under twm or any X window manager? Other windows keep obscuring the dialog box.
ref: Grab the pointer, with or without confine-to, so the user deals with the dialog first. That's what popup menus and alerts do. Or make the dialogs children of your app's windows so you control stacking. A private window manager protocol is hackish and may violate the ICCCM.
replies:
If this is a serious problem with your dialog boxes, perhaps you should
be doing a grab pointer (with or without a confine-to) so that the user
handles your dialog box before anything else (such as the window
manager).  Most clients do this with popup menus and high priority
dialog boxes (alerts).

Another method would be to make your dialog boxes children of other
application windows.  That way the application can control their
stacking order.  Window groups are supposed to do the same thing for
top-level windows, but don't seem to work very well.

You might want to experiment with a private protocol between your
client and your window manager, but this is somewhat hackish and may
violate the ICCCM.

subject: 16 bit characters

subject: msc 3.0

ref: MSC 3.0 copies the environment into the program's data space at startup so getenv works like Unix, so a large environment eats stack and heap. The fix is an 80386 in 32 bit mode, which needs hardware and software changes. No easy way, sorry.
replies:
MSC 3.0 copies the environment into the program's data space at startup to
allow getenv() to operate as it does on Unix.  A large environment will
reduce the space available for the stack and heap.  The solution is to use
an 80386 ("what the 286 SHOULD have been -Bill Gates) in 32 bit address mode,
but that requires hardware and software changes.

subject: Active Sensing
q: What is the "Active Sensing" function in the MIDI menu of my synths and samplers for? Is it only used when sending Sys Ex?
ref: It's an optional MIDI byte, hex FE, sent several times a second to say the device is still alive when no other data is flowing. If a receiver that has seen FEs stops getting them, it can assume a disconnect and do all-notes-off. It can show up anywhere in the stream, so filter it. RTFM, though yours clearly won't tell you.
replies:
Active Sensing is a message passed on MIDI approx once a second that is
used to say  "I'm here and I'm functional."  Basically, it's intended
for more extensive MIDI setups to check if everything is on line, and
possibly even find out what is where.

					-Tim

The active sensing command, hex 'FE', is optional and may be sent out by
a midi device about 3 times a second.  This tells the receiving midi
device that the sending device is still up and running even in the absence
of other midi data.

Since it is optional, the receiving device should not expect active sensing
until it actually receives an 'FE'.  After that it should expect an
'FE' at regular intervals.  If it stops receiving 'FE's then it may
assume that something is wrong with the other midi device (perhaps
it has been disconnected).  The receiving device can respond in many
ways.  The most common is to perform an all-notes-off/controller-reset
operation.

While active sensing has its practical uses, many midi devices simply
ignore active sensing.  I have found that the active sensing 'FE'
can appear at any time within a midi data stream.  I have seen it
embedded in bulk dumps and other Sys Ex messages.  Midi software
should be prepared to "filter" out the incoming 'FE's.

q: I ported sendmail 5.61 to ISC SysV 3.2 i386 and the SMTP delivery core dumps in malloc or _filbuf with a stray pointer. Any idea?
ref: Check your fdopen. Some systems don't give you a buffer when it's called, which caused mega-problems on another port. The fix there was calling setbuf on a malloc'ed buffer after every fdopen call. Ugly, but it works.
replies:
You might want to check the 'fdopen' routine on your system to make sure that
they provide a buffer.  Some systems don't create a buffer when the 'fdopen'
routine is called.  This created Mega-problems for me when I tried to port it
to HCX-UX 3.0.  I finally just called 'setbuf' on a 'malloc'ed buffer after
EVERY 'fdopen' routine call, just to make sure.

- David Summers

subject: Writing to the cartridge port.
q: The ST Internals book says writing to the cartridge port gives a bus error. How does the Megadisk RAM cartridge manage to write there?
ref: Easy: you never write. Reading from FC0000 plus an address puts that address on the bus, so read from FC0000 plus A1 with the data byte in A1, and a simple PAL writes the data into RAM. Works fine as an I/O port too.
replies:
Who knows? One Meg seems a little optomistic as the ST only has
128K of address space available for the cartridge port. Where will this
extra memory go?

		Mark Powell

********************************************************************************

It's easy: whenever you *read* the adress range from FC0000+ you
actually *write* an adress to the adress bus, right?
Now: read adress FC000+(A1) with (a1).b containig the data to be
written. A simple PAL can write the Data into RAM.

Works just fine as an I/O Port. I attached an IBM-PC hard disk
controller (OMTI) to this I/O and use the interface for EC-BUS card as
well.

hase

Welding years ago is very unlikely to result in delayed damage.  Either

subject: Asked before: keeping computer vertical
q: Is it a hazard to a hard disk to keep an AT with two Seagate drives standing vertically under the desk?
ref: No, modern drives run flat or vertical just fine. Do the low-level format in the position the machine will actually live in, so format vertical if it runs vertical. Don't tilt them more than a few degrees, don't block the airflow, and yes, this gets asked every month.
replies:
Modern hard disk drives are quite happy in either a horizontal or
vertical position.  For best results, you should do the low-level
format of a disk drive in the position that it will be used in.

In other words, go ahead and run it vertically, but when you add
your other disk drive(s), format them with the machine in a vertical
position.

BTW hard disks are generally NOT happy tilted more than a few
degrees from straight horizontal or straight vertical.

You're right it has been discussed before, but it's a good thing to
bring up from time to time. Hard disks are rated to run flat or
vertical. For best reliability do a low level format in the desired
operating position.

  From experience: don't block the air flow, and some marginal cards may
run too warm vertical, since convection doesn't lift hot air away from
the boards quite as well. This is not a problem with well designed boards.
	bill davidsen		(davidsen@crdos1.crd.GE.COM)
  {uunet | philabs}!crdgw1!crdos1!davidsen

subject: Can I get more than 16M on a 4d70GT?
q: Can I get more than 16M of memory on a 4d70GT? I've heard rumours of untried double height SIMMs.
ref: SGI doesn't support more than 16MB local to the 4d70 CPU board. Add-in expansion boards reach 144MB total, in 16MB steps, on certain versions. Some boards were designed for 4MB SIMMs, never verified, so 64MB is possible in theory. Double height SIMMs? I seriously doubt it.
replies:
SGI doesn't support greater than 16MB of main memory local to the 4d70 cpu board.
It does offer up to a total of 144MB (in 16MB increments) using add-in memory
expansion boards for certian versions of the 4d70 cpu board. Also, certain
versions of the 4d70 cpu board were designed to support 4MB SIMM's (single height,
9x4Mb), but this was never verified in-house. If one had the correct cpu board and
everthing worked, then 64MB in 16MB increments would be possible. As for using
"double height simms", I seriously doubt that they would work.

Mike Anderson Advanced Systems Division Silicon Graphics, Inc.

subject: PCNFS and a Network Device (help)
q: Under PC-NFS we're trying to make an HP plotter on a MicroVax a network device with net use printerdevice: \\nodename\queuename, but we get 'filesystem access denied'. How do we fix it?
ref: Your problem is a filesystem not exported to the PCs. PC-NFS printing redirects output to a disk mounted from the directory given to pcnfsd with the -s option. Check /etc/exports on the server and make sure that filesystem is exported. This is basic stuff, people.
replies:
Rob,
	Your problem is that there is a file system not exported to the
PCs. This file system is the one that is pointed to from the PCNFSD with
the -s option. When you print using PCNFS it will redirect the printer
output (the prt.exe program) to a network device mounted as a disk. The
devices are T:\ for lpt1, U:\ for lpt2 and V:\ for lpt3. Then PCNFSD
will take the file from the UNIX dir and send it to the print spool dir
for the printer you want.

	There for what you should is check the /etc/exports file on the
file server to ensure that the proper filesystem is exported (on a sun
PCNFSD is started up either in the rc.local file or the inetd.conf for
the rpc version. For the rc.local version there should be somthing like
this in the rc.local file:

	if[ -f /etc/rpc.pcnfsd ]; then
	 /etc/rpc.pcnfsd -s /usr/tmp ; echo
	 'rpc.pcnfsd' >/dev/console
	fi

some time after YPBIND.

subject: SuitcaseII vs. MasterJuggler
q: Can SuitcaseII or MasterJuggler open sound files, and does keeping sounds in suitcases instead of the System file save memory on a 1Meg Mac?
ref: Both open files containing 'snd ' resources. Suitcase II's dialog shows Smg2 and SFIL types, and the Show all file types box handles the rest. As for memory, there is no direct relation between System file size and RAM use. Resources load only as used, so suitcases buy convenience, not RAM.
replies:
Both products can open files containing 'snd ' resources.  Suitcase II's file
selection dialog will show files having the file type codes 'Smg2' (created
by The Sound Man utility) and 'SFIL' (created by the Sound Mover utility,
which is a shareware product included on the Suitcase II product disk by
Sound Mover's author's permission).  If the file has another type code, the
"Show all file types" checkbox in Suitcase II's file selection dialog will
allow you to open it.

There is no direct relation between the size of the System file and RAM
usage.  The advantages of keeping resources in suitcase files rather than in
the System file are flexibility and convenience, not reduced RAM usage.  The
System file is not read into RAM as a whole; it is a disk repository of
resources which are read into RAM as they are used, and remain in RAM only
while they are used.  The same is true of suitcase files.

I am the author of Suitcase II.

subject: Mig-29 lands in Turkey
q: What is the role of the Mig-29, and what has been learned about it after one landed in Turkey?
ref: It's the Soviets' latest air superiority fighter, built to outfight F-16s and F-15s. Thrust-to-weight is over 1, it's about F-18 size but faster and more maneuverable, and it's not fly-by-wire. Short internal range. Of course the US wants a look.
replies:
The Mig-29 is the Soviet's latest and greatest air superiority
fighter.  It was designed to outfight F-16s and F-15s.
It has a thrust-to-weight > 1, meaning it can accelerate in a
vertical climb.  It is about the same size as an F-18, but
faster and more maneuverable  (wing loading is less than
that of an F-18).  It is not fly-by-wire.
It probably has look-down shoot-down doppler radar (also supposedly
installed on Su-27 Flankers and Mig-31 Foxhounds).
It has a fairly short range on internal fuel.
You can bet that the U.S. would love to look one over.

An interesting aside is that the Mig-29 was designed to operate from
unpaved airstrips:  it has auxialiary air intakes on top of the plane,
and the primary air intakes on the bottom of the plane have mesh covers
(or close completely, I forget which) to prevent foreign object damage.
Supposedly this is to appeal to third world buyers.

subject: My CD Player Skips

isn't caked on, or wipe it gently with a tissue if that doesn't work.  Be
very careful, as if you scratch it, you'll have an unusable player on your
hands.

subject: Random number generation in perl
q: Can I generate random numbers in perl? I'd want something like seed() and random() functions. I'm fairly new to perl and pretty sure it isn't in the manual.
ref: Pretty convinced, are you? It's been there since V2: rand(EXPR) returns a fractional number between 0 and EXPR, or 0 and 1 if omitted, and srand(EXPR) seeds it, defaulting to time. Almost exactly your spec. Read the manual.
replies:
Pretty convinced?  Care to bet on that? :-)

From the 3.0pl18 manual (although its been there since V2, as I recall):

     rand(EXPR)
     rand EXPR
     rand    Returns a random fractional number between 0 and the
             value  of  EXPR.  (EXPR should be positive.) If EXPR
             is omitted, returns a value between 0  and  1.   See
             also srand().
     [....]
     srand(EXPR)
     srand EXPR
             Sets the random number seed for the  rand  operator.
             If EXPR is omitted, does srand(time).

Almost exactly to your specifications.

print "Just another Perl hacker," if "you can't think of anything better..."

subject: Real Time Clock Chip source
q: My old Mac's clock jumps to random dates or dies completely. The clock chip is an 8-pin with 8504 on it and I can't identify it. Is it the chip, and where can I get one?
ref: It's your dead battery, not the chip. The little battery inside the case keeps the clock and the other PRAM values alive while the power is off. When it dies, the clock starts fibrillating. Swap the battery before you go hunting for chips.
replies:
Sounds like your battery has run dead.  The clock chip is probably fine.  In
order to keep time while the power to the Mac is off, there is a little
battery inside your case.  When it dies, your clock starts "fibrillating."

The clock time is just one of several values which are stored in PRAM and
sustained by this battery.

subject: Freq. and Cap. meter questions
q: Is there a chip or circuit to convert frequency to voltage for a homebrew meter, and how would I build a crude capacitance meter?
ref: Use a phase-locked loop like the CD74HC4046 with one resistor and capacitor; it works to about 20 MHz and costs under $2. For capacitance, use a clock, a counter, and an accurate R/C timer chip gating it. Or let a PLL lock to a fixed frequency and read the voltage. Simpler than your DMM's A/D.
replies:
Try a phase-locked loop; for few percent accuracy, you
can use a CD74HC4046 (the data sheet claims 0.1 %; that seems
perhaps optimistic to me), with a single resistor and capacitor.
This includes a high-impedance preamp, works to circa 20 MHz, and
runs on a few milliamps of +5v.  Cost under $2.

	Not necessarily: get a clock and a counter; set up an R/C
timer with a good accurate timer chip (XR320 from Exar, or LM322
from National, is more accurate than a straight '555); drive the counter
with the (constant) clock and gate it with the timer output.
This scheme is actually simpler than the A/D converter your DMM
has in it.
	Alternately, hook the capacitor into a PLL chip (like the
CD74HC4046), and observe the output voltage when the PLL locks
onto a fixed frequency.  This produces a voltage proportional
to C.  Change the fixed frequency for range-switching.

		John Whitmore

subject: Simple File Transfer
q: How do I add fields to a dBase III Plus database once it has been defined? I need to load an ASCII download that's missing a few fields we use.
ref: Easy, if not obvious. CREATE a Temp file with all the fields you want, USE Temp, then APPEND FROM Master. Only fields with matching names get copied, so get the names exact. Field order doesn't matter.
replies:
Sorry that this is not more obvious; it is, however, very easy to do.  If
you have a dbf file with fields a,b,c and you want to add d and e, just:

	CREATE Temp  && with fields a,b,c,d,e
	USE Temp
	APPEND FROM Master

Temp.dbf now contains the data in the original master file with the extra
fields added.  Note that the ordering of fields in Temp is not important,
but the exact names are--only fields with the same names are copied.

Hope it helps.

/alastair/

subject: Weapons (was Re: Blasters != Lasers)
q: Do sonic disruptors work in space? Can tightly beamed sound travel in a vacuum, and what's the principle behind them?
ref: No. Focus is irrelevant: sound is a disturbance in a medium like air, water or glass, and has no existence without one. A vacuum has no matter to carry it. Basic physics, people. As for causing real damage with sound, nobody has an answer.
replies:
It doesn't matter how focused the sound wave is, (and it is possible to
create fairly highly directional "beams" of sound, especially with
high pitched sounds) it is impossible to transmit sound waves without
a medium (normally atmosphere, but also water, glass, etc.) for them
to pass through.  A sound wave is a disturbance in the medium and has
no existence on its own.

The principle behind them ?  I can't tell you what the writers had in
mind, but a possibility that (at least as far as I know) doesn't violate
current physics would be an extremely high-pitched (>20 Khz) frequency
sound pulse generated at an approximate point source in front of
a parabolic sound reflector, and with a medium length barrel.  (Sort
of like a flashlight).  The problem is not how to generate a fairly
narrow beam of sound, but how do generate sound waves that will cause
major damage to something.

First I don't remember the Klingons using 'sonic' disruptors. They were
just called disruptors. Fancy name for disintegrator ray, I always thought.

sound is pressure waves (vibrations) in matter. The sound is detected by the
vibrations moving your eardrums back and forth. Sound must travel through a
substance, whether air or metal or wood, etc. It cannot travel through space
because there is not enough matter present in open space to conduct sound. That
is why it is called a vacuum.

But like I said, I don't think the disruptors were meant to be 'sonic'.

subject: SCO externs ... too many?
q: My large application on SCO Xenix 2.3.0 has a loader that can't resolve large numbers of external references. If I reduce the number of externs below some threshold the problem vanishes. What do I do?
ref: You're hitting a symbol table size limit in the linker. Work around it by grouping related externs into structs defined in header files, so the whole group links through a single extern entry. Put related programs in their own libraries too. Lousy tools, but that's what you get.
replies:
I encountered a similar problem under microport: there obviously is
some sort of limit to symbol table size.

I addressed this by putting related externs into structs defined
in appropriate header files: e.g.,
struct {int a,b;
	char c,d,e;

Presumably SAMPLE.a is coded as an offset off SAMPLE, and everything
in the struct gets linked up using only a single extern entry
in the linker symbol table.  Moreover, this simplifies tracking
large groups of externs.  For ease of management, I favor putting
related programs (related by use of specific header files)
in their own libraries when possible...

subject: Interrupt handling with a modem in CP/M
q: I wrote an interrupt routine for my modem driver under CP/M that stuffs characters into a 256-byte circular buffer, but at 2400 baud I still lose characters during scrolling. What can I do?
ref: Double the circular buffer size and rewrite the interrupt routine. Also count lost characters: bump a LOST counter whenever a new character hits a full buffer, then check it. If it's nonzero, your buffer is too small. Basic bookkeeping, really.
replies:
Try doubling the circular buffer size and rewriting the interrupt
routine.
How does the interrupt routine handle buffer full condiitions?  Are you
detecting when the buffer fills?  My interrupt routines increment a LOST
count every time a new character interrupt tries to add a character to a
full buffer.  Then, when my program is running, I can check this value
and print an error message showing how many characters were lost.  If I
see the error message, this is a sure sign that I need to increase the
buffer size for that application.

subject: Measuring input impedance of a preamp
q: How does one properly measure the input impedance of audio gear like a mic preamp across a range of frequencies? Vrms over Irms fails because of phase differences.
ref: Drive the device from a current source and sense the voltage with a high impedance follower. Watch magnitude and phase on a dual trace scope or Lissajous figures. A network analyzer does exactly this; these days DSP is far better. Hardly rocket science.
replies:
Basically you drive you device under test from a compliant current source,
such as a common base transistor output stage and sense the voltage with
a high impedance voltage follower, such as a FET source follower.

You can observe the voltages on a dual trace scope or look at Lissajous
figures to see the magnitude and phase.

To directly read the phase takes some doing - you synchronously modulate
the drive signal and sensed voltage up to a common intermediate frequency
which will not frequency, only in level and phase.  Alternatively this IF can
be hetrodyned down to DC, or you can directly mix the audio signals down to
DC if you have linear enough analog multipliers.

A device called a network analyzer is used for this purpose.  About 15

subject: Anyway to get the '<', '>' characters in the right place on DEC?
q: Is there any way to get the '<' and '>' characters above the ',' and '.' keys on DEC keyboards in Emacs? I don't know how to specify SHIFT-, to do a rebind.
ref: Out of luck. Shifted and unshifted comma and period send the same ASCII values, since the keyboard does the decoding, so Emacs can't tell whether shift was pressed. You can swap the ` and escape keys, because those send different characters. Basic hardware, pal.
replies:
I'm afraid you're out of luck, Mike!  The problem is that the shifted/
unshifted , and . keys send the SAME ascii values to the computer - all the
decoding is done within the keyboard.  The computer and Emacs have no way to
know whether you've pressed the shift key or not, they just get the , or .
character.   Sorry!   8-(

You CAN switch the ` and escape keys because they send different characters
to the computer when pressed.

replies:
Program 100005 is the Mount protocol.  SunOS 4.1 includes support for a new
version of the Mount protocol.  The 4.1 release notes say that this is
needed for support of the "posix" NFS mount option.

servers) is that a 4.1 system will fall back to the v1 protocol unless the
"posix" option is used.

So, make sure you aren't specifying the "posix" option when mounting the
VMS system.

subject: em-dashes
q: Should em-dashes have spaces around them, or bump up against the surrounding words?
ref: No spaces. The Chicago Manual of Style says so in 2.70, and most books follow it. If you insist on spaces, use a tie before the dash so it never starts a line. Any idiot with a bookshelf can check.
replies:
The "Chicago Manual of Style" says in Section 2.70 that an em-dash
within a sentence should *not* have spaces around it.  Looking at a
couple of random books (Knuth's TEX Book, Webster's 9th Collegiate,
4.3BSD book) shows this rule to be followed by most authors.

	Richard Stevens
	Health Systems International, New Haven, CT
	   stevens@hsi.com
           ... { uunet | yale } ! hsi ! stevens

The second---by convention, I suppose.  It looks much better.  Besides, no
other punctuation marks are separated by spaces from the surrounding words.

Even if you were to use the spaces, though, you should do it thus:

	This is incorrect~--- but better than Sentence~(1) above, as
	it will never leave the dash at the beginning of a line.

In net.typing, I use two hyphens for the em dash (and the en dash), which is
conventional for monospaced text.

subject: how detect opening of message box?
q: How can my HyperCard stack detect that the user opened the message box so I can turn keytrapping off automatically?
ref: Write a doMenu handler that checks for the Message menu item, tests whether the message box is visible, toggles the lock, and always passes doMenu. That misses the close box, so use an idle handler checking the message box's visible property. It slows things, so tough.
replies:
There are two methods you might use. If the only way the user will show
the message box is by using the menu item or its command-key equivalent,
you can use a doMenu handler to turn off the lock:

  on doMenu theItem
    if theItem is "Message" then
      if the visible of the message is false then
         -- command to turn off lock
      else
         -- command to turn on lock
      end if
    end if
    pass doMenu -- DO NOT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES FORGET THIS!
  end doMenu

This method raises a problem if the user uses the message windoid's close
box to hide it; the keytrapping will not be restored. A way to handle this
is to use an idle handler to check the status of the message box:

  on idle
    if the visible of the message box is true then
      -- turn off lock
    else
      -- turn on lock
    end if
  end idle

Idle handlers slow responsiveness in some stacks, but they're sometimes
extremely useful.

subject: Goedel & programming languages
q: Does Goedel's theorem imply that for any sufficiently powerful programming language, there is a valid program that its compiler cannot compile?
ref: No, that's a misapplication. Incompleteness is about no machine being able to decide in general what a program does, not whether it's syntactically valid. Compilers can be correct and complete on syntax. Read the theorem before borrowing it from Hofstadter.
replies:
Marc's statement proposed application of Godel's Incompleteness is incorrect.

The key to Godel's Incompleteness is not that a program can't be detected
to be syntactically incorrect, but rather that NO MACHINE CAN (in general)
DECIDE ANYTHING ABOUT WHAT A PROGRAM *DOES*.

It is apparent that compilers exist, and that they CAN BE both correct and
complete.  But all they can (in general) detect is syntactic correctness of
the program; they can (in general) have *no* complete knowledge about what a
program *does*.

Example: in the comp.lang.c flame war a year ago regarding the need for
"volatile" in ANSI-C, some thought a compiler could detect if a program used
a var in a "volitale" way.  But this is (again, in general) impossible.

Back to what you *can't* do: if you claim to have written a program in *any*
language that detects *anything* about what another program *does*, you'll
be incorrect -- there will always exist programs which your program will
fail on.  (naturally, if the targe

subject: received folder becomes /tmp/snd.### (strange)
q: A user's Elm received folder, nearly 4 megabytes, vanished and an intact copy turned up in the temp directory as snd.#####. How could this happen? She may have been over her disk quota.
ref: Most likely a copy error, such as quota exceeded. Elm leaves the snd.PID temp file intact when it hits an error copying, and prints 'Emergency Exit, all files intact' with a reason. It may also have core dumped and exited. Read the screen next time.
replies:
Most likely there was a very large error message.... The reason Elm
leaves the snd.PID file intact (this is the temp file for the mailbox)
is when it hits an error copying the file (such as quote exceeded).
At that time it prints all over its screen 'Emergency Exit, all files
intact' along with some other message as to why it is exiting.

Another 'more silent' reason for this is if for some reason Elm hit a
'core dump' and exited.  It catches most of those and prints its
'Emergency Exit' message.

subject: Can you create newsgroup comp.c++ ??
q: How do I create the newsgroup comp.c++ under VMS news? VMS won't let me make a directory with a "+" in the name.
ref: Quote the name: NEWS> CREATE NEWSGROUP "COMP.C++". News 5.9C is smart enough to escape VMS-illegal characters itself, so the directory ends up as COMP.C_K_K. Without the quotes the CLI parser chokes on the trailing plus. Read the manual.
replies:
Don't know which version you're running, but News 5.9C is smart
enough to recognize VMS-illegal characters in newsgroup names and `escape'
them.  I tried

	NEWS> create newsgroup comp.c++

and it failed, but only because the CLI parser expected another parameter
after the trailing "+".  This

	NEWS> create newsgroup "comp.c++"

worked.  The directory created was [...COMP.C_K_K].  (And if you're wondering,
an underscore in a newsgroup name becomes two underscores in the directory
name.)  I note with satisfaction that when NEWS receives a checkgroups message
and emits a command procedure (encased in a mail message), the newsgroup names
are enclosed in quotes.

Use:

NEWS> CREATE NEWSGROUP "COMP.C++"

News (or the C library) is smart enough to figure it out.

subject: Malloc'ing, what strategy to use?
q: On the Atari ST with GEMDOS Malloc, is it better to allocate ten 80-byte blocks for a history buffer or one 800-byte block?
ref: One 800-byte block. If you know the size, a static array does the job. Older TOS limits the Malloc count, each Malloc eats system memory, and fragmentation isn't a real problem under TOS anyway. Don't over-think it.
replies:
If you know how much space you want in advance, then just declare a
static variable in your program, e.g.,

	static char history[10][80];

Otherwise, you are probably better off allocating 1 block of 800 bytes
for several reasons:

1.  Older versions of TOS have bugs that you alluded to that tend to
limit the number of times Malloc can be called.

2.  Even under TOS 1.4, each Malloc takes some space from static
system memory to record information about the block allocated.  Thus,
your second alternative results in more total storage being used.

3.  Fragmentation is generally not a problem under TOS anyway unless
you are doing unusual things.

subject: Using serial ports
q: I want to write a simple Mac program using the modem port. What is the Communications Manager, and should I worry about it?
ref: AAARGH, it's the Communications Toolbox and Connection Manager. Communications Manager is some other company's evil creation. It abstracts the low-level stuff, with connection tools underneath, so the same code works over serial, ADSP and so on. Learn it.
replies:
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AAARGGGGHHHHHHHH!!!!!!  Okay, once more with feeling, Communications Toolbox.
Connection Manager.  Communications Manager is an evil creation of that other
computer company.

What the Connection Manager does is to abstract the application from the low
level stuff.  Underneath the manager, sits connection tools that handle the
low level stuff for you.

How it works:
The app makes a call to read or write data.  The manager relays this to the
current tool, which takes care of talking to an associated driver.  The choice
of the tool is left up to the app, and in some instances, the user.

The big win is that the same code will work regardless of whether you're using
a Serial Connection tool, an ADSP connection tool, or the newly announced
Telepathic Conn tool.

-Why can't I resize an xfish window when using twm ?

-More generally, what window attribute allows/disallows resizing?
-What would I need to modify in xfish to make its window resizeable?

   twm uses an initialization file called .twmrc (presumable in your home
   directory.)

   that certain windows should not have a "title" (the bar with the resize,
   iconify, and focus gadgets)

      "xfish"

subject: More questions...
