subject: Implementing Malloc (was Extended Memory without dereference operator)
q: Does anyone have source or suggestions for writing my own malloc and free for extended memory under MS-DOS with Turbo C, using MK_FP? Is there anything I should know about extended memory?
ref: K&R 2nd edition pp 185-189 has source for malloc() and free(), and porting it is easy. But extended memory means protected mode, which breaks normal DOS/BIOS services, so plain pointers won't cut it. Use handles, pointers to pointers, with a GetPointer() that's valid only until the next call. Ugly, but that's DOS.
replies:
K&R 2nd edition pp 185-189 have source code for malloc() and for free().
 Porting this code is easy (I could do it...).
You have to be in protected mode for using it, and if you are there are alot
of problems in using normal DOS/BIOS services. I think that the standard
pointer approach would'nt help. It seems that the 'handle' approach for
accessing data is better. The basic idea is that a handle is pointer
to a pointer to data. You can access ther data by doing something like:

 Pointer = GetPointer(handle)
 Pointer[i] = ...
 .....
The catch is that the pointer is valid only until the next call
to GetPointer() with any other handle. Programming in this style
is not easy, but then the GetPointer() function can be very strong,
it can adapt itself to the hardware, caching into near, far, expanded,
extended, unknown memory, and even using the disk.

subject: *66, *68, *77, etc...
q: Which was the first programming language with a year in its name, like Algol 68, Fortran 66 or Forth 79?
ref: Algol 58 is the earliest I know, a precursor of Algol 60. Fortran 66 only got that name after Fortran 77 appeared, and Algol 60 predates every year-numbered Fortran. Algol 68 may be the first with no yearless name. Check Sammet's book.
replies:
The earliest I know of is Algol 58, a precursor of Algol 60.  Fortran
preceded that (specification 1954, manual 1955, software release 1957),
but when the next version appeared as Fortran II in 1958, the original
became known as Fortran I.  Fortran 66 only became known as such after
Fortran 77 had appeared.  Jean Sammett's book "Programming Langauages:
History and Fundamentals" (1969) would be the place to check up on this.
David Muxworthy
University of Edinburgh

Wasn't there an Algol60 ?  And I don't know of any Fortran earlier than
'66.  And wasn't there some Cobol standard before '74?  (This is "ancient
history" as far as computers go!)

Bet it's not - Algol 60  (the successor to the first Algol, which did
not go by year number...) is earlier than all year-numbered FORTRANs.

Note: Some people referred to Algol 60 simply as 'Algol' just as many
people often referred to FORTRAN 66 as FORTRAN IV. The first language
not to also have a yearless name might well be Algol 68.

Later,
Andrew Mullhaupt

subject: Theory Question
q: How do you find the exact density of a random sum, the sum of X_i from i=1 to Y, where Y is itself a random variable and the X_i have density f?
ref: Assuming iid X_i and integer Y, take transforms. The transform of the sum is G(F(p)), with F the transform of f and G that of g. Then you invert it. That's about all you can say in general; some cases, like exponential with geometric, give closed forms. Sigh.
replies:
I assume you mean to have the X_i iid and Y is integer valued.
I will work this out for
nonnegative X_i with Laplace-Stieltjes transforms; the argument extends to
arbitrary X_i via characteristic functions. Let S be the sum,
L(S;p) be the LST of S with transform variable p, and F and G be
the LSTs of f and g respectively. Then
L(S;p|Y=y)=[F(p)}^y
so
L(S;p)= sum over y {[F(p)]^y g(y) = G[F(p)].
Now you have to invert; as far as I know, this is about all you can
say. For some particular cases, the inversion is easy and gives a
nice closed form. For example, when F is exponential and G is geometric,
S is also exponential.
Dan Heyman

subject: printer help
q: After doing COPY of a large file to PAR:, how do I stop the print job? Turning off the printer takes forever to produce a printer trouble requester.
ref: Use TYPE file TO PAR: instead of COPY. COPY blasts big chunks at the printer, while TYPE sends a line at a time, so CTRL-C stops it almost immediately. If your printer has a RAM buffer, you're stuck turning it off. RTFM next time.
replies:
Hi there,

I usually do `TYPE >PAR: file' when I want to print something (or at least
I did until I started using Francois Gagnon's excellent Print Spooler). You
can rewrite this as `TYPE file TO PAR:' for exactly the same effect. Unlike
COPY which will send large amounts of information to the printer in one go,
TYPE only sends a line at a time. As a result, pressing CTRL-C will stop the
printer almost immediately.

The only time this is not true is if you have some sort of RAM buffer connected
to your printer which is storing the data before it gets printed. In this case,
the only solution is indeed to turn off your printer.

Eddy

subject: SFGetFile and Launch
q: Why does launching MacWrite 5.0 from my own menu item, using PBOpenWD, SetVol and Launch as in TN52, bomb with an illegal instruction when other applications launch fine?
ref: It's a bug in MacWrite 5.0's initialization. It passes whatever junk sits in a stack location as the record buffer address for _SysEnvirons. Finder happens to leave something harmless there, yours doesn't. Sloppy code, and you have to patch the binary.
replies:
(Theodore Wu) cites a problem in programmatically launching MacWrite 5.0.

The problem is a bug in MacWrite 5.0's initialization.  It passes whatever
happens to be in a certain stack location, namely 0(A6) after the first
Link instruction, as the address of a record buffer for _SysEnvirons.
The contents of that stack location happen to be innocuous when Finder
and some other launching facilities do the launch.

To fix the bug, apply the following hexadecimal patch to MacWrite 5.0:

search for: 2F0A 2056 303C 0001 A090 245F 4A6E
change to:  41EE FFF0 303C 0001 A090 4E71 4A68

This code is at offset $CA from the start of CODE 1.

subject: printf()

Most likely you would have gotten your message if you had flushed

fflush might also be necessary.

I believe the latest version is on disk 102.  You can even specify
the delay interval after each debug output line, in 0.10 second

bug crops up, you'll be "armed and ready".

-Fred

subject: New CD player technology
q: What is the new '1 Bit' CD player technology that samples at around 34 Mbps and supposedly needs no oversampling digital filter? Can anyone explain simply how it works?
ref: It generates digital pulses, which are produced far more reliably. Peaks in the signal give wider or more frequent pulses, and a low-pass filter averages them back into the original signal. Pulse high pulls the signal up, pulse low pulls it down. Marketing hype aside, that's the gist.
replies:
If I remember correctly, these 1-bit CD players work by generating digital
pulses.  Digital pulses are much more reliably produced.

But how does that turn into a time-varying signal?  Well, I DON'T remember
that correctly, but it COULD happen in three ways:
1) Peaks in the signal correspond to wider pulses.
2) Peaks in the signal correspond to more frequent pulses.
Either way, the effect is that using a low-pass filter as a "signal
averager", the original signal is determined.  You could almost think of it
this way: when the pulse is high, it pulls the signal up; when the pulse
is low, it pulls the signal down.

Boy, do I need to work on my explanations.

Michael C. Grant

There is a simple explanation starting on page 41 of Electonic Engineering
Times for June 11, 1990.  There is a somewhat more complete (and
technical) explanation on page 74 of JEI for Oct. 88. This latter is a
Japanese publication in English, of rather limited availability.

subject: Processing Power Equivalents
q: If the brain has 10 billion neurons with 1000 connections each firing 100 times a second, would a system of 1 million units with 10 connections each at 100 MHz be equivalent in processing power, since the totals both come to 10^15?
ref: Not really. Matching raw firing counts proves nothing, sigh. In most neural net models the information processed drops by four orders of magnitude (neuron count) and the information remembered drops by six (synapse count). So no, not equivalent.
replies:
Depends what you mean by "processing power."  What you're saying seems to be
that the number of neuron firings (transmission across synapses) would be the
same for the two.

However, the problem is in the way the information in the net is used.  The
way most neural net models are set up, the amount of information it could
process would drop by 4 orders of magnitude (the number of neurons) and the
amount of information it could remember would drop by a 6 orders of magnitude
(the number of synapses).

Even if you quibble with my descriptions of the uses of neurons and synapses,
it is clear that the information content would decrease by many orders of
magnitude.

subject: ISBN check sum digit

Multiply the first digit by 1, the second by 2, the third by 3, ...,
the ninth by 9.  Sum the nine products.  The last digit, the check
digit, should equal the sum modulo 11.  (An X in the check digit
position stands for 10.)

subject: Joysticks in BOTH ports?
q: How do I use both ports of an Amiga 1000 as joystick ports, with normal non-proportional joysticks, while still allowing Intuition?
ref: Open game port 0, save the trigger conditions, close it. Open the input device, send SETMPORT to set port 2, close it. Use the joysticks, then restore with SETMPORT to port 0, SETMTYPE to GPCT_MOUSE, and the saved SETMTRIG. You must open and close in that order; don't ask why.
replies:
I posted this recently, but basically you:

	Open game port 0
	Read trigger conditions and save them.
	Close game port 0.

	Open the input device.
	Send the SETMPORT message to set it to (say) port 2.
	Close the input device.

Do whatever you want with the joystick ports.

	Open the input device.
	Send SETMPORT to set it back to port 0.
	Send SETMTYPE to set it back to GPCT_MOUSE.
	Send SETMTRIG to the saved trigger conditions.
	Close the input device.

You really have to open and close the ports, and in that order. Otherwise it
doesn't work. No, I don't know why.

subject: A3000 daughter board ...

ref: Forget it. There's no room for another slot, since the IBM slots sit in auxiliary space meant for other stuff like video slots. Buster supports five slots, but those signals don't reach the daughterboard connector. You could add one with fly wires, but where it would go is a mystery.
replies:
Take a look at the A3000 bus backplane daughterboard.  There's no room for
another slot, the IBM slots go into the auxilary space, which we define and

subject: Drawing Bitmaps
q: In my Mac waveform program, how can I draw the picture into a bitmap first, so viewing is faster and stored memory is smaller?
ref: Common technique, even a tech note: TN#41. Draw into an off-screen port with your own bitmap (rowbytes, bounds, allocated baseAddr), then CopyBits it to the window on update. Redraw the bitmap when the waveform changes. Not hard once you get the hang of it.
replies:
Sure, it is a common technique, there is even a tech note on it.  TN#41.  If
you can't get a hold of that, it is pretty simple to figure out-- you make
a bitmap "by hand" (filling in rowbytes and bounds, and allocating space
for the baseAddr), open a port (with openPort), setportbits to the port,
draw the waveform into the port (which should be as big as the waveform).
Then, on update, you CopyBits the appropriate part of the waveform into your
window.  Of course, when the waveform changes, you need to redraw the bitmap.

Try establishing an off screen grafPort, then draw into it, and use CopyBits
to 'stamp' the image into the screen.  This is not a hard thing to do when
you get the hang of it.  Although to save memory I would suggest that you
write out the pixel buffer to a file(s) after you're through with each
map.

subject: Independence of Bernoulli Variables
q: I have many independent observations of a vector of k Bernoulli variables, each with mean 1/2. How can I conclude that the components of these vectors are independent, or that there's no evidence they aren't?
ref: For k=2, find the optimally correlated (ACE) transformations of the variables. The optimal correlation is zero exactly when they're independent. If they aren't, the transformations also help describe the dependence. For k>2 it might work along the same lines, but nobody's sure.
replies:
Suppose k=2. Then you might try to find the optimally correlated ("ACE")
transformations of the variables; the optimal correlation is zero iff
the variables are independent. If there is lack of independence, the
transformations might be useful in describing the dependence.

The case k>2 may be approachable along the same lines, but I'm not sure.

subject: Change bars in TeX/LaTeX?
q: Does anyone have a good general change bar mechanism for TeX or LaTeX? I wrote a simple one working a paragraph at a time, but a better one looks hairy.
ref: There's a fancy changebar style in the Clarkson archives, but it uses LN03-specific specials, so it's useless elsewhere until someone standardizes \special. Frankly, inline markup shows which words changed and can hold the old wording. I never understood the love of changebars.
replies:
There is a fancy changebar style in the Clarkson archives, but it uses
ln03-specific `\special's to draw the bars.  If we ever get a standard
for \special, this style might become more useful.

On the other hand, I have never understood why people like changebars.
(They do point out which lines have changed.  So would inline markup.
The only advantage to changebars is that they can be masked away when
the document is photocopied; but when the document is typeset
electronically, inline markup could be deleted easily.  Moreover, the
inline markup would show which *words* have changed, rather than which
lines, and could include the old wording as well.)

subject: Determining memory availabilty.
q: How can I find at run time how much virtual memory, RAM plus swap, is available before calling malloc on an SGI?
ref: Two obvious ways. Use sysmp(2) to fetch the minfo structure for free swap, plus MPKA_FREEMEM for free real memory, and add them up. Or just statfs(2) the /debug filesystem, whose size and free space are total and free virtual memory. RTFM.
replies:
There are two obvious ways to do this.

First, use the sysmp(2) system call to fetch the minfo structure (described in /usr/include/sys/sysinfo.h), which gives the amount of free swap available at any given point in time, and use the MPKA_FREEMEM option to get the free real memory available. Then do the obvious calculation.

The second, possibly simpler way is to use the statfs(2) system call on the /debug file system. /debug overall filesystem size is the same as the total amount of virtual memory available, free space is the same as the amount of free virtual space available. The inode count fields give the total number of process slots, and number free.

subject: calling main in ANSI C
q: The ARM says main() may not be called from within a C++ program. Does ANSI C have the same restriction, or can main be called from inside the program?
ref: In ANSI C, main() may be invoked recursively by a strictly conforming program. X3J11 confirmed that when asked for an interpretation. So C++ is different. Some implementations treat main specially, but that's their problem, not the standard's.
replies:
At least some implementations treat the function 'main' in a special
manner. Here's a snippet from a listing from VAX/VMS C V3.1-051 with
the "/machine_code" flag on:

  146           int main(void) {
                                          0000  main:
                                    0000  0000          .entry  main,^m<>
                              5E 08 C2    0002          subl2   #8,sp
                       00000000* EF 16    0005          jsb     C$MAIN_ARGS

The subroutine C$MAIN_ARGS is only called by main, and the call is
generated automatically by the compiler. I believe that it's purpose is
to arrange for the argc and argv parameters to be provided to the main
entry point. It's my guess that if you tried to call main() with different
arguments with this compiler it wouldn't work (main would get the command
line arguments no matter what you did, or something worse would happen).

I won't hazard a guess as to whether this is considered legitimate
behaviour according to t

I asked X3J11 for an interpretation on this point, and they confirmed
that main() may be invoked "recursively" by a strictly conforming C
program.

opposite case.

If one really had a toplogy where the CSMA model actually worked

antennae would reduce the overall efficiency of the topology.

  Since most packet radio topologies are poorly interconnected, I suspect
the CSMA model works poorly anyway, and the use of directional antennae
would not hurt very much.

   If a topology was in use where a central node was serving a number
of remotely located nodes, and these nodes could not hear each other
anyway, and the remote nodes have poor signals into the central node, then
using beams at the remote nodes would probably make sense, though the
efficiency of this topology would never be as good as a completely
interconnected topology.

Dana

subject: Does V4.1 DECnet installation also require V4.0 media?
q: After installing ULTRIX V4.1 from CDROM, setld complains DNPBASE400 needs UDTBASE400 when I install DECnet. Do I need the V4.0 media, and will it trash my 4.1 system?
ref: No, don't touch the 4.0 media. The mandatory upgrade is handled during the installation. Just go to /usr/etc/subsets and touch the 4.0 lock files, like UDTBASE400.lk, so setld thinks 4.0 is installed. It's in the 4.1 release notes. Read them.
replies:
That is correct behavior, you have
to put in the mandatory upgrade.

What you need to do is the following. Go to /usr/etc/subsets
and

# touch UDTBASE400.lk UDTBIN400.lk UDTINET400.lk UDTMAN400.lk

setld will now assume that those subsets have been created
and will properly install DECnet.

The mandatory upgrade is installed during the installation. It asks if you
have a upgrade tape, and if so it loads it during the regular installation.
Saves a kernel rebuild!

You don't have to install 4.0. What you do have to do is execute the following:

cd /usr/etc/subsets

foreach i ( U*410.lk )
 touch ` echo $i | sed -e 's/410/400/' `
 touch ` echo $i | sed -e 's/410/400/' | sed -e 's/lk$/ctrl/' `
 touch ` echo $i | sed -e 's/410/400/' | sed -e 's/lk$/scp/' `
end

chmod 744 U*400.scp

This creates the 4.0 control files so products like DECnet think that 4.0
is installed.

This is mentioned in the 4.1 release notes (or installation guide).

Roland

We did the same rather uneventful install last weekend (Ultrix 4.1 and DECnet
4.0(?)).  The DECnet install also compained about not finding the UDTBASE400
subset.  So I manually created the lock files to make it appear that the
4.0 subsets were loaded:

	/bin/cp /dev/null /usr/etc/subsets/UDTBASE400.lk
	/bin/cp /dev/null /usr/etc/subsets/UDTBIN400.lk
	/bin/cp /dev/null /usr/etc/subsets/UDTCOMM400.lk

So far, everything seems to work ok.

ref: Don't sweat the racking if you've no means of doing it. Mine turned out fine for years, though it won't be as clean. Two weeks in the fermenter guarantees it's done. Bubbles in the lock lie, since the sludge keeps bubbling. Take a hydrometer reading if in doubt.

It depends on how particular you are about your beer.  If you have no means

and it always turned out well.  If you later decide you wish your brew to
look and taste as clean as possible then you will have to start taking steps

get pretty consistent brewing temps in the 70s.  Naturally the colder it is
the longer it will take and if the temperature varies much you will have to
use a hydrometer.

subject: Smail or Elm??
q: Should I run smail or ELM on a 3B2/300? All I need is a mailer that forwards mail to a smarthost when it can't figure out where to send it.
ref: You're comparing apples and oranges. Smail is a router that works out uucp paths and calls binmail and uux to deliver. Elm is a user interface. Run both: smail for routing, elm on top, and turn off elm's own path handling.
replies:
ELM and SMAIL are different kind of mailing systems.  You should compare elm
with mail (or berkeley Mail/mailx) and smail with sendmail.
Smail is a smart mailer what can sort things out for you, like what uucp
mail path to use etc. it can work in combination with or without sendmail.
So on SysV systems without sendmail it will run just fine not having sendmail.
But you do need a 'user mailer' on top of it like ELM, mailx or mail.

You are talking about two different things.

Smail is a mail router, which finds out (more or less) how and where to
transport mail to. It calls upon local and remote services (binmail and
uux) for the actual delivery. Smail is not intended to be used directly.

Elm is a mail user interface. It is very friendly, and has a number of
features built-in which are also handled by the mail router & delivery
services.

So you can (should?) run both - elm as a user interface, and smail as the
router. You can disable most of elm's "own" handling of uucp paths, routes
and such and leave those to smail.

subject: Variable length arrays in Pascal--can it be done?
q: Can I do variable length arrays in Pascal by declaring a huge array type, a pointer and handle to it, allocating just enough with NewHandle, and resizing with SetHandleSize while tracking the count myself?
ref: Your technique is sound, it's how Apple does it for lists and color tables. Just turn off range checking with {$R-} wherever you index, or the runtime will bark at you. Pascal checks ranges, remember. Honestly, RTFM.
replies:
[Reason for having variable length arrays deleted]

Umm..not quite. Pascal is defined to Range Check at RUN time. That is,
if you access outside of the declared range it's a runtime error. So
as long as your dynamic array is smaller than your declared array,
you'd be OK for the range checking (assuming you don't write outside
the actual size of the array, as you said). But if you ever tried to
write to a location beyond the end of your declared size, you'd get a
runtime error.

MPW Pascal (and I believe Think Pascal also), have the ability to turn off
runtime range checking. You'll need to turn it off everywhere you index
into your dynamic array.

In MPW Pascal you use the directive:
  {$R-} to turn runtime range checking for sets, arrays and strings off.
  {$R+} to turn it back on.

Mitch

Your technique is sound. I think that's how TextEdit's lineStarts array and
the List Manager's cellArray work. Notice that only the lower array bound
matters: it determines whether the array starts with element 0 or 1. The
upper bound is immaterial since you'll never create an instance variable
of this type, only a pointer to it.

Moreover, you can keep the count with the array
	Type MyArray = record
			count:Integer;
			elements: array[1..1] of MyArrayElemnt
			end;

Finally, I recently "discovered" the ToolBox Utility PtrAndHand. It's great
in this context since it does the GetHandleSize, SetHandleSize and
BlockMove stuff you'ld have to do yourself. You can always get a Ptr to
the source data with the @ operator and the destination handle can be unlocked
(PtrAndHand does the right thing internally, I think:-).

Hope this helps, John

o----------------------------------------------------------------------------o
o------------------------------------------------------------------------

I believe this is similiar to the way Apple does it for CTabHandles and other
variable-length arrays.  They declare theirs to be
TYPE
	CSpecArray: Array [0..0] of ColorSpec;
and turn off range checking so the references succeed.  If you want range
checking effective for other arrays, your method should work.

subject: Moon Hardware
q: There's hardware left on the moon, lunar module stages, buggies and so on. Could any of it be reused or reconditioned if you just swapped the battery?
ref: Don't count on it. Extreme day-night temperature cycles wreck electronics, the Surveyors only lasted a day or two without an insulated shell like the Lunokhod rovers had. Most of that gear was built for a single use and a short service life to begin with, so good luck finding anything still alive up there.
replies:
Sender: ouz044@cck.cov.ac.uk (USENET News Owner)

(personally, I'd just take a real big tax write-off)

   There's a lot of hardware on the moon in the form of lunar module
   second stages, and moon buggys etc.  I wonder if any of it could
   possibly be reused or conditioned. I realise that the enviroment isn't
   exactly the best for storage, but would any of it still work??
   If we could replace the battery on a buggy it would be one big
   plus for the manufacturer.

"The Vulture Has Landed!"

It's true that most of the LM ascent stages were deliberately crashed into the
moon, but I think you meant lunar module FIRST stages.  They should be more
intact, though they were subjected to the ascent engine wash as the crew left
the moon.  Recall that spent booster stages can explode years after use due to
their unburned propellant.  I'm sure none of the LMs landed with no propellant
left (Eagle may have come closest).  While I'm almost certain the LM fuels were
not highly explosive, I expect you'd still have to be cautious poking around an
abandoned stage.

Not fundamentally impossible, but not something one could count on.

The extreme temperature cycles are very hard on electronics in particular;
the Surveyors typically survived only one or two day/night cycles despite
precautions like heaters for crucial components.  The Soviet Lunokhod rovers
survived much longer only by being designed to close up into an insulated
shell overnight.  Most of the equipment left on the Moon was designed for
daylight only.

For that matter, a lot of it was designed for a very limited service life
because it was only going to be used once.

subject: Problems converting to HC2
q: After converting a stack from HyperCard 1.2.5 to 2.0, 'send Next to this card' gives 'Can't understand arguments to this keyword', though the same with Prev works. Why?
ref: Because next is a HyperTalk keyword, and 2.0 no longer lets keywords be sent as messages. Others are do, else, end, exit, function, global, if, on, pass, repeat, return, send, then. Rename your handler to something like doNext. This will bite everyone converting.
replies:
This is going to be a very common problem for HC 1->2 conversions.  "Next" is
a keyword in HyperTalk, and HT 2.0 is not as lenient as HT 1.x.x about
allowing keywords to be used as names for messages and variables.  So
when you use message/variable names such as "next", "div", "me", etc. they
will probably have to be changed.

I ran into this converting an important stack for a friend.  I told him
a year ago not to use "me" as a variable name, but would he listen?  Nooo.

'send Next to this card' no longer works because the word 'next' is a
keyword in HyperTalk, and keywords can no longer be sent as messages.
(I'll leave it to Dan Winkler to provide an explanation of why this
is so, perhaps in his next book.)

Here's the complete list of keywords:  do, else, end, exit, function,
global, if, next, on, pass, repeat, return, send, then.  If you have
handlers with any of these words as names, you won't able to invoke
them in 2.0.

Your stack will run fine under 2.0 if you change the name of the handler
from 'next' to something that's not a keyword, such as 'doNext'.

We're working on a complete list of the incompatibilities between
1.x HyperTalk and 2.0 HyperTalk and will post it widely when it's
ready.

Kevin Calhoun
HyperCard Engineer
Apple Computer, Inc.

subject: Problems with file systems with more than 2000 Files
q: I read the Finder has problems with more than 2000 files on one disk, and our 140 MB SCSI disk's filesystem got corrupted. Is that limit real?
ref: No, that's garbled in translation. There's no limit on files per disk. The limit is on the number of different applications, because the Desktop file is a resource file and the Resource Manager can't hold more than 2,727 resources. See Tech Note 141. System 7.0 fixes it. One poster has 15,000 files and no trouble.
replies:
[ Problems with > 200 files on one disk ]

A problem that exists and will exist for the forseeable future is the
problem with the Desktop file. It is a resource file, and as such cannot
have more than 32767 resources in it. Now, some (generically typed
applications with the "Standard application" icon and without file comments)
add NO resources to the Desktop, while others may well add 20 resources,
or more. There are two ways to avoid this, either by partitioning the
disk or by modifying the Finder/Desktop structure (a task for the Apple
Operating Systems Development Team) but neither may be appropriate for
Your needs. (This is described in a TechNote, my TechNotes were updated
in April or May, I think.)

Hope this clarifies, sez'

They are wrong; something got lost in the translation.  There is a limit
to the number of different applications that you may have on one disk.
There is no limit on the number of files on one disk.

Information about each application is kept in an invisible file called the
Desktop file.  The current method for maintaining this information uses
the Resource Manager.  The Resource Manager can't have more than 2,727
resources in one file.  See Tech Note 141 for details.

The Desktop problem will be fixed in System 7.0.  See Tech Note 210 for
more details on the current implementation and its limitations.

I have 15,000 files on one hard disk in my office, with no problems.

subject: How Doy you get a real random number in LSC?
q: How do you get a real random number in LSC? rand() and Random() both give the same sequence every time at startup.
ref: Seed it, genius. Take the system clock value modulo the max seed size and set the seed to that, and you stop getting the same sequence each run. Any idiot knows a PRNG is deterministic.
replies:
Well, rand() works pretty well if you remember to change the seed each
time.  The best way I've seen to do this is by using the value off the
System clock.  You have to take it modulo the max seed size and then
set the seed to this value.  This will keep you from getting the same
"random" sequence every time.

Last attempt at connection actually.

The date is the internal format, which is defined as the number of seconds

subject: RS232 interrupt reset?
q: I enabled the modem status interrupt on a serial port, but the interrupts stop if I don't read the modem status byte. Is reading that status register required to reset the interrupt?
ref: Yes, you must read the Modem Status Register to reset that UART interrupt. Every interrupt type has its own reset: line status register for receiver line status, receive buffer for received data, IIR or a write for the transmitter holding register. RTFM.
replies:
I think you're saying that you enabled Modem Status interrupts. If so then
yes, you have to read the modem status register to reset the UART interrupt
status for that interrupt.

Per the National Semiconductor manual, the following are the interrupt
types and the actions necessary to reset them.

Receiver Line Status int	Read Line Status register
Received Data Available 	Read the receive buffer register
Character timeout (16550)	Read the receive buffer register
Transmitter Holding Register	Read the IIR, or write to Transmit Holding
				Register.
Modem Status			Read Modem Status Register

The Received Data Available interrupt may also be cleared in a 16550 series
UART by the number of characters in the FIFO dropping below the trigger
level. Note that this does not necessarily mean that there are no more
characters in the buffer, so it's best to use the Line Status Register to
determine whether there are still characters to get.

Hope that helped.

subject: Problem with SCO directory routines in C
q: On SCO UNIX 3.2, the <sys/ndir.h> directory routines seem incompatible with <dirent.h>, and my directory lister drops the first letters of filenames. -ldir isn't found either. What should I do?
ref: Stop using <sys/ndir.h>. It's only compatible with the readdir in libx, not libc or libdir, and it reads 16-byte entries straight off the directory, which breaks on other directory formats like BSD. Use <dirent.h>. It's filesystem-independent and uses getdents(). Mixing libraries is your own fault.
replies:
Yes, this is true.  There are three directory-reading routines in 3.2:
readdir in libc (COFF, that is; it's in Slib3.2 for OMF), readdir in libx
(both COFF and OMF), and readdir in libdir (OMF only).  <sys/ndir.h> is
compatible with the readdir et al defined in libx.a (both coff and OMF), but
it is, as you said, incompatible with the one defined in libc or libdir.

You should *not*.  First of all, you didn't use -lx in that case, and mixed
versions.  Second of all, do *not* use <sys/ndir.h> unless you expect to run
the program on a pre-xenix 2.3.0 system; the ndir routines open up the
directory directly and read out 16 bytes.  Obviously, this is not correct.
In particular, it won't work too well on systems that have different
directory formats (BSD for one).

It's for OMF only.

You don't use ndir.h.  Use <dirent.h> instead; that will give you
filesystem-independent routines, which use the getdents() system call to
find out what's in the directory.

subject: Mac PostScript on NeXT
q: How do I print Mac PostScript files on a NeXT? Embedding a laserprep header gave no errors but no output.
ref: Hit Command-K, not Command-F, in the Mac print dialog so the driver writes the laserprep header. Then edit the file so the first line is %!PS-Adobe-2.0. Without it the NeXT treats it as plain text and spews streams of PostScript source. Basic stuff.
replies:
I've had success transferring postscript files from the Mac to
the NeXT and printing them.  When generating the postscript files
from the Mac, at the print dialog box, issue Command-K, not
Command-F.  Command-K tells the driver to write the laserprep
header that's needed to process Mac-specific print files.  Edit
the resultant postscript# file so the first line contains
%!PS-Adobe-2.0.  The default laserprep header doesn't have this
so the NeXT will think you're printing a normal file without it,
giving you streams and streams of postscript source code.
Alternatively, you can hack the laserprep LROM and include it.
(It's in LaserPrep, resource POST, ID -8192, string #1.  After
modifying, it should look like:

%!PS-Adobe-2.0
%%Title: "Laser Prep -- The Apple PostScript Dictionary (md)"
%%Creator: Apple Software Engineering
%%CreationDate: Thursday, March 19, 1987
)

subject: MicroEMACS and VMS MAIL
q: How do I use MicroEMACS 3.10 as the callable editor from VMS MAIL, as described in the reference manual appendix? I can't get it to work.
ref: Define a symbol ME to run the program and MICROEMACS$LIB to point at its library directory. Then set the mail editor to a small command file in SYS$LOGIN that copies P1 to P2 if P1 isn't _NL: or empty, defines sys$input as sys$output, and runs me on P2. Works here, no thanks to the manual.
replies:
I'm no VAX expert, but this works for me:

Define a couple of symbols, one to run the program and one for it to
find the emacs library.  For example:

  ME == "$DISK$CEFIS:[737EFIS.UTIL]ME.EXE"

  MICROEMACS$LIB == "$DISK$CEFIS:[737EFIS.UTIL]"

Set the mail editor to SYS$LOGIN:MEMAIL.COM.

Contents of SYS$LOGIN:MEMAIL.COM:
$ if "''P1'" .NES. "_NL:" then if "''P1'" .NES. "" then copy 'P1' 'P2'
$ define/user sys$input sys$output
$ me 'P2'
$ exit

subject: Starving Your Fish
q: Is it a good idea to skip feeding your aquarium fish one day out of seven? Does anyone actually do this, or does it just stress them?
ref: Plenty of people do it. One day a week with no food, or a 36-hour gap, and the fish show no stress, though they act a bit anxious. Overfeeding fouls the water, which is worse than a missed meal. Sigh, appetite always exceeds need.
replies: Mine don't eat on Saturdays.  Hasn't bothered anyone yet.

I normally feed my fish once every evening.  About once a week, I skip
the evening feed and then feed them the next morning and skip the
evening feed that night.  Thus my feeding intervals in hours for a week
are:

	24 24 24 24 36 36

My fish are not showing stress.  They act kind of anxious the evening
they don't get fed though.  It seems to me that most critters in
nature are supposed to look a little hungry.  Consider your typical
mammal pet (dog, cat, human).  If you feed it the recommend healthy
amount of food, it will still act hungry and often beg for more.
Appetite always exceeds need.

My domino damsel will tend to graze a little bit on algae when it
hasn't been fed in a while.  I've heard that young tangs can starve if
you don't feed them often.  I'm sure feeding requirements vary with
species, age, temp, etc ie 'your millage may vary.

I used to feed my fish twice a day.  Then I went to once a day.  Now I
let them go a day and half once a week.  They still look fine.

I feed my fish about once a week and that's it! They've gone a month
without any food from me. I think the amount of food you give your
fish depends on your setup and the number of fish in the tank.
I have only four fish (2.5" Potters Angel, 2" Royal Gramma, and
2 1.5" Percula Clowns) in a 55 gallon tank. I also have about
80 or 90 pounds of live rock. There is lots of stuff on the rock
for the fish to eat. A fish store I used to go to in D.C. had
a great reef tank (125gal w/ about 6 fish) that they had never
feed!

I think the added stress from poor water conditions caused by
overfeeding is worse on the fish then the stress which occurs
when they miss a few "meals".

I may get flamed for being "cruel" to my fish but they

subject: Symbol table?

Debuggers can.

The normal program loader discards it. SID and DDT load programs differently,
and keep the info around.

- Bruce

subject: Finder flushing
q: I moved and resized a Finder window, then the power went off and the window was back in its old position after reboot. Does the Finder buffer changes, and can I force it to save them?
ref: Finder saves its window configuration when it launches an application or when you restart or shut down from the Special menu. Crash out or shut down some other way and it never does. The RAM cache probably isn't the culprit. Learn how your machine works.
replies:
Finder empties the trash and saves its folder/window configuration when
it opens an application, or when your Mac is restarted or shutdown from
the Finder Special menu.  If you use some other launching device (possibly
in conjunction with Finder, like PowerStation) or shutdown thru non-
Finder means (like System Errors); Finder won't do this.

I'm not sure, but I believe this is *not* the case.  I think the cache
buffers all disk i/o, without "write-through" protection or forced
flushing.

gunk produced by the cycling process.  Why leave it around in the tank

"worm feeders", so that worms don't get a chan

subject: CPIO/TAR Standards
q: Where are the latest CPIO and TAR archive standards documented, and will Open Systems like OSF, AT&T and POSIX actually use them?
ref: The POSIX archive format is in IEEE Posix 1003.1, Chapter 10. Anything POSIX-compliant will support it; OSF and the rest will if they want to be compliant. Anyone not supporting it in the next few years would surprise me. Go read the standard.
replies:
The arhive format which was standardized by POSIX is in the IEEE Posix
1003.1 standard in Chapter 10.

As far as implementations supporting the standard, POSIX definitely will
since it is a part of the standard.  OSF, UI, etc. will support it if they
wish to be POSIX compliant.  If they don't wish to be POSIX compliant, they
are not bound (except by their customers) to support any standard at all.

I would be very suprised any Unix-like operating system which is released
in the next few years does not support the Posix standard.

subject: WorkBench 2.0, Help!!
q: My new Amiga 3000 has 2.0 ROMs, and when iprefs runs from the Startup-Sequence I get an "Intuition Preferences" requester asking me to close windows to reset the Workbench screen. What causes it and how do I stop it?
ref: You put something in your startup-sequence that prints to the CLI, so a window is open when IPrefs runs. IPrefs can only reset the screen before any windows open. Move your added commands after IPrefs, or redirect their output to >NIL:. Basic stuff.
replies:
The A3000 _Release_ version of 2.0 has these version numbers (Kickstart
36.141, Workbench 36.68).  The dealer demo units have a late beta with
smaller version numbers, but the "for sale" units have the release 2.0.

You have put something in your startup-sequence that outputs text
to the CLI.  The initial CLI has been trained to not open until
the first text is spat out.  IPrefs can reset the screen for you under two
conditions:  Before any windows are open, and when only Workbench's
windows are open.  The standard startup-sequence runs IPrefs before anything
spits text out, hence no windows are open, hence IPrefs can do its job
silently.  Try moving the commands you added to after the "wait" command
after IPrefs.  Or redirect the output of the commands you added
to >NIL:.  Otherwise you have to wait until Workbench is up, and
hit "Retry".

     Peter

Unlike 1.x, 2.0 "tells" the workbench what mode it should be in when
Iprefs is run. The system configuration information is more for colors
and such. WARNING: DO NOT USE CONMAN with 2.0 as that will cause your
console to be screwed up. Bill Hawes is reportedly working on a
replacement.

[can't help you on #2]

If you are a developer, send in your Non-Disclosure agreement and
$20 if you are certified. Commodore will send to the latest beta
(or is that Gamma :-)) If you aren't a developer then wait until
Commodore announces the "Native Developers Update" for 2.0 which
should be available some time after 2.0 is officially released for
"real".

That requester comes up if you have a SHELL window open.  Simply close the
shell window before you start IPREFs (or alternately, don't cause any output
to be sent to the shell before starting IPREFs) and everything should be fine.

At the moment, the only updated programming docs for OS 2.0 are in the AutoDocs
available RSN from CATS.

subject: Sun 3.0, Text: table is full
q: What does the Sun 3.0 console message "Text: table is full" mean? It started appearing on our diskless 3/50s and the 3/160 server once the load went up, and new processes get aborted.
ref: It means the text table is full. That's the kernel array of program texts, one slot per distinct program running. Fix it by configuring a new kernel with a larger maxusers. Sigh, also stop sprinkling the sticky bit on everything, which was one reply's culprit.
replies:
I got the same problem when I installed MH on my machine.
I think that you have some programs with the save text bit set
(chmod +t), this mode saves the text segment so it will not help to
kill some processes. The solution is to do a chmod -t on "all" files,
and then reeboot the system.

It means the text table is full.

(The text table is an array that holds information about program
texts.  Every program you run takes one slot; running the same
program many times simultaneously still takes only one slot.)

The fix is to increase the size of the text table, which is best
done by configuring a new kernel with a larger `maxusers' parameter.

subject: differences now between 300 and 800?
q: Wasn't HP-UX 7.0 supposed to merge the 300 and 800 series? What are the differences that make software vendors support one but not the other?
ref: 7.0 is not a complete merge; the C compilers differ. The 800 is RISC-like with the portability limits that implies, a different stack direction, strict alignment, and different peripherals. Each line needs its own dev, QA and support. Marketing said otherwise, naturally.
replies:
A non-inclusive list:

1) HP-UX 7.0 is not a complete merge.  For example, they have different
   C compilers.

2) The 800 series is a RISC like architecture with all of the portability
   constraints of that class of architectures.

3) The stack direction is different.

4) The 800 is a strictly aligned architecture.

5) The peripherials are different.

For these reasons, supporting each of the HP series requires a software
vendor to devote significant resources to development, capital
equipment, QA, support and sales.

regards,
fletcher

subject: Displaying text with XView

replies:
The textsw package is being rewritten, so expect changes in the
future... On the other hand, there is -currently- no way to
send a bunch of textsw_insert() calls as a "batch" and have the

have found to be quite reasonable both aesthetically and performance-wise
is to write all the data to a tmp file and use TEXTSW_FILE_CONTENTS
to have the textsw display the file.  No scrolling is done and the
text just pops right in.  Immediately remove the tmpfile -- this does
not affect the display.

ref: Possibly both are correct. ASN.1 allows definite length encoding, where the length gives the content octets, or indefinite length, ended by 00 00. One compiler may emit one and the other the other. Read the spec.
replies:
I don't know if this is what is happening in your case but it is
possible to produce two different (but correct) encodings from the same

length encoding.

Basically there are two types of length encoding. "Definite length
encoding", whereby the "length" part of the asn1 "type-length-contents"
actually specifies the length in octets of the contents octet string.
Or, "Indefinite length encoding", whereby the "length" part does not
contain the length but instead the end of the contents is indicated by
a "00" followed by "00" in the byte stream (sort of like an end-of-file
indicator). A special value in the length part indicates which type of
length encoding is in use.

It may be that one compiler generates encoders which produce definate
length encoded octet strings and the other compiler indefinite. I've a

subject: (M) How long until damsel eggs hatch?
q: My damselfish in a reef tank laid eggs and the larger one is guarding and fanning them. How long until the eggs hatch, so I can have baby brine shrimp ready for the fry?
ref: Damsel larvae hatch in 3 to 7 days, depending on species and temperature. Brine shrimp nauplii are too big anyway: the first food should be marine rotifers, about 100 microns. Culturing microalgae to feed rotifers to feed larvae is beyond most hobbyists. Good luck.
replies:
I have observed this type of behavior, anbd I think you do have a bonifide
pair.  While the incidence of false spawnings are high in damsels,
you may have fertile eggs!

The larvae hatch out in 3-7 days depending on the species and temperature.
At hatching they will be 1.1-4.5 mm.
They may or may not have a yolk sac. If not,  they feed immediately.
If a yolk sac is present, they won't feed untill it is adsorbed.

I am not aware of widespread rearing of the reef damsels (not counting
clownfish, in the same family). Partly due to size. The hatchlings
first food should be marine rotifers, which are 0.1 mm (100 microns).
These are much smaller than brine shrimp naups. Setting up a
routine to culture the microalgae, to feed the rotifers to feed
the larvae is beyond the desire of most hobbyists.

Draw into an offscreen pixmap, then copy it onto screen.

subject: 8087 Coprocessor
q: I have an XT with a V20 running at 8/4.77 MHz. What speed 8087 do I need? Can a 4.77 MHz 8087 work at 8 MHz, or will it overheat?
ref: The 8087 runs synchronous with the CPU, so buy one rated for the highest clock you'll run: 8 MHz. A 4.77 chip at 8 MHz will drop clock pulses and fail, or at best run very hot. It works only if you stay at 4.77. Any idiot knows that.
replies:
Unlike the 286 machines, your coprocessor runs at the same clock speed
as your 8088 or it your case V20. So if buying a 8087 you want to get
one designed for the highest clock rate you'll be running.... 8 Mhz.
You *could* if you so desired, purchase a 4.77 Mhz chip and run your
machine at the slower clock rate.

   I ran into an interesting situation regarding 8087's. When I bought
my first XT-class machine way back when it was to be a standard 4.77 Mhz
unit. I had applications which insisted on a coprocessor. So I ordered
ahead of time a 4.77 Mhz 8087. When my machine arrived, low and behold there
was a note telling me they were shipping "turbo" machines (8 Mhz) at no
extra charge. I could not return the 8087 for a faster one so I put it in
anyway. I ran that machine that way for about 3 years. I can't really
advise you to intentionally buy a slower chip and run it at the faster
speed but if you alread have a chip I would certainly try it. In my case
had I known I would be getting a 8

If you plan on always running at 4.77 MHz, no problem. If you switch to 8 MHz,
chances are the system won't even boot/run. This is based on trying the same
experiment with a 4.77/10 MHz XT. YMVM. Even if if does boot/run, the 8087
(which normally runs pretty warm) will run VERY hot and this will decrease its
life significantly.

8087's run synchronous with the CPU. Therefore, if you
want to run at 8 MHz, you need an 8 MHz 8087. When you are running
a 4.77 MHz 8087, there is no possibility at all of having it run
at 8 MHz. It is not merely a matter of the chip overheating: it
simply will not be able to keep up with the fast clock rate. It
will stumble and drop clock pulses and just royally fail. It will
be totally useless. So, if you want to run at 8MHz, you must have
an 8 MHz 8087.
	80387's share with the 8087 this trait of the coprocessor
clock operating synchronous with the CPU clock.
	80287's, on the other hand, do not HAVE to be operated
synchronous with the 80286 CPU. Most often, in fact, the 80287
is clocked at 2/3 the CPU rate - but this is more convention
than requirement. As I understand it, one may buy whatever rate
80287 one wishes, and if you can find a clock on the motherboard
to clock it with (or you can provide your own), you can run it at
that rate.

Good luck...

subject: ... HELP HELP ... TROUBLE PRINTING WITH eroff ...
q: I'm printing a text file with eroff to a LaserJet, and several lines at the bottom of each page get dropped. How do I make it print continuously?
ref: A roff is the wrong tool. Laser printers can't print to the page edges, so you lose lines in the unprintable top and bottom margins. Add formatting like a macro package such as -ms to generate margins, or use a simple line printer filter instead.
replies:
A *roff program is not quite the right tool for the job.  If
eroff is like troff, it is actually trying to do what you want
(i.e in the absence of any formatting instructions, print on all
lines of the page).  The problem is that most laser printers
cannot print all the way to the top and bottom edges of the
paper.  If you're going to use a roff-style formatter for the
job, you'll have to somehow insert enough formatting instructions
(simply asking for a default macro package such as -ms might
suffice) so that top and bottom margins will be generated to
avoid the unprintable regions.

For simple, line-printer output, laser printers (especially
PostScript printers) often use simpler filters designed just for
that purpose.  (Adobe's TranScript package has a program called
psof for this purpose, named for the Berkeley lpr printcap field
it occupies.)

Actually, since a LaserJet is more like a "normal" printer than a
PostScript printer, you might be better off just shipping your
file to it

subject: dallas/frisco game
q: A defender made a face mask penalty and knocked the ball loose from the receiver near the goal line, and the offense got the ball on the 3. Shouldn't the penalty be enforced from the previous line of scrimmage?
ref: No. A defensive foul while the receiver has the ball, or while it's loose from a fumble, is enforced from the spot of the fumble. Only a foul before the catch is enforced from the line of scrimmage. Same in NFL, NCAA and Federation rules, whistle or not.
replies:
It was a bad call all the way around.  The final ruling was a catch and
a blown wistle before the fumble.  The call was clearly wrong.  It should
have been pass interference.  Holt grabbed Rice's face mask before the
ball arived.  I think they originally called it an incomplete pass and
a 5 yard face mask penalty.

I didn't see the game but from your description it sounds like the
penalty was enforced correctly. Assuming Rice caught the ball and was
then fouled (from the above it does not sound like it was the other way
round), any defensive foul occuring while the receiver had possession of
the ball, or while the ball was loose from the fumble, would be enforced
from the spot of the fumble. If this was the 6 yard line, then indeed
the 49ers would get the ball 1st & goal on the 3.

The penalty would have been enforced from the previous spot (line of
scrimmage) only if it had occurred before the pass was caught.

This ruling applies equally in NFL, NCAA and Federation rules, and
applies irrespective of whether the official blew an inadvertant whistle
or not (penalties always supersede inadvertant whistle provisions).

Jim Briggs
Secretary, Rules and Mechanics Committee
British American Football Referees' Association

subject: Doubling Font sizes and Shrinking Photographically

ref: PostScript uses a single master shape for every point size, so you don't get different designs at different sizes. Just take the 300 dpi printout, stat it down, and treat it as 600 dpi. Only phototypesetters bother with multiple masters, and those are already high resolution.
replies:
Well, PostScript uses a single "master" (ie, character shape definition) for all
point sizes, so you don't actually get different shapes for different  sizes.

treat it as 600 dpi.

Other than this, I don't know of any systems which do deal with multiple
masters, except for phototypesetters.  If you have a phototypesetter, you're
already getting high resolution output.

subject: Paging in SunOS
q: On SunOS, if a diskless workstation runs an application mounted from a file server that is a different machine than its boot server, how are text and data pages handled, and how does that affect the load on each server?
ref: Assuming a ZMAGIC executable, text is paged straight from the a.out, so it comes from whichever server holds that file. Data is backed by swap, so it goes wherever swap lives, usually the boot server. Obvious, really; the question nearly answers itself.
replies:
First, I assume by "boot server" what you really mean is "the server
that provides swap space".  This is usually the boot server but, I
think, need not be.

I also assume the executable is a ZMAGIC executable, so that the text
segment is paged from the a.out file; otherwise the source of the
executable is not interesting.

That said, the question more or less answers itself: the text segment,
being paged from the a.out file, is obtained from the server on which
that file resides; the data segment, being backed by normal swap space,
is paged to and from swap, wherever that is.

Yes, this means that dataless (ie, local root&swap only) machines
running remote executables may paradoxically run NMAGIC binaries faster
than ZMAGIC....

					der Mouse

subject: What does this message mean?
q: What does this 4.3 BSD MicroVAX II console message mean: "machine check 80: vap 7fffe594 istate 10001 pc 30d5 psl 3c00000, mser=0x2c1 page=11872"?
ref: It's a memory parity error. Decode the mser bits: bit 9 set and bit 8 clear points to memory expansion module #1 on the KA630. If errors are random and your PMI cables between boards are long, shorten them to minimum. Or blame cosmic rays, I suppose.
replies:
Bob - When one of the two cpu parity bits <6-5> is set (bit 6 is), the
memory cd bits <9-8> are loaded with a 2-bit code which indicates the
source of the parity error:
	00 - Q22 bus mem or device
	01 - KA630 on board memory
	10 - MEM expansion module #1
	11 - MEM expansion module #2

bit 9 of your mser is set (8 is not) therefore, I suspect memory expansion
module #1 is where your problem is.

Good luck!!

Mike Kitchen
South Central Bell

It could be one of a number of things,

1. if you get the same error every time, it could be a bad memory chip
	mser tells you the board its on, the error above is on module 2.
	(see KA630AA CPU Module User's Guide - EK-KA630-UG-001 in
	conjunction with the kernel code))

2. if you get random errors, and your memory boards have *very long* PMI cables
	between them, shorten the PMI cable to *MINIMUM* length, ie so you can
	only just fit it between boards.
	This is generally a problem with 3rd party memory (mine that caused this
	problem was Cammington, but once the PMI cables were shortened we have
	had NO recurrence of the problem in over a year)

3. you could have a radiation source nearby zapping your bits ;-)

subject: Device numbers in a stat entry vs. the kernel i_node table
q: On System V, the st_dev from stat() never matches the i_dev in the kernel inode table, though the inode numbers match. Why are they different, and how do I relate them?
ref: Because i_dev carries extra bits flagging 512- versus 1024-byte block filesystems. Use st_dev == brdev(i_dev), with brdev from <sys/sysmacros.h>. So i_dev is like 0x2204 while st_dev is 0x0204. Read the headers next time.
replies:
st_dev == brdev(i_dev)

where brdev is a macro defined in <sys/sysmacros.h>.  There are some bits
masked off of i_dev which are used to indicate whether the filesystem
uses 1024-byte blocks or 512-byte blocks.  i_dev should be something like
0x2204 while st_dev would be 0x0204.

subject: windowing question
q: Is there any way to open an Amiga window that won't become active when clicked, so one window gets all the keyboard input?
ref: No, any clicked window goes active. Share one IDCMP port across all windows and call Activate() on your input window when ACTIVEWINDOW arrives, or just read keystrokes from every window. Users will be confused by ghosting borders. Closing windows gets tricky.
replies:
I suggest you use a single IDCMP port for all your windows.  This way, if you
get an ACTIVEWINDOW message, you can call Activate() on your input window
right away.  Or you could even read the input keystrokes from all windows,
thereby doing away with the necessity for an input window.

I did this in PickPacket, if you can find a copy take a look at the window
code.  Closing windows gets a little tricky.

No, all windows get active if they are clicked on. But why, if the
input window is covered by the output window, you could just get
inputs from your output window too. With a covered window
you could only get keyboard and menu events, but gadgets would
be confusing if they aren't visible.

Michael van Elst

No, But...

You can get messages from your other windows when they are activated and,
when you receive one, call ActiveWindow() for your keyboard input
window.

One possible negative point to this is that users might try to activate
your output windows and be confused by their inability to do so (The
border will de-ghost and reghost.)

Another way would be to use the same IDCMP port for all your windows
and receive keyboard input from any or all of them.

subject: How fast can a typical Laser printer Centronix Interface go?
q: A vendor told me the Centronics interface on a typical LaserJet II only moves data at about 50 Kbaud. Is that true, and if so is a Centronics interface worth having on a printer?
ref: Not really a limit. A 30 page-per-minute printer at 80 columns and 60 lines needs only about 24 Kbaud, and the link itself can do around 166 KBytes/sec. On a PC the bottleneck is DOS software, around 1K/sec through the normal driver. Use copy /b and it's far faster. Sigh.
replies:
We recently drove a parallel interface printer at a full 30PPM, 80 columns,
60 Lines Per Page.  That works out to (excuse me while I !bc) 24Kbaud.
If you can find a printer faster than 30PPM, maybe it matters.
We also found that the 37PPM printer didn't like our UNIX a whole lot.
We would blast data to the printer at 50KBytes /second (yes it is Byte wide),
then go away for a while, then blast more data...
The data link is theoretically capable of 6uSec cycles, or 166KBytes,
but the priorities aren't keen on high printer load.
A serial link at 19.2K turned out to be much better.

Using a typical PC (what does this mean anymore?) running DOS, the
Centronics interface is software bound.  You can expect to get a maximum
of about 1K bytes/sec (equivalent to a 9600 baud serial connection).
A program that drives the port directly (*NOT* reccommended) can reach
speeds that violate the Centronics timing specs.  I wrote a replacement
DOS printer driver to speed things up.  If you use "copy /b file lpt1"
(/b is important), it will drive just about any printer at close to its
rated transfer speeds.  We've seen bursts of 30K bytes/sec to a PostScript
printer and speeds in excees of 90K to a dummy card with a scope
attached to it, when using a modest 286 machine.

If there is enough interest, I'll ask the boss if I can release the
driver.

P.S. The /b option of the copy command is equivalent to using MS-DOS
function 44h to set the "raw" (uncooked) mode on a character device.

Also: You can probably reach speeds of 10K bytes/sec by using the
BIOS int 17h function call to pri

subject: SRBs
q: On the shuttle launch video the SRBs were still burning when they separated. Doesn't that waste a significant part of their thrust?
ref: No. SRB burnout is gradual, and separation happens after thrust has dropped to something insignificant, though they still put out a little exhaust for some seconds. Better to drop them while burning than carry dead weight. Think before you worry.
replies:
The SRBs may still be burning when they are jettisoned, but they may
not be producing USEFUL thrust.  If the thrust from an SRB is less than
its combined mass and contribution to atmospheric drag, it is dead weight,
and actually detracts from the useful payload, since the SSMEs must
carry the difference.

#
#	Watching the 30-second video on the news of yesterday's shuttle
#launch, I noticed that the SRBs were still burning when they separated, and
#kept doing so for at least a few seconds (i.e. as long as they showed
#them).  To me, this means they waste some significant fraction of the SRB
#thrust after separation.  Is that really true?

It's probably better to separate while they are still burning, before
they become dead weight.

SRB burnout is a gradual process.  Separation occurs after thrust has
dropped to something fairly insignificant -- it is not possible to do
the separation while the SRBs are at full blast -- but they do go on
putting out a little bit of exhaust for some seconds.

subject: Setuid on expreserve and exrecover
q: Why are /usr/lib/expreserve and exrecover set-user-id bin or root?
ref: On BSD it's needed because chown() requires root. System V doesn't need it, so chmod 555 them and chmod 777 /usr/preserve, since expreserve has a well-known security problem. Vendors still shipping it setuid deserve a stern talking-to.
replies:
Needed on BSD but not on System V due to chown() requiring root privileges.

Do us all a favor and if you are a V. system chmod 555 ex*preserve and
chmod 777 /usr/preserve.  ex*preserve has a well-known security problem.
If any vendor is still delivering systems with ex*preserve setuid they
should be shot at sunrise.

Email bounced, so:

Uh, yeah:  The setuid root or bin is so that the /usr/lib/expreserve
program can write the file in the directory /usr/preserve, which should be
owned by bin and mode 755, e.g.:

$ ls -ald /usr/expreserve
drwxr-xr-x   5 bin      bin           80 Mar 22 10:56 /usr/preserve

(Otherwise it would not be able to write to the directory....)

  In this way, only you (and root and bin) can remove any of your files
stored there, and only you can change them, as the files are normally
stored mode 600 or 700.
  "/usr/lib/exrecover" should be the same mode as expreserve so it can
retrieve them for you....

   To the person saying that its distributors should be shot: I do beleive that
the superuser bug has been fixed! (about eight years ago...)

Randy

subject: Tar - max filename length 100; why ?
q: The tar manual says file names are limited to 100 characters. Is that an artificial limit? Tarring a CAP filesystem with long Mac file names fails with 'File name too long'.
ref: The traditional tar header only has 100 positions for the name, and changing it would wreck tar as a least-common-denominator interchange format. Use dump(8) for backups, or cpio(1) if you need to swap data with non-BSD systems. Read up on the format next time.
replies:
The traditional tar header format only allows 100 positions for the file
name.  If this is changed, then resulting archives are less useful as a
least common denominator interchange media.

The alternative is to use dump(8) if the intent is for backup purposes or
cpio(1) if you need to exchange data with other than BSD derived systems.

subject: Stereo TV
q: What exactly is in a stereo TV broadcast? Is it like FM stereo, and could I receive it with an FM receiver hooked to cable?
ref: Same basic system as FM, except the L-R subcarrier is at 31.5 KHz instead of 38 KHz, so the pilot is 15.75 KHz. One guy runs an LM1800 stereo decoder chip tuned to 15.75 KHz off his VCR's MPX output. A plain FM receiver won't cut it, so don't bother.
replies:
TV uses the same basic system as FM except the L-R subcarrier is at
31.5 KHz instead of 38KHz.  Therefore a 15.75 KHz pilot frequency is
used.  I use an LM1800 stereo decoder chip tuned to 15.75Khz  connected
to the MPX output of my VCR and it works great.

There may be other subtle differences that I am not aware of
but my LM1800 does not seem to care.

ref: No, you're confused. The coating isn't laid in concentric circles; it's cheaper to coat the whole surface, and not all drives share a track density. It's like regular cassettes versus chrome: the two need different recording bias, so the coatings differ. Basic stuff.

<format with the state of the raw diskette.

Yep.  You're confused.  The coating is not laid down in concentric circles
for a multitude of reasons including:
	1) cheaper to simply coat the entire surface.
	2) potential head alignment problems.
	3) not all drives use the same track density (IBM is not the world).

With 360KB vrs. 1.2MB, the distinction is like regular cassettes vrs Chrome.
A different recording bias is required by the hardware, so the two types of
disks are coated with different materials.

The actual disk capacity is determined by other differences (number of trac

subject: Scrolling bitmaps (help needed)
q: How can I do a smooth wrap-around vertical scroll of a bitmap on the Amiga? ScrollRaster is too slow, scrolls a plane at a time, and messes up the colors. The RKMs don't say how.
ref: Use hardware scrolling. Allocate a bitmap twice as tall as the display, make the RastPort handle that height, increment RyOffset, then call ScrollVPort(). No flicker and no WaitTOF needed. Reset RyOffset to zero at half the bitmap height. The reset is left to you.
replies:
For vertical scrolling, allocate a bitmap twice as high as the
display (for 200 lines, allocate a bitmap with a height of 400,
etc).  Set up a Dwidth of 200 lines.  Make the RP handle 400 lines.
You now have a drawing area 400 pixels tall, but you can only see
200 pixels.  Increment RyOffset then call ScrollVPort().
Notice no flicker, incredible speed and smoothness; the result of
hardware scrolling. (you don't need WaitTOF() or WaitBOVP())
  You can't increment RyOffest forever, so you'll have to set
RyOffset back to zero when it is equal to BITMAP HEIGHT / 2 (If your
Bitmap is twice as high as your viewport display).
  The last excersize is left to the reader:  How to handle the reset
situation described above.

  John

subject: whoami
q: Problem with "who am i" on System V: when the login id is exactly 8 characters long it prints nothing and just returns the prompt. Anybody seen this, and is there a fix?
ref: Yes, it's a known bug, present from SysVr2.0 through 3.2. Work around it with the LOGNAME variable (less secure) or keep logins under 8 characters. AT&T boxes can get the fix from the hotline, bundled with a passwd fix. Other vendors, go bug your vendor.
replies:
I assume you mean "who am i" - my SysV machines don't have whoami.  This
has been the case for at least SysVr2.0 ->3.2.  I reported it a long time
ago.  One possible workaround (the one I used..) is to use the environment
variable LOGNAME instead, although that is less secure.  Or just make all
your login id's less than 8 characters long.
A related problem with the longer names is that mail to names which match
the 1st 8 characters of a login name is accepted and stored even though
the name differs past the 8th character.  For example, if you have
"longname" as a login id, mail to "longname5" will land in /usr/mail/longname5
instead of being rejected.

Les Mikesell

If you have an AT&T computer, you can get a fix by calling the hotline.  The
fix for this bug is included with a much more important bug fix for the
"passwd" program.  I would contact your vendor if you don't have AT&T
equipment.

subject: Help On Kermit Under OS9
q: Kermit 1.6 under OS-9 on /t1 transmits fine but nothing is echoed when receiving. I tried iniz /t1 and shell i=/t1&, on level 1 and level 2. Is there a problem running Kermit through the bit banger port?
ref: Sigh. You're not supposed to see anything during a Kermit receive. Check from another window that the file grows in chunks, $800 on floppy or $2000 on hard disk. And drop the shell, it blocks other I/O. The bit banger is a poor choice for full duplex anyway; use a real serial port.
replies:
Firstly, the INIZ shouldn't hurt anything, but the shell will. The
shell will block other I/O while it sits there waiting for a command
with an I$readln..

Secondly, you're really not supposed to see anything during a Kermit
receive. What you could do to verify that the file is being received
is pop to another window and see if the size of the file increases
every now and again (it is buffered, and pre-extension occurs, so
you'll likely see the file grow in chunks of $800 if floppy or $2000
if hard disk).

Last - the bit banger is a poor choice for full duplex communications
under OS9. A hardware serial port is much easier on the CPU and you
have a significantly greater chance of getting the protocol transfer
done successfully.

subject: Mail drop path for mode line
q: How do I tell Emacs that my maildrop is somewhere other than the default /usr/spool/mail/$USER? I can't find the variable in the C or Lisp sources.
ref: It's in the Lisp, you just missed it. Set rmail-spool-directory to your mailer's spool directory, or set rmail-primary-inbox-list to your inbox files. Customize the defaults in lisp/paths.el or site-init.el if building it yourself. RTFM, or at least INSTALL.
replies:
Try one of the following:

- set the rmail-primary-inbox-list variable to your list of inbox files
- set the Mail: babyl option in your rmail-file-name file
- pass an explicit argument to rmail-get-new-mail
- set the rmail-spool-directory variable to your mailer's spooling directory

Paragraph 4 of INSTALL suggests that you look at $BUILD/lisp/paths.el
and customize things in $BUILD/lisp/site-init.el if the defaults
aren't appropriate for your system.  You probably want to change the
value of rmail-spool-directory.

subject: A suggestion: .... == ../../..
q: Could Unix get a feature like Netware's, where cd ....\run means cd ..\..\..\run, so ... is the grandparent directory? Has anyone done it?
ref: Why bother with the kernel? The . and .. entries are real files, and ... is already used by some applications. If you're lazy, alias '...' to 'cd ../..' in csh, or set cdpath to ( .. ../.. ../../.. ). Don't modify the kernel to save typing.
replies:
If you mean the operating system sold by AT&T it's UNIX.  Fair enough?

Not so fast, see below.

It's ok.  I like the / or \ as a separator to help parse the dots.
... is already used by some applications under UNIX.

Changing something like this at this point is almost impossible
but you are free to do so if you have access to source code.
You should ask the Free Software Foundation folks, they might
consider it for GNU (their UNIX like operating system).

The beauty of the current implemenetation is that the file system
does most of the work. That is, the files '.' and '..' are really
there.

	ANY process can make use of those files.

You can always put the files '...' and '....' in there if you wish.
True - this would need some sort of kernel mod if you wanted mkdir(2)
to automagically add those files.

I think there are better ways of being lazy - myself.

Csh example 1:

	alias '..' 'cd ..'
	alias '...' 'cd ../..'
	alias '....' 'cd ../../..'

Csh example 2: use cdpath

	set cdpath = ( .. ../.. ../../.. )

then when you type
	cd a
the system will check for
	./a
	../a
	../../a
	../../../a

Quote for the day: "If's you're lazy, don't modify the kernel' :-)

Side note: Athena runs 4.3BSD + NFS (U Wisconsin merge, VS2/VS2000
workstations). Directories . and .. are what you'd expect (current dir
and parent). If however you attempt to create/use a file named ... you

stat of it returns ENOENT. If you try to create such a file, it will
appear not on the remote filesystem, but in the local one, in the
directory that the filesystem is mounted over[2].

Under the 4.3BSD+NFS on our IBM PC/RT workstations, ... works fine.

Anyone else seen this bug? It has been reported and filed here, I
don't know how far the report would have gone though.

subject: Audio DAT recorders as computer backup devices
q: Audio DAT recorders are coming to the USA for about $900 and falling. Could they be used as cheap computer backup devices?
ref: No. The audio I/O format needs an expensive interface, and the decks are made for real-time record and play, not start/stop data. They have no computer control, so no unattended backups, and their error concealment hides errors instead of flagging them. Want a data recorder? Buy a data recorder.
replies:
[...]
[...]

1)	The (Sony/Philips) digital audio I/O format is quite specific
	to digital audio applications. You would have to build an interface
	to/from that format ($$$).
2)	Audio DAT recorders are designed for real time record/play operation.
	They are not start/stop data recorders.
3)	(Consumer) DAT recorders generally have no type of control interface,
	except for a handheld remote controller. Therefore, unattended backups,
	which are possible with a data recorder with a computer interface,
	would not be practical.
4)	The error concealment used in the event of uncorrectable errors is
	designed to minimize audible disturbances. For data recording an error
	flag is desired.
5)	Etc., etc. etc. ....

The moral(s) of the story is(are):
	If you want a data recorder, buy a data recorder.
and
	You get what you pay for (or, to be more correct, You don't get what
	you don't pay for).

All of the above apply in principle to digital video recorders as well (so don't ask...).

subject: 1.4 Wishes and 3.5" drive question
q: Is there a program to map out bad blocks on an Amiga floppy? I have a batch of sub-standard disks that keep giving errors during downloads.
ref: The terse answer is no. The Amiga reads and writes whole tracks, not sectors, so there's nothing to map out. Format with Tom Rokicki's DFC, which verifies as it goes, and toss any disk that fails. Or just buy real disks instead of whining about nickels.
replies:
You may have noticed that the FORMAT program that comes with the Amiga
simply writes the formatting info to the disk; it does not verify that
it can read what it just wrote.  I have been using Tom Rokicki's DFC
program that is on Fish Disk #131.  It verifys the disk as it is formated,
so that you can identify bad flopies and throw them out before they cause
you grief.  Downloading onto an unverified floppy is not very smart.

The terse answer is: no.

The verbose answer is that the Amiga reads and writes entire tracks at
a time, not individual sectors (blocks).  If such a program were to
exist, it would have to map out bad tracks.  I think the best solution
is to format the floppy using format or Tom Rokicki's dfc to format
the disks.  If the floppy won't format then don't use it.

I know this is not the answer you were looking for John, but it seems
to be the answer this forum comes up with every time the question is
asked.

Kevin

The answer isn't to make it possible to use substandard disks on the Amiga,
the answer is to fork over the extra nickel or dime to get real disks.
You don't ask GM to fix your car so that you can run it on methanol do
you? Do yourself a favor and sell those substandard floppies to someone
else. [I'd guess they are not substandard, rather they are only single sided
and you get hosed trying to write to the back side of them.] You are only
asking for trouble if you continue to use them. The even more insidious
problem will be two weeks from now when you go to read back the data and
it is now unreadable. Save yourself the hassle. Dump these loser disks.
