subject: Multiple screen/display applications
q: How can I control multiple X displays from a single keyboard and mouse? Has anyone used X with more than one physical monitor?
ref: Two ways. One CPU with two monitors, where one X server treats them as separate screens. Or two CPUs, each with its own X server, where the application opens a separate connection to each over the network. Costlier but more flexible.
replies:
There are a couple of different ways to do this:

1.  One CPU with 2 monitors.  DEC sells some machines like this.  I'm
sure other vendors do, too.  With this configuration, one X server
manages both displays, considering them to be separate screens.  The
application interacts with either screen through a single connection to
that X server.

2.  Two CPUs, each with 1 monitor.  This configuration is more
expensive, but more flexible.  Since each CPU will have it's own X
server, the application must create and manage separate connections to
each.  Since X supports networking, this is pretty simple to do.

Note:  I use the term CPU for lack of a better term.  It can be a
workstation, X terminal, or whatever.

subject: Help removing password protection
q: A user password protected his only copy of a HyperCard stack, and the DeProtect XCMD didn't help. Are there other ways to remove the password protection?
ref: DeProtect removes passwords fine on all previous HyperCard versions, so you likely have a different problem. Some stacks set UserLevel and CantModify on entry. Set the maximum user level to 5 in the protection box first, then in the message box set the CantModify of this stack to false and set the userLevel to 5.
replies:
Deprotect does remove passwords just fine.  You may have a different problem.
Some stacks will set the UserLevel and CantModify upon entry (I do this with
my front-end network stacks so they will be sharable by users).  I haven't
tried it in HC 2.0, but DEPROTECT DOES REMOVE PASSWORDS EFFECTIVELY ON ALL
PREVIOUS VERSIONS OF HC.  I could be mistaken - that does happen from time
to time, but I've deprotected a bunch of stacks this past week.  Try the
following in the message box when the stack is loaded:

Set the CantModify of this stack to false
Set the userLevel to 5

That should clear up access problems (to scripts and the like).  One other
note - you have to set the maximum user level to 5 BEFORE you do that (in
the protection box) - otherwise no go.

Mike.

subject: Rename the Earth?
q: Why do astronomers use Latin names like Olympus Mons and Mare Tranquillitatis instead of Mount Olympus and Sea of Tranquility?
ref: Because Latin was the international language of science when the lunar features were named, back in the 1600s. Riccioli set the system in 1651. New names get approved by an IAU commission. The English forms came later for monolingual students. Do some reading.
replies:
"Earth" is considered to derive from Indo-European 'ar' meaning the
(plowed) ground, via lots of Northern European intermediate forms including
Hertha the Icelandic earth goddess.  It is in no sense less appropriate
than the Latin 'tellus' form.  The latter just sounds more exotic to our
Anglophone ears.  If there were Latin language SF writers they would
probably call their characters Earthlings for that nifty sound. :-)

At the time Lunar features were first mapped, Latin was the universal
language of Western science.  Mare Tranquillitatis was the first "official"
name the feature had; "Sea Of Tranquillity" came along later for the
benefit of monolingual English and American students.

I believe Olympus Mons was first tentatively identified early in this
century or late in the last, as a feature visible only to serious
astronomers, among whom Latin was still the accepted lingua franca. :-)
I seldom see it it called Mount Olympus except in Golden Books type
bowdlerizations and the occ

--
Officially, the "Sea of Tranquility" never _has_ existed on the moon:
it has been "Mare Tranquillitatus" since at least the mid 1600's.  The
lunar features were named by early astronomers shortly after the invention
of the telescope; the modern system of lunar names was established by
Riccioli in 1651.  At that time Latin was still the international language
of science.  As for features on Mars and other celestial bodies, the names
are not official until they are approved by a commission of the
International Astronomical Union.  I suppose the names are given in Latin
because that is the way it has been traditionally done (just as in biology
the names of species are given in Latin).

The approval of a name can take some time, which is presumably how the
name started (unofficially) as Mount Olympus and ended up as Olympus Mons
(the official name).

subject: CDEV crash (Help Mgr Problem?)
q: My cdev crashes in _FindDItem+$01B2 with an Illegal Instruction or Address Error. What is _FindDItem looking for at that moment?
ref: It isn't dying in _FindDItem at all. MacsBug just shows the nearest public routine it knows, and FindDItem is nowhere near $1B2 bytes long. You're probably in some internal Dialog Manager subroutine after it. Do a stack crawl to see how you got into the ROM.
replies:
Your Macintosh isn't dying in _FindDItem. What Macsbug is showing you
is that _FindDItem is the closest public routine that it knows about.
FindDItem is very short, and is certainly not $1B2 bytes long. Instead,
you are probably in some internal subroutine of the Dialog Manager that
is situated after FindDItem.

The best thing to do would be to do a stack crawl, try to find out
how you got into the ROM, and take things from there.

subject: Help compiling elm on Multibus under Xenix
q: Compiling elm on Xenix 3.5 on a Multibus system, the link fails with 'group DGROUP larger than 64K bytes'. How do I fix this?
ref: Set ccflags='-Ml -Mt128' and ldflags='-Ml -Mt128 -F 3000' in config.sh, so objects over 128 bytes go in another segment and the stack is 3000H. Then hunt down the VAXisms, like uncast 0 pointer arguments, and make big buffers static or malloced. Have fun.
replies:
Glad you got the system up!

I know. It was hell here too. See the associated discussion on coding practices
in one of the UNIX groups. You need to do this... in config.sh:

ccflags='-Ml -Mt128'
ldflags='-Ml -Mt128 -F 3000'

That specifies that any object greater than 128 bytes will be put in another
segment, and sets stack to 3000H bytes. This should leave a DGROUP that you
can live with.

After that, you'll have to dig through all the source files for VAXisms. It's
full of places where it's calling a function expecting a pointer with an uncast
0 as the matching argument. Plus, there are a couple of places where the code
generator gets crazy and tries to stuff a pointer into 16 bits. It will warn
you with a cryptic message about NEAR and FAR pointers.

Plus, you will need to play with the stack size, and probably make a few
auto-allocated buffers static or malloced.

Have fun. If you get a recent ELM working under 3.5 I's like a copy. I gave up
upgrading it months ago.

The fault lies not in the drive but in the Mac OS.  The problem you're

subject: No reply to duplicate NFS Write
q: A Symbolics Lisp Machine with a flaky I/O board dropped replies to its NFS Write requests. The SunOS 4.0.3 server never replied to the retransmitted writes, and the Lisp machine timed out. Is the server keeping a cache of recent writes, and does 4.1 behave the same?
ref: No. SunOS 4.0.3 has no dup request cache for writes, and it answers every request unless it's overloaded and dropping them. SunOS 4.1 uses the Chet cache, with an in-progress bit. It ignores a duplicate only while the original is still being worked on. Read the Usenix paper.
replies:
There is no dup request cache for writes in 4.0.3 NFS.  There is a cache
of sorts that is used to return a useful response to failures caused
by duplicate non-idempotent requests, but this is not consulted for
writes and in any case a response is always returned.  If you`re
talking to a SunOS 4.0.3 server then you'll get a response to every
request (unless the server is so overloaded that it's dropping
requests).

SunOS 4.1 utilizes a "Chet" cache (See Chet Juszczak's paper in
Winter '89 Usenix proceedings).  This cache not only reduces the
chances of incorrect results from duplicate non-idempotent requests,
but also allows the server to avoid unnecessary work generated by
non-idempotent requests.  The Chet cache maintains an "in-progress" bit.
All incoming requests are checked against the cache.  If a request is
a duplicate and the "in-progress" bit is on then the request is
ignored since a response is forthcoming anyway.  You should eventually
see a response to the original request a

subject: What functionality does one need? (Was "IP over Ethernet to printers")
q: Is Imagen's TCP printing just a simple byte pipe with no way to query printer status or do accounting, so a printer out of paper sits idle all night?
ref: No, read your docs. Imagen TCP/IP has TRANSPORT1 as the byte pipe, a UDP STATUS1 channel reporting not ready, out of paper, jam, low toner and job in progress, and an ACCOUNTING1 channel. On Berkeley hosts lpq reports STATUS1.
replies:
Well, according to my documentation (dated August 1986), Imagen TCP/IP
supports a TCP "simple byte pipe" called TRANSPORT1 for sending data,
a UDP connection for obtaining status called STATUS1 and a UDP based
connection for accounting (both reliable and unreliable) called ACCOUNTING1.

TRANSPORT1 and STATUS1 are seperable or can be used together. The status
that is available through STATUS1 include:
   - Engine not ready
   - Engine out of paper
   - Paper jam
   - Lacking consumables (toner)
   - Job in progress

Using our host software on a Berkeley system, lpq will report back the
STATUS1 status for a given printer. I'm not sure how status is reported
on System V.

Tomorrow's printing will probably be like today's printing, you have
work-group, satellite, or centralized printing. This boils down to whether
you have an operator and how far you have to walk to pick up your printout.

     Mark

subject: Color Blindness in Utah
q: Why is the Green River called green when it looks muddy red? Does anyone know the real story?
ref: It depends on the flow. In late summer with low water and no flash floods upstream it's reasonably green. After spring runoff or rain it runs brown, red or whatever. Presumably it was named on a clear day. Go figure.
replies:
We canoed the Labyrinth Canyon stretch of the Green this spring.  It goes
from Green River, UT to Canyonlands NP.  The water there is definately
green.

Late in the summer when the flow is low the Green is reasonably green if
there have been no flashfloods etc upstream. In the spring and after heavy
rains the colors run a full range from brown, red, green, etc.

I have always commented that at the confluence of the Green and the
Colorado the Colorado has been more green almost every time I have been
there.

If you have an aversion to nonclear water you must definitely stay off
of all the desert rivers except (alas) the Colorado below the Glen
Canyon dam.

In Utah we have the Dirty Devil river and Muddy creek (neither are more than
creeks) and there waters will discolor your skin until you shower vigorously.
I am sad every time I have to wash away the silts of these wonderful rivers.

Bret Webster

/ hpspdla:rec.boats.paddle / noel@giga.slc.unisys.com (Eileen Noel) /  6:51 am  Sep  4, 1991 /

We canoed the Labyrinth Canyon stretch of the Green this spring.  It goes
from Green River, UT to Canyonlands NP.  The water there is definately
green.
----------
It depends on how long it's been since the last rain storm.  I've been on the
Green and the Colorado a few times.  When it is raining up stream, you could
leave the river and hike up a side canyon for a few hours.  When you leave, the
river is blue-green.  When you come back it is "Too thick to drink and too thin
to plow".
The river was named on a clear day.

subject: How does wavetable synthesis work?
q: How does wavetable synthesis work, as in the Ensoniq VFX and Waldorf Microwave? Is it easy to make expressive patches?
ref: In practice you have tables of related single-cycle waveforms, and a digital oscillator sweeps through them under envelope, LFO or modulation control. It gives lots of spectral activity and is easy to program. Whether that's expressive is a loaded question, but it sounds gorgeous.
replies:
Theoretical? Don't know. The practical basis is that you have tables
of different but related single-cycle waveforms and allow the digital
oscillator to sweep through these tables under envelope/LFO/modulation
control. Some literature claims that the wave generator "interpolates"
between waves as it sweeps, whatever this means.

"Expressive" is a loaded term; I claim that the ol' DX7 is pretty
expressive if you program the envelopes properly, since then
different attack rates and note durations leave the operators at
wildly different levels. Wavetable synthesis *does* allow a lot
of sonic/spectral activity over time or under MIDI control, and
it's quite easy to program. The effects may not be "expressive",
but it's a gorgeous sound, nontheless. The strength of the Waldorf
machine is the analogue filtering which really adds to the colour and
richness of the wavetable sound. The strength of the VFX is the
number of digital oscillators available at once, each with many
modulation paramete

subject: MIDI on UNIX systems (was: Performer on the NeXT?)
q: Is UNIX the problem for MIDI, since the Atari ST and Amiga handle MIDI interrupts fine on slow 68000s while a NeXT supposedly can't?
ref: Oh, foo. UNIX isn't the problem. With a smart peripheral like an MPU-401 clone and a decent driver, it handles MIDI fine. Expecting a multiuser system to do interrupt-per-character I/O on the main CPU is silly. It's not ideal, but neither is most else.
replies:
Oh, foo.  The problem is *not* UNIX.  Given a reasonably smart
peripheral (an MPU-401 clone is smart enough) and a decent device
driver, UNIX will handle MIDI just fine.  It's silly to expect a system
capable of handling dozens of simultaneous users/windows/processes/etc
to handle interrupt-per-character I/O.  And it is even sillier to expect
such a system to handle the timing required by MIDI using the main CPU.

I'm not saying UNIX is an ideal system for MIDI--it isn't.  There are
too many daemon processes floating around to allow real-time in-and-out
MIDI filtering, for example.  But few OS's (other than specialized
real-time OS's--of which there are UNIX flavors) can handle this; arguably,
it is a job for another intelligent peripheral (alas, an MPU-401 clone
doesn't do here).

so you can pry them out).  This will reveal two black screws.  Remove
The screws.  Slide the back *up* relative to the front.  (There is a
J-style hook between the front and the back at the base of the keyboard).
The two parts should come off revealing:

One printed circuit board connected to the calculator's keyboard by
a line of spring-clip pins.

The battery contacts are round soldered-on disks that extend from the
PC board.  I've found that in mine the solder connection to these disks
sometimes gets a fine hairline crack in it.  Re-soldering the connection
might fix some of your problems.

subject: Elm 2.2PL14: Inconsistency in recording Mail Sent

ref: It's a feature. If elm finds a folder for the user you're mailing, it appends the copy there instead of your sentmail folder. Mail with no matching recipient folder goes to the default. Check your folders directory for the missing copies. RTFM.
replies:
I had the same question some time ago. If elm finds a folder for the
user you are sending mail to, it appends the sent mail in that folder

subject: double spacing a file w/ SED
q: How can I double space a file using SED? I tried s/$/$$/g on my IBM PC and it doesn't work.
ref: Replace each line with a newline followed by the line itself, using s/.*/ with a backslash-newline and & in the replacement. That works with MKS Toolkit sed. Honestly, awk or a shell script is far easier; sed is line-oriented and you're fighting it.
replies:
S='
s/.*/\
&/
'
sed -e "$S" $@

with the MKS Toolkit sed should work.  It does under **IX, and I've
never had conversion problems from **IX to MKS sed.  I can't speak to
other PeeCee sed(s).

It would be a whole lot easier to do it with a shell script or with
awk... SED is oriented to lines, yet you're trying to do something that
involves more than a line (at least in the output)

subject: Help My SO wants a CAT !!!
q: My girlfriend wants a cat to keep our 16-month-old Bernese Mountain Dog company. How do we introduce the dog to the cat?
ref: Keep them separated for a few days so they smell each other without seeing. Then introduce them with the dog on a down-stay while the kitten is set in the room. Wagging tails usually win the cat over. Don't just let the dog loose.
replies:
I have never had a cat, so I don't **really** have any business
answering this, but:  when my mother would get a new dog or cat, she'd
always keep them separated for a number of days, such that they could
smell each other but not see.  After a few days, when they would meet
for the first time, they would accept each other as "old friends".  I
think the largest dog she ever had was a spaniel, and I don't know how
big a Bernese mountain dog is, so this might or might not work.

Tom

Well, we went through kitten introductions with my husky 3 times when
we were in the 'roomate' phase.  It generally went very well.  I would
put the dog on a down-stay.  Then the kitten would be set down in the
same room.  The husky would want to play with the mobile squeak toy,
but she would stay.  Depending on the kitten's prior experience with dogs,
it might hiss at her or not.  Friday-the-husky, still in a down-stay,
but very interested in the new toy, would start wagging her tail.  None
of the three kittens we tried this with could resist that big, fluffy
cat toy for long...

Two of the three cats ended up very tolerant of the dog.  They played
'chase' with her - they ran, she chased, and when they were tired, they'd
lie down.  Friday would nose them in the side, as if to say 'hey, I'm
not tired yet, get up and run some more!'

Alison

subject: making GNU Emacs talk SMTP

ref: Unnecessary. Emacs runs on plenty of machines with no SMTP, using POP, uucp and so on. You'd still end up writing the sendmail.cf, since the SMTP server is usually sendmail. And sites may swap in their own sendmail replacement. It wouldn't be hard in Elisp, just pointless.
replies:
I have to disagree.  There are a number of problems with this.

1) GNU Emacs runs on many machines that don't have SMTP, or that don't use
SMTP for mail delivery.  There are sites that use POP, uucp, and other
mailer configurations.

2) You would still have to write the sendmail.cf.  Look at MH (the Rand
Mailer).  The default configuration is to connect to the SMTP server.
(Normally this is localhost, but you might want all mail to be delivered to
one machine.)  Since the SMTP server is usually sendmail, you wind up
writing the sendmail.cf.

3) Most mailers deliver mail by invoking sendmail with flags.  There may be
a reason for a site to replace sendmail with a program that does something
site-specific.  For example, sites that use NFS without lockd might want to
force all mail to the server machine.

It would not be difficult to write an SMTP package in Elisp (see the NNTP
package in GNUS).  I just think that it is unnecessary.

Besides, you could always use the MH-E package that is

subject: post-mixer amplifier
q: Why do professional SW radios from R&S and Collins put a diplexer between the double balanced mixer and the post-mixer amplifier, when a grounded-gate amp seems to work fine over a wide range into 50 ohms?
ref: The diplexer acts as a low-pass filter and gives the mixer a nice resistive 50 ohm termination at all frequencies, which it wants for good IMD performance. Feeding an amplifier directly degrades the mixer's third order intercept. You didn't measure IMD, did you? Go do that.
replies:
The diplexer filter after the mixer serves as a low-pass filter.  It typically
has a high (>= 20dB) return loss at the IF frequency and terminates higher
frequencies.  The mixer ports like to see nice resistive 50 ohm terminations
for optimal IMD performance.  It doesn't sound like you measured IMD.  Feeding
the mixer output into an amplifier such as you have degrades the mixer's third
order intercept point compared to a resistive termination.

I suggest trying the diplexer filter and compare the results with what you
obtained using the amplifier.  And make some IMD measurements....you'll find
the results interesting.

subject: detecting user inactivity
q: How can I sense user inactivity in Windows, like a screen saver does, so I can set a timer that goes off if there's no keyboard or mouse input?
ref: Write a DLL with a system-wide hook that watches for WM_CHAR, WM_SYSCHAR and WM_MOUSEMOVE. Record GetTickCount() on each event, and use a timer to detect the lack of messages. The code MUST live in a DLL, not a normal app. See the hooks overview in the manual.
replies:
One approach that springs to mind is to write a .dll and
install a system-wide windows hook in it (SetWindowsHook()
type WH_GETMESSAGE since user generated events are posted to
the event queue).  Each time you get a user-generated event,
call GetTickCount() and store the result in a static.  Before
doing so, however, compare the returned value with the old
contents of the static, and if the elapsed time is greater
than your threshold, install your timer.

This is a pretty rough sketch, but it should work.

cheers - Paul Bonneau.

create a DLL that used a system hook that looks for WM_CHAR, WM_SYSCHAR, and
WM_MOUSEMOVE messages to any application.  Add a timer so that you can detect
the lack of messages and that's it!  See the hooks overview in the manual.

subject: Sparse addressing info wanted
q: Some Lisp and Prolog systems put type tags in the top byte of an object's address, which needs sparse addressing from the virtual memory system. Which hardware allows sparse addressing, and does software like UNIX malloc get in the way? Do VAXes not support it?
ref: I don't see what hardware has to do with it. Memory management just maps virtual to physical addresses, and pages need not be contiguous. Address space is never fully contiguous anyway. Even on a VAX under VMS you can map whatever ranges you like with system services, one range per type.
replies:
I don't quite see what the hardware has to do with this.  As far as I
know, most (all?) memory management schemes simply map virtual to physical
addresses.  Thus, although address must be contiguous within a segment
or page, the segments/pages themselves need not be contiguous.  It's
entirely possible that I just take this for granted in the systems I
use, however, and everyone else does it wrong... :-)

In any case, to be more specific, I don't see how you can say VAXen
don't support "sparse addressing".  Under VMS (I don't know about UNIX)
you can map whatever addresses you want.  In general, address space
for a process is never completely contiguous.

If you really want (and for your purposes you do) you can use system
services to map virtual address ranges of your own choosing.  Thus,
you could map a range of whatever size you like for each type you need.

subject: Page Numbering in Books
q: In FrameMaker I have a book with Doc A (3 pages) and Doc B (4 pages), and a header of Page <$curpagenum> of <$lastpagenum>. The last page of Doc A prints as 3 of 3 instead of 3 of 7. Can I make $lastpagenum show the total for the whole book?
ref: No, $lastpagenum doesn't propagate across book files. Kludge around it: make the header's last-page number a cross-reference to a $lastpagenum variable in the last document. Put that variable in a paragraph by itself, on an unused master page if need be. Sigh, the manuals won't tell you.
replies:
No, $lastpagenum does not propagate.  However, there is a somewhat kludgy
way to do what you want.  Make the header entry for last page number a
cross-reference instead of a variable.  The cross reference would be to a
$lastpagenum variable located in the last document of the set, in this case
Doc B.  Since a marker designates the entire paragraph, the $lastpagenum
variable would have to appear in a paragraph by itself in that last document.
If there's nowhere visible that would be convenient, putting it on an unused
master page will work.  I had a need to do this a while ago, and came up with
this roundabout way of getting it done.  If you need more info, just drop me
a note.

subject: SNA over Ethernet via NDIS
q: What does it really mean that SNA can operate over an Ethernet LAN, given that SNA presumes a reliable data link and Ethernet LLC type 1 has no acknowledgments or recovery? And how is address resolution done?
ref: Can't speak for the new PC product, but IBM's RT AIX 2.1 already did SNA over Ethernet, with name services much like NetBIOS. You broadcast an Add Name Query, get a Name Query Response, and use Find Name Request and Name Found Request to locate a physical address. Hardly new.
replies:
A little known IBM product is their SNA support over an Ethernet for the RT.
(I'm not an RT user and this information is dated January 87, so I have no
idea about its current status.)  I have no idea if this announced PC
product is meant to interoperate with this RT product.

In the manual "SNA Services Guide and Reference" for the RT AIX V2.1,
Appendix D gives the name services provided over an Ethernet.  (The manual
says "Ethernet" everywhere but the frames they diagram are all 802.3.)
They provide 4 services:

(1) Add Name Query.  You broadcast this to see if any other node has the
	name you want already registered.  Hummmm, sounds like Netbios ...

(2) Name Query Response.  The response to (1) if someone already has the name.

(3) Find Name Request.  You broadcast this to locate the physical address
	corresponding to an 8-byte name you want to contact.

(4) Name Found Request.  The response to (3) if the name is found.

	Richard Stevens
	Health Systems International, New Haven, CT

subject: What do InitGraf (etc) do?
q: Why do my Mac programs have to call InitGraf, InitTE, InitDialogs and the rest? The Finder is already running QuickDraw and dialogs, so isn't initialising unnecessary?
ref: Some managers, like the resource and memory managers, are initialised once globally. InitGraf sets up the QuickDraw globals for your application, so it and the QD-dependent inits must run whenever a new application heap is set up. Even under MultiFinder. Read Inside Mac.
replies:
(I'm sure you'll get lots of answers...)

Some "global" managers are, in fact, initialized once, e.g. the
resource manager, memory manager, etc ... Inside Mac spells this out
for each appropriate manager ("The application should never need to do
this" type of comment).  Other managers deal with structures and
processes "local" to the application and its heap.  InitGraf
initializes the QD globals for the application, clears the screen to
the default desktop pattern(*), resets the cursor, etc. -- note how
all this always happens when a new application is launched.  So
InitGraf and initialization procedures for all the managers dependent
on QD need to be called every time the application heap is
initialized.

	/JBL

(*) While this does not all happen under MultiFinder, each application
has its own heap and QD globals, so InitGraf is still needed.

q: Why does vi on the Unix-PC write the file out when I use a shell escape or :n, and how do I stop it?
ref: You've got autowrite turned on, probably from EXINIT or a .exrc file. Remove the aw there, or put set noautowrite in your .exrc. Use set noaw inside vi for one session. Read your own startup files, for crying out loud.
replies:
???  This has not been my experience with any release of the
Unix-PC software.  I suspect you've set your vi sessions up using
'autowrite' mode.  To find out, the next time you're in vi give
the command
and see what's listed.  Dollars to donuts you get autowrite.  There's
this places it could come from: your EXINIT environment variable,
a file named .exrc in your home directory, or a file named .exrc in
your local directory.

The reason vi is behaving as you describe is because you have the
autowrite feature on.  In the .kshrc file a line sets EXINIT to
'set ai aw sm' or there is a similar line in your .exrc file.  You
simply need to remove the 'aw' from that line, or from a 'set' command
in the .exrc file if one is used.  Or you can issue from within vi the
command 'set noaw' if you simply want to turn the feature off for the
one editing session.  Hope this helps.

Yes, stick this in your ~/.exrc file.

set noautowrite                 -or-  set noaw

Then you'll get your desired effect.

-Lenny

subject: clntraw_create(), how to use?

Run rpcgen several times with the option to only generate one
of the files and use sed or awk to deconflict the procedure names.  I
have often tossed rpcgen out after several iterations and maintained
the generated code because it is easier.

subject: Procedure Variables and Records and Sorting
q: In Modula-2, can I write a generic sort routine that works on different record types, using procedure variables?
ref: Yes, no object-oriented magic needed. Pass the sort routine procedures for swapping two elements by index, comparing, and maybe copying. Those procedures know the array types; the sort doesn't need to. See the sorting chapter of The Modula-2 Software Component Library, volume 4.
replies:
The sort routine should be given routines for swapping two elements given an
index as well as routines for comparison and perhaps copying. The procedures
are aware of the different arrays by the sort routine need not be. See 'The
Modula-2 Software Component Library' volume 4, the chapter on sorting.

subject: Interference on 2454 MHz (extraterestral ?)
q: We run TV point-to-point links across the U.S. and see odd interference on 2.5 GHz channel 8A (2454.5 MHz). It's irregular, covers about 10 MHz, varies in strength and shows up almost everywhere. Any idea what it is?
ref: Microwave ovens. They sit right around 2450 MHz, free-running magnetrons with lousy frequency control, modulated by 60 Hz and swept 5-10 MHz by the stirrer. It's an ISM band, the spectrum trash heap. Sigh, what did you expect there?
replies:
You have been hearing microwave ovens.  Welcome to the wonderful world
of shared (microwave) bands and interference!  Now you understand why
it's so important to get those part 15 devices off of the amateur bands.

In the rare case that original ideas   Kenneth J. Hendrickson    N8DGN
are found here, I am responsible.      Owen W328, E. Lansing, MI 48825
Internet: hendrick@frith.egr.msu.edu   UUCP: ...!frith!hendrick

..

Gee, I know where _I'd_ look first!

Guess what frequency most microwave ovens operate on?  600 watts out of
a magnetron free-running oscillator into a small but still slightly
leaky cavity...  with very poor frequency control!

I'm surprised that video relays still operate in that area, since it's
an ISM allocation (spectrum trash heap) or close to one.

I am not sure whether this posting is serious or not.

	But microwave ovens operate at 2450 mhz (I didn't think anyone
operated any other services there).  They generate a ragged spectral
peak modulated by both 60hz (they usually don't use much of any filtering
on the power to the magnetron) and the energy dispersing stirrer which
typically sweeps the signal up and down 5-10 mhz at a few hertz rate as
the phase of the rf reflected back to the tube changes and pulls
the oscillation frequency up and down.

	Even though the leakage from a operating oven is supposed to
be pretty small, with a decent spectrum analyzer and a 20 db gain horn one can
usually find several microwave oven signals going at one time from a built up
area such as a city rooftop.

subject: Does anyone remember the Phantastron tube and how it worked?
q: How did the old phantastron tube in an FM transmitter work? I was told a magnet forced the electron beam into a helical path, and electrodes stretched the helix to phase modulate the signal.
ref: Sounds like the serrodyne effect to me. I worked on a travelling wave tube that modulated a GHz signal this way: a sawtooth under 10 kHz fed the helix, and raising the amplitude lowered the frequency. Never disconnect the helix, or the tube blows.
replies:
What you describe sounds similar to what I think is called the "serrodyne"
effect (spelling from memory). I once worked on a system which used
a travelling wave tube to modulate a (GHz) signal like this. I don't recall
magnets, but there was a sawtooth input (<10Khz) to the helix, as you
increased the amplitude, the signal freqency reduced. ( My instructor gave
strict instructions that the helix was never to be disconnected or
the TWT would blow. I subsequently found out that the TWiT's cost
over 1K pounds. :-) )

subject: Fractals & Chaos
q: What is the relationship between the mathematics of chaos and fractals? Does anyone know more about this field?
ref: Read Mandelbrot, who coined 'fractal'. His books 'Fractals: Form, Chance, and Dimension' and 'The Fractal Geometry of Nature' cover turbulence, critical-point fluids, galaxy distribution and bursty channel errors, though only briefly. Go read them instead of guessing from a magazine article.
replies:
That's exactly what Benoit Mandelbrot, the man who coined the term
"fractal", has tried to do. I recommend reading his books "Fractals:
Form, Chance, and Dimension" and "The Fractal Geometry of Nature".
He shows how fractals may apply not only to the shape of mountains,
continents, etc. but to the distribution of stars and galaxies, to
fluid turbulence, the distribution of errors on a bursty channel,
the behavior of a fluid near the critical point, and more, though
he just touches on each field.

you can't alloc more than that many global objects (note, windows
uses some itself).  Any program that reaches this limit is written
wrong.  On x86 you have to be aware of the number of selectors
available.

Chris

subject: Overlays

ref: Zortech's VCM linker doesn't have the function pointer problem. Overlays load on demand and go wherever there's room in memory, and get dropped when malloc runs short, much like virtual memory. subject: OS/2 Security
q: Is there a program that gives OS/2 EE 1.2 Unix-style per-user protected directories and passwords?
ref: Microsoft Lan Manager 2.0 does it. Access control lists live in the file system itself, so without a valid name and password you can't touch restricted parts of the disk. Permissions go down to the single file, for users or groups. Local security is new in 2.0.
replies:
Microsoft Lan Manager 2.0 provides such a secure file system. The
access control lists for a file or directory are stored as part of
the file system itself and unless the local or remote user has
logged on with a valid name, password pair he will not be able to
access parts of the disk restricted from him.

The access permissions can be any combination of Read, Write, Create,
Execute, Delete, Change Attributes, & Change Permissions and can
be applied to users or groups of users with a granularity down
to the single file level. New directories and files aquire the default
permissions for that drive, the per-drive defaults being settable by the
administrator.

There are four classes of user:- Admin, User, Local & Guest. These
are treated as special user groups and you can assign permissions
to a person according to the groups he belongs to.

Local security is a new feature of Lan Manager 2.0. This local security
is a feature of the workstation software as well as the server software.
Wor

replies:

information; Novell NetWare, for instance, maintains time and date information
for file creation, last modification, and last access (though the latter
will be meaningless most of the time if you back up your network regularly).

subject: Should I switch to Minix St?
q: Should I switch to Minix ST from TOS and MiNT? Is -DBsd enough to compile Unix code for Minix, given it's supposed to be V7 compatible?
ref: Not worth it for me. Minix ST is a decent V7 clone, but BSD is generations past V7. SysV programs port more easily, though it takes a fair bit of editing either way. TOS is still faster, and my applications are written for TOS. I'm giving up on Minix.
replies:
I set aside 50 meg of disk for Minix on my system, and I'm finding that
it's at least 30 meg of wasted space. The applications I want to run
have all been written for TOS, and it's a lot of effort to support both
TOS and Minix simultaneously. I am probably going to trim the Minix stuff
off sometime soon. (Maybe not entirely, but who knows. I haven't booted
it up in months...)

BSD is several generations beyond plain 7th Edition Unix. ST Minix is
a pretty good clone of V7, but not enough to make things that easy. Both
BSD and SysV Unix are derived from V7, but generally it seems to be easier
to port SysV flavor programs to Minix. It takes a fair bit of editing,
regardless. There are a lot of good ideas in Minix, but performance-wise
I think TOS is still faster. I'm kind of torn between working on MiNT
and RTX and adding new features to Minix, but I think since MiNT and RTX
allow me to continue using things like Uniterm, I'm eventually going to
give up on Minix.

subject: How do you get rid of <defunct> processes? (AT&T UNIXpc)
q: How do I get rid of <defunct> zombie processes on my AT&T UNIXpc that won't die with kill -9? And how do they get created?
ref: Sigh, you can't kill what's already dead. A zombie is just a process table slot waiting for its parent to wait(). Make the parent sh exit, init inherits the zombie and reaps it. It eats almost nothing, so stop fussing.
replies:
A process goes through basically three stages startup, run, and
shutdown (defunct).  The defunct stage is after the program has received
the kill/quit signal (which is why you kill has no effect) and is trying
to close all open files (stdin, ... etc) before it is removed from the
process table.  If you happen to do a ps after the program is killed but
before all clean is done you will see <defunct>.  I have seen your
problem before on a megaframe (which is also a convergent product).
The convergent people told me at the time to ignore the defuncts on the
megaframe that it would case no harm ( and it didn't).
In your case it would be anoying if they are still in your "W" window.
Are you running multiple gettys on the console?
Does it only happen with one program?
Does it only happen to programs that use the screen?

The process is in an in-between state ... the process itself has
exitted and all of its' core is deallocated, the only thing left
is a process table slot.  That slot will go away whenever its' parent
does a wait().  "wait()" reaps zombies.  Probably the parent isn't
ready to do any wait()'s?

hmm... I just looked a bit closer at your example.  How in the world
did you get an "sh" with init as it's parent?  Are you running
without the window manager?  (er... /usr/bin/ua?)  (Yes, I already
know that you're running on a Unix PC).

Anyway ... a less drastic way of reaping that zombie is to have the
"sh" exit ... the zombie will then be inheritted by process 1
(init), and since init is doing wait()'s all the time eventually
the zombie will get reaped.  In general, this is the way of getting
zombies to be reaped is to cause them to be inheritted by init
somehow.

He's not tying up much resources.  I have a dim memory, however,
that a zombie can, in some cases, keep some device which can

subject: Tree drawing
q: Has anyone written a Prolog routine that displays a structure like s(np(d(the),n(dog)),vp(v(barked))) in tree form, for showing parser output?
ref: The Quintus library has several tree displays, but rotated 90 degrees from what you want. Frankly that term is a poor way to represent a parse tree beyond toy programs. Rotated pictures with +-- branches are easy to print and easier to read.
replies:
The Quintus library provides several ways of displaying trees, but
rotated by 90 degrees from what you want.  The basic problem is that
s(np(d(the),n(dog)),vp(v(barked))) is not a very good way of representing
a parse tree, except for toy programs and tiny illustrations.  (You
really should allow for non-atomic category labels.)  "Rotated" pictures
	s
        +-- np
        +-- vp
	    +-- v barked
are quite easy to print, and rather easier to find your way around.

subject: fatal error 26 (Xenix 386)
q: Compiling large C programs under Xenix 386 gives fatal error 26, a parser stack overflow, yet it works in 286 large mode with -M2l. How do I get around it?
ref: The 286 and 386 modes use different compilers, which explains why one works and the other doesn't. The 386 parser most likely has an internal array that overflows. Why its limits are smaller is anyone's guess. Vendors, bah.
replies:
I assume you are running SCO Xenix with the 2.2 development system.
First thing is to know that the 86 and 286 mode use a different compiler
than the 386 mode.  That will explain why  it works in 286 large mode,
and not in 386 mode.

The stack overflow is harder.  I would assume that there are some
internal constants in the compiler which are being exceeded.  The parser
probably has it's own internal stack stored somewhere in an array.  If
the array is exceeded it would generate this error.  As to why the 386
compiler would have smaller constants than the 286, your guess is as
good as mine.

JB

ref: There's no wand of remove curse, so no uncursing a pile at range. Make a stack of junk scrolls, dip them in a fountain, write remove curse on them with the marker, bless them with holy water, then read one per packload. A wand of cancellation also works, but it strips enchantments too. Sigh.

Dave.

Spoilers ahead (sort of)

There is no wand of remove curse, so you can't uncurse a pile of stuff.

Get a pile of scrolls that you don't care for (punishment, destroy armor,
light, detect monsters, etc.).  Dip them in a fountain.  Use your magic marker

together.  Dip them in a potion of holy water (one potion will get them all).

rings you're wearing.  Do an assembly-line remove curse on the batch of stuff,
using one scroll each time you have picked up all the items you can carry.

much of it will turn out to be useless anyway.  I just try to pick out the
good stuff.

subject: 7300 hard drive controller
q: What exactly is a buffered seek on a hard drive, versus a plain ST506 seek?
ref: A buffered seek is a seek command with no specified time per cylinder step. The drive coordinates the move and tells the controller when it's done. A timed seek has the controller issue step pulses at a fixed rate. Buffered is much faster on long seeks. Most current drives do both.
replies:
A buffered seek is a seek command without a specified time-per-cylinder
step. The drive is supposed to coordinate the request, and let the
controller know when the operation is complete. This is in contrast to a
timed seek, where the controller issues step pulses at a fixed rate. The
advantage of this is that on a long traversal of the media, you can often
speed up in the middle, getting *much* better performance (since the head is
already moving, inertia can be disregarded on the middle seek pulses, and
thus, the seek is completed faster).

Most current drives can perform this task -- and drives which can do
buffered seeks can usually handle 'regular' seeks as well.

Assuming by "clause1,...", you actually mean "goal1,...", the following
might be one _simple_ way to do this:

    ...
    ListOfGoals = [goal1,goal2,...,goalN],

subject: Actor question: a:=new(ClassA);
q: In Actor, when I create an object with a:=new(ClassA) and no longer want it, how do I get rid of it? Is there a garbage collector?
ref: Just set a := nil. Actor keeps two variable spaces and copies live objects between them when idle, so whatever you've dropped gets left behind. Yes, there's a GC. No free() needed, grumble.
replies:
a := nil;

   Actor keeps two variable spaces and copies objects back and forth
between them when the system isn't busy. By setting a to nil, you leave
whatever a refered to hanging, and when things get copied that information
gets left behind.

subject: 5 1/4 Latch circut and A2000
q: My home-built 5 1/4 motor latch and Tandon drive worked as a PC drive on my A1000 but not on a B2000. PCcopy says 'root directory full' and PCformat gives 'error -4'. What differs between the 1000 and 2000 floppy interfaces?
ref: Check for heavy 180 or 220 ohm terminating resistor packs on the drive. The A1020 is specified for 1K terminators. The A1000 used discrete TTL buffers, but the A500 and A2000 use a modified 8520 with high-current outputs, which overloads easily. Hardware 101.
replies:
You might want to make sure that your drive doesn't have any heavy-duty
180 or 220 ohm terminating resistor packs.  The A1020 drive is specified
to use 1K terminators to avoid overloading the driver circuitry.  The
A1000 used discrete TTL buffers to drive the floppy signals, whereas the

subject: div() & ldiv() behavior?
q: What do div() and ldiv() do when the arguments are negative? I know what they do when both are positive.
ref: The quotient is always truncated toward zero, per the standard. So div(8,-3) gives quot -2, rem 2, and div(-8,3) gives -2 and -2. Plain 8/(-3) is implementation-defined, so don't mix them up. RTFS.
replies:
Sec 4.10.6.2 of the standard says that div(int numer, int denom)
"computes the quotient and  remainder of the division of the numerator
numer by the denominator denom.  If the division is inexact, the
resulting quotient is the integer of lesser magnitude that is nearest to
the algebraic quotient.  If the result [can] be represented, ...
quot * denom + rem shall equal numer."

This means, as I read it, that the quotient is always truncated toward
zero.  Thus,
	div(8,3)   gives quot=2,  rem=2
	div(8,-3)  gives quot=-2, rem=2
	div(-8,3)  gives quot=-2, rem=-2
	div(-8,-3) gives quot=2,  rem=-2
There's a similar table in sec 4.10.6.2 of the rationale, with 7
substituted for 8 and 1's or -1's for the remainders.

BTW, note that this is may be different from the result of 8/(-3) etc.
Sec 3.3.5 says the result can be -2 or -3 (implementation-defined).

Stan Brown, Oak Road Systems, Cleveland, Ohio, USA    +1 216 371 0043
                   email (until 91/4/30): browns@iccgcc.decnet.ab.com
My

For the normal division operator, the results are machine-specific.  For
div() and ldiv(), however, the quotient is truncated towards zero.

subject: Quintus Prolog Problem
q: In Quintus Prolog, setof(X, recorded(woof, X, _), Set) gives Set = [term2] and then Set = [term1] on backtracking, instead of one answer [term1, term2]. Is that a bug?
ref: No bug, you're missing something. Prolog has no true don't-care variable, so the anonymous variable gets a different value on each backtrack. Name it and quantify it: setof(X, Ref^recorded(woof, X, Ref), Set). Don't put anonymous variables inside setof or bagof.
replies:
As near as I can tell, setof and bagof don't work properly with the
   "recorded" predicate in Quintus Prolog (version 2.5.1, sun3-4.0).

   If I record:  recorda(woof, term2, _),
		 recorda(woof, term1, _).

   and then query:  setof(X, recorded(woof, X, _), Set).

   I receive the answer Set = [term2], and on backtracking the answer
   Set - [term1].  It seems to me that I should receive a single answer
   Set - [term1, term2].

   Am I missing something?  Or is this a known bug?

   Bradley

It is trickey.  This would work:

	setof(X, Ref^recorded(woof, X, Ref), Set)

Prolog doesn't have a true don't-care variable.  The _ is really
just a shorthand for some particular variable that you haven't
bothered to name.

# As near as I can tell, setof and bagof don't work properly with the
# "recorded" predicate in Quintus Prolog (version 2.5.1, sun3-4.0).
#
# If I record:  recorda(woof, term2, _),
#               recorda(woof, term1, _).
#
# and then query:  setof(X, recorded(woof, X, _), Set).
#
# I receive the answer Set = [term2], and on backtracking the answer
# Set - [term1].  It seems to me that I should receive a single answer
# Set - [term1, term2].
#
# Am I missing something?  Or is this a known bug?
#
# Bradley

You're missing something.  That's the correct behaviour.  Look again at
the incantation:

?- setof(X, recorded(woof, X, _), Set).

That anonymous variable will be given a different value on each
backtrack.  To state that you want all values to be included in Set, use
the existential quantifier and give the variable a name:

?- setof(X, Ref^recorded(woof, X, Ref), Set).

setof or bagof unless you *know* what you ar

subject: Changing the environment in sh
q: How do I change an environment variable like PATH from a /bin/sh script so the change shows up in my login shell? Setting and exporting it in the script only changes the script's shell.
ref: Source the script with the dot command, like ". script", instead of running it. A child shell can't change its parent's environment, and there is no other way. This is one of the first lessons of shell programming, so quit calling yourself dim and learn it.
replies:
Instead of having the shell execute the script, as in

$ sh script
(or)
$ script          # assuming script is chmod +x

have the shell evaluate, or source the script:

$ . script        # `dot script'

You're not dim, just apparently a novice with the shell.  This is one of
the first difficult lessons of shell programming.  You cannot change the
value of a variable (environment or otherwise) from a subshell, since
the environment of a superior shell is not available to the subshell.
The only way to do this is with the "." (dot) command which can loosely
be understood to mean "read in the following file (using PATH if
necessary) and execute it as if I had typed the commands directly into
my keyboard".  Of course, if you include the dot command in a shell
script, it will execute the commands AS IF THEY WERE PART OF THE CALLING
SCRIPT.  There is NO OTHER WAY to change shell environment variables.

subject: Programs compiled under xenix run slower under unix?
q: Do programs compiled under Xenix run slower under Unix than if they'd been compiled on the Unix system? Does translating Xenix programs slow them down?
ref: No. Xenix 386 binaries run natively under SCO Unix with no translation or emulation, so nothing slows them. Only 286 binaries go through /bin/i286emul for system calls, and recompiling those as 386 would be faster. Whoever refused your binary was spreading myths.
replies:
There is nothing inherent in a Xenix (x.out) 386 binary that would cause
it to run slower under SCO Unix.

The common assumption stated above, that Xenix programs are "translated"
to run under SCO Unix, is absolutely incorrect for 386 programs. SCO went
to a lot of trouble to put true native execution of Xenix binaries in SCO
Unix.  There is no translation or emulation. Full support is there, just
like it was in Xenix.

286 binaries need translation for system calls under SCO Unix. Xenix 386
handled system calls from 286 binaries directly in the kernel, but when
SCO Unix execs a 286 binary, /bin/i286emul is invoked to run the program.
If the program in question does a lot of system calls, it may be slower than
under Xenix. If the program is medium or large model 286, system call
translation is not nearly as much of an issue as having 286
code - recompiling as 386 would make it faster, but not necessarily
because of translation. This is less true for small model programs.

subject: vertical line registration in tbl...

ref: It's not the pipe character, it's the box vertical rule \(br that gets used. The real problem is that many typesetter fonts lack proper vertical and horizontal rule character definitions. -Here is the problem.  The vertical lines in the table

-overshoot the bottom-most horizontal line.
-

-fix for this?

No, the "box vertical rule" character \(br is used.
It works fine in many environments, including ours.
The real problem is that many fonts supplied for

horizontal rule character definitions.  A good
explanation of these matters can be found in
"Adventures with Typesetter-Independent TROFF" by
Mark Kahrs and Lee Moore in the Summer 1984 USENIX
conference proceedings.

subject: HelpPlease: Device Drivers for hard disk partitions
q: I want to partition my hard disk into logical volumes like D: E: F: G: to limit damage from corruption and get past the 32 meg limit. What's the best way to do it?
ref: Switch to MS-DOS 3.30, the first release that fully supports disk partitioning, and you stay compatible with later DOS and OS/2. Older clone-maker schemes aren't compatible, so you must back up, reformat, repartition and restore. Tedious, but that's life.
replies:
The most satisfactory way of doing this, and one which would keep you
compatible now and in the future (with DOS *and* OS/2), would be to switch
to MS-DOS 3.30, the first MS release which fully supports disk partitioning.

We, like many clone manufacturers, modified Dos 3.2x to support this
feature, but, as you would expect, our partitioning is not fully compatible
with the method later chosen by IBM/MS for 3.30.  A conversion from a
pre-3.30 partitioning scheme to the new 3.30, requires that the disk be
backed up, reformatted and partitioned, then the contents restored.

As far as partitions >32Meg, I expect you won't have to wait too long
(nudge, nudge, wink, wink, say no more)!

subject: os9 and Unix

ref: No deficiency. OS9/68K is smaller, faster and cheaper than Unix, and has better programmer tools; Unix just has more user tools. It's mostly used in embedded gear, since it can be entirely ROMable with minimal RAM. Mostly ignorance keeps it obscure, sigh.
replies:
OS9/68K is smaller, faster, and cheaper than UNIX. Why would anyone
want to sell that? Actually, OS9 is not common because ignorance is.
All we can do is keep telling people to check out OS9 before they
buy. If they want a user system, UNIX comes with more tools. If
they want a programmer's system OS9 comes with better tools, e.g.
very good compilers.
BTW, a company in Wisconsin, Heurikon, sells systems that run
OS9 or VRTX or VRTX32 (not on the same machine of course). I just
got their latest catalog, and boy, they sell neat stuff. And yes, I
do have one of their systems and it has been rock solid.

				Richard Piner

industry, but I think you will find that at present OS9 is used mostly by
companies producing microprocessor controlled equipment, eg digital servo
motor control, to name one I am familiar with.
    The great benifits of OS9 in target systems ( eg single-PCB micro-computer
mounted along side high power servo drive amplifiers ) is that the system
does not need to be disc based, i.e. totally romable, in the microware jargon.

minimum, you compared that to the simplest UN*X system.
I think it will just take time for this to spread to the home market.

subject: Bug in batch ?
q: On my NCR Tower, batch jobs sometimes mail back an error that lpirun was not found, even though output is redirected. Is it a bug in batch?
ref: We've seen intermittent batch failures too; hard to debug, and gone in SysV r3 based releases. You only redirected batch's own output, not the script cron runs.
replies:
We have seen intermittent problems of batch jobs not running.  Difficult
to reproduce and debug.  Seems to have gone away in SysVr3 based releases.

If the file xyz has been created then the message is coming from
lpirun.  If not then the shell is having trouble finding lpirun
or the script has been botched.  You can find the script that cron
sees in /usr/spool/cron/atjobs.

When cron runs, it starts up a shell to handle the script, saving the
stdout/stderr and mailing it to the user.  All that's been redirected
to /dev/null is the output from /usr/bin/batch, and not the script
that runs under cron.

subject: Getting rid of "disk almost full" message
q: How do I stop the 7300 from displaying those annoying 'disk almost full' messages every few minutes when free space drops below 5%?
ref: It's in the source, so you can't configure it away. Buy a bigger disk, kill smgr, or patch smgr with adb so the free space check is always satisfied. On 3.5, change the bge.w at upd_time+1be into a bra.w. Cleaning your disk is cheaper.
replies:
You don't.  It's imbedded in the source and cannot be changed.  Well, you
COULD get a larger disk!  Or, on the other hand you could kill the smgr.
And, as an afterthought, you could run mgr instead of the 'luser agent'.
I recently installed the software driver version and can't wait until I
can get the daughter board.  BTW, even with the software driver, mgr is
still a faster windowing system than X on my Sun 3/50!!!

Brian Rice

Assuming you're running 3.5 as I am, you can

*	$ su
* ()
*	# adb -w /etc/smgr
*	upd_time+1be?i
	upd_time+1be:		bge.w	upd_time+236
*	.?w 6000
	upd_time+1be:	6c00	=	6000
*	.?i
	upd_time+1be:		bra.w	upd_time+236
*	<EOT>
	#
(*) = you type

which causes smgr to think there's lots of space regardless of your usage.

subject: squirrels
q: Squirrels freeze by the side of the road until my bicycle is right on them and then dart out in front. Any squirrel-scare methods, and what survival purpose does this behavior serve?
ref: Shout "HOLD YOUR LINE" and most squirrels respond. As for why, small animals can't outrun predators in a straight line, so they change course constantly. It may not know whether you've seen it. Or squirrels could just be stupid.
replies:
Maybe some sort of ultra sonic noise maker in densely squirrled areas
to scare the little dolts away, rather than into your tire path?

A squirrel can kill you if it gets caught in your front spokes and
locks up the wheel. Or if you are cornering hard on a descent and
the squirrel gets under your front wheel, you may not be able to hold the
bike up.

Whether of animalistic or bicyclistic persuasion, most squirrels
respond favorably to a stern shout of "HOLD YOUR LINE."

Small animals such as squirrels and rabbits do not have sufficient
straight-line speed to outrun larger predators. So they compensate
by changing course frequently. The squirrel may wait until the last
second to burst out in front of you because it was not able to decide
whether you had seen it and were chasing it earlier.

Also, some animals run around in front of predators to draw them
away from their young. I don't know if squirrels do this, but some
birds do.

Then again, squirrels could be stupid.

subject: Hawk in the city?
q: I saw a hawk eating a wren in my city of about 30,000. I rarely see a hawk in town, much less eating prey. Has anyone seen this before?
ref: Quite likely. Peregrine falcons have nested in big cities for years, since tall buildings are ideal cliffs and pigeons make a smorgasbord. Boston has two known nests and New York had one on a bridge. Hardly news.
replies:
It is certainly likely.  Peregrine falcons have been known to make their
nests in large cities for the past several years.  Tall buildings are
an ideal habitat for this cliff-nesting falcon, and as the bird is a
bird-eater, the presence of pigeons creates a real smorgasbord!  There
are two well-known nests on two skyscrapers in Boston, and one nest
was reported last year on the Verazzano Narrows Bridge in New York.

Some cities actually "hacked" peregrines within the city limits for
the express purpose of reducing pigeon populations.  I've heard that
this was done a number of times in Manhattan....but not Manhattan,
Kansas, where Mr. McCall posted from!  It's still possible that this
city has its own population of 'grines who find buildings as comfortable
as cliffs.

If you could see that it was eating a wren, you probably got a good view.
Did you note any identifying marks colours etc?
How did it fly when it departed? Did it make any noises?

Here in sunny London (~10^^6) a falcon called the kestrel is fairly common,
(I saw one within the last week), and it feeds on small birds and rodents.
Like some other city birds (crows, pigeons) it is also often found on cliffs
and hills.

same packet types.  Even if you convince the packet driver to forward the

generate replies, etc.  Bad news.

subject: On hiding HyC 2.0 under multifinder
q: Under MultiFinder on a 9-inch screen, HyperCard 2.0 no longer hides itself when I switch to another program, unlike the old version. How can I fix this?
ref: Use the suspended, a new 2.0 global property that is true when HyperCard is in the background. In an idle handler, hide card window if it's true, else show it. Or put suspend and resume handlers in your home stack that hide and show the card window. RTFM.
replies:
Sure; put the following into your home stack script.

on suspend
   hide card window
end suspend

on resume
   show card window
end resume

Personally, I view this as a feature.  Now, if I don't want the card window to
be hidden on my SE/30 it doesn't have to be.

chaz

The basic idea you need is "the suspended", a new 2.0 global property.
Under 2.0, the suspended is set to true whenever HyperCard is in the
background. A basic handler would be

  on idle
    if the suspended is true then hide card window
    else show card window
  end idle

Of course, you may want to get fancier (take multiple windows into account,
refrain from hiding if the right edge of the window is far enough over to
expose the Finder's icon row, etc.). But this gives the general idea.

subject: Computing power in three phase circuits
q: How do I compute apparent power in a three-phase Y-connected AC circuit if I know the three phase currents and the nominal line-to-line and line-to-neutral voltages, assuming unity power factor?
ref: Complex power is S = V times the conjugate of I, but V must be the line-to-neutral value. Get that by dividing the line-to-line voltage by the square root of 3, then sum the three phases. Everything rotates 30 degrees going between the two, so mind your angles.
replies:
Good..because when you go from line-to-line to line-to-neutral, everything
rotates 30 degrees. The complex power S is V(I*) (I conjugate, so flip the
sign on the angle of I) except that V is V line-to neutral.

To get the 'real' portion of V, divide by the square root of 3, so then
effectively, your apparent (real?) power is...
3**-2(VI+VI+VI).

subject: PowerSat Options
q: Could a power satellite beam its energy down with a laser instead of microwaves? How do the two compare?
ref: Sigh, lasers focus tighter, but power-to-laser and laser-to-power conversion is far less efficient, maybe 9% end to end against about 85% for microwaves at Goldstone. Weather hurts lasers more too, and they'd make better weapons. A sunlight-pumped laser could be smaller, but clouds still kill it.
replies:
The laser boys keep telling us that by using lasers instead of microwave
transmission, we would get less spillage and therefore, greater efficiency
and lower the safety risks.

Unfortunately, I have yet to read about a high efficiency ( > 50 % )
laser or photoconverter so to me, laser power transmission would offer
at best about 9% dc-to-dc efficiency (using 30% efficiency for the laser
and the photoconverter which I suspect is generous).
This also ignores attenuation within the atmosphere which can reach
100% in bad weather conditions.

On the other hand, microwave transmission with a dc-to-dc efficiency of
85% was demonstrated at Goldstone back in the 70's (over a range of about
10 km I think). Using a frequency of 2.45 GHz, attenuation due to atmospheric
effects is not a problem (I studied the problem for my final year thesis).

The big problem is putting the Space Power Satellites up into orbit.
Just about all other technical problems have been solved.

Greg Kaan.

Lasers have the advantage that they are much easier to focus into a tight
beam, and the disadvantage that the power->laser and laser->power conversions
are much more difficult and much less efficient than for microwaves.  They
are also somewhat more subject to attenuation due to weather.  They would
also make much better weapons, which is a potent argument against them if
an unambiguously peaceful device is desired.

It wouldn't make much sense to use PV cells at a powersat to drive a laser
-- the efficiency is just too low.

For laser powersats to work, you want to chuck the light-->
electricity--> light conversion, and go with a laser pumped directly
by sunlight.  Some varieties of solar pumped lasers do exist, but I
don't know how durable or efficient they are.

The big advantage of a laser powersat is that it can be much smaller,
at fixed beam power density; megawatt scale satellites are possible.
Technologies that require you jump immediately to gigawatt scale
plants are very hard to develop.  But clouds would be a problem.

subject: How make champagne?
q: How is sweet champagne made? My carbonated wines always ferment dry, and I'm trying to avoid exploding bottles.
ref: Real champagne uses methode champenoise: second fermentation in the bottle, twist and tilt the bottle to move sediment to the cork, disgorge it, then top up with sweetened wine and recork. Artificial carbonation is cheapest and worst. Do it properly, or don't whine about it.
replies:
According to Anderson and Hull, the method is to
1) make a wine (preferably ~10% alcohol)
2) add sugar and champagne yeast
3) give the bottle and occasional spin along the long axis to get the yeast
       to the bottom)
4) after a few months, chill the bottle to 26 F, so that carbonation is not
       lost), and transfer to another bottle
5) use a stabilizer, sweeten to taste

     Voila! A sweet, sediment-free champagne.  Of course, I haven't tried it
yet, but that's what the book says.  Any takers?

There are several ways to make sparkling wine; artificial carbonation
is the cheapest and least satisfactory.  Champagne is made by what is
called the `methode champenoise' (surprise!).  There is also an
in-between method, where the secondary fermentation is done in large
closed vats (cuve close).

Methode champenoise:

   Second fermentation in bottle (creates bubbles).
   Bottle manipulation to move sediment towards cork.
   Disgorging to remove sediment.
   Bottle topped up with (usually sweetened) wine and corked.

The bottle manipulation involves joggling the bottle with sharp
twists, and moving it in stages to a bottom-up position.  This can be
done by hand (tedious but requires considerable skill) or machine.

Disgorging is done either by simply taking off the cap (they often use
beer-type bottle caps) with the bottle still upside-down, and quickly
righting it; or by freezing the sediment in the neck of the bottle,
and having it pop out vertically.

subject: Kodachrome 64 at ASA 80
q: I hear many people shoot Kodachrome 64 at ASA 80. Does that increase color intensity, does it need special processing, and can I switch midway through a roll?
ref: Yes, it's common. Just set the camera's speed dial to 80 any time, even mid-roll. Processing is the same, since Kodachrome allows no special processing. No manual setting? Dial in -1/3 exposure compensation. If you have neither, why bother with Kodachrome?
replies:
Yes. And I shoot my Kodachrome 25 at ASA 32 as well. This was systematicaly
done by the National Geographic photographers as related by Gallen Rowell in
"Mountain Light". The best way to judge by yourself is to proceed as he did:
choose a few typical scenes, shoot each of them at the nominal sensibility,
then increase and decrease the exposure by 1/3 f-stop. Then for each scene
mark the one you prefer. A roll should be sufficient to do this experiment.

The only thing you have to do is to adjust the sensibility indicator of your
camera to 80 instead of 64. It can be done at any moment. The processing is the
same (however no special processing can be done with Kodachrome).
Of course you can do it only if your camera has a manual film sensibility
tuning device. Otherwise look for a exposure compensation device and adjust it
to -1/3. If your camera has neither, perhaps it is not worth using Kodachrome!

Tuan.

subject: MacRecorder sampling rate
q: Downloaded MacRecorder files often have the wrong sampling rate. How can I change the playback rate by editing the resource fork or some other way?
ref: The rate lives in the INFO resource, ID 1000, longword 7: 1 is 22kHz, 2 is 11kHz, 3 is 7kHz, 4 is 5kHz. Open the file in ResEdit and change it. If there's no resource fork, open and re-save it in SoundEdit. It's in the manual, page 211.
replies:
Look on page 211 of the MacRecorder User's Guide.  There you will find that
the sampling rate for a file is stored in the INFO resource (ID=1000) in
longword 7.  It is encoded as follows:
1 ->22kHz
2 ->11kHz
3 ->7kHz
4 ->5kHz

There must be a better way than this, but I have found it to work:

Open the sound file with ResEdit.
Open the Resource called INFO with ID = 1000.
Change the last four characters in row 18 accoring to this pattern:
    0001 = 22K sampling
    0002 = 11K sampling

Sometimes sound files do not have a resource fork.  If this happens, then
open the file with SoundEdit and save it again.

subject: exceed 64K memory allocation in MS C 5.10
q: Microsoft C 5.10 gives an 'exceed 64K memory allocation' error on a 640x480 array even with the huge model (-AH). How do I get past the 64K barrier?
ref: Your array is an automatic variable on the stack, which can never exceed 64K. Make it static or move it outside the function, or use a huge pointer and halloc. Any idiot knows the stack is small.
replies:
I suspect that your friend is doing something like this...

main()

{

        int array[640*480];

           ...

Which is an error because MSC thinks this is an automatic variable, which
it will try to allocate on the run-time stack, which can never be bigger
than 64K.

What he should do instead is create a huge pointer to said array and use
the huge memory allocation (halloc.)

Or alternatively declare the array static, or move the array outside of
the function, either of which gets the array out of the stack and into the
DGROUP, which can be as big as you like (within limits.)

.

Chewey, get us outta here!

subject: wrap vs. bypass
q: With regard to FDDI, what is the distinction between wrapping and bypassing?
ref: Wrapping is when a dual link goes down and the nodes at each end join the primary and secondary rings into a single C-shaped ring, restoring full connectivity. Bypassing is a node disconnecting a failed or inactive local ring or host from the backbone while still repeating frames. The names are descriptive, for pity's sake.
replies:
I am familiar with the terms from Pronet-80 and I assume they
carry over intact to FDDI, but wrapping and bypassing are descriptive
terms.
	"Wrapping" is when a dual link goes down (infamous backhoe
cut) and the nodes on each end of the failed link detect the loss of
primary and secondary rings and loss of neighbor and then they "wrap"
the primary and secondary rings together, connecting the two
counter-rotating rings together into a single ring in the shape of a
"C".  Full connectivity restored.
	"Bypassing" is when the FDDI node detects a problem with the
local ring or host and disconnects the local network from the
backbone.  It bypasses a failed or inactive host/ring.  This maintains
the two counter-rotating rings intact and fully operational, since the
bypassing node is repeating frames around the ring and is fully
participating in the dual ring management, etc.  It's a necessary
token ring fault management technique.

	Kent England, Boston University

subject: GNU/Sozobon C question
q: What's the difference between Sozobon, GNU gcc, and compilers like Laser C or MWC on the Atari ST? Are they different languages or just different compilers, and what's the big deal about GNU?
ref: They're all just compilers. All are more or less K&R first edition with their own extensions, but gcc also does ANSI C. The catch is that gcc pretty much needs a hard disk and 2 megabytes. Without that, Sozobon is decent and the price is right.
replies:
Well, they're all just compilers. But they all support different features.
There are two standards for C; K&R first edition (the original book by
Kernighan and Ritchie) and ANSI C, which is the new standard (and which
is covered in the second edition of Kernighan and Ritchie). All of the
compilers you mention are more or less compliant with K&R 1st edition,
and they all have (different) extensions to it. The GCC also complies
with the ANSI standard (and has extensions to *that* as well!).

I've used Laser, Sozobon, and the GCC. I only use the GCC now; I find the
other compilers quite limiting in the features available. On the other
hand, the GCC pretty much requires a hard disk and 2 megabytes of memory.
If you don't have this much, you might consider one of the alternatives.
Sozobon is a pretty decent compiler, and the price is certainly right.
And the commercial compilers do have the advantage of better documentation
and (often) nice graphics shells, if you care about that.

subject: Changing the width of script windows.
q: How can I change the width of HyperCard script editor windows under HyperTalk control, so they show a full 80 columns of Monaco 12?
ref: The script editor keeps window positions in a global called scriptWindowRects, one rectangle per line. Declare it global and put your rectangle in it at startUp, like putting 0,0,599,400 into scriptWindowRects. New windows use the first unused one. No resource hacking needed.
replies:
The script editor saves the locations of script windows in a HyperTalk
global, "scriptWindowRects".  Whenever you move, resize, or close a
script window, the editor updates this global.  Whenever a script is
opened, it scans scriptWindowRects for a rectangle that no other script
window currently occupies.  The first unused rectangle becomes the
boundary for the new script window.

If there are no unused rectangles in scriptWindowRects, the script editor
calculates a location based on screen size.  You can set up your scripting
environment on startUp by putting rectangles, one per line, into
scriptWindowRects (and be sure to declare it as a global).

For example:

   put "0,0,599,400" into scriptWindowRects

where scriptWindowRects is a global.

Kevin Calhoun
HyperCard Team
Apple Computer, Inc.

subject: Mac IIsi memory quirks - help
q: Why does my Mac IIsi run benchmarks like Speedometer slower for the first application than for later ones, and speed up as my system gets bigger? What causes this quirk?
ref: One of the IIsi's memory banks is slowed down by video access and the other isn't. Programs sitting entirely in the slow bank run slower. Use fewer colors or black and white, or buy a NuBus video card. Quadras have separate video RAM, so no.
replies:
The difference is due to the fact that one of the banks of memory in the
IIsi is slowed down by video access and the other one isn't.  If programs
are completely in bank A, they will be slower, and if they are completely
in bank B, they will be faster.  You can reduce the effect by using fewer
colors or black and white (thus reducing the memory bandwidth used up by
the video system), and you can eliminate it completely by buying a
nubus video card.

It is unlikely that  Quadras suffer from the same problem because they
have separate video RAM.

subject: How do you do this query in SQL?
q: How do I write an SQL query to select drivers who have both RED and BLUE cars, with each driver's id appearing only once in the result?
ref: Self-join the table, one alias per color: driver.id = c1.id and c1.color = 'RED', driver.id = c2.id and c2.color = 'BLUE', and so on. Use outer joins for optional colors. That's ORACLE's (+) notation; INFORMIX differs. Basic stuff, really.
replies:
.
[stuff deleted]
.

Assuming you have a fixed number of color possibilities, you can
accomplish this with a self-join as follows:

select driver.id, c1.color, c2.color, c3.color, c4.color
from driver, color c1, color c2, color c3, color c4
where
    driver.id = c1.id and c1.color = 'RED' and
    driver.id = c2.id and c2.color = 'BLUE' and
    driver.id = c3.id (+) and c3.color (+) = 'GREEN' and
    driver.id = c4.id (+) and c4.color (+) = 'TAN'

The (+) is ORACLE's notation for 'outer' join, which will give you nulls
if there are no matching rows.  INFORMIX has a different syntax and I
assume other vendors supply similar functionality.

subject: HDB system forwarding restrictions?
q: With HDB UUCP, how can I restrict which systems can forward mail to which other systems?
ref: You can't with UUCP permissions, which only restrict which systems may run which commands. Easiest is pointing COMMANDS at your own wrapper script for rmail that checks last-hop and next-hop, then calls the real rmail or bounces. Basic UUCP, folks.
replies:
You can't do this with UUCP permissions. All you can do is restrict
which systems have access to which commands. So that, for example,
you could say:

	MACHINE=a:b:c COMMANDS=rmail
	MACHINE=OTHER COMMANDS=

which would only allow those three machines to run rmail.

The easiest way to do this with your software is to write a shell
script or program which would check last-hop and next-hop for
whether they are allowed to do what they want, then if they are
invoke the real rmail, otherwise bounce the mail. To do this do
something like:

	MACHINE=OTHER COMMANDS=/usr/lib/uucp/rmail

or whatever you want to call it.

subject: Coalescing memory for DOS
q: What is memory coalescing, why is it needed, and when? I'm asking in the context of DOS not coalescing freed memory.
ref: Coalescing means merging adjacent free blocks into one larger free block. Skip it and a run of allocations and frees fragments memory until even a small request fails despite hundreds of K free, just in useless pieces. Basic stuff, really.
replies:
Coalescing is the process of combining adjacent free blocks into a single,
larger free block.  If you didn't do that, a sequence of allocations and
frees would eventually fragment the memory to the point where even a small
allocation would fail even though there are hundreds of K available--but none
of the free blocks large enough for the request.

subject: HELP mail problem

replies:
We have a similar problems running just Suns but OS version 3.5 and

NFS mounted (e.g. remote) filesystem as it would a local filesystem.
For sendmail to deliver the mail, it wants root privledges to get around
some obvious security problems (as in being able to write a file it
doesn't own).  On the Suns, I bet you have it set that root from certain
