subject: Text Spacing on Laser & Fractional Font Sizes?
q: For justified text on a LaserWriter from QuickDraw, am I right that the endpoints come from drawing text accurately with fractional widths and SpaceExtra? And how do you specify fractional font sizes, like 5.9 point?
ref: Correct. The LW driver does a MeasureText with your FractEnable, SpaceExtra and CharExtra, and uses that for the line endpoints. For fractional sizes, use StdText with numer/denom, say 59/100 on 10 point. Compensate for the width change, and keep the same ratio in a TextBegin-TextEnd comment.
replies:
That is correct.  The LW driver will do a MeasureText using your settings
for FractEnable and SpaceExtra (and CharExtra), and use the results as the
endpoints for the line.  Actual spacing, character-to-character, will be
different on the Laserwriter.

Use the StdText procedure to draw the text.  You can specify fine scaling via
the numer and denom parameters.  Try, e.g. 59/100, with 10 point type.
Note that this will change the measured width, (above), and you will have
to compensate for that.  Within a TextBegin-TextEnd comment, ALL calls to
StdText must have the SAME numer/denom, or you will get funny results.

It sounds like your program is in Applesoft and is not managing memory

0  N=64 :

subject: time-constructability of (t(n)^(1/3))
q: Given a time-constructable function t(n) greater than n log* n, is a(n) = ceiling of t(n)^(1/3) time-constructable without computing t(n)?
ref: In general, no. Take a big easy-to-compute s(n) like 2^n and a 0/1 function f needing about s(n)^0.5 time. Let t be s(n) if f is 0, else 8 s(n). Computing a(n) in time a(n) would compute f too fast. Basic diagonalization, nothing silly.
replies:
In general, no.

Let s(n) be a large function which can be computed in time <<s(n)
(e.g. 2^n).  Let f(n) be a 0/1 function that requires time s(n)^0.5 to
compute.  Define t(n) as:

If f(n)=0 then s(n)
else 8*s(n).

Then a(n) is 2^(n/3) when f(n)=0, 2*2^(n/3) when f(n)=1.  Since s(n)
is easy to compute, if you could compute a(n) in time a(n), you could
compute f(n) in time a(n).  But a(n)<s(n)^0.5, so you can't.

subject: BMW 325 recall info
q: After the emissions EEPROM recall on my '86 BMW 325e, the engine temperature gauge reads higher, especially in summer with the A/C on. The dealer says it's fine if not in the red. Any clues?
ref: Likely the new chip has a more retarded timing curve for lower NOx. Later ignition puts less combustion energy into the piston and more into heat in the cylinder walls, so it runs hotter and loses some efficiency. If it's not in the red, the dealer's probably right.
replies:
You probably don't have to worry.  Have you been using the same oil?
  Also, how's your coolant, and how's your thermostat?  Is your radiator
  clean and unobstructed?  Do you have the correct spark plugs in?

  I thought in Europe they measured fuel economy (consumption?) by the
  unit "l/100 km" ?  At least that's what my car says when I switch its
  computer to metric...
							Jason

The EPROM controls engine temperature but turning on and
off the electric fan. At least that is how it works on my '87 Vette.
They probablly had to raise operating temperature to more completely
burn the mixture in the engine. That supposedly lowers the bad emissions.
It should also lower performance as well since a warmer engine might mean
lower less dense air/fuel mixture in the engine. Part of the aftermarket
"performance" EPROM they sell for the Vette is to lower the operating
temperature to get that denser mixture. They also reccomend you buy a
lower temperature thermostat.
	So, I reccomend looking around for a lower temp. thermostat for
your BMW. If you can find one for your car this may be the answer to your
problem. In fact the dealer is probablly right, as long as it is not
in the red you don't have anything to worry about.

	Tim

Based just on what you've written, I think the new EEPROM has a more retarded
timing curve.  This is desinged to reduce NOx emissions which can't be directly
measured but causes the most irritating forms of pollution: smog.  To obtain the
most efficient use of the fuel, the combustion should be timed so that the
maximum pressure is produced when the piston just passes TDC.  When the
timing is retarded, the ignition occurs at a later phase of the combustion
stroke.  What this does is is to cause more of the combustion to occur after
the piston is already going down toward BDC.  Now, less of the combustion
energy is being used to push the piston, but the energy has to go somewhere.
This energy now turns into heat that is transfered to the cylinder wall, and
thus makes everything much hotter.  Since less of the energy is being put to
useful work, this also means that you WILL lose power and efficiency.  However,
the changes to your car may be small enough that you won't notice it.

eyc

P

subject: Shared memory help on 800 series needed
q: Is there a way to configure the kernel on an HP 9000/800 series to set the maximum size of individual shared memory segments? On a 300 series you use SHMMAX, but I heard it won't work on an 800.
ref: Of course it works. Put shmmax in the kernel configuration file, shmmni for the system-wide segment count, and shmseg for segments per process. shmmax interacts with dmshm, so change both together. Also pass NULL as shmaddr to shmat(2); the 800 picks the address.
replies:
Well, the following shared memory parameters are available in the
configuration file:

shmmni          100;
shmmni is the max number of shared mem segments systemwide.

shmmax          0x4000000;
shmmax is the max size of a shared mem segment.
Warning: interacts with dmshm...change both at the same time.

shmseg          12;
shmseq is the mex number of shared mem segments per process.

All of these came from prcrs' configuration file.  prcrs is a 9000/850.

There is one issue that you will encounter with porting shared memory
stuff to the 800's.  Your shmat(2) call must specify NULL for shmaddr.
The 800's must be free to decide where in the address space to put the
segment.  But it will chose an address off in hyperspace.  You will never
have a shared memory/malloc collision.

subject: New vlt user (w/ problems).
q: I'm a new vlt user on the Amiga and get rexx messages, font errors and can't open a Tek window. How do I get it working?
ref: Vlt needs to find its stuff. Put its fonts in FONTS:, its defaults in S:, and its libraries in LIBS:, or assign them to the Vlt disk, like assign FONTS: Vlt:Fonts, then save your configuration. RTFM, it's all in the docs.
replies:
[ list of problems deleted ]

You must have vlt's fonts in your FONTS: directory. Either copy them
to your WB disk, or 'assign FONTS: Vlt:fonts'.

Same for the S: directory and the libs: directory. Vlt needs to find
its defaults in the S: directory, and its libraries in the LIBS: directory.

If you have Vlt on a separate disk, before you start it make sure you
type something like this: (the Vlt's disk name being VLT)

   assign FONTS: Vlt:Fonts   (for the 3 vlt fonts)
   assign LIBS:  Vlt:Libs    (for libraries (review.library, arp.library, etc))
   assign S: Vlt:s           (for config files)
   assign REXX: Vlt:rexx     (for macros)

Then configure your system and save the configuration.

                                                     aliu@nunki.usc.edu
                                                       Forwarded (MD)

subject: Cat's Teeth
q: My vet wants me to rub my one-year-old cat's teeth with baking soda paste, but he's a biter. How do I go about it? Also, he was taken from his mother at seven weeks, and the vet thinks he can't groom himself properly. Is that likely?
ref: Don't wrestle him. The harder you hold a cat, the harder it fights, so get the vet or a groomer to show you the right hold. As for grooming, kittens taken at six weeks learn fine, maybe slower. Honestly, technique beats brute force.
replies:
Have the vet (or some other type of animal handler/groomer) show you
how to hold the cat effectively.  Generally, the harder you hold the
cat, the harder it will work to get away.  You need to have the right
type of hold to make it easy on you and the cat.  If the cat stays
calm, you (probably) won't get hurt.  I realize that this is much
easier said than done which is why I suggested having someone show you
rather than trying to explain it.  With cats, technique is everything.
He may not end up being cooperative, but he will probably be less
uncooperative.

I've hand fed kittens from birth and they have learned to groom
themselves just fine.  They might be a little slower, but they learn.
More to the point, a kitten can generally can be taken from its mother
at six weeks (as soon as it learns to eat).

subject: PC video interface help needed
q: Has anyone used large screen TVs with direct video inputs as PC displays? My video card output looks fuzzy with poor color convergence on a 27 inch monitor. Is the monitor to blame?
ref: Probably not, since monitors have no brain to be dead. Check that bridged video loops are terminated with 75 ohms. Also make sure your scan converter matches the graphics card, since a CGA one won't work with EGA or VGA except in CGA mode.
replies:
Yes..we often convert CGA, EGA, and VGA output to NTSC for display
	on projection TVs and other NTSC devices.

	As we aren't using converter cards, but scan converter frames, I can
	only speculate that the problem is with your scan converter card, and
	not the monitor (they cannot be brain dead...as they have no brain
	to qualify themselves as such).

	Did you:

		1> Make sure that bridged video loops through the monitor are
		terminated with a 75ohm terminator?

		2> Make sure that the scan card is compatable with the
		graphics card output format?  (i.e. a CGA scan converter won't
		work with an EGA or VGA card, except in CGA mode, because the
		scanning frequency is _much_ different).  This doesn't
		generally account for the type of problem you have encountered,
		but it has been known to happen.

	Hope it helps in some way...

subject: protecting my HD20
q: How can I unmount the internal HD20 on my SE so I can test dangerous programs without risking infection of my files?
ref: Restart with a floppy inserted, and hold Shift-Option-Command-Delete during boot until it starts from the floppy. That disconnects the SCSI port, so no hard drive mounts. It's only a software disconnect, so it's not perfect. Kids these days.
replies:
"It was not like this when I was a kid", ah yes, the good old days.
If I was testing some dangerous software on my computer and I had a external
drive I would disconnect it, turn the power off, and take it to the other
end of my house.  But since you have a internal drive, like me, you can do
the next best thing.  Do this:

	1) Restart your computer and insert disk right after.

	2) Hold down the  SHIFT-OPTION-COMMAND-DELETE  at the same time
		during reboot, until the computer is booting off of floppy.

This will disconnect the SCSI port.  It is only a software disconnect, I
think, so It may not be perfect but you will not be able to mount any hard
drive.  Hope this helps.

Bruce.

subject: Aztec C?
q: Has anyone used Manx Aztec C? I need to port C code from the IBM PC to the Apple II, and it's the only C compiler I can find for it.
ref: One person's impression of the PC version was unfavorable. Keys that generate two characters, like arrows and function keys, returned only the second one from getchar, so you couldn't tell them from ordinary ASCII. A sloppy screwup like that makes it hard to trust the rest.
replies:
I've used the Aztec C compiler for the PC several years ago, and my
impression was not favorable.  The PC keyboard has a number of keys
that generate two characters (00 xx) for a key code.  Typically these
are arrows, function keys, etc.  When I read a keystroke with getchar,
it returned only one character -- the second one.  There was no way
to distinguish what I received from the normal ASCII character with
the same code.  It struck me as a problem of someone porting over the
getchar function to the PC hardware and not looking carefully enough
at the funny codes generated by that keyboard.  It was hard to get
much enthusiasm for trusting the rest of the compiler after such an
obvious screwup.

Clayton E. Cramer

subject: 'g' protocol over X.25 - why not?
q: Why does the uucp 'f' protocol work over an X.25 connection through PADs while the 'g' protocol doesn't?
ref: It's not that 'g' doesn't work. You have to set the X.28 parameters as transparent as possible: no forwarding characters, forward on timer or full packet, and watch flow control. Also widen the uucico window from 3 to 7 so ACKs return before timeout. 'g' is slower than 'f', but it's everywhere.
replies:
generally, yes

it's not that 'g' doesn't work, you just have to mung the X.28 parameters
appropriately and maybe adjust your uucico window variable.

i did extensive playing with this on a past project and finally achieved
an average of 160 cps over 2400 baud X.25 links.

two tricks:

1) under SCO Xenix 2.2, we adjusted the windows variable in uucico (using
adb, yech!) from the default of 3 to 7.  this means that as many as 7
(formerly 3) packets could be sent before the protocol would wait
for an ACK from the first packet.  opening the window allowed the ACK's
to return before the protocol timed out.

2) X.28 parameters must be set to as transparent a mode as possible.
no forwarding characters, forward on timer or full packet.
also watch those flow control parameters.  depending on the network
(private, DataPAC, Tymnet, Telenet, etc) these parameters may change.

'g' over X.25 may not be as efficient as 'f', but at least 'g' is available
in almost all uucp implementations.

a pleasan

subject: DECwindows on PCs
q: DEC announced DECwindows on a PC, PCSA Version 3.0, for $250. Is DECwindows just another name for X, and does it run over TCP/IP as well as DECnet?
ref: No and no. It's DECnet only, and it isn't X windows. You run DECwindows as supplied on DEC systems, and your PC is just a display server. It takes over the whole machine, leaving no room for anything else. Wants 2MB or more to run well; 640KB barely limps along swapping disk. Marketing, as usual.
replies:
Note that PC DECwindows is available in the current version of
PCSA (2.2), although it is not as good.  v3.0 uses extended or
expanded memory, there are 286 and 386 specific versions, it
works wonderfully as long as you have a couple of megabytes of
memory minimum (barely works with 640KB and disk swapping, okay
at 1MB with some extended memory, and great with +2MB memory),
only uses DECnet (as part of PCSA software) and is not Xwindows.
The last point simply means that you run windows as supplied
on DEC systems, which is DECwindows.  You are only a server
(display).  It completely takes control of your PC, there is
no space left for anything else.

subject: /etc/killall, what is it?
q: What is /etc/killall on our Apollo? It seems to kill all of a user's processes, and as root it kills everything but init. Is that right?
ref: It's the System V killall, which kills all active processes not part of the shutdown procedure, default signal 9. Only the super-user is supposed to run it, but yours is mode 555, so anybody can. Read your manuals, and complain to the vendor about that.
replies:
Straight from sys5.3 man page:

=======================================

     killall - kill all active processes

SYNOPSIS
     /etc/killall [ signal ]

DESCRIPTION
     killall uses /etc/shutdown to kill all active processes not directly
     related to the shutdown procedure.

     killall terminates all processes with open files so that the mounted file
     systems are freed and can be unmounted.

     killall sends signal (see kill[1]) to all processes that are not part of
     the above group of exclusions.  If you do not specify signal, the default
     signal - 9 - is used.

FILES
     /etc/shutdown

SEE ALSO
     shutdown(1M), kill(1), ps(1)
     signal(2)

NOTE
     Only a super-user can run killall.
            ^^^^^^^^^^

However, I could run this program as a regular user. The default permission
is 555 in our system. Wonder why...

It is not the first time that someone discover an undocumented program
that happens to be dangerous. I suggest that every such program be considered
suspect and that we ask the software provider what does those programs are
doing there. Are they trapdoor ones ? Do their lawyers will provide compensationif any wrongdoing happens because of those ? Remember, they do not want to ship
perl with domain/os because they fear etc. But at the same time, they provide
us with undesirable nasty pests.

Just say no to undocumented programs, ask for the source!

subject: landmark & SI speed test, are they real ????
q: Are the Landmark and SI speed tests a perfect measure of a PC's performance? My Gateway 386 20MHz scored lower than an advertised competitor and I wonder why.
ref: No. Any benchmark only reflects a program with one particular mix of instructions, and it's only as good as the designer's choice of mix. Norton's SI is infamous for this, did a poor job, and exaggerates the performance of non-8088 machines. Ads quoting it are marketing noise.
replies:
$Has anybody ever tried using landmark speed test or si speed test  ???
$Are they the perfect measurement of your system's perfomance ?? I am using

   No.  Any benchmarks, and Norton's SI is infamous for this, will only
accurately reflect the performance of the computer when executing a program
made up of a particular mixture of instructions.  How well the benchmark
reflects reality is determined by how well the designer chose the mixture
of instructions to include in the benchmark.  Norton apparently did a
poor job; it exaggerates the performance of non-8088 machines.

ref: Wrong, the basic A2000 has just one built-in floppy. You need the optional A2090 controller card, about $399 list, with ST506 and SCSI connectors. Check the list of drives known to work with it first, since SCSI isn't universal yet. Or buy the bridgecard for PC-side disks.
replies:
Right now, you can purchase an A2090 hard disk controller card, suggested
list is $399, and it is a DMA controller with 2 ST506 interfaces, and
SCSI (50 and 25 pin connectors).  Then you simply open PC World magazine...
and buy one of the million third party hard disk drives... :-)

	Paul.

I sense confusion.  The basic A2000 comes with a single built-in floppy.
The *optional* A2090 hard-disk controller card supports both ST506/412
disk drives and floppy drives.  If you go for the bridgecard, you can also
add hardcards or other disk controller/drive combinations on the PC bus
side of things.

Warning: be sure to check the list of drives known to work with the A2090
controller that is included in the package.  SCSI drives are not quite
universal yet, and it would be unpleasant to be stuck with a drive and
controller that don't talk to each other...

subject: Survival in Rolemaster
q: How do you keep characters alive in Rolemaster, given how deadly the critical tables are?
ref: Several ways. Have a healer in the party, who can live through nasty crits with spells. Or give out Fate Points, one per level up to three, each negating a crit. Or just warn players how lethal combat is and run non-combat adventures. Anyone dumb enough to lose a fight deserves it.
replies:
Simple.  Having one healer in the party makes everyone in it immortal
(assuming he's smart and goes for spells almost exclusively.  By fifth level
he can routinely live through punctured hearts and such!  and if he got
Transerral, then he can take anybody elses punctured heart onto himself and cureit.  oh this is inconvenient in battle.  I have a player who really enjoys
being this masocistic(sadistic? I always get the two mixed up)  and I love
it because I can be as nasty as I want without discouraging the PC's too much.
Only on the rare occasion that someones brain gets fried or something does
he actually die.  I also limit the transferral spells to working only on `kind'
, humans, elves, etc.  So my spell-users familiars tend to die on occasion.

I have been playing Rolemaster for about 2 years with this GM who
has this system of Fate Points.  The Fate Point system involes using
a Fate Point to negate a crit, any type of crit - including a ESF or
anyother damage giving circumstances.  The Character gains a Fate
Point every level gain, with a maximum of three.  Thus a player can't
have three, say at fourth level, and then go up to fifth and expect
to then have four to use.  These Fate Points are gone after their use
and can only be replaced by going up a level, one at a time.

 When the player uses the Fate Point, the concussion damage still
happens, if appropriate, and thus the player survives a major
injury or death.

 This works for our group, so maybe it will work for your group.

I hope this helps,
Tracy

********************************************************************

RPGA Network - Role Playing Game Association Network
               ( The right formula for gaming entusiasts )

I have a very simple system for keeping the characters alive.  I don't
worry about it.  I warn the players before the game starts how dangerous
the combat system is (giving examples) and then run non-combat oriented
adventures.  Anyone dumb enough to pick a fight that they can lose
deserves the consequences.  8-)

I've found, IMHO, that most good role-players will avoid combat anyway
given a choice.  The only people I need nursemaid are those raised on a
non-lethal system like AD&D, who don't understand that if someone points
a crossbow at you and says "Freeze!" you freeze.

	-kitten

subject: Question about MIDI (guitar related)
q: How can I use several guitar preamps, MIDI delays and analog effects together through MIDI, switching the signal path around? I want a system that is easy to change over the years.
ref: If your MIDI preamps support MIDI mapping, wire them in line and pre-program patch numbers so the unwanted ones are bypassed. For non-MIDI gear with footswitch jacks, try the MIDI Octopus from Scholz R&D: 8 switches, up to 99 patches. Nobody makes MIDI power amp switching. Get a MIDI foot controller.
replies:
If you have several MIDI preamps which support MIDI mapping (that is
if you can afford more than one :-), you should be able to wire them
up in-line and pre-program patch numbers such that the ones you don't
want will be bypassed.

For preamps and effects which don't support MIDI but have jacks for
footswitches, you might want to look at the MIDI octopus from Scholz
Research & Development.  They claim that it supports up to 8 switches
which can be pre-programmed in up to 99 patches.

As for power amps and speakers, well I don't know of any MIDI
controllable power amp or speaker select switch, but sounds like an
interesting project for some aspiring electrical engineering student. B-)

Oh, and don't forget the MIDI foot-controller---life's a hell of a lot
easier with one.

Hope this helps
-Blaise

subject: What the hell is the "K directive"???
q: My AmigaDOS Execute no longer runs my startup script and gives a "No K directive" error. How do I fix it?
ref: Put .bra { and .ket } at the top of your script. AmigaDOS uses < and > as default brackets, which collides with redirection like >NIL:. This comes up every week, and it belongs in the FAQ.
replies:
Put the following lines at the top of your script:

.bra {
.ket }

The problem is that AmigaDOS (in its ininite wisdom) uses the < and > as its
default brackets for things like variable names etc..  This is fine unless you
have some redirection in your script (i.e. command >NIL:). and things get a bit
confusing for ADos.

**NOTE** I think this point should be in the FAQ!!!!! I had this problem, and
hit my head against a wall for a week until someone told me the answer.  I have
since seen it about half a dozen times since then (in the past 2 months!).

subject: Alternate Terminal apps?
q: I dial in from my NeXT to Wyse 60 terminals and need 43 lines and a bigger font. Terminal doesn't do that. Is there a way to get more lines and larger fonts?
ref: Resize the terminal window, log in, set term to vt100, and run stty rows with your line count, say 43. Change the font size with the font panel in 2.0, or dwrite Terminal NXFixedPitchFontSize nn in 1.0. Not exactly rocket science.
replies:
There should be no problem for that. e.g. on our SUNs I do the
following to get a nice big window remotly:

I resize my terminal window, log in with kermit, and then when at the
shell prompt, I do the following:

% set term=vt100
% stty rows 66

where 66 happens to be the number of lines that I'm using. So you
would have to resize the terminal window to 43 lines and use 43
instead of 66. There might be some different commands on the WYSE, but
there should be no problem in principle.

The font size you can alter with the font panel in 2.0 and with the
dwrite command in 1.0 (if I remember correctly like that):

% dwrite Terminal NXFixedPitchFontSize nn

where nn is the point size.

subject: TCP/IP and WIN3.0
q: I can't get ftp and telnet to work twice under Windows 3.0. The first window works, but after I exit and try again I get a Cannot Attach Init Error. Any ideas?
ref: Your telnet is a TSR that unloads itself whenever it sees the host connection break. Start a TCP/IP session under WIN3 and log out, and the TSR is gone, so you can't start another. Read what your TSR actually does before blaming Windows.
replies:
**stuff deleted**
I'm not sure about the ftp program, but telnet is a TSR that unloads itself
whenever it detects a break in the connection to the host. Thus if you load
telnet, then load WIN3 and run a TCP/IP terminal session (logging out of the
host when finished or otherwise breaking the connection), you will not be
able to initiate another TCP/IP host session from within WIN3 because telnet
is gone.

Two possibilities, the first being by far most likely:

1) you must tell mountd to use the '-n' option in sun4:/usr/etc/inetd.conf
since Apollo NFS can not use privileged ports.

2) the mount point already exists on the Apollo (I think the error
message is different for this though).

ref: Signal handling is the big issue with child processes, and plain Xlib gives you nothing for it. XView's Notifier handles it well and works independently of XView. The XView programmer's guide covers it. Xt works similarly, so extrapolate.
replies:
I discuss this rather extensively in the XView programmer's guide
(which happens to be Volume 7 of the O'Reilly series on X programming).
Unfortunately, it is rather notifier-intensive rather than general
enough to be applicable to any X application.  However, since the
notifier does many things similarly to the way Xt does things, you
could extrapolate the information and devise a way to do it in Xt.

there is nothing built into Xlib to do signal handling.  Whenever
you have child processes around, signal handling becomes a very
big issue.  This is a great win for XView since its Notifier does

so you don't have to use XView to use the Notifier.  The book shows

doing just plain old Xlib programming using the notifier, but again,
this should not be too

subject: BSMPT envelope
q: Could somebody please send me an example of a BSMTP envelope?
ref: It's plain SMTP commands in a file: HELO with your host, MAIL FROM, one or more RCPT TO lines, DATA, the body, a lone period on a line ending in CR/LF, then QUIT. Optional TICK and VERB lines go before MAIL FROM. Fields work just like Internet SMTP, so read the RFC.
replies:
OK, here's one.

HELO OREGON1.UOREGON.EDU
MAIL FROM: <556@oregon1.uoregon.edu>
RCPT TO: <costigan@cscma.dec.com>
RCPT TO: <user@node.domain>
DATA
                .
                .
      <mail body goes here>
		.
		.
.<crlf>			; note: period followed by CR/LF pair
QUIT

Fields are defined exactly like the Internet SMTP protocol. There are
two optional field (TICK <nnn> and VERB <ON | OFF> that can be
included BEFORE the MAIL FROM line, but are used only when the sender
requires a transcript of the session returned from the processing
agent.

Drop me a note if you need more info.

subject: NeXT dimension video output
q: How do I get the NeXT Dimension board to send an NTSC signal out so I can record a live demo on video tape? I heard a program keeps the mouse centered on the NTSC screen.
ref: That's ScreenScape, delivered with the ND board, found in /NextDeveloper/Demos. It sends a 640x480 portion of the screen to the video output, tracking the mouse or frozen in place. The whole screen can't go out, since there's no hardware to resample it. For that, buy a high-res RGB to NTSC encoder, and bring money.
replies:
A program called "ScreenScape" which is delivered with the ND board
does what you want.  It outputs a portion of the screen (640x480)
to the video output ports.  You can either let this output window
track the current mouse cursor (tracking mode), or you can freeze
the position of the output window anywhere within the screen.
The ScreenScape output window is invisible on the ND display itself
so it won't interfere with the megapix image.

Another way is to build in NXLiveVideoView into your program.
I don't know what you would buy by doing this.

There is no way to output the whole screen to the video output, however,
as this requires resampling/resizing from 1120x832 (?) down to
640x480.  ND lacks hardware to do this in real time.
If you need to do this, you have to use a high-res RGB to NTSC
encoder.  One example is RGB/Videolink 1400AX, which lists at
$15,995 (RGB is in Berkeley, I think -- No I have no stake in the
company.  I used this box once and it did a good job.).

Yes, you can use the demo /NextDeveloper/Demos/ScreenScape. It will output a
rectangle from the screen to the video output ports on your ND board.  With it,
you can adjust various parameters on how the rectangle tracks your mouse.

subject: Software Carousel and the PC
q: Has anyone used Software Carousel for running multiple programs and switching between them on a PC? Any comments?
ref: It's solid and nearly bulletproof, with little overhead. It swaps the whole program image out to extended RAM and brings in the next, so it's not multitasking, and there's no cut and paste without Magic Mirror. If you can live with that, fine. Don't expect miracles.
replies:
Some people use Software Carousel where I work, and over all, it's quite bullet
proof. The toughest test I've ever seen was where we had two databases open, a
network database open, network mail, a compile and a Procomm session. It didn't
crash. Works quite nicely with very little overhead!

-->Chris

I have used Software Carousel for almost two years and find it very
useful and well-written.  I have 640K + 2MB of RAM.  Using Software
Carousel, I can switch between applications very rapidly.  The program
basically writes out the current program memory image to the 2MB of
RAM and swaps in the new program from the extended RAM.  Note that it
is not a multi-tasking system.  Programs don't continue to "run" while
swapped out.  It also doesn't provide a way to cut from one program
and paste to another, but Softlogic has another program, Magic Mirror,
that will work with Software Carousel to do this.  If you don't need
real multi-tasking, I highly recommend Software Carousel.

subject: Trouble killing processes in Sy
q: Why can't I kill some processes? Are those stuck processes the "zombie" ones, and what does a kill signal actually do to a process?
ref: Not zombies, any idiot knows that. Zombies are already dead and just hold the PID until the parent waits. Stuck ones are in uninterruptible sleep. Kill sets a signal and, for an interruptible sleeper, makes it runnable so it sees the signal soon. Multiple kills on a hung process do nothing.
replies:
Correct.  Zombies merely hold the PID until their parents do a wait()
for them or until their respective parents die causing them to be
inherited by init() (PID 1).  They need to wait for the wait() so that
the exit() status can be returned to the parent's wait().

Correct.  Thus sending multiple signals to a process hung in a system call
or otherwise not getting cycles doesn't do anything.

It does a bit more.  If the affected process is sleeping interruptably,
it is made runnable and has its priority raised to PUSER if it is now
lower.  If it is actively running, its killing itself arranges for an
`AST' (no not the Minix AST :-) ) so that it will be sure to see the
signal.

In other words, the affected process is arranged to be run soon, so that
the signal will happen.

subject: CHX, CHD in OS9 startup?
q: Is there a simple way to put chd and chx commands in the OS9 startup file so their effect persists after the startup script finishes, given that scripts run in subshells?
ref: Start a shell from inside the startup file, and redirect its standard input. That works, though if you pop out with an EOF you land back in the startup file in an unchanged shell. Otherwise use tsmon, or fuss with init and sysgo. RTFM.
replies:
Starting a shell from inside the startup file will work.  You can
change directories and start a shell but be sure to redirect standard
input for it.  The only problem I remember having with this approach is
that if you pop out of the shell (with an EOF) you get back to the startup
file and wind up in a shell that hasn't been chd'd.

Using tsmon is another trick.  The password file lets you specify directories
and an initial program to execute (typically shell).

If you want to go back to the beginning you can fuss with init and
(perhaps) sysgo.  The default directories and program for the system
are given in init.  Sysgo looks at init and gets things going.  On my 6809
system I use sysgo to change the execution directory and system disk from
/d0 to /h0 after the system is mostly booted.  OS9boot is on /d0, but
everything else (CMDS and startup) is on /h0.

Peter Dibble

RFC-959, section 5.1, "Minimum Implementation", Page 43.  The
mandatory commands are user, quit, port, type, mode, stru, retr, stor,
and noop.  So an implementation without list and nlst is legal, just
not very useful.
						don provan
						donp@novell.com

My recollection (and it was more than 15 years ago) was that as we
designed the FTP we imagined that there might be read-only file transfer
sites (e.g. a card reader) and write-only sites (e.g. a line printer)
that one would want to do FTP to (especially using the "three party FTP"
feature), so we should not _require_ both STOR and RETR.  I guess if we
weren't going to require those we didn't see the point in requiring
anything else.

Alex McKenzie

subject: modem answering at wrong speed
q: My 2400 baud Hayes-compatible modems on SCO Xenix sometimes get stuck answering at 1200 baud after a 1200 call, even though getty sends 2400. Is it getty or the modem, and how do I fix it?
ref: It's the modem, a very common problem with these: it never resets after a 1200 connection. If yours can reset when DTR drops, set that. Otherwise write a wrapper around getty that resets the modem each time, and fork a child to talk to the tty. Cheap modems.
replies:
this seems to be a very common problem with 2400 baud hayes compatible
modems, hence the posting.

the problem arises whenever a connection is received at 1200 baud and
the modem is not reset.  some of the modems have a setting which allows
the modem to be reset whenever DTR drops.  i'm unfortunate enough to not
fall in that catagory, so i know of what i speak ;-(

if you modem does not have a command option to reset the modem on hangup,
and you are equally unfortunate to have the 1200 baud problem, there is
nothing you can do outside of resetting the modem on each hangup.

the simple fix is to write a wrapper around getty and have it reset
the modem on each invocation.  just a word to the wise, you have to
fork a child to do the actual talking to the tty port because the
process group will get messed up.  not enough room to explain it here,
just trust me.

if you are unfortunate enough to be stuck with micropoor unix and its
perverse getty, you are in real trouble.  i understand insta

I have had similar problems. A partial victory might be achieved by setting
your modems to reset on a dtr change. I.E. ATD0 I believe. Thus, when the
getty drops the line (dtr low) the modem performs an ATZ on itself and
resets back to 2400 baud. This has worked somewhat well on my machine but
sometimes the modem just loops on itself and continually resets for hours
until someone turns it off. I am using a Hayes 2400 external on an
Altos 2086 running Xenix. If someone else has a more elegant solution
I'd sure like to hear it.

subject: How do I disable Mouse Input?
q: How can I temporarily disable all mouse input to the system in Windows while leaving keyboard input and buffering enabled? EnableHardwareInput() only works if I want to disable both.
ref: Do a SetCapture so every mouse message goes to your window, then just ignore them there. ReleaseCapture puts things back, and the window needn't even be visible. Or hook WH_GETMESSAGE and turn mouse messages into WM_NULL, though that's untested. Sigh, read the SDK docs.
replies:
You could install a WindowsHook of type WH_GETMESSAGE (since
all user input is posted and must be retreived with
GetMessage() or PeekMessage()).  If you want mouse input
disabled, turn the mesage into something innocuous like
WM_NULL.  I have never tried this but it *should* work.

cheers - Paul Bonneau.

The program that wants to disable the mouse could do a SetCapture.
This will send all th mouse messages to the specified window.  There
you can do whatever you want with it (like ignore it).  ReleaseCapture
sets everything back.  The window that sets the capture doesn't
has to be visible.

subject: Password Program!
q: I wrote a Pascal program that checks a password when you log in to a PC, but you can break out with Ctrl-C. How do I stop that?
ref: Write a keyboard interrupt handler that checks whether Ctrl is down and passes everything else along. So no Ctrl while typing a password. Big loss. Or make the whole password program an interrupt handler that intercepts all keyboard input until the right keys come, so Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break do nothing.
replies:
...
A simple solution would be to write an interrupt handler to
check if Ctrl is being pressed.  If it is not, just pass the
input to the regular interrupt handler.  So, you can't use
Ctrl while entering your password.  That shouldn't be a
problem.

If anyone would like to see how this is done, e-mail to me
and I'll get to it tomorrow, then post the solution.

Another thing that can be done is to make the password
program an interrupt handler.  It unloads itself once the
right keys are pressed - otherwise it intercepts all keyboard
input.  Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break have no effect on this type of
program.

subject: Opening one window and then another but still using the first window
q: In my IRIS program I open one window, then a second, and I need to keep using the first. I put the second window to sleep to hold it open, but that delays everything. How do I do this?
ref: Stop discarding the return value of winopen. It gives you an integer ID for each window, so save it and call winclose on the right one when done. Forget to close in a loop and you'll dump core, and there's a window limit too. RTFM.
replies:
Actually, your question sould read, "How do I close the second window
without closing the first one also?", right?

Don't discard the return value of winopen; it returns an integer
which uniquely identifies each window.  Then, you can use 'winclose(win1);'

Try:
win1 = winopen("...");
...bla...bla...
winclose(win1);

By the way, I forgot to issue a winclose in a long running loop like
the one you have and witnessed my program silently dumping core.
The error  was cryptic enough, try not there, so that
the cure was not obvious :-),  but I eventually found it.

Also, isn't there a limit of 64 open windows?  Whatever the number
there is a limit, so utilizing 'winclose' for *busy* programs is
helpful.

subject: Forcing /bin/sh in a script under V/386 3.2 Korn shell
q: How can I force a script to be interpreted by /bin/sh instead of the Korn shell under System V/386 3.2? The colon trick works for csh, but not for ksh, and #! /bin/ksh doesn't work either.
ref: System V has no #! support, unlike BSD. The best substitute, swiped from Perl v2's Configure script, is this first line: (alias) >/dev/null 2>&1 && (exec /bin/sh $0 ${1+"$@"}). Ugly, yes, but that's what you get for running a vendor-mangled csh.
replies:
On a BSD Unix, one could put "#! /bin/sh" at the start of your script
and it would work. Unfortunately, System V doesn't have this (and
worse yet, your vendor has gratuitusly hacked csh so many scripts will
break under it), so the best substitute (swiped from Perl v2's
Configure script) is:

	(alias) >/dev/null 2>&1 && (exec /bin/sh $0 ${1+"$@"})

subject: Help with Tandon drive
q: My $5 Tandon full height 80 track diskette drive gives "Drive 0: Seek failure" at boot, though it grinds at power-up. How do I get it working?
ref: Old drives that sit unused often have the oil on the head guides dried up into glue. With power off, put light oil on the two polished rods and slide the head assembly back and forth a few dozen times. Oil the motor bearings too. Basic maintenance, kid.
replies:
i've had similar problems with old drives, and drives that have not been in use
for a length of time. quite often the problem is that the oil on the guides
along which the read/write heads move dries up and acts like glue, preventing
the heads from moving in and out. the solution: put some light grade oil on the
guides (usually two polished metal rods, about two 1.5" long, running from
front to back of the drive), then, with power removed, move the head assembly
back and forth a few dozen times to work in the oil. it might also be an idea
to oil the bearings in all the motors as well.
  to get at all this stuff in the tandon drive, it is necessary to remove the
board on the top of the drive; two screws, one on each side, near the front of
the board, you only need to unplug the plugs at the front of the board (that go
to the heads), and hinge it at the back. good luck.

Robert Rozee  (ROZEE@ELEC.CANTERBURY.AC.NZ)
EEE Department, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand.

and...

subject: Leaving the hard disk on continuously
q: If I leave my PC on all the time and park the hard disk heads, how do I unpark the disk? Is there a utility? Should I leave the monitor on too?
ref: You don't unpark. The next disk access moves the heads back on its own. Parking just puts them over an unused area. As for leaving things on, that's a religion; I'd switch off the monitor at night. Don't fret.
replies:
No, no.  The next time you issue any instruction to the disk,
it will unpark itself.  In fact, the PARK utility I have brings
the CPU to a grinding halt after it parks the disk, precisely
to avoid this happening!

I would not place bets on leaving the disk running all the time,
though I know plenty of people who do just that.  I am just a little
uncomfortable with the idea that some environmental problem may
crop up while I'm away (like jack-hammering on the floor below --
don't laugh, this happened to me).  Also momentary power failures
(e.g. during electrical storms) can make it go bonkers (you will have
to reboot anyway, since your controller will have gotten confused).

I wonder if there are some authoritative engrg. types out there who
can address this issue as something other than a question of "religion".

Probably, you should just switch it off.  Transients won't be any good
for the things you can't see, too!

Parking the heads just means moving them over a part of the disk that
you don't care about (a place where you don't have any data stored -- usually
the extreme inside (or outside) of the platter).  This is done so that if the
drive is disturbed in some obscure (or not so obscure) manner, and the heads
somehow try to change some data, the data will be garbage anyway, and not
something that you care about (usually the heads are "parked" over a cylinder
which is not in the area for storage, so there's really no data there at all).

	You don't need to worry about unparking the heads: just use the drive
as you normally would (pretent it's not parked), and the heads will return to
the storage area to read data -- it just takes them slightly longer to do so.

							Anand.

Your next disk access should unpark the heads. There are several PD
programs which park the heads after N seconds of non-use. I don't use
any TSRs anymore, but I test one at some time and it seemed to work.

  I definitely wouldn't cycle power on the monitor during the day, I
would shut it down over a weekend (unless you're going to use it). I
personally power down my monitor every night, but the rationale for this
is primarily that this particular type of monitor has been know to burst
into flames at out site. The one I'm using has burned twice, although it
hasn't actually had flames coming out of the case yet.

  Mono monitors may be more sensitive to phosphor burn than color and
should be turned down when not in use. There are several programs which
do this after N sec on non-use.

subject: Nice value worthless??? / Renice?
q: Why does nice seem worthless on my 386 running System V, when it worked on a VAX 11/730 with BSD? Is there a renice for Sys V?
ref: Nice affects only CPU scheduling. On the slow 730 you waited for the CPU, so nice mattered. On your 386 you're waiting on a slow disk and swapping with little RAM, so it does nothing. Niceness doesn't control disk queue priority. Look for renice in a UNIX source archive.
replies:
A 730 is *so* slow that you were probably waiting for the CPU most of
the time, and the nice value determines how much CPU you got, so it
determined responsiveness.

A timesharing 780 was usually like this too - a bit faster CPU, but
usually pretty fast disks and often several controllers, so you were
still mostly waiting for the CPU.  But on the Compaq, you've got a
processor that is faster relative to the disk.  So you're waiting for
the disk most of the time, the CPU runs whatever it can whenever it can
and still has lots of idle time, and nice just doesn't have any effect
- every process gets as much CPU as it can use.

What you really want is for niceness to control the priority of
requests in the disk queue.  But it doesn't.

Nice affects the scheduler priority.  It does not deal very well with the
lower level system performance issues like "do I have more than 1 process
able to run", etc.  This is important with a machine with small RAM and
a slow disk.  Swapping or page faulting a running process blows it out
for approx. that 40ms of drive seek time.  No RAM with a large make (read
at least 6 processes that must run to do your compile) can make for swap
or DPVM thrash VERY easily.  If your vi is paged out, it will not run until
the page it needs make it through the diskIO queue, which can seem like
forever.

In summation, if a job is IO or memory (or both) bound, don't expect nice,
(which is really affects CPU advantage) to do squat for you.

One of the UNIX source groups has renice in its archives.  Look there.

subject: Which mail routing program do I need?
q: We have several mail readers (mailx, elm, mush) on our 3B2s, but the mailing list aliases are only in mailx's global rc file. Do I need sendmail, smail, pathalias or uumail to make aliases work for all of them?
ref: You want smail. Either 2.5 or 3.x will run on a 3B2 and use /usr/lib/aliases, and 3.x does a fair impersonation of sendmail. Skip uumail, it's just a crippled smail 2.5. If aliases fail, your install is probably botched or the aliases file isn't sorted. Read the docs.
replies:
Which smail?  Smail 2.5 works just fine with /usr/lib/aliases.  However,
if you've not installed smail quite right, your mailers may not
invoke it properly.  I suppose that goes ditto for smail 3.x (you
don't really need smail 3).  Smail 2.5 does not permit mail-to-file
or mail-to-pipe in the aliases file - Jon Zeeff wrote a program
called lmail which can do it in conjunction with smail.  "deliver"
will also do that.  I can send you a copy of a fixed version of lmail
if you want.

uumail is a less functional version of smail 2.5 - don't bother.

Pathalias is useful with smail too - smail has support for the pathalias
map file.

You should be able to use either smail2.5  or smail3.21.  They are very
different programs but either should compile and run on the 3B2.
 Smail2.5 only does alias and forward file lookup - you need to use
other programs for local and remote delivery.  If this is what you
tried and it didn't work, perhaps you have something configured wrong
or your aliases file wasn't sorted.  Some patches have been posted to
fix a bug in finding the last entry in the aliases file, though.
 Smail3.x does a fair impersonation of sendmail, including SMTP (optional),
forwarding to files and pipes, and handling most of sendmail's command
line options.  It's a bigger program with more options to configure, but
it is also more versatile and robust.
 Either version would normally be installed as /bin/rmail in a sysV
environment with a small front-end program installed as /bin/mail which
decides (based on the command line) whether to run the old /bin/mail for
reading mail or smail for sending.

subject: Solid State PA's
q: Why are early 1980s solid state rigs derated on 10 meters, like 200W PEP down to 160W PEP?
ref: All transistors lose gain as frequency rises. Rule of thumb is an fT of ten times the operating frequency, but big power transistors are hard to build for high frequency. A maker could save money with a 250MHz part instead of 300MHz and just sacrifice some gain on 10 meters.
replies:
All transistors exhibit declining gain with increasing frequency.  The general
rule of thumb is to select a transistor with an "f-sub-T" (the frequency at
which the gain of the transistor is 1) of 10 times the maximum operating
frequency, so that the gain will be high enough that the circuit around the
transistor determines the stage gain.  However, since (big) power transistors
are hardest to design for very high frequency work, a manufacturer could
generally save quite a bit of money by using a transistor with an fT of, say,
250MHz instead of 300MHz, and just sacrificing a little power gain on 10 meters.

might see some of that "more" with Apple II developers, but it probably
won't happen unless there are major *direction* changes with the Apple II

subject: CLK_TCK vs. CLOCKS_PER_SEC
q: The POSIX sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK) is supposed to return CLK_TCK, said to be defined by ANSI C, but I only find CLOCKS_PER_SEC in the Dec 1988 ANSI C draft. Did the name change? Which is correct?
ref: CLK_TCK is the right one for POSIX, but it never made it into ANSI C. It comes from the /usr/group 1984 standard. Define it in <time.h> under _POSIX_SOURCE. Early ANSI drafts misused the name; CLOCKS_PER_SEC is the ANSI thing. Sigh, standards committees.
replies:
CLK_TCK is correct, but as you note it turned out to not be part of ANSI C.
POSIX implementations should define it in the shared (between POSIX and ANSI C)
header <time.h>, under control of _POSIX_SOURCE (so that it is not visible in
pure ANSI C mode).

Several drafts of X3.159 had used CLK_TCK incorrectly where CLOCKS_PER_SEC is
now used.  CLK_TCK really originated with the /usr/group 1984 Standard and was
intended for the sort of use that 1003.1-1988 assigns for it, not for the sort
of use that X3.159-1989 assigns for CLOCKS_PER_SEC.  This was realized in the
final stages of preparation of X3.159, after 1003.1 had already finished their
standard.

noticed this problem before it was too late for 1003.1 to fix it in their
document.  However, by following my recommendation above the damage is limited

subject: 9600 baud transfer problems
q: I get errors transferring files at 9600 baud between my ST and a UNIX box, with chopped lines in captures and xmodem and kermit failing to sync. Can I fix this without dropping to 4800 baud?
ref: You need handshaking at 9600. Check that the Unix side honors XON/XOFF, since Flash can't keep up and sends an XOFF when its buffer fills. If the Unix box ignores it, characters are lost. RTS/CTS is flaky on the Atari. Gulam or Uniterm may also behave better.
replies:
Does your *NIX box respond to XON/XOFF (DC1/DC3)?  Flash, for one,
can't keep up with character input at 9600 baud, and will send an XOFF
when the buffer gets nearly full.  If the *NIX box ignores it, the
buffer will overflow and characters will be lost.

Alternatively, you could enable hardware handshaking (Ready-to-send
[RTS]/Clear-to-send [CTS]), but in my own experience these don't work
properly on the Atari side.  You *will* need some sort of handshaking
at 9600 baud, in any event.

subject: tty2a trouble - Please help me!
q: On a Dell 386/25 running SCO Xenix, tty1a works but enabling tty2a gives "getty can't open tty2a : err. 6". I also have two Intelliport boards. Any idea?

interrupt during POST. If so it disables the 2nd port. This means that
when you reboot the early 325, you must first disable the port, or it
will see it self, get confused, and turn itself off. Later versions
fixed this, I'm told, and it isn't in the new ones which set the CMOS

try to avoid it, or for a buck you can run a switch out the back,
connect to the reset (RST) jumper on the motherboard behind the cache
controller, and *after* you shutdown clean, pop the switch and reboot
that way.

subject: Animating Cursor

ref: It's in the MPW 3.x manual, volume 1, appendix F. RotateCursor loads the acur resource, a list of curs IDs, and steps through them each call. It allocates in the A5 globals, so it's tricky from a DA or XCMD. Spinning cursors are a poor progress indicator anyway.
replies:
It's described in the MPW 3.x manual, volume 1, appendix F (pp525-30).

list of IDs for curs resources, and with each subsequent call, increments (or
decrements) a counter by a specified amount, moving through the list of
cursors. To do this, it allocates space in the A5 globals, so use of this
routine from a DA or XCMD is tricky. I have previously posted an XCMD which
does this; it should still be in the sumex-aim archive info-mac/card/xcmd
directory as spinning-cursor or such. If you can't find it, mail me and I'll
send it to you.

that successful for me as a way of convincing users I still love them while my
code grinds away for more than 3-4 seconds. An indicator box which moves at
least once a second seems better tolerated, as the user has some idea how far

subject: Comparing screen values in Oracle
q: We're building a banking transaction form in SQL*Forms with Oracle, and a trigger compares one screen value to another. Does Oracle permit this? We're having trouble with it.
ref: Of course it works. Use a select 'x' from dual where :blk.val1 = :blk.val2, and the trigger fails if they differ. Gotcha: SQL*Forms compares number fields as strings, so '7' beats '11'. Wrap both fields in to_number. You'd know that if you'd tried it properly.
replies:
You should have mentioned the way in which you compare, because it
should of course work. Whatever may be the cause in your case, the
following works (assuming the two values are in one block called blk
and named val1 and val2 resp):

select 'x' from dual
where :blk.val1 = :blk.val2

The trigger fails if the values are different.

I think the trigger mechanism using SQL is quite powerful; I built an
entire application and didn't have to resort to host language user
exits.

        Leo.

I have had a similar problem when the fields were number fields.  It
appears that SQL*Forms does string compares even on number fields.

If you have a block called blk and number fields called fld1 and fld2 and
fld1 has the value 7 and fld2 has the value 11 then the statement

select 'x' from dual
where :blk.fld1 < :blk.fld2

will fail because the string '7 ' is greater than '11'.

To fix this do the following,

select 'x' from dual
where to_number(:blk.fld1) < to_number(:blk.fld2)

This should properly do the number compare.  That's how it works on
our Oracle at least.  Sorry if a previous article without the ':blk'
references in the statements got into the world, I tried to cancel it.

subject: How do I transfer files through a telenet connection?
q: How do I transfer files with Xmodem, Kermit or Vtrans through a Telenet connection? The transfer fails in the first packet.
ref: Packet networks add delays beyond the timeouts of simple protocols like Xmodem. Use a windowing protocol instead, such as Zmodem or Ymodem, with rz/sz on both ends. For Kermit, check that the parity settings match on both sides. Basic stuff.
replies:
Well, you are out of luck, as you suspect.

Packet networks introduce delays which are in excess of the timeouts
on simple protocols.  Increasing the timeouts would work, but at
tremendous (5:1 or greater) cut in throughput.

The only protocols which will work are of the windowing variety --
like the X.25 used internally by the nets themselves.  (Windowing
means keeping track of a list of packets which have been sent but not
acknowledged yet, and marking them off/resending as necessary.  There
are many flavors with various sophistication about this).

You might like to try Chuck Forsberg's YAM protocols -- he recently
posted a set of sources for them in C.  Either Ymodem or Zmodem (don't
have doc handy...) is an upgrade to Xmodem which has windowing.
You'll need to compile and run them on both your host and home
machine; must have matching set.

Clive Steward
Resident Visitor (That's what AT&T calls contract workers and consultants,
whatever field you happen to be working in.)

Your Kermit problem may be caused by the two programs having different
parity settings.  Check the parity settings on both programs to make sure
they agree.  It is also possible, but unlikely, that one of the other
myriad Kermit parameters may need tuning.  Normally, Kermit works over
Telenet, alebit quite slowly because of the short block length and high
overhead.

XMODEM will not work unless all 256 code combinations pass through the
network, and the parameters used for your session may be "eating" some of
them.  The same problems may apply to the other protocol you tried, which
may be an XMODEM mutant.

Assuming that the interface between your host system (presumably Unix) and
Telenet is not stripping the 8th bit, you should be able to use the rz/sz
programs posted to net.sources a while ago for ZMODEM file transfers with
your PC.  ZMODEM escapes the characters and sequences that Telenet uses
for flow control and supervision, and the streaming technique gives high
throughput with Te

subject: How to detect if printer is on-line?
q: How can a program determine the printer status, such as off-line or out of paper, especially on an ImageWriter?
ref: Printer-dependent only, no PrGeneral. The dumb ImageWriter I doesn't wire the out-of-paper signal, so all you get is checking CTS. The ImageWriter II is smart: get the manual, find the control codes in the appendices, and query it through the serial drivers.
replies:
This may be way off base, but I believe that this can only be done in a
printer-dependant way (i.e. no PrGeneral).  That being said, I don't
believe it is possible for the 'dumb' ImageWriter I, because the out of paper
signal is available only on pins not connected (you can check CTS to see
if it is ready or not, but that is the best you can do).  The ImageWriter II
is a 'smart' printer, so you should probably obtain a manual and look in
the appendices for the control codes (they MUST be there, at least in the
version for the Apple II series).  Then you use the serial drivers to determine
the printer status.

subject: getting machine names
q: With gethostent, gethostbyname and gethostbyaddr, a particular name like machine.eng is found by name, but it doesn't appear when I list all entries with gethostent. Why?
ref: gethostbyname and gethostbyaddr go through DNS or NIS to the nameservers. gethostent only lists what's in your /etc/hosts, or the NIS equivalent. Listing the whole Internet is Not An Option. And stop cross-posting.
replies:
Gethostbyname and gethostbyaddr are most likely using either the DNS protocol
or NIS to resolve the machine name or address by talking to Internet
nameservers.  See the man page for "named" and/or "resolver" on your system.

Gethostent is only going to be able to list the machine explicitly listed in
your /etc/hosts file (or in what NIS uses as your /etc/hosts file, if you're
using NIS).  Listing all of the files on the entire Internet is just Not An
Option.

By the way, your message probably didn't belong in comp.unix.admin, and it
certainly didn't belong in comp.unix.wizards, and you didn't really need to
post it again after you posted it the first time in only comp.unix.internals.

2. Buy a 387.

subject: Orbital Mech Tutoring (was Re: HST crazy idea)
q: Why can't the Hubble orbit be given a precession rate to follow the terminator as the Earth goes around the Sun?
ref: You'd need rotation in the plane of the ecliptic, but the precession from Earth's equatorial bulge is in the plane of the equator. At reasonable altitudes below the inner Van Allen belt, the best you get is about ten months of constant sunlight and two with short eclipses. Orbital mechanics, kid.
replies:
What you need for this is a rotation in the plane of the ecliptic, but
the precession you get from the Earth's equatorial bulge is a rotation
in the plane of the Earth's equator.  At reasonable altitudes (i.e. below
the inner Van Allen belt), the best you can do is about ten months of
constant sunlight and two with short eclipses.

subject: Password type? (was Re: Changing LaserWriter names)
q: What is the type of the exitserver password under the PostScript language standard? LaserWriters use a number but I remember DEC's LN03R using a string.
ref: exitserver isn't standard PostScript, so its semantics are only in your printer's manual. Just use 0; only DEC printers ship with anything else, and theirs is the string (LN03R) or (LPS40). Shipping a product? Don't use it at all.
replies:
The "exitserver" verb is not a standard part of the PostScript language,
even though it happens to exist in virtually all printer products to
date.  Since it is an `extension' to the language, its semantics are
not specified except in the manual for the printer that you buy.

However, only DEC printer products ship with anything other than zero
as the password.  I don't think you get a "typecheck", you just don't
exit the server loop ("invalidpassword" error, I think).

In truth, the incantation "serverdict begin <password> exitserver"
should itself be treated as a single operation, since none of
"serverdict", <password>, or "exitserver" is guaranteed to be there
(and are not, for example, in Display PostScript implementations).

But for the most part, to hack around this feature or that feature,
just use "0".  If you're shipping a product, you probably should not use
it at all.  If you have a DEC product, you already have learned, the
hard way, that your password is (LN03R) or (LPS40)

subject: Sets
q: How big should a set be in Modula-2? Wouldn't it be better if the limit were effectively unbounded?
ref: In practice it's one machine word. None of Wirth's compilers support sets bigger than BITSET, because it was done for bit-fiddling. A Modula-2 set is an image of a machine word, not an abstract data type. Call it a set if you like.
replies:
I rather believe that this was done to support bit-fiddeling in Modula-2, since
BITSETs aren't really good for anything else. None of Wirth's compilers support
sets bigger than BITSETs. In this sense, a Modula-2 set is not an abstract data
type but an image of a machine word. The question is  whether they ought  to be
called "sets".

subject: -geometry or how do I specify size and location independently?
q: How can I set the size of my xload window in .Xdefaults and the location on the command line with -geometry? The size from .Xdefaults gets ignored.
ref: The geometry resource is only a hint to the window manager. Set XLoad.width and XLoad.height in .Xdefaults instead, and keep using xload -geom -100-0 on the command line. The missing dimension comes from your defaults. RTFM.
replies:
There are.  The geometry resource is just a hint to the window manager.
This hint is also used along with the x, y, width and height resources
of the top level shell.  Depending on the type of shell being used
you can set these resources separately to the geometry resource.

What you want to specify in .Xdefaults is:

	XLoad.width: 94
	XLoad.height: 94

and still use
	xload -geom -100-0 &
etc.

This also lets you do ...
	xload -geom x300		# explicit height of 300 pixels
	xload -geom 200			# explicit width of 200 pixels
	xload -geom x300+4+4		# height = 300 @ (4,4)
with the missing dimension taken from the user defaults.

subject: Display Enhancer
q: Can the A3000's display enhancer show the 1280 modes without resolution loss? And if not, why?
ref: No. The enhancer samples one pixel every 70ns, but the 1280 modes are 15kHz with 35ns pixels. You get two pixel positions per sample, so the scan-converted display misses every other pixel. It would need a redesign. Commodore strikes again.
replies:
No.  The Display Enhancer (both the DE for the A2000 and the one built-in
on the A3000) would require a redesign to work with the 1280 x XXX resolution
modes.

   This is one of my beefs with the A3000.  Commodore spent millions of
dollars fabricating the ECS Denise with these new resolution modes, and
then does not support them with their flicker-eliminating display device.
I wish Commodore would have designed the A3000's built-in DE to support
these modes or, at the very least, designed the more expensive standalone
DE for the A2000 to support these resolution modes.

  -------------------------------------------------------------
 / Marc Barrett  -MB- | BITNET:   XGR39@ISUVAX.BITNET        /
/  ISU COM S Student  | Internet: XGR39@CCVAX.IASTATE.EDU   /
------------------------------------------------------------
\        The great thing about standards is that          /
 \       there are so many of them to choose from.       /
  ----------------------------------------------------

Haynie

No.

The display enhancer samples one pixel every 70ns, and it knows how to get out
of the way of display modes that are already at 31kHz sync rates.  The 1280
pixel modes are 15kHz, but use 35ns pixels.  So you get two pixel positions for
every one sample taken by the display enhancer, resulting in a scan-converted
display that's missing every other pixel.

subject: physmem config for 16mb DECstation 3100
q: My config file has physmem set to 8, but my DECstation 3100 has 16MB. Is that correct?
ref: No. Physmem sets the maximum memory the kernel tables support, so with 8 you only get 8M. Set it to 16, re-config, relink and boot a new kernel. Probably you're staring at the GENERIC file. RTFM, if the manual had it.
replies:
Is it possible that you're looking at a copy of the GENERIC config file?
if your system had 16 Meg at installation then the installation should have
put 16 in your host-specific config file.  physmem should be 16 if you have
16 Meg.

Hopefully all 16 Meg are being recognized by your system (i.e. are working).
How much memory do you see when you utter

csh>  uerf | grep mem

-chris

The physmem parameter is used to size the system page table , so it should be greater
than or equal to the amount of memory actually in your machine.  Other than that, it has
no effect.  When you have a chance, change physmem, re-config, relink and boot a new
kernel.

Regards,
					Frank

No, since physmem defines the maximum amount of memory that the kernel
tables are prepared to support.  With this definition of physmem, you
should only get the use of 8M, and this should show up in the boot-time
memory configuration/memory available messages.

subject: NiCd behavior
q: My 7.2V 1000mAh camcorder NiCd, with a 10 ohm 10 watt resistor across it, won't drop below about 2.2V. Is that a full discharge, and if not, how do I drain it further?
ref: Fully discharged is about 6.0 volts for a pack like that, so yours is quite dead and some cells may be reversed. To drain it harder, wire lots of 1157 car bulbs in parallel; their resistance drops as they cool, so they keep drawing current.
replies:
The 7.2 NiCads I work with are considered fully discharged when
their voltage reaches about 6.0 volts.  I imagine that your battery
is _quite_ discharged and several of the cells may even be reversed.

Keep at it. Unless you COMPLETELY kill it it will still retain memory.
You are probably at a charge region where some crystals inside are
breaking down, at about the same quantum electric level.
A friend of mine came up with an excellent way to completely
drain these things. :
Get 10 1157 dual element car light bulbs. Wire all 20 filaments in
parallel. Then, hook up heavy lead wire (try 10g or so) to appropriate
connectors to go to the battery.
The neat thing about this is that the bulbs act like variable
resistors. As the voltage across them decreases, the power decreases,
the bulb cools down. The resistance of the elements then decreases, so
the bulb still draws near the same current (loosely) Bulbs such as
1157's range from about .45 ohms cold to about 2.5 ohms hot. They
will also have no problem dissapating power (they can't burn up).
I think .045 ohms at a limit will have no problem in completely
killing the battery!
Regards,
Gordon.

subject: how long to ammend your taxes?
q: How long do I have to amend my tax return in the IRS's favor before they might consider me for an audit? I don't want to delay my refund by amending before it arrives.
ref: You get 3 years from the filing date to amend. The IRS doesn't care meanwhile; it just charges you interest on what you owe. Not amending isn't an audit trigger, though an amended return may make them look twice. Why not just wait until your taxes are done before filing? Sigh.
replies:
You have 3 years from the date you filed your tax forms  to file an ammended
form.  Either way, the IRS doesn't care (it will charge you interest on
the money you owe them, or pay you interest on the money they owe you) for
the duration.   Not ammending the form is not a basis for an audit (i.e. if
they are thinking about auditing your return, and ammendment to the form will
probably not change their mind), although an ammended return will make them
look twice at your return which probably increases your chances of getting
audited.

Why don't you just wait until your taxes are complete before you file?

subject: High-value Button capacitors: Where to get?
q: I found surplus capacitors that give 47000uF in a thimble-sized can at 5.5v, and 1.0F ones the size of an oreo. How do these things work, and where can I get more?
ref: They pack conductive powder loosely so it's full of pores, treat the surface to make a dielectric, and fill the pores with a conductor as the other electrode. That huge internal surface area is the capacitance. Series resistance is high, so they're battery-backup parts for keeping memory alive. Don't use them as filter caps, you'll cook them. Sigh.
replies:
If they're the ones I'm thinking of, they are made by taking a conductive
powder, packing it loosely so there are lots of pores, and then treating
it to make the surface a dielectric.  The powder is one electrode, and a
conductive material filling the pores is the other.  The enormous surface
area inside the pores is what gives the massive capacitance.

A consequence of this setup, however, is that internal series resistance
is quite high, which limits the applications to ones in which frequency
response is not an issue.  They are primarily battery replacements for
keeping nonvolatile memories alive.  Don't use them as filter capacitors,
they aren't built for it.  You might even overheat them.

q: My .DBF is indexed on str(invnum,4)+str(seqnum,6), and I want to SEEK on only the first part. The seek hits EOF. How do I do this in Clipper/dBase?
ref: STR pads short numbers with leading blanks, so SEEK "123" misses; you need " 123". Better: build the index with LTRIM around each STR. Or SET SOFTSEEK ON and seek str(invnum,4) + space(6), which leaves you at the first entry not less than the key. RTFM.
replies:
Unfortunately you did not specify what your SEEK command was,
however, I am going to guess what it is by looking at your INDEX
command.

The STR function takes the numeric field and if the value of this
field is LESS THAN 4 DIGITS, say 123, 10, or 5, then it will add
leading blanks to make it 4 characters long when returning a
character-type data.

For example, suppose you have a record whose INVNUM field has value
of numeric 123.  If you SEEK "123" you will not find this record.
However, if you SEEK " 123", the pointer will point to the record.
Please note there was a blank space before 123 (in character type).

The best thing to do is to index the file by removing the leading
blanks.  LTRIM function will accomplish that.  I know dBXL and FOX
and of course dBASEIII+ support this function, but I am not sure
about clipper since I do not use it.  The command looks like:

INDEX on LTRIM(STR(invnum,4)) + LTRIM(STR(seqnum,6)) to idx_file

Now, if you seek "123", the pointer will point to th

	SEEK STR(4892,4)

What problems are you having?  The driver SHOULD report 2 drives found --

/dev/ct    c  41  8     ; rewind-on-close
/dev/nrct  c  41  0     ; no-rewind-on-close

DLP

Incorrect major/minor device numbers (see section on HPDD in the

Incorrect DMA channel. Verify that the hardware DMA (should be
5 or 6) matches the value in software. This value is stored in

/etc/conf/cf.d/mdevice

on the line that begins with "TAPE" in the far left column. The

subject: Question about generating a multivariate normal distribution
q: What is the cheapest way, computationally, to generate pseudo-random vectors from a multivariate normal distribution, given an approximation to the dispersion matrix?
ref: Standard method, and I know of no cheaper one. Once only, take the Cholesky decomposition S = TT' with T lower triangular. Then each time compute x = u + Tz, where z is a vector of independent standard normals. Good methods for T and z are easy to find, so go look.
replies:
A fairly standard way is as follows. I know of no cheaper method.

1) Suppose S is the dispersion (variance) matrix.  Find the choleski
   decomposition, ie the lower triangualar matrix T such that

	S = TT'

   (This step is done once only.)

2) If  u  is the desired mean vector, then each time calculate

	x = u + Tz

   where  z  is a generated vector of independent standard normal variates.
   x is the desired multivariate N(u,S) variate.

Good methods for calculating T and for generating z are easy to find.

Bill V.

subject: Amount of chip memory is different each time I boot, what's the deal?
q: My A3000 with 2 megs of chip RAM gets a different amount of chip RAM available on each boot, from about 900K up to 1.9 megs. What's going on? Bad memory chips?
ref: Probably a flaky chip, maybe a marginal one or a bent-under pin. Exec sizes chip RAM at cold boot in chunks and stops at the first one that fails the test. Since you're not crashing, the first meg is fine. Get the second bank looked at.
replies:
Sounds to me like you have at least one flakey chip.  That's not necessarily
a bad chip, you might have one with a bent-under pin, or other such atrocity.
Basically, as I understand it, when Exec wakes up from a cold boot it goes
out and calculates how much Chip RAM is available, on a reasonably fine grain
(maybe 64K or 128K chunks).  It doesn't really expect to find flakey Chip RAM.
So in testing memory, it'll most likely go until it finds a chunk that doesn't
test out.  If you're not crashing, this indicates that the first meg is still
fine, and that you never get to the second meg.  That's actually a good sign,
as it indicates that nothing is likely being shorted out and you _probably_
don't have a severely dead chip, as these things tend to drag down the whole
chip bus.  You should have that second bank of Chip RAM looked at carefully.

My first suspicion (as a software guy) would be a bad memory chip
(one that's marginal, so it fails the chip-ram existence test at different
places).  It also could be making intermittent contact, perhaps (less likely).

subject: Structured loops (WAS:Re: Turing programming language.)
q: Is there any existing language with a loop construct like 'do ... while condition ... od', where the test sits in the middle of the loop body?
ref: Sure, it's the old loop ... exit when <boolean> ... end loop with the test sense reversed. Turing has it. Knuth credits Ole-Johan Dahl with inventing it, in his 1974 paper on structured programming with go to statements. Hardly news.
replies:
This is the same as the loop ... exit when <boolean> ... end loop;
except that the sense of the test is reversed.  This exists in Turing.
It also exists in an in-house language I designed and implemented a couple
of years ago.  I don't know of any other languages that use it, however.

I checked a little further and found that Knuth (Structured
Programming with go to Statements, ACM Computing Surveys, v6, n4,
December 1974, p. 261-300; see page 279) credits Ole-Johan Dahl with
"recently" inventing:  "loop; S; while ~B; T; repeat;", but he does
not cite a reference.  (He strongly implies that the negation on the B
is important, but when I read the paragraph carefully I found it very
ambiguous as to just what he thought was better.)

[useful examples deleted ]

The do ... while <condition>  ... enddo construct exists in a not-too-well-
known language in this part of the world, namely in the application language
of "NorSoft", a Norwegian application generator/database system, which has
a remarkably powerful language (with which I am hopelessly in love and wish I
could use for other things as well :-)

As an aside, I think that Pascal's While-Do and C's while/do-while/for(;;)
constructs are infinitely more readable than the general (admittedly power-
ful) loop construct in Turing.

hi ho
--lth

subject: need to raise ulimit
q: I'm running Microport V/AT 2.3 and compiled the Korn Shell large model, but ksh dumps core as soon as I run it. Is it the kernel, compiler or linker?
ref: None of them. ksh assumes an int is the same size as a pointer, and in 286 large model it's 16 bits against 32. No workaround, just bad coding. Compile small model with only your favorite edit mode and optimize. So much for portable code.
replies:
...
...

The K-shell is written to assume that the size of an integer is the same
size as a pointer.  In the 286 large model, an integer is 16 bits, and
a pointer 32.  There is no workaround, this is just plain bad coding
practice.

Best bet is to compile ksh small model with everything but your favorite edit
mode turned off (e.g., -DVSH or -DESH) and make sure to optimize it.  It will
then fit (just barely) in the small model, where the size of an integer
really is the same as the size of a pointer.

So much for portable code.
