subject: Hard disk parking
q: Is it a big advantage for a hard disk to auto-park its heads on power failure or powerdown? Is it a problem if I have to run a park program or shutdown myself?
ref: Don't buy a drive without auto-park. An unparked head can damage the disk surface, and a power failure won't wait for you to run your park program. A crash may be unlikely, but a head crash or damaged media is what you risk. Sigh.
replies:
I strongly do not suggest buying any hard drive without auto-park.
Parking retracts the disk read head from the disk surface (and
sometimes parking locks the head in place). When the head isn't
parked, it can damage the disk surface. "Is this likely?" Well,
probably not likely, but possible which is enough to scare me off.

Can you say head crash or damaged media?

phil...

subject: Question about graphics.library
q: When using graphics library routines like BltBitMap on the Amiga, should I call OwnBlitter first, or does BltBitMap do it for me?
ref: Don't call OwnBlitter first. You only need it when you poke the hardware blitter registers directly: OwnBlitter, WaitBlit, touch the registers, then DisownBlitter. The library routines handle it themselves. The RKMs should have said so.
replies:
)When using OS routines in the graphics library such as 'BltBitMap' should one
)call 'OwnBlitter' first, or will 'BltBitMap' do this for me?

Don't call OwnBlitter first.  The only time you need to OwnBlitter is when
you're addressing the hardware blitter registers directly: e.g.
    OwnBlitter()
    WaitBlit()
    <access the hardware bltxxx registers directly>
    DisownBlitter()

- Kodiak

subject: DCD questions
q: Do current packet radio TNCs have any carrier detect, or do they just wait for a flag? Is carrier detect necessary?
ref: All TNCs I know of came with some form of carrier detect, though many just look for energy and are unreliable. Better ones look for something like a real data signal. It isn't needed for the receiver to work. It only inhibits the transmitter when the channel's busy.
replies:
All TNCs that I know of have came with some form of carrier detection.  The
problem is that many such circuits are not very reliable, particularly those
that simply look for energy in the channel. The better carrier detect
circuits look for something more closely resembling an actual data signal,
thereby making them much less susceptible to falsing by background noise.

A carrier detect circuit is not necessary to make the receiver work. With
any TNC, you can simply open the squelch and feed the random noise into the
receiver. When a valid frame arrives, the TNC will decode it. The carrier
detect circuit is needed to inhibit the transmitter when another station is
already using the channel.

Phil

subject: 386/ix directory(3) library is broken; how do I replace it?
q: The 386/ix System V closedir() is broken because it uses a structure after free(), which makes GNUtar run out of fds. How do I replace the directory library with a portable one, and will the vendor fix it?
ref: The SVR3 directory routines came from an early copy of the public-domain package, and the closedir bug came along with it. Replace the *dir.o objects in libc.a and the dirent.h headers with the fixed versions, or keep them separate from the vendor's. Tell your vendor to fix their code.
replies:
The UNIX System V Release 3 *dir() routines were derived from an early
release of my public-domain package.  Even the version I originally
posted to some source newsgroup contained the closedir() bug.  Many
people did not pick up the bug fix subsequently posted, nor the fix for
a problem with 14-character filenames under the old UNIX filesystem.

I'll e-mail you my current sources.  They are supposed to be fully SVR3
compatible although different in some internal implementation details.
You could replace your SVR3 libc.a/*dir.o objects and /usr/include/dirent.h
and /usr/include/sys/dirent.h with new versions from my package, or you
could maintain the headers and object modules in separate places from the
versions supplied by the system vendor.  (Personally I would opt for
replacing the buggy version, but there may be other constraints that keep
that from being a viable option for you.)

You might tell your vendor to get in touch with me..

subject: How does Excel do cells
q: How does Excel implement the cells in a spreadsheet? Are they just drawn in one window, or is each cell its own window? What does it cost to create lots of child windows, and how does Excel do the blinking selected cell?
ref: Best guess, it's all GDI calls. A window per cell would carry colossal overhead for no reason, since cells are display only. The blink is a timer plus FrameRect. Only the edit bar needs a real window. Think before you create a thousand windows.
replies:
I can't be sure (since I'm not a Microsoft developer) but my best guess says
that the spreadsheet in Excel was created entirely via GDI calls.  I don't
believe that each cell is a separate window since the overhead involved in that
would be collosal, not to mention the fact that there's no real reason to use
a window for the cell.  The blinking can be done fairly easily with a timer
and a FrameRect call (or something similar).  The only place that really
needs a window would be the edit "bar" on top of the window.  Otherwise the
cells are display only.

As I said, though, these are just guesses and it is entirely possible (if not
probable) that Microsoft did it in some other way.

subject: macros in vi
q: How do I use @ macros in vi, and how do I get the macro into the buffer in the first place besides typing and yanking?
ref: You named the buffer after @, and @ runs the contents of that register, @@ repeats the last. Yanking is the way. To set one up in EXINIT or .exrc, use map @a and so on. Read the vi reference.
replies:
\could someone tell me how to use @ macros in vi?
\the manual i have says follow the @ with the name of a buffer.
\how do you get the macro into the buffer in the first place
\(besides typing them in and yanking them). [...]

Correct.  Quoted from the Vi Reference (email if you missed it):

    @<a-z>                  | Consider the contents of the named register a
    @@                      | Repeat last register command.

If you want to set such a macro in EXINIT/.exrc:

	map @a ...

subject: Boot sector of harddisk?
q: Where is the boot sector on a hard disk? Reading head 0, track 0, sector 1 with INT 13 didn't give me the boot sector.
ref: Unlike a floppy, that first sector on a hard disk is the partition sector, which is what you read. Its partition entries hold the head, cylinder and sector of the boot sector for the entry starting with hex 80. Debug can't even touch the partition sector. Learn the layout.
replies:
Unlike floppy disks, the HD uses the first sector as the partition
sector, and this is the sector you accessed. The last 4 paragraphs
of the 512 bytes of this sector list the data of the 4 possible
partitions of the HD.  The bootable partition paragraph begins
with hex 80 and this paragraph will have the head, cyl and
sector info for the boot sector.  If memory serves me, using
INT 13, the boot sector is located as 0/1/0.  You can identify
the boot sector by looking at bytes (decimal) 4 through 11.
This will give information including the msdos version number.
Somewhere around the end of this sector you will see listed
the two hidden file names.
If you are not sure what the boot sector looks like, try this:
In debug:    l ds:1000 2 0 1
             d ds:1000 l200

The first command loads the first relative sector of the C disk
to memory starting at ds:1000
The second command reads the 512 (decimal) bytes of the boot
sector.  Debug can not access the partition sector.

Forrest Gehrke

subject: Floppy Disks and X-Rays
q: How sensitive are 3.5 inch floppy disks to airport security x-rays? I have to carry about 100 of them on a plane and they hold my only copies of the software.
ref: The x-rays themselves won't hurt the disks. It's the electromagnets in the machine's monitors and emitters that can erase data. The odds aren't great, but they're not negligible either. Have the disks hand checked, and keep backups next time.
replies:
All of the information I've seen about this say that the x-rays
themselves aren't harmful to the disks.  But, you still need to
be careful because the electromagnets in the x-ray machines monitors
and emitters _can_ erase data.  The chance isn't great, but it is
non-negligable.  The best thing would be to just have the disks
hand checked.

subject: File Servers and Network Nodes
q: What are you doing to serve 105MB NeXT clients off a file server so they can use the extended release? Do you mount everything from the server, or what?
ref: We mount /usr/local, /LocalApps, /NextDeveloper and /NextLibrary from the server, and keep a few fonts and such locally. The rest of the extended release gets replicated on the client disk, which runs about 90% full. It works, but it's ugly, and upgrades will be a nightmare.
replies:
We mount the following from our server ('040 cube) to 5 clients, each with a 105:
	/usr/local (ro), /LocalApps (ro), /LocalLibrary (rw - for MakeTeXPK),
	/NextDeveloper (ro), /NextLibrary (ro).
/usr/spool/mail (rw), & home directories are mounted from a Mips & a Sun.

On the clients, clean out most of /NextLibrary & /NextDeveloper; keep some
stuff there (fonts, etc) in case of problems with the server. Replicate
the remainder of the extended release in /NextApps, /usr/{lib,bin,include}, /lib,
/bin, (others ?).  Your local disk will be very full (90%), leaving around
20 MB for swap.

This works for us, but it's ugly. OS upgrades will be a nightmare, but I'll
probably use rdist, or similar.  If we can get more RAM for our server, I
may just make the 105's into swap disks.  However, I don't have a great deal
of confidence in the Cube as a fileserver (not the best disk performance
and inability to do sync scsi, along with the increased ethernet load).

- Steve Johnson, Systems Manager, Dep

subject: 2 monitors on an A3000

ref: No. The 1950 on the 31Khz DB15 connector just gets the display-enhanced version of the same video data on the 15Khz DB23 connector that feeds the 1084. One video source, two plugs. Look at the hardware.
replies:
No, because the 1950 being connected to the DB15 connector (marked
31Khz) is just the display enhanced output of the same video data
present on the DB23 connector (marked 15Khz) and connected to the 1084.

subject: 8mm and DAT tape drives under RISC/os
q: What SCSI addresses, device names, and tape parameters should I use for 8mm and DAT drives on RS-2030 and RC-3230 machines under RISC/os? Can they live alongside the QIC at 6?
ref: Both live quite happily. Convention: 0 system disk, 1-3 data disks, 4 data disk or high-capacity tape, 5 data disk or half-inch tape, 6 QIC, 7 host adapter. Device is /dev/[r]mt/hc[04]. Nothing special for dd, tar, cpio; check the dump.ffs man page.
replies:
Both live quite happily.  The convention is:

0 - system disk
1 - data disk
2 - data disk
3 - data disk
4 - data disk or high-capacity tape
5 - data disk or 1/2" tape
6 - QIC tape
7 - host adapter

/dev/[r]mt/hc[04]

Nothing special for dd, tar, cpio.  A recommendation for parameters for the
size and density for dump.ffs is found on the man page.

ref: Sounds like your video and ethernet boards are stomping on each other's memory, via QEMM or video BIOS shadowing. If you run EMS, exclude the memory address the ethernet card uses. It's in the hardware manual, which nobody reads.

use that mode.  16 bit mode works fine in one SX machine using the NEAT

Sounds to me like your vidoe board and etheret board are writing over
each others memory. Your computer either has qemm 386 (allowing it to
use vidoe memory) or your borad has video bios shadowing.

If you are running EMS make sure that you exclude the memeory address
that the eithernet card uses. I think they discuss it in the AE-2
hardware manual. This keeps EMS from allocating the AE-2 address to. for
instance, Lotus.

Josh Guttman

subject: v20 chip

ref: For eight or ten bucks, buy it, but don't expect miracles. Compiling got only about 10% faster, mostly the power-on memory check. Some clones hang or crash, and a few programs like COPYWRIT and COPYIIPC are incompatible. Hardly a kilo-buck CPU.

I worked with an XT clone that had its 8088 replaced with a V20 and
had all sorts of trouble.  Most things worked fine, but every once in
a while I got an "Internal stack failure - system halted" message,
which occurs (presumably) because of the high speed of the CPU.  If
too many interrupts are generated (by the keyboard, serial port, etc.)
at close intervals, the stack just crashed andthe system had to be
re-booted (turned off & on, no CTRL-ALT-DEL).  I also know there are
incompatibilites with programs such as COPYWRIT and COPYIIPC.

We're talking about 8 or 10 buck's rght? Buy it. My first PC clone was
from suntronics. their bios ran fligh simulator and every thing else I
ever tried. WHen I put the V20 in, it ran fine until the screen scrolled
up the first line! Then it hung! Repeatedly. I relaced the 8088 and
everything was fine. I all subsequent PC clones, the V20 worked fine.
The biggest speed up seemed to be during the power-on memory check.
Despite the claims, don't expect a lot overall. For example,
compiling 30K of source, exlapsed time was only reduced 10%. Still, the
ole PC is so slow, its worth it. Think of it as a percent per buck.
(Now if they only had a kilo-buck version .... :-)

subject: Window resource sharing?
q: Is it legal for multiple Amiga windows to share the same Menu list or the same Gadget list?
ref: Possible, but problematic. NextMenu pointers go every which way, and you can get propelled into a brick wall. CHECKIT flags change behind other windows' backs. Gadgets are worse because of the SELECTED bit, so it may look highlighted when you just turned it off.
replies:
Possible, but problematic.  The NextMenu pointers will be going
every which way, depending on which Window last had the menu.  This is
important because, if the user manages to interact with the Menu in one of
the other Windows before you've chased down all the NextMenu elements, you
could get propelled into a brick wall.  Also, if you have CHECKIT MenuItems,
then one Window may change the state of the CHECKED flags behind the others'
back.

	Again, possible, but problematic.  Largely for the same reasons.
However, because of the strange nature of the SELECTED bit in the current
release, it's much easier to get yourself into trouble.  It may *look*
highlighted, when in fact you just turned it off.

	Stu Ferguson would be able to comment more completely on the
subject, since he wrote Modeller 3D, which has multiple Windows using the
"same" Menus and Gadgets.

thing. Then, when you get a fill net feed, occasional articles might
be cross posted to a netwide group and local.something.  The article
would show up in the local group, even though it didn't belong. Of
course this won't happen very often.

I originally thought of using bitnet.listname, but it didn't quite seem right
with several internet lists going in.  I eventually decided on list.listname.

Be forewarned, keep a high quota on the account all the lists are forwarded
to.  When you blow out your quota, you're sure to make a lot of list managers
very unhappy.

subject: NFS Super users?
q: Can I disable the NFS behavior that maps super-user to uid -2 so I can do system maintenance and backups from one system?
ref: You can patch the kernel variable "nobody" to 0 with adb, but that's a lousy idea since anyone root on a client gets root on your server. Don't use NFS for backups. Use rdump to a remote tape drive.
replies:
NFS can allow remote root access. It is not a good idea to have NFS
permit this by default. If someone becomes root on a client, they would
then have super user access to the NFS servers. If you MUST do this,
then patch the kernel variable called "nobody". NFS servers map root NFS
requests to this user-id. Normally it is set to -2 (explaining the
behaviour you describe above). Setting it to 0 will grant clients super
user access to the server. You can patch the kernel with adb or an
equivalent debugger. Some vendors allow you to set this variable as a
option when configuring a kernel.

The way to do that is not to use NFS for backups! Use rdump to backup
files to a remote tape drive or other backup device. Alternatively, pick
up one of the many versions of tar that are floating around that have
support for driving a remote tape device.

		Jim

subject: Resident libraries on Xenix 2.3
q: Is there any supported way of making and using resident libraries on Xenix 2.3? The executable seems to need to be a COFF file, and the -coff switch to cc does nothing.
ref: You mean shared libraries, and the answer is no. The OMF/x.out formats don't support them. The -coff switch and cvtcoff are for the UNIX devsys, and Xenix ignores -coff since it can't generate COFF binaries. Read the docs next time.
replies:
You mean the shared libraries, I assume.  And the answer is:  no and yes.
No, because the OMF/x.out formats do not (currently?) support shared
libraries.  The libraries are there because 2.3 was intended to run COFF
binaries, and at least some of those needed the shared libraries.  Just the
shared libraries, though, not the stubs (/lib/libc_s.a, for example) needed
to create binaries which use the shared libraries (/shlib/libc_s, for
example).

The -coff switch, and the cvtcoff program (although what you want is
cvtomf), are for the UNIX devsys.  cvtomf converts an OMF file to COFF, and
cvtcoff does the opposite (both have their limitations; cvtomf is intended
to only be used by the compiler, and cvtcoff is only intended to be used by
cv).  Under Xenix, the -coff switch is ignored, since it is not possible to
generate COFF binaries.

subject: Windows prolog/epilog
q: What's going on in the Windows function prolog and epilog with the DS manipulation, the NOP, and the INC and DEC of BP?
ref: Yes, the MOV AX,DS gets patched at runtime. The BP tweak marks far calls so Windows can walk the stack and tell far from near. Then it can fix up pushed DS values and RETF targets when it moves or discards segments. Buy Petzold's Programming Windows, it's all in there.
replies:
Your assumption on DS is correct.  The BP stuff is to allow Windows to
"walk the stack" backwards, differentiating far calls from near
calls, so it can move data around.  When it moves data, it needs
to clean up all those "pushed" DS values that are on the stack,
or else when you start returning from functions you will be loading
DS with an out-of-date value.  And when it moves code, it must change
any RETF's (actually the value of 'CS' on the stack) to the new
value.  And if code is discarded, RETF's actually jump to the
cde which reloads the application code segment.

Windows could not know which functions were entered with a FAR
call and which with a NEAR.  If that were the case it would be
impossible to "walk the stack" accurately.  By tweaking BP on
each FAR function entry, it is possible to tell NEAT from FAR.

For more info on this and other such tidbits, I recommend picking up
_Programming Windows_  (CHarles Petzold, Microsoft Press), which is
a great addition to any Windows SD

subject: what is a ``span''.
q: I keep seeing references to the "span" of high-end SGI machines like the VGX and Skywriter. What is a span?
ref: A span is a vertical column of pixels. These machines break polygons into columns instead of rows, and rows are "scans". The parallel processors that render the columns are also called spans, so a base VGX has 5 and the multi-buffer option gives 10. More spans, faster fill. Sigh, basic stuff.
replies:
on VGX and Skywriter, a "span" is simply a vertical column of
pixels.  when a primitive is rendered, it is broken into spans
which are rendered in parallel.  the more span processors
you have, the faster the fill rate.

the base VGX system includes 5 spans.  if you upgrade to the
"multi-buffer" option, then you get 10 spans and a much faster
fill rate.

High-end SGI machines decompose polygons into columns of pixels, rather than
rows, as is more common.  We refer to columns of pixels as 'spans'.  (We refer
to rows of pixels as 'scans', or 'scan lines'.)  The parallel processors
that convert span definitions into pixels are also sometimes refered to as
spans, as in a '5-span VGX', or a '10-span VGXT'.

would be severly inconsistent with the SAA/CUA and make your users

subject: Magical Paradox
q: In AD&D second edition, if a mage casts Phantasmal Force to create the illusion of a glowing ball, does it actually light up the room, does it nullify infravision, and can the party walk around safely by its light?
ref: Only if the mage bothers to illusion the whole room lit up too, walls and floor included, which is a much harder trick. It only nullifies infravision or provides usable light for whoever fails to disbelieve it in the first place, everyone else just stumbles into invisible furniture.
replies:
The only way that the room would "light up" is if mage created the illusions
of the items in the room (including walls, floor, etc) lighting up.  This
becomes a much more difficult illusion.  It would nullify infra-vision
if the mage included this as part of the illusion (the user of infra-vision
would be so affected by the illusion).  A character trying to walk
around with the aid of this light would see exactly what the mage was
causing to be lit up.  If the mage were able somehow to light up the
actual objects in the room, then a character affected by the illusion
could walk around safely.  If the mage did not "light up" the objects
in the room, then the walking character would be bumping into
"invisible" objects.

Note that the more complex the mage attempts to make the illusion,
the less chance of characters believing the illusion.  Lighting an
entire room would be pretty tough.

Any other opinions?

Excellent.  This is why I hate magical illusions.

I guess that it will only light up the room for the people who don't
succesfully dis-believe it.  I  can't see it now:

DM:  It's pitch dark

Mage:  I cast an illusion of a quartz halogen headlight

DM:  okay, everybody can see

Dumb Fighter:  Hey, that's an illusion! (Makes roll)

DM:  okay, the dumb fighter can't see.

Perfect.

This question keeps coming up.

 The answer is simple.  You need a version of sendmail which can read MX
records.  Many systems come with both 'sendmail' and 'sendmail.mx'.  If
you have both, then: mv sendmail sendmail.nonmx;ln sendmail.mx sendmail

available on many ftp sites.  If you are inexperienced and don't want to
try this just yet, configure your 'sendmail' to forward most mail to a
host which can read MX records and deliver the mail for you.

subject: Audio Animator/IFF
q: Audio Animator saves files in 8 bit Apple IFF format, and I gather there are 16 bit and other standards. Is there a conversion program available?
ref: There's no such thing as Apple IFF; IFF is from Electronic Arts. You mean Apple's AIFF, which records bit depth per sample. Converting 8-bit samples to 16-bit changes nothing in the sound and just eats disk space. Think before converting.
replies:
I'm assuming you mean Audio Animator.

IFF is a standard created by Electronic Arts.  There isn't an "Apple IFF".
What there is is Apple's "Audio IFF" or "Audio Interchange File Format", also
called "AIFF".

AIFF is a very robust file format for sampled sounds.  The format contains
information on how many bits deep each sample is.  If Audio Animator's software
creates 8-bit samples, trying to change them to 16-bit samples isn't going to
change anything.  It will sound the same and just take up more disk space.

AIFF is not an "8-bit" format; it's me 32-bit oriented than anything else, I
would say.  It's the preferred method of audio storage and interchange for
Apple II, IIgs and Macintosh computers.

However, in the example cited, it's simple: run your Mathematica graph through
psfix, which is supplied with the Mathematica package.

subject: comp_t
q: Accounting records on Xenix store CPU time as a comp_t, a 16-bit float with a 13-bit fraction and 3-bit exponent. How do I turn it into an integer number of clock ticks?
ref: Mask the low 13 bits for the mantissa and the top 3 bits for the exponent, then ldexp the mantissa by three times the exponent. That's an empirical guess from timing known commands, so run your own trials. AT&T couldn't document it properly, naturally.
replies:
I just messed with that recently myself.  By running a bunch of commands that
took known amounts of time (sleep(1) is handy for that) and trying to make
sense of the resulting comp_ts, I came up with the following theory:

mantissa = comp_t & 0x1FFF
exponent = comp_t & 0xE000

double ticks = ldexp( (double)mantissa, 3*exponent)

The extra factor of 3 in the exponent bothers me, but it was consistent with
the various values I tried.  You'll probably want to run a number of trials
yourself.  I would be delighted, actually, to learn that I'm wrong and have
someone provide a more sensible explanation.

Wouldn't it be nice if AT&T's comment included the information that needs
to be included?

subject: domain forwarding using smail3
q: Using smail3, mail sent from my host to a user at another domain host isn't forwarded on, but mail addressed directly to that user at the domain gets routed correctly. What should I look for?
ref: Smail 3 doesn't care where a message came from when routing, so likely the upstream host resolved the domain name before sending it back. Check the uuxqt logs with uulog -s and -x to see what was on the rmail command line. Or queue-only and poke at the files.
replies:
Smail 3 doesn't consider where a message is from (or whether it is
local or remote, or how it was received) when it applies its routing,
so the most likely thing is that iuvax resolved the domain name
before sending it back.  If connection is via uucp, look at your
uuxqt logs to see what was actually on the rmail command line when
it came in using "uulog -s iuvax -x".
I'm not sure how you catch the "envelope-to" on inbound SMTP.  Setting
the mode to queue-only so you could poke around in the files as they
land in /usr/spool/smail/input/* might work.  In fact, the mailq command
should show the destination(s) of the queued files.

subject: Want HP-28S fuel gauge, program name query
q: Can an HP-28S program find out its own name, so a catalog of about 150 stored programs can print 'Output for name1' without storing the name inside itself?
ref: Technically yes, with machine code, but it's risky and eats more memory than the name. Don't. Just call the program from a wrapper: << DUP ->STR "Output for " SWAP + 1 DISP EVAL >> stored as INVOKE, then run 'pgmname' INVOKE. Simple enough.
replies:
There is a way to do this, but it seems like a lot of unnecessary work.

You can write a machine code object that will determine what variable
it is stored in and put the name on the stack.  This will use up more
memory in your program than the name itself.  Alternatively, you can
write a machine code subroutine (in another variable) that figures out
where it was called from and determines the name of the calling program.
Both of these approaches are extremely risky, which you did not want.

The best way is to avoid this complexity and simply call your program
from another program that prints the name for you.  The basic idea is:

INVOKE
<< DUP ->STR "Output for " SWAP + 1 DISP EVAL >>

'pgmname' INVOKE

The hardware in the 28S uses a simple comparator to compare the battery voltage
to an internally-generated reference value, so it cannot arbitrarily measure
battery voltage.  There are two such comparators in the calculator.  The first
tells the software to turn on the low battery indicator and the second, at a
lower voltage, tells the software to shut down the calculator completely to
avoid the chance of some incorrect operation messing up memory.

The calculator speed was set to assure correct operation down to this lowest
battery voltage; processor speed varies with battery voltage and if the voltage
gets too low some logic might not reach the correct state before its output is
sampled.  If the calculator has been sped up using one of the programs which
have been posted here it is possible that memory will be messed up or lost as
the battery voltage drops with age.

subject: Are sockets the wave of the future?
q: Are sockets the wave of the future for TCP/IP applications on Unix? We might need portability to a STREAMS-based system, so which should we use on System V 3.2?
ref: SVr4 brings the Transport Level Interface, which is meant to obsolete sockets, with STREAMS modules underneath. TLI is modeled on ISO 8072, so porting shouldn't be awful. Better yet, use an RPC facility and be shielded from all of this. Read the Sun Network Programming Guide, for once.
replies:
With respect to Unix systems, System V r4 (SVr4) presents the
Transport Level Interface (TLI). This is the transport layer interface that
will obsolete sockets; there will be STREAMS modules existing underneath
the interface. TLI is modeled after the ISO Transport Service Definition
(ISO 8072), so presumably, if your non-unix host has a similiar facility,
porting shouldn't be that bad.

SVr4 (or at least Sun's version) will be using STREAMS.

I'm not sure of the commercial availability of TLI in a Unix system
(SunOS 4.1, the current version, does NOT support it).

By the way, if your application can use some sort of RPC facility, then
you can be shielded from all of this.

If you want some TLI documentation, refer to "Network Programming Guide",
from Sun Microsystems  (part 800-3850-10).

Good luck!

Rod

subject: Looking for a fast exp(x) where -10.0<=x<=10.0
q: I need a fast exp(x) function for a float x in the range -10.0 to 10.0. A big lookup table with interpolation, or something like it?
ref: Ask yourself how fast, how accurate and how much memory first. Since exp(a+b)=exp(a)*exp(b), split x into high and low parts, look each up in a small table and multiply. Or keep a table of exp(2^n) and multiply in one entry per set bit. Trivial.
replies:
Decompose your exp(x) into exp(a+b), where a and b are
the most-significant and least significant parts of x.
exp(a+b)=exp(a)*exp(b), so get exp(a) and exp(b) from
two small tables and multiply them together.

Another idea I have used is the polynomial approximations as given in
Abramowitz and Stegun ``Handbook of Mathematical Functions''. For exp(x) you
can get accuracy to 2 x 10^{-10} for seven terms with 0<x<ln(2). Outside that
range use known results i.e. exp(x) = 2 x exp(x - ln(2)) for ln(2)<x<2ln(2).
The seven terms might be a bit much if you want real speed, but with other
suggestions given you may be able to tailor a useful algorithm depending on
your speed/accuracy/memory tradeoff.

My standard questions: how fast do you want it, how accurate do you want it,
and how much memory are you willing to use?

Actually the exponential function is very easy to compute, because exp(x+y) =
exp(x) exp(y).  So don't even need CORDIC, you can get by with one dimension.
All you need is a table of exp(2^n) for a wide range of n.  For each bit
that's on in the argument, you multiply the result by the corresponding value.
If you want it to be faster and you're willing to use more memory, you can do
many bits at a time.

subject: HP Laserjet III from a Amiga. How to control.
q: Escape sequences I send to PRT: on the Amiga for my Laserjet III print as plain text minus the escape character. What am I doing wrong?
ref: PRT: is the printer.device and driver. It parses ANSI X3.64 codes and trashes the rest. Use PAR: or SER: for raw output. RTFM, since this is what Appendix D is for.
replies:
Hmm, to put it frankly: PRT: *IS* THE printer.device! And the driver!
Perhaps you should just replace PRT: by PAR: (or SER:, respectively),
then you really bypass all those drivers.

When you talk to PRT:, it only regards valid ANSI escape sequences and
intentionally trashes all others.

                                         ^^^^
Please check again. If it really says so, it is a bug to be corrected.
It should say PAR: or SER: for getting RAW output.

Assuming the printer is connected to the parallel port you should be sending
your output to PAR:, not PRT:.
All output to PRT: is analyzed for ANSI X3.64 commands. An example of an ANSI
X3.64 command would be   <ESC>[1m   this is convert to whatever Preferences
states is the codes for Boldface on. So no matter which printer I have
connected I just set the printer type in Preferences then <ESC>[1m turns
Boldface printing on. It was designed to help programs. The program no longer
has to worry which printer is connected... Preferences which convert the codes
to what it thinks the printer wants. In your example of <ESC>[5j I can find
no equivalent in the ANSI X3.64 list (see Appendix D, Printer Escape Codes in
your Introduction to the Amiga manual) so <ESC>[ is probably pulled off then
5j is checked against the list of ANSI codes. None is found so the 5j is
printed but the <ESC>[ (which I believe is called <CSI>) is filtered out.

 If you output to the PAR: it will use the parallel.device

subject: Looking for a method to invert a function.
q: I want an analog circuit that turns f(t) into -f(t), then adds it to g(t) = f(t) + h(t) to reveal the embedded signal h(t). Is that doable?
ref: What's the great trick? That's just inverting the signal polarity. If you meant f(-t), inverting in time, that's a different story. You can't reconstruct more than the past history of an arbitrary function, unless it's periodic. Then sample-and-store a cycle digitally and play it back. Think before posting.
replies:
I don't see what the great trick is here; you are just inverting the signal
polarity!  Now if what you MEAN is to turn f(t) into f(-t) (invert in time)
that's a different story:  If f(t) does not exist before t=0, that's easy;
tie your signal input to ground :-).  If it does exist before t=0, it is
"impossible" to reconstruct anything more about the arbitrary function than
is known in its past history.  If it is presumed the function is periodic
then construction of an approximation to the time-mirror image could be done
by a simple (DIGITAL) sample-and-store-then-reconstruct circuit after
observation of one cycle.

subject: The Director
q: Under WB 1.3 my Director script that echoes to speak: sometimes makes the Amiga voice say "You need ARP library vs. 33". Why?
ref: ARP echo prints that when arp.library gets expunged and can't be reloaded, either because libs: is unavailable or there isn't enough contiguous memory. I suspect the memory; you're running on the edge. Watch your free memory with perfmon.
replies:
For this to work, several things happen. The speak handler gets loaded
from l:, the translator.library gets loaded from libs: and the narrator.device
gets loaded from devs:. Additionally, execute uses C:RUN to kick off the
process so if you don't have c: assigned to ram: it may cause a disk
access. It is unclear to me at this time if Execute really cares if RUN
is resident.

The echo command (ARP echo) will print the "You need..." message if
the arp.library gets expunged from memory and either a) it can't load
it from the current libs: directory, or b) there isn't enough contiguous
memory to load it so the OpenLibrary() fails. Personally, I suspect the
latter. Sounds like you are running right on the edge of memory availability
in your system. Run perfmon (or what ever it is called, the one with the
rabbit icon) and watch your memory usage to see if it drops way down.

subject: 100ns SC ZIPs fast enough for A3000-25?
q: Are 100ns static column DRAMs fast enough for an Amiga 3000-25, or do I need 80ns ones?
ref: The RAMSEY chip was designed for 100ns DRAMs, but the chip people can't guarantee them over the full power and temperature range, so the spec says 80ns. 100ns parts would work in most systems most of the time. Not recommended. Don't be cheap.
replies:
OK.  The deal is, the RAMSEY chip was designed to use 100ns DRAMs, for 16MHz
or 25MHz (the chip is optimized for either; it runs basic 4 clock cycles for
16MHz, 5 clock cycles for 25MHz).  However, the IC people aren't able to
guarantee operation with 100ns DRAMs over the full power and temperature
range of the chip, so we call for 80ns DRAMs.  I can tell you that 100ns
parts would work in most of the systems most of the time, but unless I can
say they work in all of the systems all of the time, I don't recommend it
(nor does Greg Berlin, who designed RAMSEY and wrote the specs, which is what
the 80ns figure from the A3000 manual is based on).

subject: A/UX trouble
q: Booting A/UX on a Mac IIfx gives "panic: ialloc: dup alloc" about a third of the way through the progress bar. What does that mean?
ref: It means a single inode got allocated to two different files. Run fsck on the guilty filesystem, though boot should have done that already. If the system is really mangled, reformat and repartition the disk from scratch. Sigh, and don't go playing with dp carelessly.
replies:
It's telling you that it has discovered a single inode allocated to two
different files. Try running fsck on the guilty party. But that should be
done automatically on boot when it discovers that the disk is "dirty" so
there may be deeper problems. You didn't my any chance do something werid
with dp, did you? (Though I'm not sure that even that could cause this
message.)

It could also mean just about _anything_ if your system is really messed up.
I'd suggest reformatting and repartitioning the disk from scratch, if
nobody else has any better ideas.

subject: Multi-spoolers
q: Is there software that lets a single print queue drive several printers, sending each job to a free printer of the right forms type?
ref: The System V lp spooler does it. Define printers and classes, a class being a group of similar printers, and lp -d with a class name goes to the first available one. You forgot to say what system you run, by the way.
replies:
You neglected to say what version of system you are using, but it is possible
to do this kind of spooling using the System V lp spooler.  By correctly
specifying printers and classes a user can send to a specific printer, or a
specific class of printers.

A class is a group of printers that share a similar characteristic.  For
example, we have three NLQ dot matrix printers here at the office.  If a
user wants the file to be printed  out as fast as possible, they may issue
the command 'lp -dlq <filename>' where '-d' specifies the destination, and
'lq' is a class of printers which contains the three NLQ printers.  The
file would get printed on the first available printer in that class.

If a user wanted the file printed on a specific printer, (i.e. the one nearest
his or her office, they would use the command 'lp -dprinter1 <filename>' where
'printer1' is the name of the printer nearest them.

There are a lot more features, but I will refrain from reciting them all here.

B. Choi, H. Shin, Y. Yoon & J. Lee, Triangulation of scattered data in
3D space, Comp. Aided Dgn., v.20, n. 5, 1988, pp. 239-248.  This journal
is published by Butterworths.

D. Avis and H. ElGindy, Triangulating point sets in space, Disc. & Comp.
Geom. v. 2, pp. 99-111, 1987. (pub. by Springer)

A couple of papers from the computer vision literature:

J-D. Boisonnat, Representation of objects by triangulating points
in 3D space, Proc. 6th Int. Conf. on Pattern Recognition, 1982, pp. 830-832.

J-D. Boissonnat, Representing 2D and 3D shapes with the Delaunay triangulation,
Proc. 7th Int. Conf. on Pattern Recognition, 1984, pp. 745-748.

L. De Floriani, Surface representations based on triangular grids,
The Visual Computer, v. 3, n. 1, 1987, pp. 27-50 (pub. by Springer).

subject: flopy disk pin assignments

replies:
Sony lists two interfaces on the back of their "Mass Storage Product
Line Card".  Most pins are the same except:

pin  Sony Interface     PC Interface
     (Shugart type)     (IBM Type)

1    Disk Change Reset  Ground
2    Disk Change        Not Connected
4    In Use             Not Connected
34   Ready              Disk Change

For 30 mm high drives, mp-f63w-01d and mp-f73w-01d are listed as PC
interface, other mp-f52w, mp-f53w, mp-f63w, and mp-f73w are listed as

(or PS/2!?)  interface.

subject: Help: Vetta 2 Computer
q: My new Vetta 2 bike computer shows absurd speeds like 67 mph, jumpy speed and cadence that never reads below 90. The clock works and readings stop when I'm still. What should I check?
ref: A wrong wheel measurement wouldn't cause sudden jumps or bad cadence. It sounds like extra pulses. Check the battery first, since low voltage can make transients that get counted as pulses, then the installation and any stray magnets triggering the pickups. Basic troubleshooting, really.
replies:
You might have the wheel measurement wrong, but that wouldn't account
for sudden jumps, nor for bad cadence values.

The two things I would check first are the battery (perhaps at low voltage
you get transients which get counted as pulses), and the installation.
It sounds like you occasionally get extra pulses, which cause the high
cadence and the jumpy speed.  Are there any other magnets which might
be triggering the pickups?

My first guess would be the battery, because that would account for
both the cadence and the speed errors.

--David Wittenberg

subject: Mail to/from Prodigy

Fat chance.  If you've been following the discussion in the Telecom digest
and elsewhere, Prodigy thinks that they're doing their users a big favor by
letting them send mail to each other at all, much less allowing a gateway to
other systems.

Prodigy was designed to be a one-to-many system, that is, users call up
regional concentrators which communicate with the main system.  Users are
supposed to spend their time looking at catalogs and stuff like that, fixed
shared screens which the regional concentrators can cache.  Since mail is
private, and they don't even know that all copies of a message addressed to
a mailing list are the same, each time you look at a mail message the
regional machine has to make a request to the main system, which loads the
regional-main links more heavily than they'd expected.  This problem is
exacerbated by their practice of delaying and censoring messages to the
public bulletin boards, which caused users to create mailing lists for their
semi-private conve

subject: creating extra swap partitions
q: How do I add a second swap partition on a second disk under Ultrix 3.0 on a PMAX? swapon -a complains that it must be a block device.
ref: Use the block device, /dev/rz3b, not the raw /dev/rrz3b, in /etc/fstab. Sigh, and mkfs has no place on a swap partition. You also have to reconfigure the kernel with swap on rz0b and rz3b, and make sure the /dev special files for rz3 exist.
replies:
The entry in /etc/fstab should specifiy the "cooked" or "block" device
rather than the "raw" device (regardless of what it actually uses).

Most likely you've put the wrong name /dev/rhp1b vs /dev/hp1b in your
entry.  Second chance would be that you don't have the correct names in
/dev for all the partitions of the disk device.

mkfs isn't used for swap partitions, since the system (normally) swaps on the
entire partition, rather than within the bounds of a filesystem layered onto
the device...

The "block device" is the non-raw partition.  The entry in /etc/fstab should
list /dev/rz3b, not /dev/rrz3b.

You do have to reconfigure the kernel to add a second swap partition.  The
configuration file in /sys/conf/mips should have a line like this:

config vmunix root on rz0a swap on rz0b and rz3b dumps on rz0b

If you want, you can run /etc/doconfig, reply to its questions, and it will
generate a config file for you.

Before you boot the new kernel, make sure that you have special files in
/dev for rz3.

Enjoy!
					Frank

subject: Scheduler changed under 2.0?
q: Under AmigaDOS 2.0 on an A3000, the system seems to lock up and jerk along when loading programs during a heavy load, unlike 1.3. Was the scheduler or LoadSeg() changed?
ref: Probably not the scheduler. On the A3000, illegal memory accesses cause a Bus Error taking 250 milliseconds each, and sloppy programs hit them. Under 1.3 emulation the address space is mapped differently, hiding it. Run Enforcer to check. Its serial reports at 9600 baud also stall the machine.
replies:
On the A3000 attempts to access illegal memory results in a "Bus Error".
(For anything not otherwise filled, the A3000 Hardware asserts _BERR).
Each illegal memory access takes 250 milliseconds.  Programs like the ones
you mention sometimes read/write/trash random areas of memory.

Under 1.3 emulation on the A3000, the address space is mapped differently,
hiding the feature.

The only way to tell for sure would be to get the developer tool called
"Enforcer", and check if the pauses are coincident with illegal memory hits.

I've seen the same thing.  I was downloading a file while trying to do
something else and the system got *extremely* slow and jerky, and the
download kept failing.  I was running some program (I can't remember which
one now) that was number crunching or rendering or otherwise using every
free cycle, but it was running at 0 priority, so I don't know why it would
screw-up the inputdevice.

Are you running a utility called "enforcer" when you're under 2.0?
It finds certain program bugs and spits error reports out the serial
port at 9600 baud -- the machine is suspended during that time.  DPaint
has a few such reports upon startup.  That would explain what you're
seeing.

     Peter

subject: 1540 and sync. SCSI drives
q: Can I connect a synchronous 4 MB/sec SCSI disk and an asynchronous 1.5 MB/sec streamer to the same Adaptec 1540 on 386/ix? Does the driver run both at async?
ref: Yes, mix them at will. Sync/async is negotiated by messages between host adapter and device, transparent to the driver. Enable sync in the board setup and each target gets sync if it supports it. Only fast-SCSI needs all devices rated fast. SCSI 101.
replies:
According to Adaptec documentation, the controller itself handles
negotiation for synchronous/asynchronous operation.  This is an option
selected by a jumper on the board.

  --jh--
John Hood, Biar Games snail: 10 Spruce Lane, Ithaca NY 14850
domain: jhood@biar.uu.net bang: anywhere!uunet!biar!jhood
Looking for a OS hacking programming job in the Ithaca area...

Sure, SCSI is downwardly compatible.  Everything on the SCSI bus is
asynchronous until the (negotiated) data phase, then a synchronous
transfer can occur.  SCSI-2's wide-SCSI and fast-SCSI are just
variations on this theme.  The negotiation occurs completely transparently
to the driver by an exchange of messages between the device (target)
and the host adapter (initiator).  You can mix and match asynch and
synch devices at will.  The one trick is that fast-SCSI is very touchy
and all your devices must be rated fast, so you won't be able to
mix and match in that case.

If you have enabled the board to allow sync. to work in the initial
setup commands, then it will do sync if the target allows it. During each
selection to a target, a bit is passed that says wether the target supports
sync mode, and the controller uses it.

				JR

subject: GCR & Stacy & HardDisk access
q: A Stacy 2 with Spectre GCR installed can't access its hard disk. Is there some trick involved?
ref: Some STacy hard disks have a bug: if they see a reference to LUN 1 they lock up. In Spectre's hard disk devices menu, turn off all LUN 1 devices, save the config and reboot. Then format a Spectre partition from the hard disk menu. Read the manual.
replies:
According to Mark Booth (from Genie), some early Stacy models would
cause Spectre GCR to lock up if SCSI LUN 1 was enabled under the
Spectre "Hard Disk --- Devices ..." menu. So, before going into Mac
mode, select "Devices..." under "Hard Disk", and try turning off LUN 1.
(This is the reason Spectre 2.65 defaults to all SCSI LUN1 devices off,
which is a change from the Spectre 2.0 defaults.)

One or more of the partitions on the STacy hard disk need to be
converted into Spectre partitions.  Just use the format command on the
hard disk menu when Spectre is started.

        If the Spectre can't access the hard disk at all (ie.  not even
from the startup menu) then they need to change the device/subdevice
menu so that the Spectre does NOT access any of the LUN 1 drives, only
LUN 0.  After they change the sub-device menu save the Spectre
configuration and then reboot and try again.  There is (or at least was)
a bug in the STacy hard disk, if it saw a reference to LUN 1 the drive
locked up.  It wouldn't even respond to commands sent to LUN 0.

subject: Expanded vs. Extended mnemonic.
q: Is there an easy mnemonic to remember the difference between expanded and extended memory on a PC?
ref: ExTended is what you get with an AT: ordinary DOS-managed address space, 286 and up only. ExPanded is a paged LIM scheme: a small 64K window that software remaps into memory the CPU can't otherwise address. Works fine on an 8088. Not hard, folks.
replies:
Another one I've seen on the net which helps me is:

exTended: what you get with an AT.  Memory is available as normal, DOS-
managed address space.  Available only on '286 and higher systems; no 8088's
need apply.

exPanded: what you get with a Paged interface like LIM, under which you
have a small (like 64K) page window with support software which responds to
special calls to remap the window address space to an area within the
LIM memory (which is not otherwise addressable by the 8088-type CPU).
Works fine with old 8088 chips since there is no need to address physical
memory beyond the 20-bit address bus.

subject: -lmalloc
q: On IRIX 3.1, programs run fine with the BSD malloc but core dump with -lmalloc. What is the difference between the two?
ref: The -lmalloc version treats a request for zero bytes as invalid and returns NULL. That NULL probably gets passed to free() or realloc() later, and boom, core dump. Your Xlib is likely compiled to allow malloc(0). A zero-byte request isn't invalid, so -lmalloc is broken.
replies:
Most likely you have an Xlib which is compiled to allow malloc(0)'s.
-lmalloc does not support this ability.

I've had the same problem with -lmalloc (also known as malloc(3X)).
The crashes are probably caused by the fact that this implementation of
malloc, for some reason, treats a request for zero bytes as invalid.
It therefore returns a NULL pointer, which is probably passed to free()
or realloc() later, resulting in a core dump.

I probably don't have to convince too many people of this, but a request
for zero bytes is by no means an invalid request.  I think -lmalloc should
be fixed.

	 - Dan Webb

subject: Two paths for one file descriptor
q: How can a curses-based program send its standard output to two different terminals on receipt of a SIGUSR1, so a remote user can watch over a modem without the user leaving the application?
ref: With System V 3.2 curses, use newterm(type, outfd, infd) to set up a new terminal and set_term(new) to switch to it. It handles different terminal types too. Or use expect: trap SIGUSR1 to log_file, spawn the program, interact. And say which OS you run next time.
replies:
If you mean one process sending output to two different terminals, and
you are using System V 3.2 curses then check out the routines;

	SCREEN *newterm(type, outfd, infd)

which sets up curses for output to a new terminal, and

	SCREEN *set_term(new)

which makes curses switch to the new terminal.

The above solution supports terminals of different types.

p.s. it helps if people mention what operating system they are using,
a lot of BSD systems still do not provide System V curses functions
(however many proprietary BSD based systems now ship the latest System V
curses libraries).

If you have expect (see comp.unix.questions FAQ), you can do this with
the following script:

	trap {log_file another-terminal} SIGUSR1
	spawn curses-based-program
	interact

You can jam this all on the command line without the script as:

	expect -c "trap {log_file file} SIGUSR1; spawn program; interact"

subject: /bin/sh memory usage
q: Why does /bin/sh show 8.63 Mbytes of memory on the NeXT when /bin/csh shows only 1.01 Mbytes? What does this do to performance?
ref: Don't believe ps on a NeXT. Mach isn't Unix, and its virtual memory differs. ps reports the pages it might map if demanded, but Mach only creates and reads in pages that are actually touched. Read the CMU Mach papers.
replies:
Never believe everything you glean from ps(1) on a NeXT machine.  Keep in
mind that while in many respects Mach looks like Unix, it isn't.  It
emulates Unix almost perfectly in most of its current implementations.
However, it's virtual memory system is quite different, and what ps(1) is
reporting is the number of pages it might map if they were demanded.
Mach only creates and really reads in the pages that are accessed.
I'd suggest picking up the Mach documents from CMU to see what is really
happening.  I haven't seen one that explicity describes how the kernel
maps in the text and data segments, but the paper on the virtual memory
stuff is pretty good and gives you a feeling for what is happening.

The thesis, though, is that ps(1) under Mach doesn't really report
the same things as ps(1) under most other versions of Unix when it
comes to allocated space.

gerrit

subject: Problem with ld and string table
q: Linking about 100 object files for Kyoto Common Lisp on a 3B2/300 under System V 2.0, ld fails with 'fail to write symbol name in string table'. How do I get around this?
ref: Too many .o's for one ld run. Link half of them with -r and without -s, link the other half the same way, then ld the two outputs together without -r. If that fails, use three passes. Sigh, basic ld stuff.
replies:
Linking a large number of .o's requires ld to be executed more than once.
You need to create intermediate output files that havent been stripped.
This means the symbol table has to be there when you do the final ld run.

Try this:

	ld 1/2 your .o's with the -r option and without the -s option
	ld the other 1/2 of your .o's with -r and without -s
	ld the two output files from the above two steps without -r

That should do it. If it doesnt, try 3 passes...

subject: Cable scanner recommendations?
q: I need a cable scanner for testing twisted-pair runs. The MicroTest Pair Scanner only reports the greatest reflection along a cable run, and I'd like something that reports all of them. What else should I look at?
ref: If you want multiple reflections, you need a real Time Domain Reflectometer. It graphs the peaks along the line and reads out in meters if you set the velocity of propagation right. Expect to pay about ten times what a cable scanner costs. Cheap scanners only find the first reflection, so what did you expect?
replies:
Microtest Pair Scanner? I'm not very familiar with that, and I don't feel
like digging through all my product literature to find it. I saw the
brochure and was not impressed enough to read it through.

ANYWAY: We use a Microtest Cable Scanner for Twisted Pair, and for coax. It
only finds the first major reflection, but it is useful. It gives voltage
and noise information also.

If you are looking for a scanner that gives multiple reflection readings,
you need a Time Domain Reflectometer. That will show the cable reflections
on a graph, with peaks and valleys where the reflections are along the
line. If you have the velocity of propagation set right, the readout is in
meters of cable, so you can find the break very quickly. The problem with
the TDR is that it costs about ten times as much as as Cable Scanner.

subject: Universal machine-readable format?
q: If I had to send a small amount of data, a few thousand characters like DNA sequences, to people whose machines I don't know, what format and media would be most likely to be readable? I was thinking a plain ascii file on a 720k DOS floppy.
ref: Sigh. Use a 360K MS-DOS floppy, since 720K trips people up. Many machines import it directly and nearly every site has a PC that can Kermit it to the host. Nine-track ANSI tape and QIC are the other common choices, so send both if you can't tell. Or just use anonymous ftp, it's the 90's.
replies:
I would recommend MS-DOS 360K disks.  Many machines can import the
files directly, and almost every site has a PC that can Kermit the
files to the host.

Having worked in industry and college environments for a couple of
decades, I have stuck this kind of problem over and over again
(usually from the other end -- someone brings along a tape or
floppy and says "I want to upload this but I don't know what
format it is...").

If this were the 60's or 70's I'd advise punched cards.

If this were the 70's or 80's I might advise 1600 bpi, 9 track
tape, fixed-length records, fixed-length blocks of 4000 bytes or
so (longer ones are trouble for some machines), ASCII character set,
no volume or file labels (or, if you must, ANSII labels).

This being the 90's you might try to forget media entirely
and let the user/customer upload via anonymous login/ftp.

-Kym Horsell

The most common interchange medium is still ANSI standard 9-track tapes.
ANSI standard Quarter Inch Cartridges (QIC) are probably second.(*)
If you don't know what kind of machines the recipients have, I would
send both.

(I once wrote a tape when the only ANSI standard specified 800 bpi,
9 tracks.  A few years later, trying to find a machine that could
read 800 bpi ... so much for ANSI standards ...)

Oh yes, if your "universe" is IBM(tm) PC computers and others that are
compatible with them, then 360k floppies also sound like a good idea.
If you don't know what kinds of machines the recipients have, I would
send all three.  Maybe a 3.whatever-inch Macintosh(tm) format floppy
as well.

(*)Although my articles are personal opinion, not my employer's opinion,
the guess about QICs is especially so.

subject: Turbo C's Run Time Error Messages
q: Turbo C prints 'null pointer assignment' at the end of my program. How do I turn that off, or at least find where it comes from?
ref: Don't turn it off; you have a wild write into memory and it will bite you eventually. The message means the start of the data segment got corrupted by an uninitialized pointer. In the debugger, watch *(char *)0,4m and (char *)4 and step until they change. Fix your bug.
replies:
OUCH!! This one's gonna' bite you in the arse eventually. You're program is
doing a wild write into memory. Change the environment and you could see some
nasty *a*ffects.

Well, do you have the debugger? I had this problem... once :^) and when I ran
the debugger the environment was changed enough that the affect of this "null
pointer" was quite obvious.

Don't let this ride. It is something that you need to find!

...

 Q. How can I find out where my "null pointer assignment" is occurring?
 A. Set a watch on the following expressions:

            *(char *)0,4m
            (char *)4

    Step through the program. When the values change, the just-executed line
    is the one that is causing the problem.

 Q. My program comes up with the message 'Null pointer assignment'
    after it terminates. What does this mean?
 A. Before a small-data model Turbo C++ program returns to DOS, it will
    check to see if the beginning of its data segment has been corrupted.
    This message is to warn you that you have used uninitialized pointers
    or that your program has corrupted memory in some other way.

subject: Objective C References wanted
q: I'm curious about Objective C because of the NeXT machine, but can't find references. Can anyone suggest good books?
ref: Try Brad Cox's "Object Oriented Programming, an Evolutionary Approach" (Addison-Wesley, 1987). It wanders and bogs down in boring detail, but it explains the language. For OOP in general, Meyer's "Object-oriented Software Construction" is better written, though it's all Eiffel.
replies:
No, but I can suggest a so-so book:

	Brad J. Cox, "Object Oriented Programming, an Evolutionary Approach,"
	Addison-Wesley, 1987, ISBN 0-201-10393-1

Cox is the creator of Objective C.  I find that the book wanders and gets
bogged down in boring detail, but it certainly explains the language.  Since
the book came out the language has changed in some small syntactic details,
but nothing major.  Cox also wrote an article on Objective C in the first
issue of IEEE Software, in 1984.

If you want a good intro to object oriented programming, try the Eiffel book:

	Bertrand Meyer, "Object-oriented Software Construction," Prentice-Hall,
	1988, ISBN 0-13-629049-3.

Meyer is Mr. Eiffel, so the book is almost entirely in terms of Eiffel.  (There
is one page on Objective C, in the chapter on other languages.)  Nonetheless,
it explains object oriented design far more compellingly and is better
written, even though Meyer is French.

subject: "Long Distance" CPO (Code Practice Oscillator)
q: What's a cheap way to build a long-distance code practice setup for Boy Scouts to talk across a few hundred feet or several miles?
ref: Try light-wave communication. Use flashlights and photodetectors, with a detector at the focus of a parabolic reflector from Radio Shack for selectivity. Modulate the light to get a tone for tuning. Hardly rocket science, kid.
replies:
How about light-wave communications?  Photodetectors and flashlights for
example.  A photodetector at the focus of a parabolic reflector can be pretty
selective (Radio Shack sells  both the detectors and the parabolic reflector,
though they think the reflector is a solar cigarette lighter.) or you can use
lenses for less distorted reception.  For better signal-to-noise, you can
modulate the light either by messing with its power or by reflecting it off a
vibrating mirror.  That would provide a tone to help "tuning" at the receive
end. (You can also modulate voice onto light with similar techniques, but who's
going to want to send code when they can talk?)

subject: Remote execution from a Sun.
q: My NeXT program does PostScript imaging and writes a TIFF file. Run remotely via rlogin or rsh from a Sun, it stops with "DPS client library error: Could not form connection, host local host". NXHost doesn't help. Can it only run remotely from another NeXT?
ref: NXHost just tells one NeXT to display on the NeXTstep environment of another machine. A Sun doesn't run NeXTstep, so of course it can't connect. If your program shows nothing on screen, set NXHost to the NeXT itself. It may flash an icon there, so what.
replies:
The NXHost options simply tells one NeXT machine to display the results
on the NeXTstep environment running on another machine.  The message that you
got was telling you that the NeXT could not connect to a NeXTstep environment
on the host that you specified.

If you were specifying the SUN as the NXHost, this makes perfect sense.  It
doesn't run NeXTstep.  If your application really doesn't display any data on
the screen but simply uses some of the tools and automatically quits, set
the NXHost to the NeXT computer.  That should work.  It will probably also
display the application icon on the NeXT computer while the program is
executing.  Not a big issue but it could sure confuse a student who is sitting
down at the NeXT for the first time why this icon keeps appearing.

subject: Hypercard over a network.

replies:
Make sure you are using version 1.2 or later of HyperCard, as that
release was specifically targeted for support of servers and CD-ROM
drives.

on their own personal workstation in the System Folder.  There probably
should NOT be a Home stack on the server in the best of all possible
worlds.

Stacks can be opened read-only by multiple people for browsing and
copying (not cutting!), or as read-write by just one person.

HyperCard is used all the time this way at Apple with AppleShare.

subject: TOS 1.4 problem

replies:
First and most likely problem is that a pin either
a. missed the socket and is sticking out -- you can see this.
b. a pin tucked under the rom -- you can't see this.

the only way to handle case b is to CAREFULLY remove the roms
1 at a time, and check them.  Of course, there is a slight probability
that you will fold a pin under while doing this, so its a bit frustrating.

Also, are you really sure the roms are in the correct order?

Finally, you may have a malfuction, that tos1.1 didn't stress.

good luck

subject: Need Varification on fix made for PBHCreate
q: Why does a file created with PBHCreate sometimes disappear to the standard file package, and should I set ioFVersNum to zero?
ref: Yes, always set it to 0. PBHCreate can be treated as plain PBCreate on a machine without HFS or on an MFS volume, and there ioFVersNum is an input. HFS ignores it, so zeroing it never hurts. Read the fine print, people.
replies:
I think I understand the problem (we ran into a similar thing with MacApp).

The key point is that the call PBHCreate (or any of the HFS-version calls)
are exactly the same as the non-HFS versions (eg, PBCreate) if you are
running on a machine without the HFS code or if you are dealing with an MFS
volume.  MFS volumes do store the file version number, but HFS volumes
don't.

So even if you specify all the field required by the PBHCreate call, the
call might be treated as if it was a PBCreate call.  If you look under
PBCreate, you will notice that ioFVersNum is an input parameter.  Therefore,
to make sure your code works with MFS disks, you should always set
ioFVersNum to 0.

There is not problem with setting this field all the time.  If the volume is
an HFS volume, it will be ignored; otherwise it will be used.

You have to make sure either or both version number fields are set to 0, if
the call requires it.  Technically, PBHCreate doesn't use the version
number, except that a PBHCreat

subject: MicroEmacs 3.9e
q: In MicroEmacs 3.9e, ^N jumps the screen when I scroll past the last line. Can I scroll only one line at a time?
ref: Do move-window-down (^X ^N) first, then next-line. Typing three control keys annoying? Define a macro that does that when the cursor is on the window's last line, and bind ^N to execute it, in your emacs.rc. Not hard.
replies:
I don't know the reason for your first problem but for your second
question, I have a suggestion.  To scroll one line at a time at the
bottom of the window, you may first move-window-down (^X ^N) and then
goes to next-line (^N).  If you don't want to type 3 control keys, you
may define a macro to do it and then bind ^N to the execute that macro.
For instance, assume you use macro 30:

30	store-macro
	!if &equal $cwline $wline
		move-window-down
		next-line
	!else
		next-line
	!endif
!endm

bind-to-key execute-macro-30 ^N

Include the above lines in your .emacsrc or emacs.rc file

subject: Recursive descent parsers in perl?

ref: Go read lisp/rfc822.el in the GNU Emacs distribution. It's a hairy recursive descent parser for rfc822 addresses that uses regular expressions as far as it can. Only 281 lines, so translating it to perl is maybe a few months of work. Knowing Lisp helps.

When I was writing a perl program to parse rfc822 mail headers, I
   noticed that the grammar to describe the header is actually
   context-free. The comments in a header are delimited by "(" and ")"

   may not be painful; but I wonder how difficult it is to have a general
   recursive descent parser generator facility in perl. Am I asking too

expressions as much as it can.  Of course, it will help if you know Lisp.

work ...  It's only 281 lines of code.

subject: OS/2 under UNIX futures
q: What's the future of OS/2 running under UNIX or XENIX, given long-term worries about VP/ix or DOS Merge?
ref: Doubtful that OS/2 ever runs under UNIX except on an emulated machine, given how it's designed and how many hardware assumptions it makes. The reverse is likelier: patch a UNIX kernel to use OS/2 calls, and recompile everything. Slow, of course.
replies:
The way it's designed (emulation box, etc), I would doubt very much
that OS/2 would ever run under UNIX except on an emulated machine.

The reverse may not be true, however.  OS/2 makes a lot of assumptions
about the hardware of your system; most UNIX's do not.  I don't
believe it would be that hard to patch a UNIX kernel to use OS/2 calls
instead of its own.  Of course you'd loose performance with the
in-between steps, but you'd get the double OS that you're looking for.
I would imagine that the UNIX system call interface would need
redefining, so you'd have to recompile everything with new libraries.

subject: G-Dos
q: Where can I get G-Dos for the Atari ST?
ref: You don't get GDOS, you receive it. It's bundled with programs that use it, and you can't buy it separately. G+PLUS, about $35, is a better replacement. Or try AMCGDOS.ARC, a PD version, from terminator.cc.umich.edu. Simple question, indeed.
replies:
One does not "get" GDOS, one receives it (beware of anything like this!).
It is included with any program that uses it.  The first thing one does with
such a program is replace GDOS.PRG with G+PLUS.PRG.  G+PLUS is a better GDOS,
which does not slow down the machine, allows one to select ASSIGN.SYS files,
and does not screw up non-GDOS apps like the original atari GDOS does.  It is
a comercial product (G+PLUS), and costs about $35.

You can't buy gdos.  A software product that uses it has to BUY it from
ATARI, and put it on a disk for you.  Once you buy one program with it
it available for everything else.

You can get AMCGDOS.ARC from terminator.cc.umich.edu (35.1.33.8).
This seems to be a PD version of GDOS.  I believe there is also a file called
GDOS.ARC, but it just has a text file explaining GDOS, not the binary.  There
are a couple of GDOS fonts also on terminator.  I believe that the _real_
Atari GDOS is not public domain, but AMCGDOS is.

subject: Saving PICT
q: I'm trying to save a PICT resource to disk and load it back in another program with Think C, but it doesn't work, even with MacDraw PICTs. What am I doing wrong?
ref: You're confusing Handle and resource. Take the PicHandle from OpenPicture and AddResource it, then GetPicture and DrawPicture later. For PICT document files, the picture data starts 512 bytes into the data fork, which is why your MacDraw loading fails. Read Inside Macintosh V.
replies:
It sounds like you are confusing "Handle" and "resource" a little
here.  If you have managed to define a Picture successfully, it will be
stored in a relocatable memory block, referenced by the PicHandle
returned to you by your initial OpenPicture call.  You can take the
PicHandle, and use AddResource to turn it into a resource Handle.  It
then becomes a resource which is a part of the default resource file.
Displaying a PICT resource created in this manner is simple.  You just
open the file containing the resource, load it with GetPicture, and
call DrawPicture with the PicHandle.

Another method is to store the Picture in the data fork of a document file.
This is how MacDraw PICT documents are stored.  The actual Picture data
starts 512 bytes into the file, however, and that may be why you are
having trouble loading them.  A very good source for saving and loading
pictures to/from PICT files may be found in the QuickDraw chapter of
Inside Macintosh V.  Be a little careful when using i

subject: Backup of a live filesystem revisited
q: Can you safely back up a live filesystem? Is there a paper on it?
ref: No such paper exists, and live dumps are NOT always going to work. They usually do for extracting single files, but full incremental restores are likely to bomb out. tar and cpio work if files aren't changing. dump-style tools are unsafe live, and restoring onto a live disk corrupts things.
replies:
There are two basic approaches to backups:
	programs that use the file system (e.g. tar, cpio), and
	programs that scrounge directly off the disk (dd, dump, volcopy, finc)

File-system based programs can work on live systems as long as the individual
files are not changing.  They are slow but flexible, and do incremental dumps
well.  Unfortunately, they can't tell when a given file has been *removed*, and
can get horribly confused if you play games with links or modification times
between dumps.

Disk-based backup programs are normally much faster, but are unsafe on live
file systems; if nothing's being written at 3AM you may luck out.
Disk-based *restore* programs are another story; you should expect terrible
corruption if you use one on a live disk.  Suppose someone was already using
inode 443 when you try to restore it?

replies:
The problem with this is the fine print:  greater efficiency while you are
in the air AT SUBSONIC SPEED.  Propellers are a disaster at supersonic
speeds; you don't see fighters being designed with UDF engines, and although
they do use turbofans, the bypass ratios are *very* low by transport
standards.  Rockets spend very little time subsonic.  It's not worth it.

subject: floppy boot error
q: After making a standalone Coherent floppy I get 'Panic: getment: dev=0x883' on boot and the machine hangs. What does it mean?
ref: The device with major 8, minor 0x83 isn't a filesystem. This happens when you boot /coherent from floppy without a mountable filesystem on RAM disk 1. pipedev is set to that device, and pipes need a real filesystem. Mkfs it in /etc/brc, or put pipes on the RAM disk. Basic stuff.
replies:
This is an indication that the filesyetm associated with major number 0x8
and minor number 0x83 (i.e., 131 decimal) was not a filesystem. This happens
when you attempt to use a copy of /coherent from the floppy device and
do not set up RAM disk 1 with a mountable filesystem on it. pipedev_ is set
to this device, so the device needs to be mkfs'ed as part of /etc/brc or you
will see this sort of panic message. BTW, getment is a kernel routine that
gets a mount entry point. Since you don't have a valid filesystem on the device,
and since the pipe device MUST be a filesystem, getment panics the system.
The usual practice is to have pipedev == rootdev, as is the case for /coherent
on your hard disk.  If you intend to run off of a READ ONLY floppy filesystem,
you will need to put pipes on the RAM disk.

While I'm at it, kernel variable ronflag_ is set to 1 on the distribution
boot floppy of /coherent. This flag controls whether or not the root device
is READ ONLY. Patch it to zero if you wan

subject: "Shoe-shining" with 60 meg Wangtek tape on Sys V 386 3.2.1

ref: The -C option is in bytes, not blocks, and the 3.2.1 cpio has a bug giving you 10 times n bytes, so you got a 10k buffer. Use -C100000 for about a meg, or I use -C131072 or -C262144. RTFM.
replies:
According to the manual the -Cn option gives you a buffer of
n BYTES, not n BLOCKS. There is a bug in the 3.2.1 cpio however
which makes cpio give you a buffer of 10xn BYTES. So you really have
asked for a 10k buffer.

You can safely use cpio -oc -C100000 to get a 1000000 byte buffer.
I always use -C131072 or -C262144 to get a multiple of 1024 bytes
after the 10x bug.

subject: Imagewriter II smashes 1st line of output
q: The first line of the first print job on my Imagewriter II with a new SE comes out squished and illegible. Any fixes or workarounds?
ref: Pin-feed paper buckles near the pinch rollers about an inch from the top. Position the paper exactly, with the top edge or perforation right at the rollers, and tug out the slack. Try different paper, or best, buy the sheet feeder. Cheap paper, cheap problems.
replies:
Sounds like a special version of a more general problem involving squished
lines about an inch from the top of the paper.  The general problem occurs
when pin-feed paper is used, and the top edge of a page (or the
perforation) interacts with the pinch-rollers on the paper bail, causing
the paper to buckle slightly at about one inch from the top.  In this
case, if you only notice it on the first job, try just making sure that
you position the paper exactly right when you load it (top edge or
perforation right at the pinch rollers) and try to tug the paper a bit to
take out slack.

Another thing to try is a different brand or weight of paper.

The best treatment for the problem, though, is to buy and use the
sheet-feeder accessory.  The reason this helps is that you clamp the
platen when you use it, and the paper is pulled through by the platen
instead of being pushed by the pinwheels.  The paper is held at a point
much closer to the pinch rollers, and so it has much less tendency to
buc

subject: random bignums
q: Does anyone have suggestions for generating random bignums? We call random several times, shifting and adding, then take the result mod the upper bound.
ref: Generate each digit chunk in your multi-precision base separately, with the top chunk limited to the bound's top digits. If the result exceeds the bound, reject it and start over. Mod skews the distribution, which you apparently didn't consider.
replies:
Suppose we need to generate a random number between 0 and 123456789, and
our multi-precision routines work in base 1000.  I generate the bottom
three digits by taking one random integer between 0 and 999 inclusive, the
middle three digits likewise, and the upper three digits by taking a random
integer from 0 to 123.  The result will be a random number between 0 and
123999999.  If the result exceeds 123456789, then I reject it and start
afresh.  Otherwise I use this as my answer.

subject: HC returns machine type?
q: How can a HyperCard stack tell what Macintosh it runs on, so it can hide the menubar on a small screen but not on a large one?
ref: You don't need an XCMD. On a small screen the card window's top is 0, so on openStack do: if the top of card window <= 20 then hide menubar. Use SysEnvirons XFCN only if you really want machine type.
replies:
While there are XCMDs that will give you information about the machine type,
you can accomplish what you want here without an XCMD. What I'm assuming
you really want is to hide the menubar is and only if it would obscure
part of the card window. The following handler will do that:

  on openStack
    if the top of card window <= 20 then hide menubar
  end openStack

Since on a small screen, HyperCard comes up with the top of the card
window at 0, this will hide the menubar on a small screen. It will
also take care of situations in which a user (or a previously used
stack) on a large-screen Mac has for some reason moved the card window
to the top of the screen.

"The Starter Stack," by Robertson Smith, contains a PD XFCN called
SysEnvirons which returns, among other things, the type of Mac (Plus,
SE, II, etc.), the type of CPU, and whether or not there's a
coprocessor.  This stack is available from doc.cso.uiuc.edu via anon
ftp, under mac/MUG (or something like that).  It's in the file
Hypercard 9.0.  The stack is *very* big (almost 1000K uncompressed),
but very worth getting (it's kind of like the Developers Stack).  If
you just want a copy of this XFCN, I could mail just that part to you.
