subject: DZ VS DMF BOARDS VAX11/750
q: I was told a VAX 11/750 has different response times depending on whether you're on a DZ or a DMF board. Is that true, and why?
ref: Not a real issue. The DZ11 has no output DMA, so it loads the CPU more, and Berkeley Unix and Ultrix simulate DMA in software. The DMF is a DMA device, so it's a bit faster, but you probably won't notice the difference. DZ11s are nearly free used and work fine.
replies:
The DMF is an DMA device were the DZ is not. In ULTRIX and BSD 4.x
 if the number of chars through DZ in a given time reaches a given
 number the operating system turns off the interrupt on reciver side and
 polls the silo with each hardclock interrupt. The most impact on
 responce time is the number of dz on a system vs dmf or other dma
 comm devices. Also comm devices are normally at a interrupt level
 of 4 this is the lowest unibus interrupt level and the dz also does
 passive release to any npr (dma) device on the unibus. Considering
 the above it is more than possible that there would be a differance
 in responce times depending on which device your terminal was hook
 to. The dmf being the faster.

Not a real issue...

All common DEC serial interfaces have the same basic input structure - a
silo (FIFO) shared between the lines.  The DZ11 doesn't have DMA support
for output, so I presents a higher load on the system, and there is special
code in Berkely Unix and Ultrix to simulate "DMA".  I don't think you
are going to notice any diffference.

I don't know the details re: VMS, still they will work.

Here's the roster:

DH11 - PDP/11, not "supported" by Ultrix
DZ11 - No output DMA, CPU hungry in quantity
DHU11 - Output speed limited to 9600 baud
DMF32 - Only 2 ports with (brain dead) modem control
DMZ32 - Expensive, separate I/O panel

The DMF32, for all it's faults is still a reasonable choice for small systems.
It will make your life painful if you try to use it with smart modems and
DEC's "shared modem" support for uucp.

The DZ11's are available almost free on the used market and really do work
pretty well.  You might never notice the difference.

subject: Novice needs help
q: My X program dies a few seconds after I iconify it with a BadMatch error on X_SetInputFocus. I'm a novice with X. What's going wrong, or which manual should I read?
ref: Read the Xlib manual. Look up which Xlib function generates that request in the appendix. Only XSetInputFocus does, and it gives BadMatch when the window isn't viewable, as it isn't when iconified. For fancier handling, add an error handler or turn on synchronization.
replies:
The simplest way to debug an X protocol error like this is to:

1.  look in the appendix of the Xlib manual to see which Xlib functions
generate this protocol request

2.  read the description of those functions in the Xlib manual

In this case, only XSetInputFocus generates the SetInputFocus request.
The Xlib manual says that a BadMatch error happens if the window ID in

subject: Problem: aliases and exec in shells
q: In ksh and csh, 'exec foo' ignores aliases, so with ls aliased to 'ls -F', 'exec ls' runs plain ls. Is that expected, and is there a workaround?
ref: Aliases only expand in command position, so the word after exec isn't expanded. For ksh and bash, alias exec="exec " and the next word gets checked for aliases too. nohup works the same way. Not every word should be expanded, mind you.
replies:
[when the word to be aliased is not in a `command position']

[the `ls' is not expanded]

A simple work around for both ksh and bash is the following:

alias exec="exec "

Then the word following the `exec' will be checked for aliases and
expanded if necessary.  `nohup' is handled the same way.

I don't think that all words of a command should be checked for aliases
and expanded.

Chet

Well..... the problem might not be as bad as the shell's handling of 'exec'.
I think it just has to do with alias interpretation.

The thing with aliases is that the shell will only interpret an alias like
alias ls 'ls -F' if it's the first thing in the command line. (or the first
thing after a "|" , or enclosed in a ``, or the like something.) So even after
alias foo '| more', and typed w foo, it would certainly not do w | more.

It WOULD be nice if csh had a "global" alias option, but then there's the
chicken and egg problem of resourcing your global alias file after you've
already done so.

i.e

alias foo '| more'

is a global alias. The next time you sourced this file it might be interpreted
as

alias '| more' '|more' which would make no sense.

I guess this could be turned off during alias addition. Any other ideas?

				-Kartik

subject: Machine names and trademark law
q: If I name a machine foo.cs.columbia.edu where foo is a trademark, such as a video game, consumer electronics brand, exotic car or computer maker, have I violated trademark law?
ref: I'm not a lawyer, but you only infringe if your use could confuse customers about whose product it is. Odds are nobody cares, and at worst you get a nasty letter. Still, I'd steer clear of electronics names; exotic cars seem safe enough.
replies:
Caution:  I am not a lawyer.  Consult a pro before doing anything rash. :-)

The idea behind trademark law is that a trademark denotes a particular
vendor's product, so that it will not be confused with competing products.
The theory is that you infringe on someone's trademark only when you use
it in a way that could cause such confusion.  The practice is that different
companies have very different ideas about what constitutes potential for
confusion, and being sued is painful and costly even if it fails.

In practice, the odds are that nobody would care.  The odds are good that
if anyone did care, they'd send you a nasty letter saying "change those
names or we'll sic our lawyers on you".  This still wouldn't be fun, mind
you.  Me, I'd be wary of using names that have anything to do with
electronics, but the exotic cars sound reasonably safe.

subject: MFM -- RLL drive
q: Can I safely run my 2-year-old 70 MB Micropolis MFM drive with an RLL controller to get about 110 MB? Some say yes, some say no. What's the real answer?
ref: No authoritative answer; it depends on the drive. Back it up, borrow an RLL controller, and format it. A few bad sectors means buy one and count your megabytes; otherwise go back to MFM. Older drives usually work. Try before you buy, and stop asking for gospel.
replies:
The "real" answer depends on who you talk to.  There are those who have had
problem with RLL drives in the past, and there are those who have not.
I am among those that have not had any problems with RLL drives.  I own
a Seagate 238R, a 30meg RLL drive which has been running perfectly for the
last 3 three years on a PC.  I also have a Seagate 4096 formatted with an RLL
controller.  The 4096 is an 80meg MFM drive.  With the RLL controller, it's
capacity is 122megs.  You also get higher throughput using an RLL controller.
A 1:1 MFM controller will provide about 470KB/sec compared to 660KB+/sec for
a 1:1 RLL controller.

Back it up, borrow an RLL controller from a close friend, and try it.

If it formats with only a few bad sectors, then buy an RLL controller
and count your megabytes.  Otherwise, reformat it with MFM.

Drives from 2 years ago stand an excellent chance of working with RLL,
since back then nobody was sampling drives specifically for MFM/RLL.
That is probably why older drives tended to have fewer bad sectors on
average (MFM), as well.  My old Miniscribe works fine, with zero bad
sectors under MFM, RLL, and ADRT/ARLL.  My new Seagate 251-1 worked only
under MFM reliably.  Your mileage may vary, so try before you buy.

subject: PAL: no. of lines?

ref: A PAL Amiga gives 256 lines non-interlaced by default and 512 interlaced. The rest of the 625 is border and blanking. Overscan can stretch it to about 576 lines. Learn how interlacing works before asking.
replies:
Well, you never can use the full screen height. Some of these lines
are dedicated for checking purposes, don't know whether also sync is
counted with them. So, 625 is the absolute maximum and far more than
what is visible.
BTW also NTSC has more than the Amiga 400 lines, I think NTSC is
about 525 lines (or similar).

PAL video modes are made up of two 312.5 line fields being scanned out
at 50Hz each to make up a frame of 625 lines at 25Hz rate using
interlacing.  The default PAL Amiga screen is 512 lines long but of
coarse more is available via overscanning.  About the most number of
lines in a PAL Amiga would be about 576 lines more or less due to the
trade offs you are willing to have in regard to vertical blanking.  NTSC
is much the same situation but with different numbers.

Scott Hood

The PAL Amiga generates 256 lines as default in non-interlaced mode, and 512
in interlaced mode. The other 113 lines form the display border (in the
background colour of the vertically highest screen).

The height of the display can be changed using overscan modes (which under 2.0
can be set from a preferences file).

subject: What does BNC stand for?
q: What does BNC, as in BNC connector, stand for?
ref: Bayonet Neill Concelman, after the two engineers, Paul Neill and Carl Concelman, who designed it. The Navy story is folklore. TNC is the Threaded version. Honestly, this comes up every few months.
replies:
During WWII, the requirements for connectors better than
the UHF PL-269 and SO-239 ones, to be used for radar use, prompted two designs.
The first was developed at Bell Labs by Paul Neill and was identified as the
type N connector. At the same time, another connector was devised by Carl
Concelman. Named the type C connector, it was first designed as a true
50-ohm connector. Later, Neill and Concelman collaborated on the design of a
miniature bayonet locking connector. This was dubbed the Bayonet Neill
Concelman, or BNC connector. Some time after that, an improved, threaded
version for airborne use was developed and called the Threaded Neill
Concelman connector. For precise microwave use, a series of subminiature
connectors was produced - A, B, and C. Of these, the A or subminiature
(SMA) is the most popular.

BNC   -   Bayonet Navy Connector
TNC   -   Threaded Navy Connector
(& I suppose 'N' Connector is just a Navy Connector)

SMA   -   Sub-Miniture connector 'A'

subject: Rotating PICTs or BitMaps by arbitrary angle
q: Has anyone figured out a fast way to rotate a PICT or BitMap by an arbitrary angle? I need to rotate a small 40x40 one at least once a second.
ref: Fastest is to read the coordinates the PICT stores and rotate those around the center, using the sin/cos formulas. Better still, precompute the rotations beforehand and store them. Or do three shears, as in Graphics Gems. Also read UMPG.
replies:
Take a look at UMPG (Usenet Macintosh Programmers' Guide). In this case,
you will find a complete program that will rotate either a bitmap or a
PICT to an arbitrary angle.

Now that the version 1.0 is out, I guess this is good advice to anyone
who needs sample source code or help in Mac programming. Take a look at
the guide first, and then ask for help from this newsgroup.

The guide is available from sumex-aim.stanford.edu with anonymous ftp:
-r   292153 Oct 21 18:21 ./tech/usenet-mac-prog-guide-part1.hqx
-r   291192 Oct 21 18:21 ./tech/usenet-mac-prog-guide-part2.hqx

Another possibility for rotating bitmaps is described in Graphics Gems
by Andrew Glassner (actually edited by him). It describes a method where
you rotate a bitmap by doing three shear operations. This book is just
as vital for graphics programmers as UMPG is for Macintosh programmers.

Fastest way to rotate a PICT will probably (depending on how complex)
be to read the actual coordinates it stores & rotate those.
Remember to rotate around the center of the picture, in its own
local coords (i.e., within the rectangle specified in the header).
Formula for rotating ( (x,y) is the old loc., (x0,y0) is the
center, (h,k) is the new loc, th is the angle ):

	h=x0+(x-x0)*cos(th)-(y-y0)*sin(th)
	k=y0+(x-x0)*sin(th)+(y-y0)*cos(th)

(you get this from the sin/cos addition formulae)

I tell you three times: fastest way is to do it beforehand &
store the results!

subject: Multiprecision integer routines for PC Pascal
q: Does multiprecision integer code for PC Pascal already exist, and are the calling and linking conventions for external procedures in MS Pascal the same as Turbo Pascal's?
ref: The replies don't cover the conventions, but MS Pascal has an integer4 type, 32 bits, which isn't ordinal, so use ord to get a regular integer. It also has double precision reals and procedures as parameters, which Turbo lacks. Turbo is a toy by comparison.
replies:
In MS Pascal, there is an integer4  type which has a range from 2^31-1 to
-2^31.  This type isn't considered ordinal (can't be used to index an array,
as the control index in a for statement or in a switch statement).  Conversion
to regular integer requires the function ord to get an integer value from
integer4 (will retrieve the lower 2 bytes otherwise).  Also, there is
both standard and double precision reals available in MS pascal (not available
simultaneously in turbo), and it will allow procedures and functions
to be passed as parameters (not legal in turbo).

In other words, a lot of the things that are a problem in turbo are no
problem in ms.

Dan

subject: Changeing the transfer method for already queued mail
q: If sendmail routes mail over a netblazer link and it goes down or the queue backs up, can the queued mail be moved to a backup UUCP link?
ref: Sure. Queued addresses are reprocessed on every queue run, so change sendmail.cf and restart the daemon. Better, keep an alternate config and run, as root, /usr/lib/sendmail -q -C/etc/sendmail.alternative.cf &. Not rocket science.
replies:
As long as it is in the sendmail queue the address is reprocessed on each
queueing run.  Just change sendmail.cf, restart your daemon, and the queue
will be dispatched over a different routing.

  Better still, just keep around an alternative version of 'sendmail.cf'.
Then, if you need to reroute on a special occasion, do something like
the following (as root):

	/usr/lib/sendmail -q -C/etc/sendmail.alternative.cf &

subject: Using CPU instead of Blitter for speed
q: Wouldn't using the 020 or 030 CPU instead of the blitter slow the Amiga down overall? Maybe the blit routines should pick CPU or blitter intelligently.
ref: Polygons are definitely faster on the processor, even on a plain A500, but for block copying like windows and animation the blitter is much faster and easier to use. With bitplanes you only get parallelism on the last blit. Leave the ROM alone.
replies:
Unfortunately, with a bitplane oriented display, you only get parallelism
on your last bitplane blit. True, you can compute you next blit values before
waiting, but that buys you little time.  For polygons, the processor is
definitely faster, even on a nofastmem A500. But, for general block copying,
such as windows, arcade style animation, etc, the blitter is much faster,
and easier to use.  If the application is oriented such that the blits
can be interleaved with other processor operation, more parallelism could
be achieved, but this is usually not the case in a general purpose
application.

  As far as the ROM is concerned, it's fine as is. If a specific application
warrants higher performance, do what is fastest. Either directly access
the blitter with custom code, or use the processor to render polygons. I
haven't tried using the 030 for block moves as the blitter is highly
efficient in this case. Using the blitter and processor on alternate
bitplanes *simultaneously* would yield

subject: CreateProc
q: How do I know when a process created with AmigaDOS CreateProc exits? The main process has to unload the segment list but can't until the child is done. Is there a better way to start multiple processes from a main program?
ref: Send the process a startup message that its startup code fetches, and have it reply to the message when it terminates. Do the Reply in Forbidden state so the parent doesn't wake early. That's how Workbench does it. Don't expect to run BCPL CLI commands this way; use Execute() for those.
replies:
The common way is to send the process a startup message that is fetched
from its startupcode. The process the replies on the message if it terminates.
The Reply has to be done in Forbidden state, so the parent isn't awoken before
the child process is actually removed from the process list.
This method is used by Workbench.

It's a basic method, nevertheless, standard CreateProc is used with modules
that are LoadSeg'd into memory and it's a little tricky to start processes
running on the same code segment as the parent. Lattice provides some
new functions that do this in a simpler way.

Both can only be used to run processes that work similar to workbench
applications. You can't pass a commandline and stdio file handles in the
usual way (it depends on the startup code). And you'll NEVER run BCPL
programs like the standard CLI commands. These can be started only via
the AmigaDOS call Execute().

Michael van Elst

subject: Indirect function calls
q: Can I use indirect function calls like x = (*foo)(14) in Windows programs, especially far calls?
ref: Sure, as long as you use the Windows compiler flags and declare the function far. The address of a far function is really a reload thunk in your program's entry table, so the right code segment gets loaded even if it moved. Petzold's book explains it. Read it.
replies:
As long as you specified the Windows compiler flags and you define the
actual function as "far" you should have no problems with indirect function
calls.  The address that is indicated by the name of a "far" function is
actually the address of a reload thunk in the entry table for your program.
Windows keeps this table in one of two fixed segments that it builds for each
program when the program is initially loaded.  Making an indirect call will
still go to the reload thunk which will load the appropriate code segment if
it is not already in memory (or cause the correct routine to be called even
if the code segment has moved in memory).

For a more detailed explanation I recommend that you look at the section
called "Windows Runs the Program" on pages 300 and 301 of Charles Petzold's
"Programming Windows" book.  I think he does a nice job of explaining what
Windows does when relocating code and data segments.

I hope this helps.                                 Marc

subject: Run Time Libraries
q: How do Run Time Libraries work on the Apple IIgs? Will the standard APW linker in v2.0 support building and linking RTLs?
ref: Your understanding is basically correct. The loader finds the RTL in the Libraries prefix, and little extra code is needed. The APW/ORCA linkers won't build them, but LinkIIgs, slated for APW 2.0, will. Read its docs. Dumb abbreviation, anyway.
replies:
This is all basically correct, as I understand it.  When the Loaders need to
get something from a Run-Time Library, they look for the file in the Libraries
prefix (2/, usually */System/Libs).  Not finding it is a fatal system error,
methinks.  To my knowledge, little or no "extra" code is required to load the
routines from the run-time library ("RTL" is an accurate but dumb abbreviation
which is just one more reason I can't stand those things...).

The APW/ORCA linkers do not create run-time libraries.  LinkIIgs, which is
scheduled to be in APW 2.0 and is already at APDA in the APW 1.1 tools update
package, will create run-time libraries and programs that use them.  See the
LinkIIgs documentation for more details.

subject: Requirements to split domain into subs
q: We're registered on the Internet through uunet as progress.COM and want to split mail into subdomains like bedford.progress.COM. Do I have to register them, and should European offices use london.progress.com or a national domain?
ref: Probably no registering needed. If uunet gives you a wild-card MX for *.progress.com, the subdomains are already yours and land on your existing machine. Just have a mailer smart enough to field them. Separate MX and forwarding machines are only needed if you want delivery closer to each office.
replies:
If uunet provides a wild-card MX for *.progress.com (and they probably do
unless you specified otherwise), the subdomain name space should already
belong to you and you should have specified the contact person in your
domain application.  The implication of the wild-card MX, though, is that
everything is delivered through uunet to your existing machine.  That is,
something addressed to anything.progress.com will already land in your
lap and all you need is a mailer smart enough to field it (and preferably
not by throwing all unknown addresses at uunet since that will make
misspelled subdomain names loop back and forth).  On the other hand
if you want internet delivery to go to forwarders closer to the other
locations, then you have to arrange for separate MX'ing and forwarding
machines.

subject: Indexing man pages
q: When I choose "update index" for the Librarian target "Unix Manual Pages", it churns through /etc and then hangs on an entry in /dev. What is wrong?
ref: Blame the ixBuildOptions file under /usr/man/.index. Digital Librarian can't handle the trailing newline on the line in it, so ixBuild loses the directory name and indexes your current directory instead. Edit the file and remove the newline. Stupid bug.
replies:
cannot index

I have had no problem reindexing my man pages....  I don't know what
the problem is, but you might want to keep trying.

Todd Nathan
Vesalius Project, CSU

PS.  I entered the co-Xist and Xtrins and Xlibs stuff into mann direcotry
	and then just trashed my .index directory and rebuilt the index
	useing DL.  I am not sure why you are getting hung on /dev...

	Maybe I am missing something?  Please get back to me if this is cleared
up... ;')

The problem is the "ixBuildOptions" file under /usr/man/.index!  It
	contains a line like this:

-fman -Nwhatis -Ncat\* -V

	For some stupid reason, the Digital Librarian doesn't handle the
	newline (ASCII 0x0a) at the end of the line.  When it execs ixBuild,
	it appends the contents of the file to the command and the name of the
	directory buing built.  The newline causes the ixBuild command to
	ignore the name of the directory, thus assuming you're building an
	index of your current directory (usually your home directory, / if
	you're logged as root).

	To fix the problem, Edit ixBuildOptions and remove the newline!

It was my understanding this was a BUG (in big capital letters.)
Does anyone know a work around? I'd like to add man pages to the
digital librarian index too....

-Chris

subject: where is receive() defined?
q: Where is receive() defined in the Minix source? Every I/O task calls it but I can't find it.
ref: It's in the library linked into mm, fs and the kernel programs. Send and receive are just assembly wrappers that save BP, put the target process in the parameter and trap by interrupt. The kernel runs mini_send or mini_recv. Look in sendrec.s, pull it from libsrc.a with ar xf.
replies:
The "receive" and "send" are defined in the library which is linked to
each mm, fs, kernel programs.  They are just assembly encapsulations
that save BP and puts the target process address in the parameter and
call the system call by interrupt.  The kernel gets interrupted and
syscall() (I think) runs either mini_recv() or mini_send() or both
depending on the type of message passing as indicated in the
parameter.

The assembly routines are in sendrec.s I think.  You will need to
retrieve it from libsrc.a by doing "ar xf".

Hope this helps.

Occam 2 reference manual states that with a PROTOCOL OF ANY, the data sent

Input on this channel inputs the array of bytes and converts ( by retyping
conversion ) the value to the type of the receiving variable.

I am not convinced that the last statement holds true ( opinions ? ) as I
had to do the retyping manually.

Anyway, on input channel, read the data into a BYTE array of length equal to
that of the sent data as shown below.

INT16 inta RETYPES [inword FROM 0 FOR 2 ]
INT16 intb RETYPES [inword FROM 3 FOR 2 ]
INT16 intc RETYPES [inword FROM 6 FOR 2 ]

INT32 int1, int2 :    -- the data being sent.

CHAN OF ANY channel.a :

SEQ
  PAR
    SEQ
      channel.a ! int1
      channel.a ! int2
    SEQ
      channel.a ? [ inword FROM 0 FOR 4

subject: truncated inode

replies:
...

Check your /etc/uerf -R output to see if there is any hardware error
being reported.  Do a "dcheck -i 4 /dev/..." to see which of files

subject: Constrained vertex connectivity of a graph
q: In an n-connected symmetric graph where not all neighbors of any node can be faulty at once, is the connectivity 2n-2? How do I prove it or build a counterexample?
ref: No. Take the 3 by 3 grid with wraparound paths through the center: it's 3-connected, but removing the center row disconnects it, so it isn't 4-connected, which is 2n-2. And that removal doesn't kill all neighbors of any node. Counterexample done.
replies:
Consider the graph o=node,  -/\| = undirected edge.

    o-o-o
    o-o-o
    o-o-o

It is 3-connected (the path from any node to any other can go through
the center, clockwise or counter-clockwise).  It is not 4-connected, (2*3-2)
as removing the center row of nodes makes the remaining ones disjoint.
Also removing the center row does not remove all of the neighbors of any
particular node.

subject: INITs
q: Is it possible to copy an INIT into my System file instead of keeping it as a separate file, to make it more efficient?
ref: You could probably do it, but it won't make anything more efficient. The Mac doesn't context-switch between code in the System file and code outside it, only between applications. The UNIX "in the kernel" creed doesn't apply here, so quit fiddling.
replies:
You could probably do it, but it wouldn't make your INIT more effecient.
MacOS doesn't 'context-switch' when switching from code in the system to
code not in it.  So in this way, the UNIX creedo of 'in the kernel' doesn't
apply to the Mac.  The only time the Mac context switches is when switching
from executing one app to another.

subject: Help! Strange people are getting email I send out.
q: People not on my 170-address mailing list sometimes get my postings sent through sendmail and write asking why. What's causing this?
ref: Most likely some of your recipients are themselves mailing lists that redistribute the mail. Check the Received: headers in any copy you get back. If you're both on the Internet, telnet to the smtp port and use EXPN to expand the suspect address.
replies:
Most likely some of your recipient addresses are themselves mailing
lists which redistribute the mail.  If they send you a complete copy
of the mail you might be able to narrow this down by looking at the
'Received:' headers.  Then if you and the suspect destination are on
Internet, you can 'telnet' to the 'smtp' port and use the 'EXPN'
command to expand the address you are sendingto.

subject: si's and System 7, or how much memory you got...give it to me
q: Why does System 7 seem to take 11 MB on a 17 MB Mac IIsi in 24 bit mode, but only 1.4 MB in 32 bit mode? Is the Finder's About This Mac lying?
ref: Without 32-bit mode the Mac can only address the first 8 MB of RAM, so the other 9 MB is unusable. About This Macintosh lumps that unusable RAM under System Software. Turn on 32-bit mode, and watch which apps you run. Not rocket science.
replies:
Unless you have 32-bit mode turned on, the Mac can only access the first
8MB of physical RAM.  On a 17MB machine, this means that 9MB of RAM are
unusable.  (The "About This Macintosh..." display doesn't really tell the
truth in cases like this; any unusable block of RAM shows up under "System
Software" in the bar graph.)

subject: Prolog exam answer
q: Why can't Prolog predicates with arity greater than zero start with a capital letter?
ref: Same reason zero-arity ones can't. And they can, if you quote it: 'Cheap'(beer) is perfectly legal. Variables in predicate position work in some Prologs as an extension, or you use call/N. Read the manual.
replies:
(a) For the same reason that the predicate symbol part of a predicate with
    arity EQUAL to zero can't start with a capital letter either.
(b) But they _can_:
	'Cheap'(beer) :- ...
    is perfectly legal.
(c) If you want VARIABLES to be usable in predicate position, several Prologs
    support that as an extension (though they don't always do it in a
    particularly sensible way; you would expect P=f(X), P(Y) to call f(X,Y),
    but you can't rely on it).  The public-domain Prolog parser reads a
    term such as P(T_1,...,T_n) as the term call(P, T_1, ..., T_n), which,
    if you have call/N in your Prolog --- as you should! --- will do what
    you want.

Next, look in /dev/mt.  There will be several devices with 6 as the address.

Exabyte drive...   There are *some* drives that give back a vendor specific
string on an inquiry, and there is some problem talking to the drive if
that is so, as the s/w has no way of `knowing' what the heck it is.

subject: Nhfsstones
q: Why does nhfsstone read a kernel data structure for its statistics instead of having children pass operation counts to the parent through a temporary file or pipes? Is there a better way to compare other filesystems to NFS?
ref: The children generate pseudo NFS ops that don't necessarily match the actual NFS ops, so the kernel NFS stats are read to monitor the mix and adjust the load. Each child acts as a separate client. For other filesystems, try the connectathon general tests.
replies:
What the sub-processes do is generate pseudo NFS ops to simulate an
NFS environment on the client side.  Since these dont necessarily
reflect in the actual NFS ops performed, the kernel NFS stats are read
periodically and the operation-mix is monitored (couldn't figure out the
formulas used here, anybody did?) and the NFS load adjusted.

The parent merely sets up the client processes and finally gathers
the stats they record.  You dont need to pass the data around.
Each sub-process is independent and acts like a separate client (to
simulate several processes grabbing the few file-handles available).

Nhfsstone is tailored to measure NFS performance (diff. implementations).
Other file systems may use a different protocol.  You could perhaps use
the connectathon general tests for such comparison.

Only to the extent that the virus was unaware of the code... A well
built virus coud concevebly subvert the software involved in makeing
the check to always reporting a negative result (ie no virus), leading
to a false sense of security.

A better method might be to have any files containing critical
resources locked by default, with some non-simulable (is that a word?)
way of overriding the lock for legitimate tasks (such as installing
fonts, etc.  The problems with this are A. How? and B. The system etc.
would still be vulnerable at that point.

subject: Not accepted DIR command
q: CLI won't accept DIR copy 2 of XXX: for a disk named like that, though Workbench opens it fine. How do I get a directory of a disk whose name has spaces?
ref: Put quotes around the argument: dir "copy 2 of XXX:". Spaces separate arguments, and quoting the command too makes it one argument. Or assign a short name with assign XXX: "Copy 2 of XXX:". Read the AmigaDOS manual.
replies:
Try
DIR "copy 2 of XXX:"

If arguments contain space(s), you need to embrace them with
quotes, since arguments are normally separated by a space. Since
you included both the command (DIR) and the argument in quotes,
you specifically indicated just one argument, instead of a command
with argument (and you got a "Please insert volume DIR copy 2 of
XXX" requester). Each argument (or command for that matter) should
have it's own set of quotes, if needed.

dir volumename:		(or dir "volume name:" if the name has spaces)

You may want to copy the commands you need (dir, cd type, etc) to
your ramdisk and assign c: to ram:, so you can swap disks more
easily (note that if you want to use a command not in ram: you
either have to assign c: back to Workbench1.3:c again or include the
volume and pathname in the command. I.e. Workbench1.3:c/ed or
df0:c/ed if the Workbench is present in the internal drive. )

You'll find more information about this in the AmigaDOS manual,
 published by Bantam.

.ec

When you want to get a directory listing of a disk whose name has embedded
spaces in it, use quote marks. If you had typed :

1> dir "copy 2 of XXX:"

It would have worked properly. Also if you will use that disk a lot and
you get tired of typing the spaces, you can first assign it a different
name with the command :

1> assign XXX: "Copy 2 of XXX:"

And then you can look at it with :

1> dir XXX:

--Chuck McManis

subject: Can I count on any alignment from NewHandle or NewPtr?
q: Can I count on any alignment from NewHandle or NewPtr on the Mac? Is there any guarantee on stack alignment?
ref: Word alignment, yes. Longword, no. Heap blocks may be longword aligned on newer machines, but not always, and on a Plus it's definitely not guaranteed. Stack gets word alignment at best. Don't build a garbage collector on wishful thinking.
replies:
As I recall, heap blocks are word aligned on 68000 Macs and are long word
aligned on 68020 and 68030 Macs.  The best you can hope for is word alignment
on the stack since both word- and long word-sized values are stored on the
stack...

steve

You can count on word alignment, but not longword alignment both for heap
blocks and stack values. There are certain compilers which try to keep
the stack always longword aligned - one of them is described in a paper by
Michael Franz in a recent issue of SIGPLAN Notices. It *might be* that on
newer machines, heap blocks are longword aligned, but I know from painful
experience that at least on a Plus, this is not always true.

Matthias

subject: Standard behavior?
q: Given the predicate a([]). a(_). and the query :-a([]). , C-Prolog finds one match and UNSW Prolog finds two. Which is standard behavior?
ref: Vanilla Prolog says _ matches anything, including the null list, so there are two solutions. C-Prolog just says yes at top level and gives no chance to backtrack. Ask a(X) and press ; and you'll see both. Basic stuff.
replies:
I do not have the authority to say which is "standard" behavior, if by that
you mean which is found more commonly in implementations.  However, any book
on "vanilla" Prolog will tell you that "_" matches to anything, including a
null list, so I would indeed be annoyed by C-Prolog if it did not find two
matches.  Anybody disagree?

It depends what you mean by "one match".  I should think all Prolog
systems would just tell you that the query succeeds, since there are no free
variables to get bindings for in the query.

     The standard reading of the predicate in FOL with identity would be
a(X) <- X = []  \/  X = X.
...which, given the standard computation algorithm, should probably give
two responses to the query
... namely, X=[] and X=X.

--Jamie.

Hmmmm, not exactly.
Depends on what you mean by finding a match and how you apply
the query. If you type

a([]).

to the C-prolog interpreter it comes back and says 'yes', ie the
predicate can be satisfied. However, when you present such a query to
the C-prolog top level interpreter it doesnt give you any opporunity
to backtrack, you only get this opportunity if there are any variables
given in your query, and you make use of this opportunity by typing
';' which invites the interpreter to backtrack.

Below follows two dialogs with C prolog that indicate there are indeed
two solutions to the query you mentioned.(Note that '?-' is the
interpreter's prompt for you to type a query, and that ^ appears under
user input)

?- a(X).			-- initial query
   ^^^^^

X = [] ;			-- first solution, ; typed so invoke
       ^			   backtracking.

X = _0 ;			-- second solution..
       ^

no				-- prolog says no more solutions.

?- a([]), write(a), fail.	-- need to phrase it like this to
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

ref: Barely. You can coax gcc through the SGI C compiler with lots of massaging, but SGI's 680x0 assembler syntax is neither MIT nor Motorola and the floating-point rules differ from the Sun 3. You'd need new machine files. Not worth it for a dead machine.

Hi,
      I have a boat anchor model 3130. Has anyone installed gcc or g++ on one
   of these beasties? I would realy appreciate some (ok lots of) help with this,
With lots of massaging, you can get gcc through the SGI-supplied C
compiler.  This, however, will do you not much good at all, because
the 680x0 assembler used by SGI uses a syntax which is neither MIT nor
Motorola.  What's more, I'll wager the rules for accessing
floating-point are different from the Sun 3 series, which seems to
have been the driving fouce behind the 68000 ports of gxx.

and soon to be no longer supported that I gave up on it.

I looked at setting up gas, but that seemed to be just as much work.

Actually, working with the 3000 series C compiler from SGI isn't so
bad, if you:

2. sprinkle function prototypes liberally throughout your file

subject: Last post: Anyone know steppers?
q: How fast can I run stepper motors from my PC parallel port, and can I drive several motors at once? I get 20 RPM from a 72 step/rev motor.
ref: Use stepper controller chips with step and direction lines, so one port handles four motors. Check Motorola and National. For real speed you must ramp: step slow until moving, then faster, with a linear ramp between empirical min and max rates. Varying loads need an encoder and feedback, since steppers lose steps.
replies:
-Message-Text-Follows-
   There are several controllers for stepping motors, typically you have
a "step" line and a "direction" line so you could handle four motors with
your parallel port. Check Motorola and National.

   The hard part is that to get true high performance stepping you need to
take acceleration and load into account. That is you have to step slow
until you get moving and then step faster once the motor is moving. If
the load is negligible and all you have to do is account for the inertia
of the motor this is not too bad, A linear ramp in stepping speed between
a empirically determined min and max stepping rate works well. If you have
varying loads that is a much tougher problem, probably better handled by
a position encoder and some feedback than a stepper where you can loose
steps.

    A question I have:  It should be possible by watching the back EMF
of a stepper to detect missed steps. Has anybody done this?

subject: DEBUGGING X PROGRAMS
q: My X program crashes when run from the command line but runs fine under the debugger, with an Xlib sequence lost / BadLength error. What causes that?
ref: Classic. Your program has scribbled over some Xlib structure by writing into unallocated memory, like off the end of an array. Under a debugger, it uses its own memory allocation, so you scribble over something harmless instead. Go fix your bug.
replies:
This error usually occurs when your program has written over some valuable Xlib
structure by writing into non-allocated memory (for example, writing off the
end of an array).

When you run under a debugger the debugger usually uses its own memory
allocation scheme and so you're scribbling over something else in memory, not
the Xlib structures which cause this error message.

subject: Interrupt List - IRQ2
q: The interrupt list says IRQ2 is the EGA vertical retrace interrupt, but my AT tech reference says IRQ2 cascades the second PIC. What am I missing?
ref: Both are right. On the 8-bit PC and XT, EGA vsync is wired to IRQ2. On the AT that same bus line is IRQ9, routed through the second PIC into IRQ2 of the first. Use DOS function 25H of INT 21H to install the vector and old handlers work everywhere. Basic stuff.
replies:
Both are correct.

On the PC and XT with the 8-bit bus, EGA's V-sync interrupt is
indeed connected to IRQ2 and to the corresponding input of PIC.
And EGA is an 8-bit addon card.

On the AT's 16-bit bus, the same physical bus line(connector) is
now designated as IRQ9 which goes through the 2-nd PIC and then
into IRQ2 of the 1-st PIC.

I thought, when I noticed this first, that this might break the
hardware interrupt handler I wrote (for old PC) that used IRQ2,
and that I would have to modify the driver to use IRQ9.

It turns out that you can use the old interrupt handler that uses
IRQ2 without modification on PC, XT, and AT if you use Function 25H
of INT21H DOS service to install interrupt vector.

subject: Generating Octal/Hex Codes from Bourne Shell
q: How can I generate arbitrary ASCII octal or hex codes from the Bourne shell? echo "\007" works on my System V box, but on my Fortune 32:16 (Sys 3v7 and BSD 4.3) it just prints the string literally.
ref: Use tr, which understands octal escapes on BSD: echo . | tr . '\007'. It takes at most three digits. Or you may be getting csh's builtin echo, so try /bin/echo. Learn which shell you're in.
replies:
Well, one way to do it would be to use the tr command.  For instance,
to repeat your examples:

		echo . | tr . '\007'	# 0x07
		echo . | tr . '\212'	# 0x8a

Note that tr expects to have no more than 3 digits so '\0212' won't
give you what you expect.

On BSD you can use tr(1) which understands octal codes just in the
way your echo does in System V; the two examples could be rewritten
as:
      tr a "\007"  <<EOT
a
EOT

      tr a "\0212" <<EOT
a
EOT

The a character acts as a dummy and is translated to the octal coded
character. If you use these characters a lot, it would make sense to
save the output of tr into shell variables.
Hope this helps?
                   Leo.

Could you be using csh on your Fortune?  Csh has a builtin echo command
which behaves differently than echo in Bourne shell echo.  Try using
/bin/echo instead of echo.

subject: Visualization Machines
q: What are good machines for scientific visualization? I have a Cray, but I want over 100 MFlops peak and over 25 Mpixels per second output to show results at 20 frames per second. Should I look at Convex or the Connection Machine?
ref: Neither Convex nor DAP is a visualization machine. Look at Stardent, the old Stellar and Ardent. A GS2000 runs vector-parallel codes at about 27% of a Cray XMP and renders complex models at over 12 frames a second. AVS means no graphics programming at all. Cray codes port easily.
replies:
As far as I know neither the Convex or DAP are visualization machines.

I think you should consider machines from Stardent Computer Ltd
(formerly Stellar and Ardent).  They combine the sort of performance
you seem to be seeking with the visualization.  Our Stardent GS2000
can run my vector-parallel codes at 27% of the speed of a CRAY XMP
(single processor) and do geometry rendering of complex molecular
models at > 12 frames/sec.  Codes vectorized for the cray should port
easily, and the vectorizing fortran and C compilers are quite good.

The greatest advantage I find of Stardent is their AVS visualization
program which means that you can do vizualization without any graphics
programming. At all.  You should be able to integrate your codes with
AVS with a small programming effort to get the computatational module
to deliver data for immediate visualization.

subject: video signal question
q: My Zenith VM131 monitor uses TTL analog RGB signals. Can I connect it to an Amiga and get all the colors?
ref: Never heard of TTL analogue; TTL is digital. The monitor must be a 15.75 kHz horizontal scan rate type, and accept composite or separate sync. If it takes analogue RGB, you're in fat city with all the colors. Check the spec sheet.
replies:
I have never heard of 'TTL analogue' signals. TTL usually refers to a
digital ( on/off ) type of signal, as opposed to the continous analogue
variety. It is possible that your monitor accepts either type ( in which
case it most likely has a switch for selecting them ).

The amiga puts out three TTL level sync signals. Horizontal and vertical
sync, or composite sync. Most likely your monitor accepts composite
sync, although it might require the separate horizontal and vertical
sync. The key issue here is that the monitor must be a 15.75 khz
horizontal scan rate monitor. Check the spec.

As for the video, if the monitor accepts analogue RGB, you should be
in fat city with all the colors.

Hedley

subject: Numerical Integration on the HP48
q: How do I numerically integrate a program object on the HP48SX? I get Bad Argument Type with a program in level 2.
ref: Don't put the program on the stack. Use lower, upper, an expression that calls the program as name(arguments), then the variable, e.g. 2 3 'S(X)' 'X'. The program should be << -> X << code >> >>. That gave 6.333 for X squared. Read the manual harder.
replies:
Put the following on the stack:
	lower upper 'expression' variable

In the expression, calls to programs should appear in the form:
	name(arguments)

The program should have the form:
	<< -> local variable names << program code >> >>

I tried this with:
	2 3 'S(X)' 'X'

while S contained \<< \-> X \<< X SQ \>> \>>, and it worked. giving the
correct result (6.333...).

				-- edp (Eric Postpischil)
				"Always mount a scratch monkey."

subject: I need help with Smail..
q: Smail seems to ignore my paths file. Mail replies to hosts that reached me by UUCP name or domain name go through my smarthost instead of directly to them. What am I doing wrong?
ref: Your paths file must be sorted, because smail 2.5 does a binary search. Also, the smarthost belongs under the name smart-host, and 2.5 has a rumored bug that misses the last entry, so add a dummy last line. If it's smail3, run it with -v50 -N to see how it routes. Basics.
replies:
The return addresses were, of course, created on these machines, not your
smail.

Well, your first problem is that the paths file *must* be sorted.  Smail 2.5
(you are using smail 2.5 aren't you?) uses a binary search, and requires a
sorted paths file.  The above contents aren't sorted.

Secondly, you say you have "nuchat" as your smart host.  You're supposed
to have that specified as "smart-host" in the paths file.

Thirdly, "official" smail 2.5 is rumoured to have a bug that sometimes
prevents it from seeing the last entry.

So try this paths file:

cls	privsec!cls!%s
nuchat.sccsi.com	nuchat!%s
privsec.uucp	privsec!%s
smart-host	nuchat!%s
xcluud.sccsi.com	xcluud!%s
zzzzzzzzzz zzzzzzzz

Which smail - 2.5 and 3.x are very different.  If you are using smail3,
the above should work but you need to sort the paths file alphabetically.
Also, if sccsi.com is "your" domain, you may have configured the paths
router to strip that part before the search.  A good way to see how an
address is handled by smail3 is to use the -vnumber -N options with
a dummy message.  "smail -v50 -N <testfile" will usually tell you
enough and the -N supresses actual delivery.

subject: Importing postscript file and building "links" in HyperNeWS (question)
q: Is it possible in HyperNeWS to build links, meaning highlighted, mouse-sensitive areas that scroll with the text, on text from an imported PostScript file?
ref: Not easily. An EditText object can't make a sensitive area scroll with its text. Hyperman only supports SGML references, not arbitrary sensitive text, and not everything is even distributed. Sigh, read what the thing actually does before asking for miracles.
replies:
What you ask is not very easy with an EditText object, because getting a
sensitive area to scroll with the text is not part of it's current
capabilities.

Later you mention the Hyperman stack which has more capabilities.  All the
HyperNeWS documentation is developed in SGML, which allows us to convert
it to different formats of our choosing.  For instance, we convert it to
LaTeX for the hardcopy version of the doc, and we also convert it to the
online format that Hyperman uses.  The concept of a reference is what gives
the online format its hypertext capabilities.  The parts of the doc that say
"See Figure 3.1" or "See Section 7" are flagged by our SGML conversion tool.
When the resulting file is read by the Hyperman client program, it highlights
the references and makes them sensitive.

Our current implementation does not allow for arbitrary bits of sensitive
text, only SGML references.  And not all of what I have described is
distributed with HyperNeWS.

Regards,

  -- Jim

subject: 9600 Baud modems and V.42bis

error correcting abilities (I just use cu and uucp), but I have used
baud rates of "19200" and "38400" within my /usr/lib/uucp/Devices file. These
settings map to the EXTA and EXTB stty arguments. So far, I only have the
standard PC serial ports COM1 and COM2 (/dev/tty1A and /dev/tty2A). The
modem (a ViVa 9642e) does report carrier at 9600 and connection (between
the modem and my computer) at 38400 baud. But then again, I haven't installed

using error-control modems, using uuencode, uudecode, and cu's put and
take commands work pretty well. At least, it ends up being faster than

subject: Copy protection schemes
q: What is "key disk" copy protection on the Amiga? I can't think of protection that a raw track read and write couldn't beat.
ref: A key disk is a special master disk that must be present for the program to run. Once the program has verified it, you can remove it, so you can copy the program to a hard disk and insert the floppy only at startup. Decent vendors prompt for it; others just crash the system.
replies:
A program using a key disk requires that a special disk,
called the "key disk", or "master disk", be present for the
program to run.  The key disk may be removed once the program has
verified it.  Thus, if you have a hard disk, for example, you may
copy the program to the hard disk, and run of there, only
inserting the floppy when you start the program.

   If the manufacturer is reasonable, and you start the program without
the key disk, it will ask for it, verify it, and then eject it.  If the
manufacturer is a jerk ( Electronic Arts ), the program will just crash
the system.

   I complained to EA about this, and they told me that it was a feature.
( This is on the Mac.  I don't know what they do with their Amiga stuff ).

subject: NFS - heterogeneity of
q: How does NFS, specifically PC/NFS, handle the CR/LF versus LF difference between DOS and UNIX text files? Are text and binary files distinguished?
ref: It doesn't. PC-NFS gives you a utility to convert text files between CR/LF and LF, and no translation happens during reads or writes. NFS assumes smart clients and dumb servers, so don't expect the server to do anything fancy. Doing it on the fly in the client is possible, but getting it right in general won't be easy.
replies:
On PC-NFS, a utility is provided to translate text files back and
forth between MS-DOS style (CR/LF) and UNIX style (LF).
No translation is done on during any data transfers (read/write).

Thus, if a text file is created by PC-NFS on a UNIX machine, it will have
the CR/LF style.  If a UNIX user wants to use this file, the
translation utility would be used first to convert it to UNIX style.
Similarly, if the MS-DOS user wants to look at a UNIX text file, he
or she will use a DOS version of the same utility on the file.

NFS assumes that there are smart clients and "dumb" servers.  Never
expect the server to do anything fancy like this for you.  However,
if your client is clever enough to distinguish text files from binary
files (through some feat of magic), there's certainly nothing wrong
with training it to do the translation on the fly.  But it probably
won't be easy to get right in the general case.

subject: Graphics driver
q: What's the fastest way to control the screen in C for games, say moving a C64-sprite-like figure across the screen in CGA mode? Do I need a device driver? Also, a fast line-drawing routine would help.
ref: A device driver would be s l o w. Write directly to CGA memory at B800:0000, with even scan lines first and odd lines at B800:2000. No hardware sprites, so save and restore the background yourself and AND/OR pixel masks for horizontal movement. IBM never planned for this. Good luck.
replies:
If you want to modify a CGA screen, the fastest way to do it
is with direct writes to CGA memory, located in B800:0000 to
B800:1F40 (even scan lines) and B800:2000 to B800:2F40 (odd
scan lines).  A device driver would be s l o w .

You're trying to do something that IBM really didn't provide
for.  There is no hardware support for sprites or anything
resembling them; you'll have to save the original screen
contents so you can restore things when the "sprite" moves,
and you'll need to do your own collision calculations.  You
can't even do color table animation, because the color
palettes are fixed with two non-intersecting sets of 3 colors
each.  Since each byte of memory represents 4 pixels, you'll
need to OR and AND with pixel masks for horizontal movement.
Vertical movement is harder, because you need to add or
subtract your screen memory offset depending on whether you're
in an even or odd row.

Good luck; you'll need it, plus lots of patience.

(I did the animation for Championship

For the second, still use the text widget, but check out the
routines:  XawTextSourceRead(), XawTextSourceReplace().  These functions
allow you to read and replace (or append) portions of the text buffer.

subject: asld question
q: I'm converting a MASM klib88.asm back into something asld can handle, and I can't tell when to use '*' and when to use '#' in front of tokens. I figured '#' means a 2-byte operand and '*' a 1-byte one, but that doesn't match the 1.1 klib88.s sources. How does asld's operand syntax work?
ref: In theory * is one byte and # is two bytes. That's PC-IX syntax. In practice the assembler can see how big the number is, so it ignores the difference and uses one byte if it fits, two otherwise. Sigh, redundant syntax, but that's IBM for you.
replies:
In theory, * means 1 byte and # means two bytes.  This is PC-IX syntax.
Of course, the assembler can see very well how big the number is and doesn't
need the user to tell it whether it fits in 8 bits or not.  Thus it ignores
the difference between * and # ands uses 1 byte when the number fits in
one byte, and two bytes otherwise.  I don't know why PC-IX has two ways to
express constants when the assembler can obviously figure it out itself
except to mention that unlike Xenix, PC-IX is a genuine, official, IBM
product, sold in genuine, official IBM stores (back when they had such
things).

subject: How do I avoid a flood of Expose events?
q: Environment is X11R3. A widget sitting beneath a bunch of other widgets gets a flood of expose events while the stack is built, even with event compression on, causing redundant redrawing. How can I detect or avoid them?
ref: Look at the expose event structure. It holds a count of how many more expose events are still coming in that series. Only redraw when the count hits zero, or dispatch only the last one. Basic stuff, read the event structure.
replies:
geoff@veritas.uucp (Geoffrey Leach) writes...

  Is this a widget that you are writing/wrote or just using ?  In either
case when you receive the event you can check to see what kind of event
it is.

  If it is an expose event then the event structure will contain an
element that holds the value of how many more expose events are to
follow for that series.

  If you just using widgets then only do an XtDispatchEvent on the last
expose event.

  If you are getting several independent series of expose events then
you could do something like, just hold the latest one and after some
period of time dispatch it.

  Granted, things like this are band-aids/kludges but do work in the
case you mentioned.

subject: Can write in active a.out file: Bug in R4?
q: On two UNIX R4 systems a process can open(2) for writing an a.out file that is currently running, instead of getting ETXTBUSY. Is this a bug in R4?
ref: On a local disk you should get ETXTBUSY, and if you don't, complain to your vendor. Over NFS you won't, since the server only sees reads and has no idea the file is being executed. Basic stuff, really.
replies:
This is just another example of Unix trying to become Multics. One of the first
things I tried when I got a Multics login (late '70s) was to write a
program which printed one string, slept for a minute, and then printed a
second string. During the sleep, I edited the second string and recompiled the
source. The awakening process then printed the modified second string.
Arguably very silly behavior.

Conversely, I could never understand why Unix (system V only?) wouldn't let
me "rm" an executing program. It seemed to me that the incore inode should
have sufficed for any bookeeping during program execution.

If you are running an a.out which resides on a local disk you
should get the ETXTBUSY error.
Over NFS you shouldn't because all the server knows is that you're
reading the file. It has no notion of a file being executed remotely.
Your workstation executing the file can also not prevent you from
writing to the file on the server, because it cannot know if the new
attempt to write the file still refers to the same file. (One can rename
a file being executed)

If you don't get ETXTBUSY on a local disk you should complain to your vendor.

subject: runtype and systype?
q: What is the difference between the runtype and systype directives when compiling code on the Apollo? What should the values be, and what are the defaults?
ref: Systype decides where the program finds files through variant links like /usr/bin. Programs taking filenames should use "any", and the default comes from the SYSTYPE environment variable. Runtype picks the BSD or SysV version of routines whose semantics differ; you rarely need it. Read the manual.
replies:
systype determines where your program finds files when it hits a variant
link (like /usr/bin) that has the SYSTYPE variable in it.  Any program that
takes filenames should probably be built with a SYSTYPE of "any" (which tells
it to use whatever the SYSTYPE environment variable is set to at runtime).  The
default is picked up from the SYSTYPE environment variable, although you
can override it by setting the COMPILESYSTYPE variable.

runtype determines which version of a routine the program gets when it
executes a routine whose semantics are different between BSD and SYSV.
You normally wouldn't have to use this (presumably you are programming for
the environment you are coding in).  However if you're current SYSTYPE
environment variable is not the same as what you are coding for, then you
should use it to make sure your program gets the correct version of the
routines.

						-kee

subject: Mac is software - why not on NeXT?
q: The Mac is really software, so why can't we buy Macintosh system software and ROMs for NeXT, IBM, Sun and other hardware for a modest price and run Mac software anywhere?
ref: Because Apple would lose a huge market share, the way IBM did to the clones. They guard their ROMs fiercely. Your only legal option is a Mac emulator board with ROMs yanked from a real Mac. Dream on about a license.
replies:
Simple, because then Apple would lose a HUGE market share.  Look at the IBM
clone market.  IBM allowed other people to manufacture the BIOS and other
components of IBM systems, so people did the obvious thing, buy the separate
parts and make their own.  IBM's share of the PC market fell something like 40%
due to that decision.  Apple doesn't want the Mac to become a 'generic'
computer.  Thus, they vigorously protect their ROM code.  If you want to go and
'reverse engineer' the Mac Toolbox, go ahead.  Apple can't do much.  But that
is a pretty ridiculous project.  (Look at how few companies produced Apple II
clones.  2.  Only one is now still around.  Laser)  Therefore, the only real
option is to do what the Amacs cards do.   Buy a mac, yank the ROMS, and stick
them in whatever Mac emulator board you have.  That is the only legal option
unless Apple wants to license out their ROM code (not a snowball's chance in
....)

subject: auxiliary console
q: With CTTY I can switch MS-DOS to an auxiliary console, but programs like GW-BASIC and dBASE III break the connection. How can I make these stubborn programs listen to the aux console?
ref: Rewrite them, in general. CTTY only affects DOS calls, and those programs use the BIOS or write straight to screen hardware. You could try intercepting BIOS calls, but you'd be faking the whole screen. Carbon Copy-style programs do this slowly but adequately. Sigh.
replies:
Rewrite them, in general. There are three ways to to screen I/O on a PC -
through DOS, through the BIOS, or directly. CTTY only affects the DOS calls. I
suppose you could write something that would intercept the BIOS calls and aim
them at the serial port, but most programs that use them, such as Basic,
assume that they can directly move to any place on the screen and write a
character, so you'd have to fake that. You'd also have to come up with
conventions for the function keys, ALT keys, etc.

Many popular programs write directly to the screen hardware so they can update
the screen quickly; there's not much you can do about them.

You might look at programs like Carbon Copy which do their best to give you a
remote PC console by intercepting all the calls they can, and periodically
reading the screen and sending updates to the remote terminal. They're a
little tricky to set up, but once you do they work adequately though slowly.

subject: Request for opinions on AI textbook
q: A textbook claims the Horn clause calculus is equivalent to the full first-order predicate calculus for proofs by refutation. Is that really a mistake?
ref: Not necessarily. Resolution is refutation-complete, and any set of clauses can be turned into an equivalent set of Horn clauses by inventing new predicates to name negations. For example, replace (NOT (P a)) with (Q a) and add clauses tying Q and P together. Think before calling it an error.
replies:
In what sense is it a mistake? Resolution is refutation-complete and a
set of clauses can be transformed into an equivalent set of
horn-clauses by inventing new predicates to name the negation of
existing predicates. For instance (NOT (P a)) can be replaced by (Q a)
provided you add the horn clauses:

		(OR (NOT (P x)) (Q x))
		(OR (NOT (Q x)) (P x))

--Denys

subject: Where do crash dumps go on V/386 ?
q: My V/386 system panicked and said it was saving a crash image of 1532 pages. Where did that file go, and how do I remove it?
ref: It dumps to your swap partition, not a file. Copy the swap partition early in boot if you want it, otherwise it gets overwritten. Swap is re-initialized on reboot, so there's nothing to remove. Post-mortem on it isn't for the faint of heart.
replies:
It dumps it to your swap partition. If you want the dump, you copy
your swap partition to some file early in the boot sequence.
Otherwise, the dump just gets overwritten when the system wants the
swap space.

The crash image is for debug purposes only, and even that I have not
made work very satisfactorily.  The kernel image is saved to the swap
partition on the hard disk.   When you reboot you have the option of
saving the image to tape for later analysis or you can simply boot
over the saved image.  Doing post-mortem on a crash image is not for
the weak of heart.  When you reboot, the swap partition is completely
re-initialized, so you needed worry about removing it:  its already
gone.

subject: Mac emulators
q: How do Mac emulators work on an Amiga 3000? Can I run Mac and Amiga applications together, and does it work with Amiga Unix?
ref: No Mac emulator exists for Amiga Unix that I know of. A-MAX needs AmigaDOS to boot it, then flushes AmigaDOS out of memory, so you cannot run Amiga and Mac programs simultaneously. Don't expect that ever; it would be a headache.
replies:
There is no Mac emulator for Amiga Unix as far as I know.

The A-MAX emulator requires that you boot AmigaDOS to load it, but when it
starts up it flushes the entire thing out of memory.  In other words, you
*cannot* have Amiga applications and Mac applications running
simultaneously.  I doubt that it will ever be possible to run a Macintosh
emulator as an AmigaDOS task.  It would be too much of a headache to
implement, and both the AmigaDOS and Macintosh programs would be slowed
tremendously because they'd have to compete for access to the hardware.

subject: More occam questions
q: In occam, why does PAR PRI with the output of a vector alongside a matrix-vector computation run significantly quicker than a plain PAR?
ref: With plain PAR the behavior is implementation dependent. The INMOS compiler lets the computation run until completion or a time-slice, and only then starts the communication. PAR PRI starts the communication immediately, so it runs concurrently and finishes sooner. Swap the order of components and you'll see the same thing.
replies:
With just PAR, things will be implementation dependent - an allowed scenario (which
happens to be the way the INMOS compiler would do it) is for the computation to begin
immediately and run until completion or a time-slice.  Only then will the communication
be initialised.  By using PRI PAR, the communication is initialised immediately
and will proceed concurrently with the computation, the whole application completing
sooner.

You may observe the same effect by interchanging the order of the components of
the PAR.

subject: Large Scale DataBase
q: We have a database of 500,000 records with about 25 variables each, now on a mainframe with SAS. Could it be put in HyperCard for fast interactive searching, and how big would the stack be?
ref: Nobody knows; stacks that large haven't been tested well. Figure roughly 125 to 156 MB of text, and search times that get slower as the stack grows. Using a real Mac DBMS like FoxBase would be saner. HyperCard is not a mainframe database.
replies:
A really rough guess, based on my stack with 1,600 cards which takes
nearly .5 MB, would be: (500,000 / 1,600) * .5 MB, or about 156 MB.

An easy lower bound is 500,000 cards * 250 bytes/card = 125 MB; and that's
just for the text itself.  So the 156 MB above looks pretty reasonable.
Of course, if the average utilization of the field is much less than
250 chars, then it could be smaller.

Not if you update things often, since you'd have to remaster the CD each time.
Plus, a CD-ROM drive will cost about the same as a large hard disk.

Building a text stack from an ASCII file is fairly straightforward.  I do
it in my Go Games and Fuseki stack.  Let me know if you want a copy ...

The search speed of HyperCard gets slower as the size of the stack
increases, and if we assume linear degradation your searches might
take 2.5 hours since mine take up to half a minute.  (Additional searches
on the same key are much faster - I think HyperCard either builds indices
or at least scans ahead to the

To be brutally honest... WE DON't KNOW.  Stacks of cards in the 500,000
plus range have not really been tested too well.  I do know that there
may be some interesting bugs lurking in huge stacks, but we are making
progress in this area: we just got a 1.4 GB hard disk to do testing of
large stacks.

Now for a back of the envelope calcuation... 500,000 cards with a
minimum of 64 bytes of overhead per card and about 256 bytes of text per
card would give us 152 MB of text, not including room for HyperCards
internal indexing.  I guess if it was even double it would still fit on
a CD-ROM with some room for growth, but looking through the stack... who
knows the search time... I hope it would be good.

Yes, you could automatically build the stack for an ASCII file.  I built
a stack from 4 MB of ASCII text and it took an evening.  Figure
accordingly...

All in all, your proposition may not be that feasible, but it does give
us something to shoot for as we enhance HyperCard.

Dan Allen
HyperCard

Considering th size of your database, Hypercard would probably be a disaster.
It just wasn't created to manage that much data. I would suggest using one
of the faster Mac DBMSs to create an application. FoxBase would probably
be a good choice. It's very fast, and relatively easy to use.

subject: PURGE-O-MATIC AND DPII
q: What does Purge-O-Matic actually do, and why is it needed to launch DeluxePaint II under GS/OS 3.0?
ref: These programs insist on grabbing a large contiguous block of memory and give up if they don't get it. Purging the dynamically allocated memory makes sure they get it, if it's available. Sloppy programming, if you ask me.
replies:
Zink or somebody also published a Paintworks Gold patch for similar purposes.
It appears to me that these applications insist on glomming onto a large
contiguous storage array, and give up if they don't get it.  Purging the
dynamically-allocated memory ensures that they'll get it, if it's available.
The PWG patch (I think) makes PWG no longer limit its request to the lowest
1.25MB, but allows free memory from other locations to be used if necessary.

subject: Mapping algorithm question - NOT cartograpy
q: How can I map one 2D rectangular area into another area defined by four corresponding points, like a rubber sheet? Any references?
ref: Sounds ill-posed, but any triangle can be transformed to any other triangle with a 3x3 matrix in 2-d. Triangulate your regions in some standard way and go from there. It's two concatenated transforms through a canonical triangle. Think it through.
replies:
It sounds ill-posed, but maybe this will help:  It is straightforward
to transform any triangle to any other triangle*.  In 2-d this can be
done by a 3x3 matrix tranformation.  By triangulating your regions in
some standard way you may be able to achieve something like you want.

--------
* For beginners, if you don't understand this, think of it as two
  concatenated transformations.  The first transform takes the firsti
  triangle to a lanonical triangle (say with vertices (0,0) (1,0) (0,1) ),
  and then transform that to your your second triangle.

subject: Want my own logo - what is a RLE file?

replies:
RLE stands for "run-length-encoded". It is compressed version of a
Windows bitmap (BMP) file. There is a shareware utility called
PaintShop (PS.EXE) available at CICA that can read bitmaps in a

back to the default.

subject: swapfile
q: I removed a huge swapfile in /private/vm as root on my NeXT, but df shows no disk space freed. Do I have to reboot to get it back?
ref: Yup. The swap manager still holds the file open, and on UNIX you only unlink a file. The space isn't freed until every process releases it. Check ls -s, since sparse swap files can look bigger than they are, and set a high water mark; see swaptab(5).
replies:
Yup, because the swap manager is still hanging onto the file pointer, the
OS won't clear the inode and its allocated space. When you did the "rm"
you removed the directory entry, but it won't clear the space until all
processes release the file.
  Have you tried setting a high water mark for your swapfile? Check out
swaptab(5).

	   - jiro

I often tell people that the only use for a 105MB drive is to
turn it 100% over to swapfile, but that it's not really big
enough for people doing "real work."  Do they listen?

Of course not.  On UNIX, there's no such thing as "deleting" a
file; one merely unlinks it.  Even with no directory entries, the
file still exists, and still takes up space as long as the kernel
or any process (task) has it open.  If you're swapping on it,
it's open!

Probably.  But the LENGTH of a UNIX file isn't the same as its
size; if NeXT is smart enough to make "holey" (sparse) swap
files, you're ok.  You should be looking at what
	ls -s
displays.  (If NeXT isn't freeing disk pages, then you can
start worrying.)

					-=EPS=-

will tell you it is not needed, but we have lost very few files in

subject: Horror in frp: how?
q: I'm running a Champions superhero campaign and want a horror scenario, but the characters are nearly invulnerable. How do I craft something players find genuinely horrific?
ref: Threaten them as people, not heroes: families, spiritual selves, phobias from their disadvantages. Use nightmares where they're suddenly vulnerable, kill off NPC heroes, add a ticking clock, and never let them figure out what's going on. Keep them guessing and don't go soft.
replies:
yes, that is a bit of a problem, when you have a party as invulnerable as you
imply. there are always, however, weaknesses.

 the primary use of horror in frp's, as i see it, is to create a sense of
desperation and of course fear in the players. fear is easily created by
playing on the players' fears. Nightmares help with this too, dreams in which
they are suddenly vulnerable to all those things that can't actually hurt them.
this opens the door for sudden power failures in the waking world. an effective
dream-playing technique is to start out without letting on it's a dream..

 for a sense of desperation it is important to cause some sort of threat to
them, as people, not necessarily as heroes. hint: do they have any family?
risk their spiritual selves if their physical selves are too tough..

i think that can give you enough ideas.

How to scare 'em eh?  Well, the best way I've come up with running a horror
scenario is to never let the party figure out what is going on.  Oh, by all
mean throw clues, but always keep them guessing, don't be afraid to hurt them,
and never let them see you sweat (had to put that in there).

In a campaign I did for a Fantasy game I had a vampire trapped on an island that
the players had discovered.  The space was limited (ie no where to run)
and the everything going on was a complete mystery.  By putting pieces
together and working at solving a mystery, tensions were high.  This
combined with a little physical worry, put the fear into the players
as well as the characters.  I guess the best advice in horror is to always
keep them guessing.

Just a few thoughts to get you started:
     -  The violent deaths of a few NPC superheroes is usually a great
       lead-in to a new adventure, and introduces a "horror" element...
       for more effect, make it a coincidence (a good place to use
       a PC's luck) that it could have the PC's life had he stayed in a
       bar just a few minutes more, etc...

     -  Take a look at the PCs disadvantage lists... any phobias there?

     -  I think a time element always heightens the tension... NPCs are
       dying each day, etc...

     -  Give the badguys the power to strip PCs powers... draining, etc...

I realize these are probably obvious ideas, but ya never know!

Jim

subject: Anagram
q: Does anyone know an algorithm for producing the complete set of anagrams of any string of length N?
ref: Trivial recursion: for each character in the string, put it in front of all anagrams of the string without it. Slow, sure, but it works. For real use, derecursify it and clip impossible word beginnings like QKL early. CS 101 stuff.
replies:
Well, if you're not concerned with performance, the trivial recursive algorithm:

  anagrams(N-string) =
     for all characters C in string: C concat all anagrams(N-string without C)

In the real world, you would want to derecursify this and, assuming you're going
to run your near-infinite mess through a dictionary, clip off impossible
word-beginnings (like "QKL") without evaluating the whole tree.

Eli

subject: 2 questions
q: As a new news admin, I get cron mail saying "df: /usr/spool not block special", an expr syntax error, and a sendbatch test error. What do they mean? Also, how do I create newsgroups manually without sending control messages everywhere?
ref: You're on a lame machine. Either /usr/spool isn't the root of a partition, or your df wants a /dev/PARTITION argument. The other errors come from a variable unset because df choked. To add groups by hand, use $NEWSBIN/maint/addgroup and rmgroup; put that directory in your PATH.
replies:
1.  Can anybody tell me what the following messages mean:

           df: /usr/spool not block special
           expr: syntax error
           /usr/lib/news/sendbatch: test: argument expected

It means you're on a lame machine.  More specifically, your /usr/spool
is either not the root of a partition or if it is that your df
requires a /dev/PARTITION as an argument.  I suspect the latter.  The
other errors are probably coming from a variable not being set because
df tossed its cookies.

   2.	 When you get a notice for a news group and you are set up
           to manually create them, how do you do it without sending
           control messages throughout all of creation?

By using $NEWSBIN/maint/addgroup and ..../rmgroup.  It is useful to
have $NEWSBIN/maint in your news admin account PATH.

subject: Wsh and pathnames.
q: When I start wsh with -c, it seems to use a different path than the one in my .cshrc, and sometimes can't run the command. How does wsh get its path and how do I change it?
ref: It inherits the environment from whatever started it. Launched from 4sight, which starts before your environment loads, you get the wrong path. Quick-and-dirty fix: put a (PATH) (...) putenv line in user.ps in your home directory. Ugly, but it works.
replies:
When you run wsh -c, it inherits its environment from whatever
started it.  If you start it from your shell, then it will inherit
the environment from the shell, and all should be fine and dandy.

If you start it from 4sight, then it inherits the environment from
4sight.  This is the most common problem, because 4sight is started
before your environment is loaded up.  A quick-and-dirty solution
is to add the following (sample) line to your user.ps in your
home directory:

(PATH) (/d/kipp/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bsd:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/etc:/etc:/usr/bin/X11:/usr/local/bin/ctools) putenv

this does mean you have a copy of the information in your
.login/.profile, but thats why its quick-and-dirty.  Better yet, is
to use the ``exporttonews'' program (I believe its floating around
on the net somewhere).

				kipp

subject: How to disable command-M?
q: How can I disable command-M in HyperCard so users can't get the message box? How do I check for menu commands like command-H or command-F in a script?
ref: Intercept it with an on doMenu handler. If cmd is Message, answer something rude, else pass doMenu. Nest more ifs for the other menu items. Setting userLevel to 1 or 2 may also lock it out, I think. Figure out the rest yourself.
replies:
Try the following script...

on doMenu cmd
  if cmd = "Message" then
    answer "Bleah!!"
  else
    pass doMenu
  end if
end doMenu

You can have a series of nested if's to check for the various other
menu calls (e.g. Help, Find... etc).  Also you could set the userLevel
property to 1 or 2 or whatever to lock out the message (I think!)
