subject: Outlining bitmaps
q: Can anyone point me to references on algorithms for outlining bitmaps?
ref: Look at Capson's 1984 paper on sequential boundary extraction from a raster scan, in Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing, and Grant and Reid's 1981 boundary tracing paper in the same journal. Gonzalez and Wintz's Digital Image Processing, chapter 7, covers boundary detection too. Go read them.
replies:
Having just done this for the company I work for (sorry I don't think I can
give you code :-),  I can point you to the references I used:

1)  Capson, David W., "An Improved Algorithm for the Sequential Extraction of
    Boundaries from a Raster Scan",  in *Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image
    Processing*, Vol 28 (1984), pg 109-125.

2)  Grant, G. and Reid, A.F., "An Efficient Algorithm for Boundary Tracing
	and Feature Extraction", in *Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image
    Processing*, Vol 17 (1981), pg 225-237.

Capson's article provides the entire algorithm and is quite fast, although
there are improvements that can be made to his algorithm.  With improvements
and optimizations this algorithm easily yields the contours for a 512*512
raster image (of high complexity!) in less than 100ms (on a Sun4).

(Does this make me a graphics guru? :-)

Rob.

subject: Higher octane unleadeds
q: In Singapore the supreme unleaded has 98 octane, versus 92 here in California. Would that fuel be acceptable under US and California emissions rules, and would cars here need modifications to run it?
ref: You're comparing apples to oranges. Most countries rate octane by the R (research) method, which reads higher, while US pumps post the (R+M)/2 average. Read the pump label before you get excited. Sigh.
replies:
There are two standard ways to measure octane:  the R (research)
method and the M (measured?) method.  One of them (R, I think) usually
yields a higher rating than the other, and most countries specify
fuel octane ratings in terms of that method only.  If you read gas
pumps in the US, however, you'll note that octane ratings are listed
as using the "(R+M)/2 method" -- i.e., the average of the two ratings.
In other words, you're comparing apples to oranges.

subject: READING HD HYSICAL SECTORS
q: I can read physical sectors on my hard disk by setting bit 3 in the Rwabs rwflag, but the sector number is an int and can't go past 32767 or 65535. How do I read higher sectors?
ref: The real answer is you don't. Bit 3 was only meant to reach sector 0 and maybe 1 and 2, and after that partitions cover the disk, accessed by drive and offset. Want long absolute sectors like Spectre and Minix? Write your OWN driver.
replies:
The real answer is you dont.  And this is why.
The use of bit 3 is/was really to get to sector 0 and maybe 1 and 2.
(1 and 2 might contain a list of bad blocks).  After this, very limited
area, it is expected that partitions will cover the physical disk.

TOS partitions can then be accessed by drive and offset.

What about Spectre and Minix partitions?  Then you need your OWN driver
that will access sectors as a long absolute value.  Thats what Spectre
and Minix do.

subject: clists in ATT SysV/386 R3.2
q: What are clists in AT&T SysV/386 R3.2, how do they get used up, and how do I free some or add more?
ref: Clists are character buffers. Set five to ten per terminal, a bit more if you run networking over serial ports. Run out and the console will tell you. Smart serial I/O controllers may need almost none, so ask the maker. The Monitor reference manual says all this, so read it.
replies:
Quoting from "Monitor: Performance Analyser for UNIX Systems
Reference Manual"

	"The number of clist buffers (character buffers)
	should be set to five to ten per terminal.  If you
	are running networking software over serial ports,
	you may need to allocate somewhat more.  If you run
	out of clist buffers, a message on the console will
	tell you so.  On systems with intelligent serial I/O
	controllers, it is often possible to reduce clist
	buffers to a minimum, leaving only enough to keep
	the console operating.  You should check with the
	manufacturer of your serial I/O controller to check
	whether clists are used and free unwanted buffers."

ensure that your graphic is centered in the bounding box.

is full, the fork cannot succeed and you get the message from

subject: Scrap Management, User Preferences
q: Should I use the Scrap Manager for my own private object types, and what's the official way to save user preferences in a Mac application?
ref: Use the scrap manager even for private types, so users can save scraps in the scrapbook. Put a TEXT version alongside your private one. For preferences, use a file in the System Folder found by a poor-man's search path, so each user gets their own. Don't stuff it in the app.
replies:
If you externalize your scrap, and use the scrap manager, even if it is a
private type, the user can save scraps on the scrapbook. That can be very
convenient for the user.  By rights, you should put a dual representation
on the scrapbook: a TEXT, say,  and your private type. That way the user
can see some difference between two scraps from your program.

A file, either data or resoruce, that you find using poor-man's-search-path,
is the recommended way to go. That way, if you're application has been
marked read only, and is being shared over a net, each user can have their
own preferences in their own system folder.  Or, you can encourage users
to double click on "Stationery" files.  This solution is better, since it
allows the user the effect of multiple preferences files (say two people
share one mac.)

subject: New Car vs. Body Shop
q: My two month old Celica was badly damaged in an accident and repairs now cost about 80% of its value. Should it be totalled, and can I still have it totalled while it's in the shop?
ref: A car that wrecked should generally be totalled. A unibody absorbs the crash through the whole body, and straightened metal is never as strong as before, like uncrumpling paper. But after a month of work, the insurer probably won't pay full value, if they go for it at all.
replies:
A car which has suffered as much damage as you mentioned (I can't say for
sure, as I haven't seen it) should in general be totalled.  The Celica uses
what's called a unibody chasis;  that is, the floor pan work in conjunction
with the roof and pillars to give the body strength.  There is no separate
frame.  When such a car is crunched, the entire body absorbs the energy,
which might be good from a safety standpoint since the load is distributed.
(There may be opposing viewpoints to this)  If the body shop can pull the
body straight and remove all the wrikles, it still won't be as strong as it
once was.  You can think of crumpling up a piece of paper, and then try to
straighten it out again.  The next time you crumple it, it will wrinkle up
at the creases created the first time, with less effort.

Since they've already worked on the car for so long, I doubt that the
insurance company will pay you the total totaled value of the car, if
they go for it at all.  Of course, I'm only guessing

subject: FTP'ing files
q: Every file I ftp and then try to unARC gives a 'bad header' error. What am I doing wrong?
ref: Type 'binary' at the ftp prompt. ARC files need all 8 bits, and ftp defaults to ASCII, which mangles things like end-of-line characters. Switch back to 'ascii' if ls misbehaves. This comes up every week.
replies:
Well, when a file is ARCed it turns it from whatever format it was in
into binary format (ie. requiring all 8 bits in a byte). ftp, by
default, transfers ASCII which is only 7 bit data and it will do
conversions on things like 'end of line' characters etc. To stop it
doing all this you need to type:

ftp> binary

at the ftp prompt. This allows any kind of data to get through without
change.

I hope this works for you.

Thats ok,

Frank.

Make sure you set it to binary mode (usually the command 'binary').  To get
ls to work after you have done this, you must set it back to ascii (with, you
guessed it, 'ascii').  If you still have the problem, try setting it to
telex (I think, something like that).  Usually a '?' will get you a help sheet.

subject: How to do this in hermes
q: In Hermes, my server must always be available, so it spawns worker processes to service requests. How does the server tell a new worker to send the reply back to the original client?
ref: Easy. The return address is hidden in the callmessage. Have the server use SEND, not CALL, to hand the original callmessage to the worker. When the worker returns it, the reply goes straight to the client. Read the manual.
replies:
Easy.  The "return address" to which the callmessage returns is
hidden in the callmessage.  If the main server spawns a worker
and uses the SEND command (rather than CALL) to give the original
callmessage received from the client to the worker, then when the
worker returns the callmessage, it will return directly to the
client.

There are other ways to do it involving two send-style channels
between the server and workers, but I won't get into this here.

                   -- Darren

replies:
AT&T sells (I think as part of the Documenter's Workbench?) a product called
"sroff".  It's about 10 times as fast as nroff; if you include the mm macro
package it slows down to 3 times as fast.  The mm stuff is compatible;
the macro facility is more limited, and it doesn't handle eqn or troff.  But
it's fast, and even runs on MS-DOS PCs.

As an alternative, consider getting a cheap 68000-based UNIX machine, and
having it just do nroff.  You can get them for as low as about $4000
and they can be almost as fast as a 750 (i.e. still slow, but you don't care.)
We have an internal product which is a 68000 board with 750K memory and a small
PROM monitor that knows how to download n/troff and process jobs.  It's a
single-process machine, but there's almost no overhead, so it's only limited by
communications bandwidth, and it does a good job of offloading the main CPU.
Avalon builds a similar board that plugs into a UNIBUS; it costs more but does
more.

subject: inappropriate checks when mailing to a file

ref: Mostly yes, you're probably right. The tests in recipient.c are perhaps too paranoid. It's why many people use "|/bin/cat >> /path/to/file" instead. Or chmod 4600 the file: suid set, no x bit, and sendmail uses the file owner's uid. Sigh, rediscovered the wheel.
replies:
You have probably rediscovered why many people prefer to use

 "|/bin/cat >> /path/to/file"
rather than
 /path/to/file

At least in recent versions of sendmail there is another option.  Simply
do:  chmod 4600 /path/to/file
and since the 'suid' bit is on, but no 'x' bit is on, sendmail uses the
uid of the file owner.

 Apart from that, you are probably right.  The tests in recipient.c are
perhaps too paranoid.

subject: Making a PC-XT hard-disk bootable again...
q: I messed up the DOS system files on a PC-XT hard disk and it won't boot from C: anymore, though A: works. How can I make it bootable without reformatting?

replies:
Greg, I believe the problem is that dos 3.0 and above use 2k minimum
disk allocation units, and that 2.11 dos uses 8 k. A 1 byte file under dos
2.xx will use 8k of disk space. This is the 'slack' that Norton Utilities
reports in disk usage. One of the improvements incorporated in version
3.0 and above is the minimum disk allocation of 2k. Much more efficient way
of handling file space.

To make the most of the upgrade, re-low-level the HD, create the partition,
and reformat with system (/s).

I don't know about DOS 2.10, but with DOS 3.30 you would use the FDISK
command.  When you put DOS 3.30 onto the harddisk, did you also leave
DOS 2.10 on the harddisk?  Anyway, there is an option inside of FDISK
to make a partition active.  This is how you specify which partition
you want to have the harddisk boot.  So, if you had several operating
systems on you harddisk, you would have to specify a particular partition
as active before it would boot.  Try using FDISK to make your DOS 3.30
partition active, and then reboot the computer.

subject: Info Requested
q: How do I read or dump the code from an Atari 800XL ROM cartridge?
ref: Cartridge ROMs read just like RAM, starting on a 4K boundary and running up to C000, for instance B000-BFFF. Bank select cartridges are where it gets weird, since 32K carts map into 16K of address space. Physically copying the ROM is another matter, and probably illegal.
replies:
I wrote a program back in '81 or '82 called CARTDISK+ that moved a
cartridge contents to disk and let you patch it using CARTDISK's
specialized disassembler. The program then created a loadable binary
file out of the 'fixed' binary data. As far as I remember, the ROM
cartridges were just like reading RAM memory...the started at a 4K
boundary and went up to C000 (i.e. B000-BFFF). Things only got weird
when the bank select cartridges came out (i.e. 32K carts that mapped
into 16K of address space.

On the other hand, if you are asking about how to physically copy the
ROM cartridges, then I have no idea (and would imagine that it would be
illegal.) The main reason I wrote CARTDISK was because my cartridge
port got flakey on me early on in my 800's lifetime (back before those
days that you could go into Target and buy an Atari 800 for $75 and
get a $100 rebate from Atari...)

subject: Sass vs ASAP

ref: Not better, a quick hack. I wrote ASAP just to get CHIP-48 assembled because nothing else existed. Sass is smaller, faster and more elegant, but it couldn't compute a constant by subtracting two labels, which CHIP-48 relies on heavily. Sigh, that's the whole reason.
replies:
Actually they were written roughly at the same time, but Sass was
published a bit before ASAP.

I wrote ASAP as a quick hack just to get CHIP-48 assembled somehow,
because there was no other Saturn assembler available at the time.

Sass is certainly smaller, faster and more elegant, but the main
reason I haven't switched over to it is that when I last looked, it
lacked a crucial feature: it doesn't let you calculate an
assembly-time constant by subtracting two labels.  The CHIP-48 source
relies heavily on this construct to calculate the addresses of fixed
tables within a relocateable Code object.  Consider the following
example:

	add.a	a,c			; calculate address of "hexfont"
	move.a	c,d1			; now d1 points to the hex patterns
	...

hexfont:
	data.5 #F999F
	data.5 #72262
	...

I think with Sass you need to either do the subtraction at runtime
(making the program bigger and slower) or kee

subject: Help on a programming issue...
q: How do I type the backslash character in HP-48 programs that start with %%HP and a backslash before the <<, and how do I enter such a program?
ref: You don't type the backslash or the two characters after it; translate them using the table on page 627 of the manual. Don't type the %%HP line either. Set the modes it describes, type everything after it, press ENTER, then store it in a variable. RTFM.
replies:
The "\" character is described on pages 626 to 627 of your owner's manual.
When you see such a character, you do not type it or the two characters that
follow; you should type the proper translation according to the table on page
627.

Do not type the %%HP line.  Read the description of this line on pages 629
to 630.  To enter a program:  Set your calculator's modes as described by
the %%HP line.  Type everything AFTER that line to the end of the program
and press ENTER.  Then store the program in a variable.

subject: managing pixmaps in the server?
q: Is there a way to manage pixmaps in the X server so clients can share them by name and the server frees them when all clients are gone?
ref: Store the pixmap as a property on the root window; look it up and create it if it's missing. Fake a refcount with an integer property, grabbing the server while you update it. A client that dies without decrementing still breaks it. Live with it.
replies:
You could always store the pixmap as a property of your root window.
Your program could then get the appropriate property, and if it's not
there, create the appropriate pixmap and store it there.

You could probably fake this by having an integer property to go with
the pixmap property, and have each application that uses the pixmap
increment it when it starts using the pixmap, and decrement it when it's
through.  You'll probably want to grab the server while you get the old
count, increment it, and put it back, in order to avoid race conditions.
This, of course, won't handle a client that increments the count and
then dies without decrementing it.

subject: Some new questions Re: RFC on my "abuse"
q: If a sysadmin gets a complaint about my script probing hosts, is an email warning the appropriate first response? What follows from that?
ref: Yes, for all but the most serious problems, though killing background jobs or removing huge core dumps may happen too. The aim is a talk where you explain what you were doing, so you reach agreement on what's reasonable. Admins can't read minds. Communicate, for crying out loud.
replies:
At this site an email warning is the appropriate first response for all but
the most serious problems.  However killing background jobs or removing
100Meg core dumps may also be appropriate at the same time.

 I would hope most administrators would agree.

 One would hope that the result of the email warning was a discussion where
you would explain what you were doing, why you didn't think it was a problem,
whether it was random or following some plan, etc.  The aim should be a meeting
of the minds as to exactly what is reasonable.  It might be you would convince
me that what you were doing was already reasonable.  Perhaps I would "persuade"
you that it was not.

 The problem here is that you were doing something that in your mind was
well planned and intelligently done to minimize impact.  But the site
administrator cannot read your mind, and to him it is likely to look
suspicious.  It takes communication to resolve these differences.  Mind
reading is not a well developed art.

subject: Information on Graphics Formats
q: Is the IFF picture format simple? I want to write a C program on my Unix machine that turns an array of integers into an Amiga picture file.
ref: Not really simple, but straightforward once you understand the mechanisms. Every IFF file carries detailed info about the graphics mode and sizes, so you'll have to learn a bit about Amiga display modes. Stick to the pure IFF standard and skip the one-off formats.
replies:
Not really, but straightforward once you understand the mechanisms.
But to port pic files to the Amiga means in addition that you must
learn a bit about the available graphics modes on the Amiga, because
every IFF file comes with detailed informations about which mode to
use with which sizes etc.

There might exist also other specialized formats (e.g. for some

subject: Is there a way to unpause a workstation?
q: Users pause their workstations under Ultrix and never log out, and I need to shut the machines down for system chores. Is there a way to remotely unpause a workstation so I can make sure their editor files are saved first?
ref: Set the session manager resource rootPasswd to true in /usr/lib/X11/app-defaults/SessionManager, and the pause screen accepts the root password too. Killing processes won't do it, since killing dxsession just logs the user out. Mind the security implications, if you care.
replies:
There's a resource for the session manager, "rootPasswd", which, if set,
means that the pause screen will accept the root password as well as the
user's password.  To enable this system wide, change the second to last
line (at least in Ultrix 4.1 and 4.2) of

/usr/lib/X11/app-defaults/SessionManager

from

*rootPasswd: false

to

*rootPasswd: true

The user can override this in .Xdefaults, but I figure if s/he does, that's
her/his own lookout.

I don't believe the session manager logs incorrect guesses, so this may
have security implications if you are running at the upgrade or enhanced
security levels, and are at least moderately paranoid.

I don't think you can do what you want by killing processes--the pause
window is owned by the session manager, and killing dxsession logs the
user out.

subject: Laser Disk Quality Control
q: Are laser disk quality control problems as bad as they seem from this net? Will I be returning every other disk for defects, and are things improving?
ref: No, it's mostly nit-picking by people who paid for perfection. Serious flaws that hang a disc happen maybe 1 in 100, and dealers take back anything defective. One reader returned 1 of 30 titles. LPs were far worse, and tapes are hopeless.
replies:
Go for it!!  The defects being discussed on this net are mostly nit-
picking.  Remember the technology promises high quality and the
discs are more expensive than CDs, LPs, and tapes.  So when there
is a little flaw most of us demand our due.  Furthermore both the
dealers and distributors are VERY good about taking back discs with
ANY kind of defect.  I would guess that in discs I have bought,
SERIOUS flaws (causing a hang up of the disc so it is unwatchable)
occur maybe 1 in 100.  Most other problems are flaws in the visual
image which I won't stand for, but which you could just pass over.
Defects in LPs were far greater and it was far more difficult to get
them replaced unless you had an audiophile release.  Tapes are hopeless.
CDs probably have about the same defect rate for unplayable - the small
audio flaws are less obvious because of the error correcting circuits
and because the sound is not state-of-the-art to start with.

I guess that depends on what you watch.  I've been collecting discs, mostly
recent issues, for 18 months now and I've only had to return 1 out of the
30 titles so far.  Roughly half of these are multi-disc sets, so I'd say
I'm very satisfied with the defect rate.

The one disc, incidentally, was Batman, which had minor traveling line
segment glitches in a 7-second section.

-dave

subject: Solar Flares
q: If a solar flare flips bits, could international computer networks be affected, given they rely on satellites to route data?
ref: Hardly. Most network links, satellite ones included, are protected by CRC or similar error detection. A flipped bit makes the receiver reject the data and ask for a resend until it gets through or the link is declared down. Any idiot who knows networking knows this.
replies:
I can confirm this report since I am that Computer Scientist/Psychologist!
Moreover, the storm was so severe that as well as changing professions,
the storm has made me more susceptible to junk mail.  I now get all that
psychological junk as well as the computing stuff.  I believe it is the
South Atlantic Anomoly setting up a branch here in Glasgow!

Cheers,
	Kevin

----------------
Psycho-analysis rates on demand.  No loonies please.

Here in Tucson I heard numerous reports of excess noise from those that do
local data telecomm activities. I also noticed that the noise level jumped
significantly, in some cases causing an immediate disconnect. Perhaps it
has something to with the large number of phone lines we have draped from
poles, instead of being buried.

Most network communications (including satellite based) are protected by
CRC or similar error detection).  In addition, the transport layer will
retransmit portions of data detected as bad.

Translation:

If a bit gets flipped while travelling through the net, the receiving
host rejects it and requests a resend.  This repeats until the correct
data gets through or the net link is declared down (from two many
errors/to little good data).

subject: dynamic yacc-tables?
q: Can yacc parse tables be extended dynamically during parsing, say with a yynewrule function, for declaring mixfix operators and overloading? Are there parser generators that handle this?
ref: Read Heering, Klint and Rekers, Incremental Generation of Parsers, in SIGPLAN '89 and IEEE TSE 1990, and Horspool's paper in Computer Languages. Or use lex with a growing table, per Sibley's distfix operators paper in CACM, February 1986. Updating tables mid-parse is still an open problem.
replies:
Take a look at the paper:
    "Incremental Generation of Parsers"
    by J. Heering, P. Klint, & J. Rekers
    in Proceedings of the SIGPLAN '89 Conference on Programming Language
    Design and Implementation.
    SIGPLAN Notices Vol. 24 Num 7  July 1989, pages 170-178.

They treat specifically this problem: updating an existing parser
according to new grammar rules.  You may even be able to get source
for their experimental parser generator from the authors.

You may want to attack the problem with lex instead of yacc.  Read:
PARSING DISTFIX OPERATORS by Edgar H. Sibley in Commmunications of the ACM
February 1986, Vol 29, num 2, page 118.
Abstract:
    The advantages of user-defined distfix operators -- a syntactic
    convenience that enhances the readability of programs -- can be
    obtained as an extension of almost any programming language without
    requiring dynamic changes to the parser.
Conclusions:
    We have described a simple technique whereby a fixed BNF grammar can
    describe languages including user-defined infix, postfix, and distfix
    operators.  The technique requires only that the parts of disfix
    operators be lexically distinguishable.  ...
    The idea has been successfully implemented [with YACC] with minimal
    effort.

Note that "lexically distinguishable" means that lex can look up the
answer in a table, which can grow dynamically.  I'm not sure how Sibley's
ideas interact with overloading.

Joshua Levy

This problem has partly been addressed in at least two articles:

J. Heering, P. Klint, and J. Rekers
Incremental generation of parsers
IEEE Transactions on Software Engeneering, 16(12):1344-1351, 1990

R.N. Horspool
Incremental generation of LR parsers
Computer Languages, 15(4):205-233, 1990

How to update an LR parse table _during_ parsing without disturbing the current
parse is an open problem.

Jan Rekers (rekers@cwi.nl)    Centrum voor Wiskunde en Informatica (CWI)
			      P.O. Box 4079, 1009 AB Amsterdam, The Netherlands

subject: Function Argument Evaluation
q: Could a conforming C compiler make printf("%d %d\n", *(p = &x), *(p = &y)) print "200 200", given the unspecified order of argument evaluation?
ref: No, it can't. The arguments are the dereferenced results of the assignment expressions, not reads of p. The value of (p = &x) is &x, so you get x. Output has to be "100 200". Read the draft more carefully.
replies:
No, it can't.

      ^^^ These are not in fact the second and third arguments of the
function. Stick an asterisk in front of each of the subexpressions you
listed above and then you have the second and third arguments. It is not
the value of p at the time of the call that is being dereferenced here.
It is the result of the assignment expression that is being dereferenced,
and that has nothing to do with any side effects that take place anywhere
in this example. Nowhere in the example are you "reading" p's value.
The value of the expression "(p = &x)" is "&x". Therefore,
"*(p = &x)" is "*(&x)" which is x.

So, the output has to be "100 200".

subject: Image operator anomaly?
q: Photoshop made an EPS with a 497 by 673 one-bit image but uses a string size of 63, which doesn't divide evenly into the total data, yet it works. Changing it to 497 prints nothing. What is going on?
ref: The image operator pads each scanline to a byte boundary. A 497-sample, 1-bit line needs (497+7)/8 = 63 bytes, hence the magic number. Your string must match the scanline, not the sample count. Read the manual again.
replies:
The image operator expects each scanline of the image to be padded to
a byte boundary.  Your 497-sample wide image is only 1-bit per sample
and therefore has to be padded to the nearest byte.  A single scanline
thus requires

   (497 + 7) / 8 = 63

bytes of data.  Hence the magic number 63.

Two of the great strengths of U*IX are orthogonality and synergy; to
realize these strengths, each "software tool" should work with data
generated by every other one, as far as is practical.  Almost all
tools know how to deal with the filesystem; each tool has a consistant
view of the filesystem name space plainly available to it, and when it

additional special-purpose namespace, like VMS logicals, small

subject: preamp question
q: My preamp has CD, video, tape and phono inputs. When I plugged the CD player into the phono jack the sound came out very distorted, though it was fine on the video and tape jacks. Does the phono input accept a different kind of signal, or is something broken inside?
ref: Nothing's broken. The phono input expects a tiny cartridge signal, about 5 mV, and follows the RIAA curve, while a CD player puts out around 2000 mV. You drove the stage into clipping, which is murder on tweeters. Don't do that again.
replies:
*DON'T DO THAT*  You will do many unpleasant things to your system.  Your
phono jacks (I presume magnetic cartridge) are rated for a nominal input of
about 5 mV (if memory serves me correctly).  Although the inputs will not
likely be damaged by the output of the CD player (about 2000 mV) you will
drive many parts of the preamp into clipping.  This will put lots of
high frequency components into the output signal which will probably do
unpleasant things to your tweeters.  In addition, the frequency curve of
the phono input is not linear, it follows something called the RIAA curve.

Yes, there's a difference in what the preamp expects from phono and line
level jacks. Typical phono outputs are several dB below line level (I
don't remember how much, and it depends on what kind of cartridge you
have). Since the preamp expects a lower signal level, it's designed for
more gain, so you were driving the input stage to the point of clipping.
That could potentially hurt your amp & speakers at high levels; I doubt
you did any damage though.

subject: Unix on PC
q: What's the best way to partition a 200M SCSI drive with an Adaptec 1542B for both MS-DOS and Unix? Can I also use an old Seagate ST-251 MFM drive alongside it?
ref: Give DOS what it needs and the rest to Unix; a 32 MB DOS partition plus ISC works here with a boot menu. Set the 1542B to defaults. The MFM controller must be a secondary at IRQ 15 and the secondary port address, which usually means cutting the IRQ 14 trace and jumpering. Messy hardware, as usual.
replies:
Give as much as you need to MS-DOS and give the rest to Unix on the
200 Mb SCSI.  We have a 32 Mb MS-DOS 3.30 partition and the rest is
given to ISC 2.0.2.  Works rather nicely with the WDAP4200 here.  You
switch boot between the two OS'es via bootmenu.

You just set up the 1542B to the default settings.  The only problem is
configuring the ST412/506 MFM controller as a secondary controller.  To
do this you need to put it at IRQ 15 and the secondary port address.
Most ST412/506 MFM controllers do not have a configurable IRQ setting.
What most people do is break the trace on the controller to IRQ 14 and
run a jumper or patch to IRQ 15 and set the jumper blocks to the
secondary port address.

If you don't set your controller to the secondary port address and
IRQ 15, your BIOS will try to boot from it providing that the ISA drive
type is set to anything other than not installed.  The other problem is
an ST412/506 controller setup as a secondary controller is NOT
recognizable by your BIOS

subject: Hypercard question
q: How do I build a linked list of cards attached to a primary card in HyperCard, with a count of attached cards and a way to look at each one?
ref: HyperCard cards are linear, first/next; there are no one-to-many relationships. Put a button on the primary card for each card you want reachable, with a script that does go to card by name. Or use a stack of stacks. Read the manual.
replies:
It sounds like Chuq could use a field in each card or background with
the first line holding the number of linked cards and the names or
id numbers of the linked cards in the following lines of the field,
but this brings up a problem that I've been having:

I'm trying to go to cards by a name composed of a string constant
and a variable number, as in

  go to card "Sheetnum"&snum    -- and variants, incl. putting "x"&y in parens

but Hypercard usually fails to go to the proper, or any, card.
This occurs only (or primarily) in scripts; if I execute the same
line in the message window, Hypercard takes me to the proper card
without complaining.  Have I overlooked some requirement of the
go command, or can anyone suggest some other likely oversight on my
part?

Cards in a HyperCard stack are linked in a linear fashion.  In other words,
there are no one-to-many relationships.  There's no problem with attaching
the count of the number of cards in a string to a primary card, but the
other cards have a first/next order; they aren't arranged in a fan-like
set-up.

The card count can be part of a script attached to the primary card, but you
may find that you don't need it. A simpler strategy is to
put a button on the primary card for each card in the list that you
want to reach directly from the primary card (i.e., not in first/next
order).  There are two ways then to set up the transfer.  You can link the
button to the card or you can write a simple script attached to the button
which simply goes to the required card (either by name or ID#).  Personally,
I prefer the latter, using names, because it requires fewer changes as the
stack changes.  My buttons all "go to card x", where x is the name of card.
This way, if I move things around in the stac

It sounds as if you need a stack of stacks, not a stack of cards.  In other
words, you could have a bunch of stacks that belong to a "superstack".  The
background of the superstack should define forward and backward buttons that
allow navigating among the primary cards of each aggregate stack.  The primary
card of each aggregate stack should define additional buttons enabling browsing
through its cards.  You could even put in a fast browse button.  Copy it from
one of the provided stacks if you don't know advanced HyperTalk.

To know how many cards are in a stack, you can define a button in its primary
card that performs a HyperTalk "domenu stack info".  This will bring up the
stack information menu.

Try browsing the provided stacks.  It's likely you'll find a similar
application.  You can copy this and use it as a template for developing your
own.  Have fun.

subject: mapcolor
q: mapcolor() is far too slow when I update 2000 or 3000 color table entries one at a time in my colormap editor. Is there a faster GL routine to update a range of the map?
ref: You're probably getting all the speed you'll get. The colormap can only be loaded during vertical retrace, and the calls get buffered, so the hardware spreads many entries over several retraces. Speed depends on the machine. That's hardware for you.
replies:
Unfortunately the speed you are getting is probably as fast as you are going to get.
The bottleneck is the speed of the hardware and the fact that the colormap can only
be loaded during the montor's vertical retrace.  That doesn't mean that your program
waits around for vertical retrace for every mapcolor() call, these calls get buffered.
But the hardware can't load that many entries in a single vertical retrace so they
are spread out over multiple vertical retraces.  The speed also depends on the system
you are running on.  What system are you using?

before the "read" fixed things for me. [This sounds like a bug to me,
but, since I haven't seen anyone else mention it, I'm not certain.]

subject: SCO VP/ix - X-WINDOWS
q: Running SCO VP/ix, I only found an EGA file in the defaults directory and nothing for a Hercules card. Is there a Hercules driver? Also, will SCO's X-Windows support VGA?
ref: That file, romega, isn't a driver, it's an image of an EGA BIOS ROM. Hercules cards have no BIOS, so nothing is needed, and VP/ix supports them fine. SCO supports VGA graphics in 2.3 and later. As for their X-Windows, no idea. Read the docs.
replies:
The file you see in there (romega) is not a driver per se, but an
image of a BIOS ROM for an EGA card.  VP/ix maps this file into the
address space instead of the EGA card's own BIOS because most of the
EGA BIOSes don't have some features necessary for VP/ix's screen
switching.  Hercules cards have no BIOS, so no such file is necessary
for VP/ix to use them.  VP/ix supports Hercules cards just fine; I
have one and have run several Hercules-supporting graphics programs
under VP/ix.

SCO supports VGA graphics in 2.3 and later (and maybe 2.2.3) in
general.  I have no idea what their X-Windows support will look like.

subject: Sound problems
q: My NeXT program records a second of sound, processes it, and records again in a loop, but it locks up after about five minutes and sometimes [Sound record] returns error 30. Why?
ref: Check the SND functions, especially SNDSoundError. I think 30 is the bad tag error. If you're using the Sound class, reuse the same object and just throw away the data before recording again. Less overhead, fewer thread screwups.
replies:
Look at the SND... functions. Especially: (char *)SNDSoundError(int). I think
30 is the error for a bad tag. Do you use SNDAlloc(), or the Sound class? If
you're using the Sound class, why not use the same one, and just get rid of the
data before you start recording again. That way you have less overhead, and
chance of the threads getting screwed up.

subject: Mush 7.0.0 dumps core.
q: Mush 7.0.0 built with gcc 1.35 on an AT&T 3b1 dumps core with a memory fault. With gcc -traditional I get an unterminated #if in glob.c. How do I get it working?
ref: The 3b1 has a strange memory layout that confuses xfree(), which mush uses to check what it frees. That's why INTERNAL_MALLOC exists, so compile with it. Also try #if 0 around the #ifdef BSD stuff in glob.c, since gcc probably supplies those directory routines.
replies:
3b1's have a strange memory organization that confuses the xfree()
function.  This is the function that mush uses to check whether it is
about to free() memory that was not malloc()ed.  This 3b1 problem was
a primary reason why the INTERNAL_MALLOC package was provided back in
6.5.something; try compiling with that definition and see if you get
better results.

It's probable that the gcc libraries and header files already provide
the BSD-style directory access routines that are compiled into glob.c
when BSD is not defined.  I don't know if this could cause the problems
you describe, but you might try editing glob.c to #if 0 .. #endif all
the stuff that is currently surrounded by #ifdef BSD.

subject: Think C 4.0 questions
q: In Think C 4.0, if I declare an array in an object class and fill it as a 1K buffer, is it safe to pass it to FSWrite, or must I copy it or lock it down? Also, can I assign a subclass object to a superclass variable?
ref: File Manager calls don't move memory, so it's fine. For calls that can move memory, like EraseRect, HLock it or copy to a local. Better, declare a pointer in the class and allocate it in your init method. And yes, a subclass object goes in a superclass variable. That's the whole point of inheritance.
replies:
As long as you are calling a routine, such as File Mgr calls, that
	don't move memory this is OK. If you are calling a routine, say
	EraseRect(), that can move memory, either HLock( this) temporarily
	or copy the instance variable to a local variable.

	Yes, you can do this.
	It's very nice :-)

	Hopefully someone else can give a concise answer for your other
	two questions.
--------------------------------
Dan Podwall
CS student, University of Houston
COSC10S4@jane.uh.edu
--------------------------------

I would declare a pointer in the class declaration and allocate it in your
initialization method and DisposPtr() it in your Dispose method.  This way
you won't have to worry about locking it down.  And, of course, the C syntax
for accessing the data will be the same as if it were an array.

Yes, most certainly.  This is the whole point of inheritance.  Look at the

subject: Need design tips for battery backed memory
q: What are some design tips for a battery backed memory holding about 65K bytes for several hours? Are there power-fail detect ICs, good batteries, and memory types?
ref: Maxim makes power-watchdog chips, and the MAX638 does efficient 9v to 5v with a built-in low-battery comparator. A 9V battery drawing 7mA lasts about 100 hours. Or just use Dallas Semiconductor SRAM with an integral lithium cell, good for 10 years. Get a databook.
replies:

for this purpose.  You'd have to scare up a databook and look through it.

totally a function of the power draw of your circuit.  I've used another
MAXIM chip, the MAX638 to convert 9v to 5v.  It is very efficient, on the
order of 90%, using switching techniques instead of shunting off the
excess power.  It can handle on the order of 20-40mA.

From past experience with 9V batteries, I think that if you draw 7mA
from a 1605-type (most common) it will last about 100 hours.

The MAX638 has a built-in comparator and bandgap voltage reference
that you can use to program a low-battery level.  You are supplied
with an open-collector output to signal the lowbattery condition.

Look at Dallas Semiconductor memory.  They make SRAM with intergral Lithium
power source which does automatic battery back-up, good for 10 years.

Rick Ales

subject: HST Images

ref: Not trivial, with the microwave frequencies and esoteric modulation and coding, but a determined amateur could do it. You'd pick up the TDRS downlink, since HST points at TDRS. Legally, listening is generally fine but passing it on is seriously illegal, and it varies by country.
replies:
#
#  What's to stop some enterprising amateur (or professional) astronomer
#from intercepting the signals from the HST and decoding them himself?

The downlink goes into White Sands Missle Range. Not a very large area
to have a receiver in. I don't know how large of a dish you would
need. The decoding of the signals would not be trivial.

-Greg Hennessy, University of Virginia
 USPS Mail:     Astronomy Department, Charlottesville, VA 22903-2475 USA
 Internet:      gsh7w@virginia.edu
 UUCP:		...!uunet!virginia!gsh7w

digital coding schemes, it would not be trivial but probably could be

subject: Physical backup of a DEC rz56 partition?
q: How do I make a physical, byte-by-byte backup of a DEC rz56 partition to tape, so I can later recover a deleted file? Is dd on the raw device right?
ref: Use dd, as you suspected. Tar and cpio work through the filesystem, and dump skips free blocks. Watch the transfer size: a long read at the end of a partition can give an I/O error and drop the last blocks, so pick a size that divides the partition.
replies:
[ Customer asks: How to do a physical backup. ]

	Use dd(1), just as you suspected.  Cpio and tar operate through
	the file system.  Dump reads the raw disk, but understands the
	file system and ignore free blocks.  You could use cp(1) if you
	don't mind an 8 KB block size.  Cat(1) would also work, though
	I don't know what output block size you would get.

	Something to watch out for using dd(1).  It has been my experience
	that long reads at the end of a partition will generate an I/O
	error rather than out-of-space.  This will cause it to miss the
	last few blocks of the file system.  There might be interesting
	data there.  As example, using a 64 KB transfer size, if the size
	of the partition isn't a multiple of 64 KB, then you won't be able
	to read those last blocks.  File systems are multiples of the file
	system block size.

subject: converting from apple writer to UNIX

ref: UNIX wants a linefeed after each carriage return. Print the file to disk to get a CR at each line end, load that back into AppleWriter, then do a find and replace that turns each CR into CR plus ctrl-J. Ancient stuff.
replies:
The main difference is that UNIX needs a carriage return after each line, and
a linefeed after each carriage return.

The easiest way to add a <cr> to the end of each line is to print the file
to disk (use [P] pd 8), then load the printed file into applewriter.

To get the <lf>s after each <cr>, do a
[F]<><>J<A
where you replace the 'J' with a ctrl-j (downarrow).  This command tells
AppleWriter to find each <cr> (the '>') and replace it with a <cr> and <lf>
(If that command doesn't do it, try using '>' for the delimiter and '<' for
the <cr> token.  It's been a  l o o ng  time since I've used AppleWriter). l o o

subject: Sending data from one '386 to another via STARLAN
q: How can I send data from one 386 running AT&T V/3.2.2 to another over Starlan without writing STREAMS t_* code?
ref: Skip the STREAMS code. Use uux to pass the data to a remote program, which is pretty fast over Starlan. Or with a common RFS mounted area, copy files across and use a FIFO only to signal completion, or do the whole job in one process. Why program when it's already there?
replies:
If you don't want to do any special programming you might want to consider
just using uux to pass the data to a remote program.  It's pretty fast
using e protocol over a starlan link.

Also, if you have a common RFS mounted disk area you can create a FIFO
that spans machines while maintaining normal pipe semantics.  The throughput
seems fairly slow on the FIFOs, but if you need bulk data transfers, just
copy files over RFS and only use the FIFO to notify the remote process
when the file is complete.  Or, with appropriate RFS mounts, you may be
able to do the whole job in one process and forget the IPC entirely.

subject: Power...
q: Will an Amiga 500 be harmed if I leave the power on for days or a week? It has no fan, so is it cool enough?
ref: No problem. The A500 is designed to be cooled by convection, so don't block the airflow. Nonstandard internal expansion boards might make it overheat. Fans only matter on bigger machines, so quit worrying.
replies:
I haven't had any problems leaving my Amiga (lorbit.UUCP, a.k.a.
uunet.uu.net!ukma!lorbit) on for really extended periods of time - like
the last four or five months or so. (I also run a BBS as well as UUCP
site. So far, though, users can only read news - not post. I'm working
on software for it, and - yes, dambit - I'll make sure only non-goofballs
have write access). I _have_ had a hardware failure, but that was static
(first time I've ever been bitten in 13 years of playing with computers!)
that hit while the system was off!
     Of course, I have a separate power supply (XT type) and that _does_
have a fan. But the A500 has done fine without one by itself. Oh, if your
house gets unusually hot - we have air conditioning - you might have a
problem in the summer.
                                               - R'ykandar.

No problem.  The A500 is designed to be cooled by convection.  When air inside
the machine is heated, that air rises and leaves the case, bringing in cooler
air from under the machine to replace that which leaves.  This technique work
only for smaller machines, and assumes that you aren't going to restrict the
air flow for your A500.  Nonstandard internal expansion boards may cause the
system to overheat.

With the larger machines, you not only have to cool the basic system, but
account for any expansion goodies that might be inside, and also the additional
heating that an internal power supply will cause.

subject: Accelerator Boards

-----------------------

memory. The only catch is that it only works in the standard speed (i.e.

the standard clock rate.

The System file contains patches that fix bugs and add functions to the Mac
ROM.  There are various versions of these patches exactingly tailored to
the specific quirks of specific versions of the ROM.  The Mac LC contains a
version of the ROM that did not exist when System 6.0.4 was released.  There
are bugs in that ROM that 6.0.4 cannot fix, but that 6.0.7 can.  There are
probably other things specific to the LC ROM of which the operating system
must be aware in order to function properly.  Apple recommends version 6.0.7
or newer for the LC for a reason.  Follow their advice -- you'll be happier
if you do.

subject: SCO 386 rsh problem
q: SCO 386 rsh has /bin:/usr/bin coded in as the default path and my users' .profile won't override it. Is there a fix, patch or alternative for restricting users with rsh?
ref: Wrong premise. The rsh(C) manual says it reads .profile when invoked as -rsh from /etc/login, and the PATH restrictions apply after .profile is interpreted. The /bin:/usr/bin path is only the default if .profile sets none. Set PATH in .profile. RTFM.
replies:
This is not correct.  The rsh(C) manual entry states:

    When invoked with the name -rsh [as is done by /etc/login], rsh
    reads the user's .profile.  It acts as the standard shell while
    doing this....  The restrictions above [i.e. forbidding changes
    to PATH] are enforced after .profile is interpreted.

"/bin:/usr/bin" is the default if PATH is not set in .profile.  However,
if PATH is set in .profile, the path will be correctly restricted.  I
verified on a 2.3.2 system that this is indeed the behavior of rsh.

subject: ASDG Floppy Accelerator (and other rumors)
q: Has anyone heard of ASDG's Floppy Accelerator for the Amiga? What does it do?
ref: It's software that adds intelligent track caching at the device level instead of DOS's block caching. The cache can sit in FAST memory, and you can add or remove caches any time. With enough tracks cached you get essentially a RAMdisk overlay of the floppy.
replies:
We were discussing ways to speed up floppies on BIX and began hypothesizing
about a utility to cache tracks of a floppy in fast ram. It was pretty much
spec'd out how you would do it and Perry complained every time he figured
out a neat hack to make into a product everyone else did too. So I can put
2+2 together and guess that that is what he was talking about. Which brings
up two things of interest...

First the developer community is moving right along up the learning curve,
as they do the Amiga gets better and better. Every time I think I have to
totally whomp on the O/S to do something I find there is a 'nice' way to
do it. Thanks Dale, Carl, Bob, Rob, RJ, Bob, Bob, Sam, Jim, Neil, et al
for a very well thought out hacking path.

Second, I firmly believe that good programmers share a subconcious(sp?)
esp. Whenever one thinks of a good idea everyone seems to pick up on it
until everyone announces the same idea at the same time. It is really
weird.

There was a thread about this going on in BIX awhile ago, at least I think
that's what this product refers to.  Simply put, its a program that adds
intelligent track caching (i.e. at the device level) instead to DOS's block
caching.  Also, the caching memory can be FAST memory; its not required to
be chip memory as are normal floppy buffers or DOS's block caches.  From
what Perry said, you have the power to add or remove caches at any time.
With enough tracks cached, you get what essentially amounts to a RAMdisk
overlay of a floppy disk.

Distribution:all

lastdrive=c:

(This assumes you have drives A, B, and C)
If I recall correctly, with DOS 3.n, you need to include that statement

Syntax:	int 11H
  On return in AX:
	bit(s)
	14-15		number of printers
	  13		reserved (PCjr: serial printer installed)
	  12		game adapter attached
	 9-11		number of RS232 cards
	   8		reserved
	 6- 7		number of diskette drives installed (if bit 0 = 1)
			00 = 1, 01 = 2, 10 = 3, 11 = 4
	 4- 5		initial video mode
			01 = 40x25 color, 10 = 80x25 color, 11 = 80x25 B/W
	 2- 3		system board ram size
			00 = 16K, 01 = 32K, 10 = 48K, 11 = 64K
	   1		8087 installed
	   0		diskette installed

subject: Teleportaion and Pets
q: Why does a shield of reflection not protect me from an Umber Hulk's gaze in Hack, when the spoiler sheet says it wards off gaze attacks?
ref: Umber hulk gaze only works when you meet their eyes, so reflection doesn't help. Same for Medusa, where you have to look at her. Read the spoiler properly: it protects against gaze attacks that work whether or not you meet the monster's eyes.
replies:
Hmmm.  Perhaps we should go into a little more detail in the spoiler.
The spoiler goes like this (umber hulks aren't specifically mentioned):

Shield of reflection - ray attacks (like lightning, fire, gas) are reflected,
   and also prevents gaze attacks where the monster gazes at you.  Note that
   this will not help if you look at the monster (i.e. the medusa).
   Especially useful against dragons and floating eyes.

I guess it really comes down to figuring out what constitutes a gaze attack.
When a monster uses its gaze as an active attack, and it does not matter
whether or not you meet its gaze, that constitutes a gaze attack.  Umber
hulks have four eyes, and their gaze attack only works when you meet their
eyes (see AD&D Monster Manual, p98).  Thus, shields of reflection would not
protect you against medusas or umber hulks.  It would seem that this would
mean it also wouldn't work against floating eyes, but it does.

	  - Paul

subject: Network Wiring Scheme

ref: Perfectly reasonable. Network managers like Ethernet over twisted pair because the star topology is far easier to manage than a bus, and standardizing the medium matters more than raw performance. And tcp-ip doesn't care if it's baling wire. Wrong group.
replies:
Many of us network managers like Ethernet over twisted pair because
the topology/architecture is much easier to manage than a bus
architecture/topology.  The technical performance on the medium is a
secondary consideration to the standardization of the medium and the
star topology.

Follow-up to comp.dcom.lans or the big-lan list at syracuse.  Lots of
discussion on these issues there.  tcp-ip doesn't care whether it's

subject: How to intercept speaker output ?
q: How do programs intercept the PC speaker beep and change its sound? I couldn't find anything in the interrupt list or DOSREF20. Where can I find the literature?
ref: You won't find it, because there's no interrupt to change the sound. The BIOS has a hardcoded routine invoked when a control-G goes out through the TTY Write function. Programs change the beep by intercepting that function and handling control-G themselves. Think before you grep.
replies:
That's because there is no interrupt to change the sound.  The BIOS has a
hardcoded subroutine which is invoked when a control-G is output via the
"TTY Write" function.  The way other programs manage to change the beep is
by intercepting that function and handling control-G themselves.

subject: xterm bug ????????????????
q: Why does the twm iconmanager show 'xterm' instead of my title when I run xterm -T 'foobar', yet shows the right title if I add -e csh?
ref: Sigh. -T sets the window title, not the icon name. Use the -n option, which is shorthand for the iconName resource and is not the same as -name. So: xterm -T 'foobar' -n 'foobar'. It's in the man page.
replies:
I had this problem, too until I realized that -T or -title sets
the window title and not necessarily the icon name.

What you should do is use the -n option.  Note that this is *not*
the same as the -name option and is really shorthand for the
"*iconName" resource.

So use:

xterm -T 'foobar' -n 'foobar'

subject: Xenix Getty timeout disable?
q: On SCO Xenix 2.3.1, how can I disable the getty login timeout on one terminal port, tty2A, so my screen saver stops getting a new login: prompt every 90 seconds? Why does inittab say 'off' there?
ref: Xenix getty apparently times out depending on the case of the device name. Use tty2a, lowercase, and it won't. And Xenix doesn't really use inittab, it just fakes it. Read /etc/ttys instead, and don't run telinit or it clobbers your edits. Learn what Xenix actually does.
replies:
(for benefit of the onlookers-- I'm the one that installed FAS 2.08 on
Dave's box.  It was a standard Xenix installlation of FAS source.)

The best I can guess is that getty has yet another special Xenix
'feature' that decides whether or not to timeout depending on the
device name case-- 'tty2A' enables timeout, 'tty2a' disables it.  I
think the way to fix this one is to use tty2a.  As far as I know,
this, um, peculiar behavior has nothing to do with FAS.

Because Xenix doesn't really use inittab.  It just fakes it.  Look at
/etc/ttys instead.  Don't ever try to edit inittab and run telinit,
because this will overwrite whatever you (or, more to the point, I)
did in /etc/ttys.  SCO added /etc/inittab and a 'telinit' shell script
to make life easier for people accustomed to real System V.  The only
problem is that it's so far from what System V does that it's quicker
and easier to just learn what Xenix does right off the bat.

subject: lopsided biceps
q: My biceps are growing mostly at the shoulder end and on the torso side, not near the elbow. Is lopsided growth natural, or bad technique? Should I add another exercise?
ref: Bench press and pushups hit the triceps, not biceps. Lats and back work, like narrow grip chins, hit the biceps. Biceps aren't supposed to be symmetrical anyway. Try a curl machine for the elbow end, and drop the wide grip.
replies:
Well, I would have to disagree with this statement.  Since a muscle works
by retracting, we work the bicep whenever we "pull" something.  When
we "push", we are constricting and thus working the tricep.  So, IMHO,
both bench press and push-ups are tricep exercises.  If you want other
bicep exercises, try pull-downs, rowing, or pull-ups.

Matt

Are you doing full repetitions?  I'd guess that the portion of a curl that
affects the elbow end of your bicep is when your arm is straight or nearly so.
But except for preacher curls and machine curls, this part of the exercise
involves little work since the weight is moved horizontally more than it's
moved vertically.

Why use a wide grip on the curling bar?  I think this could exaggerate
uneven lateral development.

These exercises affect the triceps rather than the biceps.  Exercises for
your lats and back affect your biceps.  (Especially narrow grip chins.)

I don't think the bicep is supposed to be symmetrical laterally.  Mine aren't.
Unless they're excessively unbalanced I wouldn't get too worried about that.
But you might try a curl machine if you have access to one to improve the
insertion end of your biceps.

subject: XView...How does it find the fonts?
q: I'm building XView on a Sparcstation and my programs can't find the fonts. Which setting do I use, the fonts directory variable or FONTINSTDIR?
ref: They're two different problems. FONTINSTDIR only tells Imake where to install the fonts. The X server, not the client, finds fonts, so that directory must be in the server's fontpath. Use xset to check and change it, then run xset fp rehash. Basic X stuff.
replies:
There are two distinct problems here. The first is getting the fonts
installed on your system; this is what the FONTINSTDIR macro is for. It
tells Imake where to put the fonts when it installs them. So if you
had problems installing the fonts, this is where you'll want to take
a look. The second problem is getting the XView clients to work with
the installed fonts. Recall that with the X Window System, it is the
server's job, not the client's, to locate the fonts. Hence, once you've
installed the fonts, you need to make sure that your server can get to
them. Whatever directory you've installed the XView fonts in must be
in your server's fontpath, or it won't be able to find them. Use
the "xset" program to examine and change your server's fontpath. You
may also have to rehash the fontpath when done ("xset fp rehash").

If you encounter more difficulties, please get in touch.

	-Doug

replies:

on Opencard or on Deletecard handlers *in* the background or stack
scripts, you will get the 54321 error.  If you comment the handlers
out, you can delete the cards.  You can also use version 1.0.1.

subject: dd curiosity solution

		    sense only when input is a magtape or similar
		    device).

	  block	    Convert  variable  length  records	to  fixed
		    length.
	  unblock   Convert  fixed  length  records  to	 variable
		    length.

     The block and unblock options cannot be  combined	with  the
     ascii,  ebcdic or ibm.  Invalid combinations silently ignore
     all but the last mutually-exclusive keyword.

files=##	specifies the number of files to read from the
			device (usefull for tape only)

	conv=unblock	reverse of block

q: In vi, how can I map the V key to act like H while mapping the H key to 12h? I can only get one of the two to work.
ref: Maps are text replacement, so V mapped to H then runs your new 12h. Also, mapping H reuses the slot and deletes the V map; I always thought that a bug. Issue the maps in reverse order so both exist, and set noremap so V stays the real H.
replies:
The first problem is that the mappings are not doing exactly what you want
them to.  Think of them as "text replacement" more than changing how a
particular capability is invoked.  If you issue the two MAP commands
you have above then the "V" command would actually issue the "12h"
command.  If you remap the "H" key, there is no way (except with
other sequences of commands which provide the same functionality) to
obtain that same function.

The second problem is that when you issue the commands as shown above,
the mapping of V is deleted when you do the mapping of H.  The reason for
this is that that the "source" for the second map command ("H"), is found

thought this was a bug.

Issue the MAP commands in reverse order and you will find that both now
exist.

subject: Threads vs. Modal Sessions
q: On the NeXT, can I use runModalSession:for: to run a long process while letting the sliders in my main window update, instead of using a thread or a timed procedure?
ref: It'll work, but the app only responds to events each time you call runModalSession:for:. Call it once a second and response is choppy and poor, and it only takes events in the one window you give it. A timed entry at high priority (NX_MODALRESPTHRESHOLD) is better, since sliders enter a modal loop.
replies:
This is a good solution.  The user-interface thread will block when you
are not twiddling the UI controls.  It doesn't busy-wait, so it shouldn't
get half the cpu.

Another good solution.  You will probably want to register the timed
entry function at a relatively high priority (NX_MODALRESPTHRESHOLD);
A slider will enter a modal loop when you slide it, so your timed entry
will have to be at least this high of a priority if you want it to continue
getting called while you slide the sliders.

This will work too, but you must remember that that your application will
only respond to events each time you invoke runModalSession:for:.  If you
only invoke it once a second, your response to events will be very choppy
and poor.  Also, it will only accept events in the one window you specify,
which may not be a problem in your case.

Hope this helps,
-sam

subject: IDL Internals manual

ref: It's a thin softcover describing IDL's internal data structures and subroutines. If you're writing C functions to link with IDL, it's an absolute necessity; if not, it's utterly useless. Fairly well written, with example code fragments. Figure out what you actually want first, sigh.

We have a copy (Version 2.0.7), sent to us by RSI.  It is a thin,
softcover manual describing the internal data structures and subroutines
used by IDL.

If you are writing C functions to be compiled and linked with IDL, then this
manual is an absolute necessity.  To do static linking, of course, you
would need the object files (_not_ normally supplied by RSI), and I understand

Depending on whether this sort of thing is what you want to do, the

internals manual, though, it is fairly well written, with useful
fragments of example code.

Hope this helps.

subject: Problems with SHARE
q: I upgraded to a 125Meg hard drive and now have to use SHARE. I load it near the start of Autoexec.bat and MEM shows it loaded, but I still get "Warning: Share should be loaded for large media". What am I doing wrong?
ref: You're loading it too late. The warning comes before Autoexec.bat even runs. Put INSTALL=C:\DOS\SHARE.EXE in Config.sys, adjusting the path to wherever your SHARE lives. Sigh, read the manual once in a while.
replies:
Well, your mistake is loading it  in Autoexec.bat, it needs to be loaded earlier than that, i.e. either by the boot process or in Config.sys.  To load it at boot time just place it in your root directory (DOS will find it). If it doesn't, then to explicitly load it - put the line  INSTALL=C:\DOS\SHARE.EXE  in your Config.sys file (this assumes that SHARE is in C:\DOS, if not substitute your drive and path).

	/s/	Bob Gettys

BTW - the error message is happening prior to running Autoexec.bat, not after.

subject: Silicon Graphics X11R4 server and default ColorMap
q: With the X11R4 server from Silicon Graphics I can only allocate sixteen colors from the default colormap. Is that a known problem, and is there a workaround?
ref: Not a bug, a "feature." GL and X share the hardware colormap, so the server preallocates all but sixteen cells for GL. Start the server with the -gl switch, for example Xsgi -bs -gl -su in your .xSGINeWS.cmd. Read the man page.
replies:
You can specify the colormap behavior when you start up Xsgi.  Check out
the man page for Xsgi and notice the descriptions for the -pseudo, -static,
-gl, and -envm.

If you start Xsgi automatically in you user.ps file with startXsgi, you can
specify the argument to Xsgi in $HOME/.xSGINeWS.  See the man page for
xstart.

You won't see this problem under 4.0.

This is not a problem, but a "feature."

Since GL and X programs must share the same hardware colormap, and GL
programs tend to expect that the colormap is populated by certain
colors, the default behavior of the X server is to preallocate all of
the colormap cells except for sixteen of them.  Therefore, GL programs
tend to display in the correct colors while X programs have only
sixteen to play with.

If you run predominately X programs and/or you want your X programs to
display in their true colors at the expense of GL programs, you can
start your X server with the -gl switch which will cause it to only
preallocate sixteen colors.

To make this the default, create a ".xSGINeWS.cmd" file in your home
directory and put this in it:

	/usr/bin/X11/Xsgi -bs -gl -su

subject: Translation-Invariant Pattern Recognizer NN's
q: Where can I find more on translation, rotation and scale invariant pattern recognition networks, like the Widrow and Winter Madaline work?
ref: Look at von der Malsburg's Dynamic Link Architecture. It's layered and self-organizing, representing patterns as labeled graphs of correlated cells, and recognizes by graph matching. See 'Pattern Recognition by Labeled Graph Matching', Neural Networks vol. 1, 1988. Go read it.
replies:
A different approach to Invariant Pattern Recognition may be found in
Christoph von der Malsburg's Dynamic Link Architecture. Malsburg
also uses a layered architecture, but his approach is self-organization.
Patterns are represented as labeled topological graphs composed of the
*correlation* behavior of neighboring cells in a layer. Pattern
recognition is then implemented through graph matching. The correlational
graphs express neighborhood relationships between features in the
input and yield a robust invariance to translation, scaling, or distortion.

See "Pattern Recognition by Labeled Graph Matching"
	Neural Networks, vol. 1, pp 141-148, 1988

subject: (none)
q: On a Power Series 120, f77 with -pfa made my double DO loop code slower (26.4 sec versus 16.3 sec without it), and only got back to 16.2 with extra options. What am I doing wrong?
ref: Profile it, genius. Compile with -p, run, then look at the per-process mon.out files with prof. Likely some small loops don't have enough work to cover the sync overhead. Strip those doacross lines from the .m file, rename it .f, and recompile with f77 -mp -nocpp.
replies:
Everything in your note sounded fine, and the code certainly sounds
like it should multi-process well.

The thing to do is to profile the code. e.g.
     f77 -pfa keep -WK,-O=4,-UR=4 -O2 test.f -o test   -p
                                                      ^^^
and then run it again.  This will produce "n" pc-sample files (one for the
master process, and one for each slave process).  Then by looking
at them with prof e.g.
     prof test mon.out12345
you should be able to see what's going on.

One thing that comes to mind is that you might have some initialization
loops, etc... that are parallelized, but don't have enough work in each
chunk to justify the synchronization overhead.  If you haven't already,
profile the single processor version (using both pc-sampling [-p] and
pixie) and compare the results to the intermediate files generated by
pfa.  Look for loops that use 1% (or less) of the execution time of the
program being parallelized.  The next trick is to remove the unwanted
doacross's from the .m and file and rename it as a .f and recompile like
so

f77 -mp -nocpp foo.f -O2 -o foo

to generate a new parallelized executable.

Hope this helps,

Archer Sully
archer@sgi.com

subject: WARNING: DiskManager and DOS 5.0
q: I used a DOS 5.0 boot floppy with the new dmdrvr.bin to get at my DiskManager-partitioned hard drive, and it said my partition was upgraded to DOS 5.0. Now my DOS 3.3 won't work from the hard drive. Is there a way to reverse that upgrade?
ref: Not really. DOS 3.3 and 5.0 don't coexist once 5.0 has touched the drive. Floppy-only won't save you; you'd have needed a full 5.0 install, which makes an UNFORMAT disk to go back. Pick one, and with a 286 or 386 just stay on 5.0. RTFM next time.
replies:
First off, why WOULDN'T you want to upgrade you HD to 5.0?

But, to answer the question, you can't reverse the process if you only
installed 5.0 on floppies.  In order to reverse this, you will have to
completely install 5.0 on the hard drive, which will create a disk called
"UNFORMAT".  You can use the Unformat disk to re-make your hard drive into
DOS 3.3.  That is the only way.  Directions on how to Unformat using this
technique are described in the manuals.

For further information, the first place to look is the manual, the READ.ME
files on the upgrade disks, then try calling the Microsoft Technical Support
Line.  The nubmer is printed on you registration card. (not the one you sent
in, but the piece that you keep, that was attatched to this card.)  If you
have lost or misplaced this card, you can find the number from your local
Microsoft dealer.

hope this helped...

[booted up with a DOS 5.0 disk and new Disk Manager]

    Bingo!  Versions 3.3 and 5.0 of DOS don't coexist.  Once you've used
DOS 5.0 to access a hard drive, it's not a good idea to go back and
use DOS 3.3 on it.  I'm surprised that you got the "upgraded" message,
but I suppose it's a good way to let you know.

    Nope.  If you use the actual upgrade procedure on the hard drive,
then it saves what it changed on a floppy, but I don't think that even
that would have saved you in this instance.  You have to make a choice
between DOS 5.0 and 3.3.  If you have a 286 or 386 machine, I'd stick
with 5.0, myself.  Also, if you can, just reformat your hard drive
with DOS 5.0 and you won't even need Disk Manager.  Big win for you.

subject: Multi-line Edit controls, and the enter key
q: How do I make a multi-line edit control in a Windows dialog accept the Enter key as a new line instead of triggering the default pushbutton?
ref: Normally a new line takes Control-Enter, since plain Enter always hits the defpushbutton. Subclass the edit control, check WM_KEYDOWN, WM_KEYUP and WM_CHAR, and replace the \r in wParam with \n. Then Enter makes a new line when the MLE has focus. The docs are wrong about ES_AUTOSCROLL.
replies:
I don't know of your problem, if you don't have a defpushbutton.
But the docs are wrong. ES_AUTOSCROLL means, the text scrolls, when the
user creates a new line. The new line can normally only be created with
Control-Enter, not Enter alone, this always triggers the defpushbutton.

However, I have dealed whith this at work just today. You can get a
multiline edit control on a dialog accept the ENTER key just like
carriage return/line feed (Control-Enter) if you subclass the edit
control and check each WM_KEYDOWN, WM_KEYUP and WM_CHAR and replace the
\r with \n characters in wParam.

The behaviour is now: if the MLE has the focus, ENTER acts just like
Control-Enter and creates a new line. Otherwise, the defpushbutton
gets it.

Hope this helps,
Kai Uwe Rommel

subject: Problem in loading unsupported subsets
q: Installing the unsupported X11 subset on a DECstation 2100 gives a 'not enough file system space' error even though /usr has over 40 MB free. How do I get it to load?
ref: Bypass setld. In /usr/etc/subsets, find the subset's .ctrl file and its mtloc line, which gives the file position on the tape. Skip that many files, then run dd piped through compress -d and tar xvpf. Make a .lk file so setld thinks it's installed. Be careful, or you'll load the wrong crap in the wrong place.
replies:
Go into /usr/etc/subsets and find the files associated with that subsets,
one of these, XXXX.ctrl has a line mtloc x:n, where n is the position of
the file on the distribution tape.  Skip n-1 filesthen do a
"dd if=/dev/... bs=20b | compress -d | tar xvpf -".

Creating a file XXXX.lk will make setld believe it's installed.

Proceed carefully, lest you load the wrong crap in the wrong place...

subject: Can you use an Audio CD as a CD ROM?
q: My Sony audio CD player has a "Subcode out" connector on the back. Can I use an audio CD player as a CD ROM drive on a Mac?
ref: No. Audio CDs and CD-ROMs share the same encoding, but the subcode connector only exposes the eight subcode channels for graphics or text on external gear. It has nothing to do with an outside device controlling the CD. You need an actual CD-ROM drive.
replies:
Both audio CDs and CD-ROMs are encoded using the same standard.  CDs have
eight subcoding channels labeled P through W which contain some
information.  Subtrack P contains a simple music track separator.  Channel
Q contains control information such as track number, track type, and
location (minutes, seconds, frames).  During the lead-in track, channel Q
contains table of contents information for the disc, with track number and
starting location of each track.

The other six channels aren't used in any standard way; there have been
some proposed standards that these tracks include labelling information
(e.g. track name) or graphics (e.g. the CD-Graphics standard Sony is
trying to promulgate.)  This "Subcode out" connector is probably meant to
allow access to all eight subcodes so that graphics, text, etc. could be
processed by an external component.

of a CD.  If you want this, you need a CD-ROM drive, not (most) a

subject: MacWeek waiting period
q: I got a postcard saying my MacWeek application was processed and I'm on a waiting list. Does that mean I was accepted, and why is there a waiting period?
ref: MacWeek is controlled circulation, free and paid for by ads, and ad rates depend on circulation. You qualified, but it's full. Either circulation grows by n or they purge the least desirable subscribers, and then the next n on the list get in. Simple.
replies:
MacWeek is what's called a controlled circulation book.  It's free.
What it's paid by is ads.  Advertising rates are partially determined
by circulation.  In other words, ads in a magazine with 200,000
subscribers cost more than ads in comparable magazines with 100,000
subscribers.  And if a magazine's circulation goes up enough, they
have to raise their rates.  (I'm not sure why this is, but I got the
impression that they really do *have* to.)

Now.  You have qualified for a subscription.  But MacWeek is already
fully subscribed to.  Two things can happens:  They can increase their
circulation by n, in which case the next n people on the list get
subscriptions.  Or they can purge their circulation, in which they
rank their subscribers by desired characteristics (such as how many
Macs they buy) and then drop off the lowest n people, in which case
again the next n people on the list get it.

Hope this helps.

subject: TCP/NFS
q: On ISC 2.2 with TCP and NFS, everything worked, then hostnames stopped resolving in telnet, ping and PCI, though IP addresses still work. What could cause this?
ref: Smells like a name service problem. If you're not running named, /etc/resolv.conf should hold the single line "nonameserver". Otherwise it needs your domain and the nameserver addresses. Also bump NSTREAM and NQUEUE in the kernel, and check netstat -m. Basic stuff.
replies:
I would guess the problem is the Domain Name Service (DNS). Its usage is
activated by the file /etc/resolv.conf. If this file contains the one and
only line "nonameserver" you may run into the problems described.
File resolv.conf should contain on the first line the domain you're in and
in subsequent lines the IP addresses of the NameServers to ask.

My /etc/resolv.conf reads:
                            domain zrz.tu-berlin.de
                            nameserver 130.149.4.10
                            nameserver 130.149.5.4

Frank

Assuming you are *not* running /etc/named (the BIND daemon), make
sure /etc/resolv.conf has the one line "nonameserver".  With
IP, NFS, and X all running you'll also likely want to increase NSTREAM
and NQUEUE in the kernel, you can use "netstat -m" to get idea
of your resource usage.

							Ross Ridge

subject: Decserver Question
q: I want an Ultrix 3.0 GPX station to use a PostScript printer on a DECserver. I have the printcap entry, but how do I make a /dev node carrying the LAT device and port?
ref: Use :ts=terminal-server: and :op=port-name: in printcap, so lpd knows how to connect. For a general device, use lcp -h /dev/tty00:TS1:TS1_1. LAT ttys are lta#, so run MAKEDEV lta0. Next time, say what errors MAKEDEV gave.
replies:
In Ultrix V3.0 there are two ways of associating a terminal
	server port with a special device.  One limits it's use to lpd
	and the other makes the port available for general access.
	They are:

	    1.  :ts=terminal-server: and :op=port-name:  This tells
		lpd how to connect to the port.

	    2.  The -h option on lcp(8) will let associate a lat
		port with a special device file.  For example:

			lcp -h /dev/tty00:TS1:TS1_1

		This lets anything that can open /dev/tty00 write
		to and read from the terminal server port.

	The device name for LAT ttys is lta#.  So for the first set
	of 16 LAT ports you'd use MAKEDEV lta0.   If you included
	LAT support during the installation of V3.0 it should have
	created one set for you.  Unless you have other comm devices
	on the system they will ordinarly start at tty00.  You can
	use file(1) to determine what device a special is associated
	with.
