	were the errors?

subject: Can batch files return value to C program?
q: How can a Turbo-C program get the ERRORLEVEL from a batch file it runs with system()? system() only returns 0 or -1.
ref: You can't. A batch file can't return an errorlevel at all, only .COM and .EXE programs do. And system() goes through COMMAND.COM, which doesn't pass back the errorlevel of what it spawns. Spawn the program directly, or use a utility that edits the parent's environment table. Sigh.
replies:
$I calling a batch file using the Turbo-C system() call. Is there a way
$to get the value of "ERRORLEVEL" upon returning to the Turbo-C program?
$system() is declared as an int, but it only returns 0 or -1, I believe
$it returns -1 only if it couldn't find COMMAND.COM (and maybe -1 if the
$batch file wasn't found, but I haven't tested it for that)  I can't set
$an environment variable in the batch file because when I return to the
$calling program, that environment is gone.

    Please note that a batch file can not return an errorlevel at all.
Only .COM and .EXE programs return errorlevels, and to get their return
codes they can not be executed using the system () call, since that
invokes COMMAND.COM first and COMMAND.COM doesn't pass back the errorlevel
of any program it spawns.

than their own; you may want to get your hands on one or two of those and
see if you can implement some form of return codes using

subject: NFS won't mount foreign disks
q: NFS 2.1.p on my DN10000 exports fine but I can't mount foreign file systems, getting 'Access denied' from mount. How do I fix it?
ref: Use the -n option on mountd on the foreign systems. The new mountd insists on a privileged port by default, which the Apollo can't use, and -n selects the old NFS mount port. The Apollo Hotline sorted it first time. Read the man page next time.
replies:
The Apollo Hotline figured this one out first time - you have to use the '-n'
option on 'mountd' on foreign systems since the "new" NFS mountd wants to use a
privileged port by default, but the Apollo can't; the '-n' tells mountd
to use the "old" NFS mount port. NFS now works :-).

#This routine intercepts NetNews batches and mails them to uafuts!smods

tee temp | uux - -r cseg\!rnews
cat temp | uux - -r uafuts\!/sysdevl/smods/usenet/bin/rnews

This is the easiest way that I found to do it...There might be better ways.

subject: Building Xenix 2.2.1 and partitions...
q: Why did I get only about 71 usable MB out of my 85MB Maxtor 1085 under Xenix?
ref: Do the arithmetic: 1024 cylinders times 8 heads times 512 bytes times 17 sectors is 71,303,168 bytes, or 68 real megabytes. A megabyte is 1,048,576 bytes, not 1,000,000, though most vendors can't tell the difference.
replies:
The Maxtor 1085 has the following geometry:
Cylinders: 1024
R/W Heads:    8

To calculate the usable capacity of a disk use the following formula:

UsableCapacity = Cylinders * Heads * SectorSize * SectorsPerTrack

So:

71,303,168 = 1024 * 8 * 512 * 17

71,303,168 Bytes = 68.00 Megabytes

CAVEAT EMPTOR:
-------------

1 Megabyte = 1,048,576 bytes  NOT  1,000,000 bytes

Most vendors don't appear to know the difference!

subject: /debug (again and again and again...)
q: Is /debug on IRIX my swap space, and does unmounting it affect swap? What is it, anyway?
ref: Sigh. /debug is just an informational file interface to process virtual space, used by debuggers like dbx. It neither consumes nor provides physical resources. Swap lives on its own disk partition, normally partition 1 of the root disk, and unmounting /debug doesn't touch it. df on /debug merely reports the swap size.
replies:
/debug is an file interface to system processes.  Unmounting /debug to
not unmount the swap space; unmounting only removes access to the interface
which SGI's dbx can access and debug processes.

However, playing out /debug's affectation of a real file system, many
of the standard IRIX(TM) file and filesystem commands present information
about the /debug interface and the swap partion AS THOUGH they were real
live IRIX(TM) file systems though they are not.

As part of of this, df of /debug reveals the size of your swap partion.
Thus yes, if "df -k /debug" says /debug imitation file system has
51048 kbytes, your swap partion has been partioned for approximately
51MB of swap space (virtual memory).

It is wise to take heed from Mr. Higgen and remember that /debug is not
a real file system but is a file system abstraction of the processes
executing under IRIX(TM).

				--- Dave Ciemiewicz

subject: Indirect system call
q: Reading section 2 of the Unix manual I found indirect system calls, as in syscall(2). What is the use of such a facility?
ref: On some machines the system call's operands sit right after the syscall opcode, but text is read-only, so variable operands can't go there. You put the real call and operands in the data segment and point an indirect call at it. Also handy for hiding a call, as some programs do with hostid.
replies:
While browsing through section 2 of the Unix manual,
   I came upon the concept of an indirect system call,
   as in syscall(2). Now that puzzled me. What might be
   the use for such a facility?

One thing they're good for is to "hide" specific system calls.
For example, one well known symbolic manipulation program
doesn't want you to use it freely, so it hides a call to
"hostid" inside an indirect system call, and compares the
result with that obtained via a normal hostid syscall.

You have stumbled on an interesting quirk in some implementations of UNIX.
It would seem that some processors don't expect the data for a
system call to be on the user stack, but instead immediately following
the system-call opcode in the user address space. In other words,
something like:
	syscall	5
	word	v1
	word	v2
instead of the more common way that system calls work in a CPU:
	push	v2
	push	v1
	syscall	5

(So on the OS side, it uses the saved PC to access the operands
instead of the user stack pointer).

The problem is that if the system call instruction is in the TEXT
segment you can't write variable quantities after the syscall
opcode, since the text is r/o. Thus, you put the actual opcode
and its operands out in the data segment, and the indirect system
call points at the real one.

The only time I have seen this was years ago on an Onyx running 7.

subject: Empathy and Sympathy
q: Does feeling empathy require first-hand experience of the situation? Can a man empathize with a woman in labor, or is that only sympathy?
ref: Empathy means imagining yourself in another's position, while sympathy is feeling sorry for someone. You don't need the same experience. A rich set of your own experiences, good communication and a reasonable imagination will do, though men and childbirth usually lack the communication. Sigh.
replies:
I can empathise with someone half my age; I've been in his situation.
But no equality.

Note, however, that I don't believe that you have to have been in a
particular situation in order to empathise with someone in that
situation.  With a rich set of your own experiences, a high degree of
communication with the person with whom you're empathising, and a
reasonable imagination, I believe that you can still empathise without
having been in the same situation.

I think that some men can empathise with women in childbirth.
However, I suspect that the degree of communication is too low
in most cases to do this very well.

Dave

subject: higher resolution ega/vga modes in xenix 386

ref: Xenix 2.3.0 and later has the vidi command; vidi e80x43 gives you 43 lines on EGA, and VGA too through EGA compatibility. There's no VGA 50-line mode. Put it in your .profile and add a 43-line termcap/terminfo entry so vi knows. RTFM, vidi(C).
replies:
In 2.3.0 and later there is a video mode command "vidi".
The command "vidi e80x43" will give you EGA mode 43 line mode.
This mode works on the VGA also via EGA compatibility.

There is no VGA 50 line mode at this time.

In SCO Xenix 2.3.1 see vidi(C). For example:

should put your EGA or VGA card into 80 columns by 43 rows mode.

You could put this in your .profile/.login. You will also want to modify
your termcap/terminfo database to add an ansi 43 line entry so that things
like vi know about it.

subject: about the little example program
q: In the NeXT Little example program, the app window never becomes active until I click it, and the text caret doesn't flash so I can type right away. How do I fix both properly?
ref: Run from a Shell, the Shell stays the active app until you explicitly activate another. That's by design, so you don't get surprised mid-typing. Launch from the Workspace Manager and it starts active, but give it an icon. For the caret, make the Text object the window's first responder with makeFirstResponder.
replies:
When you run apps from a Shell, the Shell remains the active app
until you explicitly activate the other app. This way you won't be
surprised & confused if you keep on typing on the Shell and suddenly the
other app starts running and Shell is deactivated.

Applications start off being active when you launch them from the
Workspace Manager. To do this properly with "little," you need to
give it an icon.

The Text object needs to be the "first responder" of the window. You can
make it the first responder with the makeFirstResponder method of Window.

Ali Ozer, NeXT Developer Support
aozer@NeXT.com

subject: Checking for single user mode
q: How can a Bourne shell script on a Sun 3 or 4 running SunOS 4.1 check whether it's in single user mode?
ref: Make root's login shell csh in /etc/passwd. Single-user mode always uses sh, so put your single-user stuff in sh's .profile and multi-user stuff in csh's .cshrc and .login. It's a hack, but it works. Not rocket science.
replies:
On our systems, we have the root user's entry in /etc/passwd specify the
C-Shell (csh). But single-user mode always uses the Bourne shell (sh). So
we put stuff in sh's .profile for single-user work, and csh's .cshrc and
.login for multi-user work. This can be used to do anything you like to
differentiate the two environments.

subject: APPLE IIGS SYSTEM FONT
q: Where in memory is the Apple IIgs system font, which I believe is Shaston 8 point? I want to relocate it, save it to disk and customize it, but I can't find it in the RAM or ROM maps.
ref: Stop hunting through ROM maps. Start up Quickdraw, which installs the system font, then call GetFont. It returns a handle; dereference it and you have the address. It's undocumented because it can move with every ROM release, so this way always works.
replies:
You can easily use Quickdraw to find the system font's address for you.  Simply
write a simple program that starts up Quickdraw.  This will install the system
font as the current Quickdraw font.  Then call the Quickdraw function GetFont.
GetFont will return a handle to the system font.  Dereference the handle and
you have the absolute address of the system font in ROM.

The reason you can't find any reference to the system font's address in the
IIGS documentation is that is liable to move with each release of the system
ROM.  Using the above technique will always find the system font, no matter
which system ROM you are using.

subject: (*(dump = GNU ? unexec : undump))("perl.$$");

ref: Not in the official perl. I looked at unexec() and rejected it: it's hard to make portable, and undump already does most of what's wanted. If you want an undumped executable, write a routine that forks, waits for the dump, then runs undump. Getting grouchy in my old age, yes.
replies:
I looked at the unexec() option and rejected it because it's difficult to
make portable, and because undump already does most of what I want.  One
pays a rather large premium to be able to restart the process exactly
where it left off, and you can get most of that effect by using the label
on the dump operator.

the other process to dump, and then runs undump for you.

unexec() in the official perl.

subject: System Security
q: After the worm, someone suggested a daemon that checks for trivial passwords. But its core is a password cracker, so the source could seed a worm. What should I do to protect the source?
ref: Don't let your users get at the source, and keep the output offline, say on a printer in a secure area. Any competent bad guy can write his own anyway, but never waste a chance to make things harder for the opposition. Sigh.
replies:
This is a general problem with many kinds of security checking and security
logging:  the programs and their output are potentially valuable to crackers.
At the very least, even if your regular sources are generally available to
your users, the sources for these programs shouldn't be.  Output preferably
should be offline entirely (e.g. on a printer in a secure area), and failing
that should at least be protected.  (This isn't necessarily sufficient,
though, even if the protection system is uncompromised.  For example, if
you run a password prober regularly, and have it send mail to folks whose
passwords it finds, the modification dates on mailboxes point to accounts
with weak passwords.)

Any competent bad guy can write his own.  However, the general principle
to follow is "never waste an opportunity to make things harder for the
opposition".  It's always possible that your program is better or smarter
than the one he would write.  You should make some effort to protect yours,

subject: Changing the opening Windows screen
q: I replaced vgalogo.rle in the Windows system directory with my own converted image, but I still get the blue Windows opening screen. What is vgalogo.rle for, and how do I change the startup screen?
ref: The startup screen is compiled into win.com, so swapping the rle file does nothing. Build it: copy win.cnf /B + vgalogo.lgo /B + your.rle /B win.com. The RLE must be 16 colors or less, no bigger than the video mode's resolution (no SVGA), and under 64k. Should be in the FAQ.
replies:
This really should be added to the FAQ.

The reason replacing the vgalogo.rle file does not work is because  the
actual startup screen is compiled into Win.com in the following
manner.

In the system directory there is a file called win.cnf.  This file is
the actual startup program for Windows minus the type of display
and the actual image.

The [cev]galogo.lgo file contains the info for how to display the image
that follows it in the final win.com.

To create your own startup image do the following:

copy win.cnf /B + [vec]galogo.lgo /B + xxxxxx.rle /B win.com

There are some limits on what the RLE file can be.  First of all
it must not be more than 16 colors, and cannot be larger than the
standard resolution of the video mode.  In other words, no SVGA modes.
Also, the entire file must be smaller than 64k.

Good luck.

subject: Format of loadable object files

ref: A JMP isn't required. The CLI does a JSR to whatever was just LoadSeg'd, so start with executable code. What you must have is a hunk_header block; without it you get the not-an-object-module error. Your JMP stub probably just forced one to be created.
replies:
The AmigaDOS routine that the CLI is calling to execute you is doing
a JSR to what was just LoadSeg'd.  So its best to have executable
code there.  A JMP isn't required.  For example, the printer.device
individual printer modules.

Of course, you have to start your object module with a hunk_header block.
If this is missing you'll get the "File is not an object module" error
message.  Perhaps (assuming you start with executable code) that
when you put the JMP in that forces the creation of the hunk_header ?

subject: IBM/Apple disk interchange?
q: Is there software that lets an Apple II read or write IBM PC format 5.25 inch disks, or lets an IBM PC read or write Apple disks, without a hardware card?
ref: No such luck. Apple drives use a software controller with its own encoding, while the IBM has a controller chip and a different scheme. So neither machine can read the other's disks in software. Buy a hardware card for the PC, or hook them up with RS232C and a comm program.
replies:
I'm afraid you're out of luck; no such program exists, nor for the Apple, nor
for the IBM-PC. The problem is that the Apple and the IBM diskcontrollers use
a different encoding scheme to read/write. As you probably are aware the Apple
has no 'diskcontroller', whereas the IBM has. Apple diskdrives use a clever
'software controller', hidden in DOS. The Woz thought up this scheme to avoid
using a lot of chips when he implemented the first version of DOS.
Since IBM *does* use a controller chip, and one with a different encoding
scheme, it is not possible for Apple's to read IBM formatted disks (because DOS
doesn't know about *that* encoding scheme), nor is it possible for IBM's to
read Apple disks (because DOS uses a proprietary scheme).

The only solution is to buy a hardware card which will read Apple disks in an
IBM-PC. There are various manufacturers who produce them.

Another -cheaper- solution is to connect the Apple and the IBM with an RS232C
cable, and use a communication program t

subject: KA9Q and serial rs232 lines
q: KA9Q TCP/IP over a serial SLIP link between two PCs works below 4800 baud but hangs at higher rates, while Ethernet works. What's wrong?
ref: If the only difference is the data rate, the serial chips are dropping characters. Replace the 8250 or 16450 with a National NS16550, which has FIFOs. You also need a recent NOS using the built-in asy driver. asystat tells you if it sees the 16550.
replies:
If the ONLY difference between a working configuration and a non-working
one is the data rate on the serial link, then the problem is almost
certainly due to characters being lost by the serial controller chips. I
recommend that you try replacing the 8250 or 16450 chips with National
NS16550 chips, which have 16-level FIFOs built into the receiver and
transmitter.

These chips function just like 8250s unless they are explicitly put into
FIFO mode by software. Therefore you need to run a fairly recent "NOS"
version and use the built-in asy driver in order to take advantage of
the FIFO feature. ("Recent" means "within the past few months".) You can
verify that you have the right version when you issue the "asystat"
command because it will mention that a 16550 chip has been detected.

Phil

subject: Record Locking in foxplus+ SCO xenix
q: Is there software that does better record locking than Foxplus? I want to load several records into an array, let a user edit them, and keep other users read-only on those records meanwhile.
ref: Just use the rlock() function. Watch out for deadlock, though: two processes each hold records the other wants and both wait forever. Lock in a consistent order, or learn the hard way. FoxPro, Foxbase's big brother, also allows this.
replies:
Then why not use the rlock() function call? The only possible problem
you may have is deadlocking, where two applications have locked records
the other application wants and they both try to lock something someone
else already has after locking records other applications want to get at.

For example
process #1 wants to lock records 1,2,3;
process #2 wants to lock records 2,3,4;

#1 locks 1, tries to lock 2, can't so it locks 3, then tries to lock 2 again.
#2 locks 2, tries to lock 3, but can't, so it locks 4, then tries to lock 3.

Both processes are now deadlocked. This is something to look out for.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

subject: Power Inverter suggestions?
q: How do I build a 12 volt DC to 120 volt AC power inverter?
ref: Depends what it feeds. If a square wave is fine, interrupt 12VDC at 60 cycles and send it through a backwards 120V/12V transformer, with switching transistors or mechanical switches. For sine wave loads, a 60 cycle oscillator into the transformer is easiest but runs hot and wastes power. Know your load first.
replies:
There are two basic kinds, depending on how clean you want the output power
to be.  Some devices don't mind a 120V square wave, in which case you can
just interrupt 12VDC at 60cps, send this through a backwards 120V/12V AC
transformer, and you're done.  This can be done with switching transistors
or with actual mechanical switches (as in the old vibrator power supplies
for mobile operation of tube style radios).

Other devices really, really want a sine wave.  The easiest way is to build
a 60cps oscillator and send that through the transformer, but the most obvious
ways of doing that dissipate a LOT of heat in your transistors and are not
horribly efficient.  There are more efficient ways to go about it, but alas
my references are at home and I'm not...

The summary answer is, what do you want to use the inverter for?

subject: ESPF
q: In EPSF, are the %%BoundingBox coordinates absolute or relocatable? If I have a 2 x 3 inch graphic, can I give (0,0) and (600,900) at 300 dpi?
ref: They're absolute, and in points, not pixels. Think device independence. A 2 x 3 inch graphic is %%BoundingBox: 0 0 144 216, where it's actually drawn. If your code moves the graphic around by page type, give up on a bounding box.
replies:
They are not relocatable.

Think device independence.... Use points, not pixels.

The graphic should be placed at an absolute location.  With it fixed
in place the %%BoundingBox comment accurately describes its position
and size.  If you then want to include this image into another image,
you can use the BoundingBox info to do the appropriate translate,
scale, and rotate.  These three operators are all that you need to get
the included image in the right spot with the proper size and
orientation.  Its generally a good idea to put a save and restore
around the image.  A clip region may also come in handy.

Sender:

Followup-To:

Distribution:

The answer is that they are absolute and given in points. The
idea is that you are declaring where on the page your program
will make black or white marks, assuming it is sent to a
standard PostScript printer.

You give the bounding box as

        %%BoundingBox: 0 0 144 216

because that is where is will actually be drawn.

The bounding box is very useful if you can provide it; the
psfig software uses it to work out the necessary coordinate
transformation to place the graphic in the desired point in a
troff document, and to scale it etc as instructed.

WARNING: if your code puts the graphic in different places
according to such things as the page type, the value of the
/Product string in statusdict (blech!) or even the current
clipping path, then you can't reasonably put any bounding box
at all! Take this as a hint about the portability of your code....

subject: Statusof a msdos file after dos error
q: In Turbo Pascal 5.0 with {$I-} set, what's the status of a file after DOS reports an I/O error, such as the user pulling the diskette? Do I have to close it, can I, and should I?
ref: Depends on how you opened it. A file opened with reset for reading is left uncorrupted. With rewrite or append, writes since opening probably never reached the disk, because in TP closing is what flushes the buffer. So close it.
replies:
The answer depends on whether you opened the file with reset or rewrite.
If you opened it with reset, to read it, then a failed operation will leave
the file uncorrupted (unless the failure is due to a dog eating the physical
disk, etc.).  If you opened it with rewrite or append, to write to it, then
the chances are very good that any write/ln's performed between the opening
of the file and the failed operation did not make it to the disk.  In TP,
closing a file is the way to insure that writes are flushed from the buffer
and sent to the disk.  Verify this by opening a file with rewrite, sending
some text to the file with write/ln, and watching the light on the disk drive;
it will not glow until the close command is processed.

Peter Suber.  Depts. of Philosophy, Computer Science.  Earlham College.
Richmond, Indiana 47374.  317-983-1214.  peters@earlham.bitnet.

subject: Watcom vs Zortech 32-bit compilers
q: Do the 32-bit DOS compilers like Watcom and Zortech give true 32-bit flat addressing, and can you make DOS calls in protected mode?
ref: You still have segments, but they run from 1 byte to 4 gigabytes, and you can point all the descriptors at the same place for one flat 32-bit space. You can't make DOS calls from a 32-bit code segment, only through the DOS extender, maybe. 32-bit protected mode compilers abound; only real mode ones don't exist.
replies:
Correct

Yes and no.  You still have segments, but these are between 1 byte
and 4 gigabytes, and can overlap.

You can however have your descriptors all point to the same place, and
have one 32 bit flat space....

You can't from a 32 bit code segment.  However, you can trhough the
DOS extender <maybe> which runs DOS as a 386 virtual mode task.

The point was there was no REAL mode 32 bit compiler.  32 bit protected
mode compilers abound - look at Intel Code Builder, Zortech, DDGPP

subject: MasterMind next-guess algorithm needed
q: Does anyone have an algorithm for generating the next guess in Mastermind?
ref: Keep a record of previous guesses and their blacks and whites. Guess a combination, and if it would have produced the same results against all earlier guesses, it's a candidate. Don't call rand each time. Changing one position at a time worked well. Not optimal, but it does the job.
replies:
This is not an 'optimal' algorithm but it does the job.  Keep a record
of previous guess and results (Blacks and Whites).  Guess a
combanation.  If it is the correct answer, comparing it to the previous
guesses should give you the same results (# of blacks and # of
whites).  If it doesn't try again, this one isn't right.

The reason this is not optimal is that some guesses give more
information regardless if they're wrong.  You might want to explore
this.

The actual guessing method is critical.  You DON'T want to call
(multiple) rand for each guess.  If their is only one solution left you
want to find it quick.  Using rand only for the first guess and then
incrementing the combination isn't much better since you're guesses
will have a tendency of having multiple 000's at the end.  I tried
chaging one position at a time and this worked rather well.

I'd give you my source but I can't find it at the moment, in fact I
might have no record of it.  If you have difficulties send me email.

subject: Help requested for file conversions
q: How do I convert Apollo typed files, like Mentor Graphics rec or hdru files, into plain ascii I can uuencode and mail, and then convert them back to typed files on the other end?
ref: Don't bother with cvt_rec_uasc. On SR10 or later, use tar -A, which saves the Apollo type info in a standard tar archive. Then uuencode and mail it. Untar on an Apollo and you get typed files back. Or use iwbak/irbak or the newer wbak to write a file. Read the manuals.
replies:
We have encountered a similar problem moving designs from one
site to another that is only networked via traditional TCP/IP.
What we do is make a backup file using iwbak then ftp the
backup file and use irbak to restore it. The apollo wbak and
rbak commands only read/write tapes, but mentor has iwbak/irbak
available. These commands can also read/write backup files as
well as tapes. You should be able to encode/decode these files
and mail them. If anyone uses iwbak/irbak for ftp-ing things,
one gotcha to watch for: you can use binary mode OR ascii mode,
but if you store it on a remote computer then fetch it from
that computer, you must use the same mode both times.

Does anyone know if apollo plans to supply a wbak-like command
that can use files or stdio like tar can? I don't want tar, since
it doesn't understand apollo's file types (and I do like having
all those file types). We currently use SR9.7, so forgive me
if it's already in SR10. (We'll be upgrading to SR10.1 real soon.)

If you are running on sr10 or later, tar -A will save the
Apollo specific type and record information in a standard
format tar archive (it actually puts two entries into the
archive for each typed file).  You can than uuencode the
tar file and mail it, and at the other end uudecode it
and untar it.  If you untar it on an Apollo, you will get the
typed file.  If you untar it on anything else you'll get
a regular file full of bytes of garbage.

subject: Chips

L means ceramic package, P means plastic.

The Amiga 68000 runs at just over 7 MHz, so the 8 MHz version
will probably be the cheapest one you'll find.  Also, you may
use either the L or P version.

subject: AT vs ST506 Interfaces
q: What does an AT interface hard disk mean, as in an ad listing ST506, AT, ESDI and SCSI? How does it differ from ST506?
ref: An AT drive uses the ST412 interface, not the ST506. The difference is buffered seek: a 506 controller does step-wait 20 times, while a 412 sends 20 steps and then waits, so seeks are faster. A 412 drive works on a 506 controller, but not the reverse. RTFM, or at least the Seagate tech note.
replies:
Recently some drive manufacturers have realized that a large percentage
of their drives are going into a very well defined market place - the
IBM AT/Clone.  (Note: I didn't say the BUS is well defined!)

Anyway, what they've done is to essentially put what used to be the
ST506 interface (or 412 - whatever it was/is) ON THE DRIVE and
eliminate the need for "all that stuff" on an interface card.  The
connection has been reduced to just a few, if any, IC's, to buffer the
signals and maybe protect one side from a fault on the other.

At least, that's what I saw in some literature the Almac salesman
brought over recently.  I wasn't really interested so I didn't question
how multiple drives are handled, floppy/hard disk controlling, etc, etc.

kEITHe

An AT does not have an ST506 interface, it has an ST412 (often called
AT) interface. The diference is that the 412 offers "buffered seek." On
the 506, to step 20 tracks the controller does a "step...wait" 20 times,
while on the 412 the controller sends 20 step commands then a wait. The
next effect is that the seek is faster since the head doesn't stop at
each track. An AT drive will work on an ST506 controller, since it's a
superset. The other way round may result in seek errors.

  This info taken from a Seagate tech note supplied by IBM when the
first AT's came out.

subject: User defined functions
q: Could Emacs let me define a function from a keyboard macro, give it a name like any other command, and save it to a file?
ref: GNU Emacs already does it, any idiot knows. Use name-last-kbd-macro and insert-kbd-macro. A string bound to a function name with fset is read as typed keys. Use standard bindings or M-x so it ports between terminals.
replies:
Multics Emacs has two things along these lines.  One is the ability to
save keyboard macros into a text file and later load the macro back
into Emacs.  You can also manually edit a macro this way (don't you
hate it when you finish creating a keyboard macro and then realize
that you forgot to make it go to the next line at the end, and have to
redo it?).

The other facility it has is a keyboard macro compiler.  It takes a
keyboard macro in a buffer and converts it to Lisp.  It works by
simply replacing each key with the corresponding (function) call.  It
doesn't work really well, though; for example, it translates the macro
sequence

	^X^F "filename"

into
	(find-file)
	(insert-string "filename")

because the compiler doesn't realize that "filename" is actually a
parameter to find-file.  It knows about a few special case (I think it
knows about ^S, since that is used very frequently in macros).
Another bug in the macro compiler is that it uses the key bindings in
effect in the macro edi

This is exactly what M-x name-last-kdb-macro and M-x insert-kbd-macro
in GNU Emacs can do for you.  The trick is that a string bound to a
function name is interpreted as if the characters in the string were
entered from the keyboard, e.g.

(fset 'insert-hello-world-in-beginning-of-line
   "^AHello world ")

However, there is a minor problem with this approach:  If you use
key bindings which are unique for the terminal on which the keyboard
macro is defined, you will not be able to use them on another
terminal.  If you want to be able to move functions defined via
keyboard macros between incompatible terminals, use only the standard
bindings and call other functions via M-x or eval even when you have
bound them to a key on YOUR keyboard.  For example,

(fset 'insert-hello-world-in-beginning-of-line
   "^[#Ghello world ")

MIGHT do what was intended on the terminal it was defined on, but not
on any other terminal!  The following version is always protable:

(fset 'insert-hello-world-in-b

subject: Micro C-Shell
q: Micro C-Shell in multi-user mode: after I change /etc/passwd and log in, it just goes back to the login prompt and never gives me a shell. Why?
ref: Bug: the colon is the passwd field separator and also part of GEMDOS paths. A home of E:\bammi gets cut off at E, which is invalid, so login refuses you. Set home to \usr\foo on the drive with the shell and put a profile.sh there that sends you to the real home.
replies:
I ran into exactly the same problem.  The problem is caused by ':' being used
as the field seperator in \etc\passwd and also being used by gemdos path names.
What had happened in my case was that i specified my home directory
to be 'E:\bammi'. Now when i login, login reads \etc\passwd and find that my
home directory is 'E' (the ':' in the pathname terminated the passwd field),
which is not a valid path, so it refuses to let me log in. I have informed
David Beckemeyer of this bug. For now the solution is to tell passwd that
your home directory is \usr\foo on the drive on which MT c shell live. In
\usr\foo you put in a profile.sh that send you off to your real home, after
modifying the home variable appropriately.

subject: Tarski's definition of truth
q: Can someone explain Tarski's definition of truth? My logic professor kept saying "'Grass is green' is true iff grass is green" and I never understood the point.
ref: Sigh. That's not a theory of truth, it's a condition of adequacy any theory must meet: the left side ascribes truth to a sentence, the right states a fact. Tarski's real work was defining truth via satisfaction, so quantified sentences inherit truth from their parts. Read his original article, "The Semantic Conception of Truth".
replies:
There's much more to Tarski's theory than this, but to start
here:

The left hand side ascribes truth to a certain sentence,
and the right hand side describes a fact about the world.
The statement asserts that the sentence is true iff the
fact holds.
This is not a *theory* of truth, but a condition of adequacy
that any theory of truth has to fulfil.
Tarski wanted to ascribe truth to sentences, via the notion
of satisfaction of formulae (sentences with object-place-holders).
He was able to explain how a sentence with multiple quantifiers
can inherit its truth value from its parts, something which had
puzzled logicians from Aristotle onwards.

The best way to start is to read the original article,
"The Semantic Conception of Truth" in his collection
"Logic, Semantics, Metamathematics", easily obtainable
from the UCB Philosophy Library.

Peter Ladkin

subject: Making command.com run different autoexec.bat upon bootup
q: Why does SHELL=C:\COMMAND.COM /P /CC:\DOS\AUTOEXEC.BAT in config.sys lock up the machine when the autoexec finishes? I'm on a PS/2 with PC-DOS 4.01.
ref: Using /C and /P together isn't well defined. /C runs the batch file and then exits, and it seems to win over /P. Your top-level shell exits and nothing is left, so the machine locks up.
replies:
The behaviour of the /C and /P options simultaneously is not well
defined.  /C invokes the autoexec.bat and then exits.  /P is supposed
to make the shell permanent.  It appears that the /C option takes
precedence and your top-level shell is exiting and hence your machine
locks up since there is no shell after autoexec.bat is executed.

subject: Question about Return-Receipt-To

replies:
In general, you cannot make return-receipt-to work reliably.

return receipt request in the header.  Suffice it to say that careless
use of this "feature" can cause lots of problems and cost someone a lot
of money.  It's best not to use return-receipt-to: at all.

subject: Anonymous ftp/password encryption
q: Why can't users log in through ftpd on an SR10.2 Apollo node whose registry was converted from 9.7 with cvtrgy? The encrypted password in the registry doesn't match crypt().
ref: SR9 didn't use crypt()-style encryption, and cvtrgy keeps the SR9-style passwords. The simple fix is to expire all user passwords, so people set new ones at login that get encrypted in the new format. Then ftp works. It's in the SR10 transition notes, I think.
replies:
=>
=>I have been trying to use the version of ftpd, supplied by sls@ocf.berekeley.edu,
=>that supports anonymous FTP.  That part works fine, except that now
=>anonymous FTP is the type that works.
=>
=>The registries on the SR10.2 node were created from the 9.7 registry
=>using cvtrgy.
=>
=>It seems that the encrypted password in /etc/passwd does not match
=>the password encrypted by crypt(), thus preventing users from "logging
=>in" via ftpd.
=>
=>Is this a known problem, or am I misunderstanding the problem?
It is not known as such, but the 9.7 passwd-entries contain a non-sr10
compatible crypted passwd. (I think it is mentioned somewhere in
	"making the transition to sr10"

The fix is rather simple. Expire all user passwds, upon login are they
required to supply a new one, which then is crypted in new format.
So next time an ftp-session is started, then access is allowed.
Ftp was created on sr10, hence it did not give any problems.

Regards,
		Willem Jan Withagen

Eindhoven Universi

Ah yes.  When a password is created and stored in an SR10 registry, the
encryption is, effectively, done by crypt(), so the normal comparison
techniques work fine.  However, SR9 did not use this encryption technique.
The SR10 registry can understand SR9-ish encryption, so when you cvtrgy,
the password will still be SR9-style encryption.

Your only hope (that I know of, anyway) is to have your master registy on
SR10, and do cvtrgy -from9to10's to get the info down to the SR9 side.

subject: Legal postscript fonts?
q: Is it legal to scan a typeface, trace it into a PostScript font with Fontographer, rename it and release it into the public domain?
ref: In the US the shape of a typeface can't be protected, so it's legal. The name can be a trademark, so rename it. Other countries may differ, and importing there could be trouble. Distributing copies can be a civil violation, and stealing others' work is unethical anyway.
replies:
Making altered copies of copyrighted material may or may not be a
copyright violation, depending on the details of the law and the
details of what you do.  Distributing those copies to other people
is a violation (although the violation is civil, not criminal -- the
government won't put you in jail over it, but you can be sued over it).
The precise method of distribution -- public domain, copyrighted posting,
availability for FTP -- is irrelevant.

If you do the copying in a country where it is not a violation, then that
is not illegal, but importing the results to a country where it is a
violation may break that country's laws.  (*This* might even be a criminal
act -- smuggling -- rather than a civil violation.)

Stealing other peoples' work is unethical even when it is not illegal.

In the US the the SHAPE of a typeface cannot be protected.  It is
therefore absolutely legal to do what you are proposing.  The NAME of the
font can be protected (Trademarks), and often is, so renaming your newely
created font would be necessary.
   The type foundries in the US often have typefaces which are identical,
in all but name.
   Adobe has recently been discussing these legal issues in
comp.lang.postscript.  They used a case very simliar to yours as an example
of what would be legal (in the US).
   of note is that though Adobe has said that this is legal in the US, but
that in some countries the SHAPE of typefaces can be protected, but they
have never given any countries as examples of where SHAPES of fonts can
be protected.

subject: HOW DO YOU INSTALL A PASSWORD ON A PC?
q: How do you install a password on a PC? I was told DOS 4.01 or 5.0 can do it with something in config.sys, but I can't find it in the manual.
ref: MS-DOS doesn't do that. DRDOS 5 can password files and directories. Compaq, IBM and others have a power-up password stored in CMOS, set with a setup disk. Or use a boot-lock program like LOCK.EXE, freeware. Forget the password and you're pulling the battery. Wonderful design.
replies:
(1) You can set passwords on files and directories using Digital Research's
DRDOS 5, not MSDOS.

(2) Some PC's have a password built into the ROM, to disable access to the
CMOS setup (nothing else, though). These are pretty secure - and just
disconnecting the CMOS RAM's battery isn't enough to clobber the password, not
on the one I tried, anyway.

(3) There are plenty of programs to force you to supply a password when booting
up, before you can run DOS. One that wasn't mentioned by others is: LOCK.EXE,
which is freeware, and prevents access to the hard disk when booting from
diskette. A new version is coming out soon, with better documentation and
options, I think including the ability to prevent boots from floppy disks.

It is now available via FTP at the University of Richmond as LOCK.ZIP, in
[anonymous.hayes.dos].  As usual, login "anonymous", password
<your_e-mail_address>.  IP number is 141.166.1.6

If it is coupled with the CMOS password, above, you get a pretty tight system,
but

He was probably referring to machines that have a power-up password.  Compaq,
IBM, and others have a power-up password check that can be used to completely
disable the machine and prevent re-booting without knowing the password.  It
is usually set via a special setup diskette and is stored in the configuration
CMOS memory.  When the battery goes, so does the password... this is the only
way to reboot if you forget it....

ref: This gets asked constantly. Apart from the busy bit on the PC parallel port, they present the same programming model, and the same software drives both. The Janus library is the basis for the more sophisticated stuff, documented in the Technical Reference manual.
replies:
The programming model is the same, the sidecar and bridgecard are different
implementations of the same basic logic.

The applications software provided probably doesn't, however there is
"Janus" library provided that can provide the basis for more sophisticated
applications and interactions.  I'm not sure whether this library is fully
documented in the A2000 user's guide that comes with the machine, however
I know the documentation is in the A500/A2000 Technical Reference manual
available from the CATS people.

You shouldn't have to wait long for the A2000, now that they are finally
shipping...

As this gets asked a lot, I'll post the answer...except for the sense
of the busy bit on the PC parallel port they do indeed present the
same programming model.  In fact, we use the same software to
drive both the Sidecar and the Bridge board.  (aside from the
LPT1 program)

As an I/O adapter for an Amiga, the PC may have its finest hour :-)

		andy finkel

subject: help with Fortran bug (sr9.7.5 ftn 9.95)
q: My large FORTRAN program on an Apollo (sr9.7.5, ftn 9.95) dies with 'unable to unwind stack because of invalid stack frame'. What does it mean, and what should I check?
ref: Don't cry BUG yet. Make sure every subroutine and function call passes the right number of parameters, since a mismatch makes non-stack memory get read as stack. Also recompile all modules fresh and check your big-array equivalence alignments. Usually it's your own sloppy code.
replies:
This may be too late, or too obvious, but if you haven't solved your
problem, make sure that all subroutine/function calls are using the
correct number of parameters. This will cause non-stack memory to be
interpreted as stack.

I hope these suggestions aren't too simplistic, but before we cry BUG
here....Has your hacker 1) made sure all his modules are freshly compiled;
and 2) double-checked big-array equivalence alignments?  A framing error
could arise from subroutine declarations being out of kilter, or arrays
attempting to wander around your operating system.

You know the old FORTRAN saying:  "If all else fails, Throw It In Common."

...lori

subject: exception #10 (not #13)
q: My small program occasionally produces exception #10 under QEMM 5.11 and DESQview 2.31. What does that mean?
ref: Exception 10 is the Invalid TSS exception. A TSS is a task state segment, which the CPU and control program use to save and load machine state at task switches. Your program probably scribbles over one. Check for dangling pointers, then call Quarterdeck.
replies:
Exception 10 is the "Invalid TSS" exception.  A TSS is a task state segment,
a data structure used by the control program (in this case DESQview/QEMM) and
the CPU to manage tasks.  Every time the processor switches tasks, it saves
the machine state for the current task into its TSS and loads the saved
machine state for the new task from its own TSS.

Since a TSS is a data structure used by control programs, I'd assume that
DESQview would mark the memory they occupy read-only, but perhaps this
isn't the case and our program accidently overwrites one or more TSS's.

Check your code for obvious problems such as dangling pointers and if nothing
appears to be wrong, try calling Quarterdeck customer service.

subject: Digital Audio
q: What happens to the harmonics of a musical note when it is digitized and then reconstructed?
ref: Any harmonic below 20 kHz is retained, since Fourier says it's all sinewaves anyway. Anything above 20 kHz is gone, filtered by the anti-aliasing and anti-imaging filters. Whether you can hear those is the real question, so quit shouting.
replies:
assuming you are refering to CDs (and "good" ADC and DAC)
All harmonics of the note theat are less than 20kHz are retained.
All harmonics above 20kHz are loss.

The real question is will we hear the lossed harmonics?
Can speakers or ears generate IM distortion which alows us to hear them?

One thought I had (thanks to jj) was that the ear may generate
IM distortion which was audible. Given the way the brain can use
changes in frequency response to detect vertical location.
Maybe it also detects and is accustomed IM distortion.

John D. Hoford

Fourier tells us that all complex waveforms are composed of sinewaves.  Thus,
if those harmonics fall in the audible spectrum, they will get digitized and
recorded just like any other signal.  If they fall above 20 kHz, thr various
filtering filters, anti-aliasing, and anti-imaging devices on record and
playback will filter them out.

subject: Chalk up another one for helmets
q: I fell and hit my head hard on concrete while wearing my helmet, but I can't see any damage on it. Should I throw it out and buy a new one?
ref: Look for crushed foam inside and out, and for cracks. A hard hit likely deformed the crushable lining even if it rebounded, so replace it. A helmet is cheap compared to your head. Or mail it to the maker for inspection.
replies:
I would look for any evidence of crush in the foam (both on the inside
and outside) as well as for cracks.  Given any suggestion of damage to
the foam, I would replace it, but obviously a helmet is meant to take
some punishment and you don't want to trash one everytime it drops on
the floor.  If you bought it recently and feel that you deserve a
replacement, mail it back to the manufacturer with a note explaining what
happened, how grateful you are that your head is still intact, and ask
them to inspect it.  Chances are they will simply replace it to save
the expense (and liability) of attempting to test it.

David States

subject: ORACLE: SQLFORMS 3.0 Problem-Bug!
q: How can I make an SQL*Forms 3.0 trigger select all records using a wildcard when the screen field is blank, without losing the index? NVL with LIKE gives ORA-00920.
ref: Test against an empty string rather than null. Use DECODE(:screenfield2,'','%',:screenfield2) with LIKE, or use an OR with :screenfield2 = ''. Or branch in the trigger to two separate SELECTs, one with no predicate. Sigh, basic Oracle.
replies:
Rather than using null to test the screen field I would recommend
using '', ie an empty string.

Rather than using NVL in the first case it could be rewritten as:

    select field
    into :screenfield
    from table
    where table.field like DECODE(:screenfield2,'','%',:screenfield2);

The second method (which is the method I prefer) would be:

   where ((table.field = :screenfield2) or (:screenfield2 = ''))

This should use an index on table.field if :screenfield2 != ''. Note
that if :screenfield2 = '' then a full table scan will take place in
both cases - thats fine as you want all the rows back anyway.

Another solution would be to test :screenfield2 within your
trigger/procedure/whatever and branch to one of two SQL statements -
one with the predicate table.field  = :screenfield2 and the other with
no predicate at all.

Hope this helps...

Martin Morris

subject: guitar audio signals
q: Can I plug an electric guitar into a home stereo amp without hurting anything? Do turntables put out the same signal as a guitar?

Plug your guitar into "AUX" at your amp. I've been doing this with various
keyboards when I've been playing with them at home and it works just fine,
so I guess a guitar would be no problem either. You will perhaps need a

response a turntable pickup has. This will destroy, if not your amp, the
sound of your guitar.

And yes, switch your amp to mono (most stereo amps have a switch for that).
Then you will get the sound in both channels. Some stereo amps doesn't like
when they have a full signal in one channel and none in the other.

subject: Kermit which will work through a TCPIP packet driver
q: Can a newer Kermit talk through a TCP/IP packet driver on an IBM clone? Our university mainframe runs MTS with an X.25-type interface into TCP/IP, where telnet works but FTP doesn't.
ref: Yes, get MS-DOS Kermit 3.11. It has its own built-in TCP/IP Telnet code that runs over Ethernet packet drivers, since packet drivers carry no protocol stack. But if FTP fails, Telnet likely will too, or MTS simply lacks an FTP program. Use long packets and sliding windows.
replies:
---------------------
Brent,
	Yes. Get MS-DOS Kermit 3.11, the current release. Btw, Packet Drivers
do not contain protocol stacks, but act as packet switchers at the very bottom
of the protocol food chain. Thus Kermit has it's own built-in TCP/IP Telnet
code which runs over Ethernet type Packet Drivers.
	Before you go too far, it might be wise to think about this. X.25
is a data transporter and should know nothing of the meaning of the data.
Telnet and FTP share TCP and IP protocol stacks. So if FTP won't work then
likely Telnet won't either. Thus maybe you don't have a TCP/IP compatible
communications channel. On the other hand maybe the MTS system simply lacks
an FTP program.
	Kermit to Kermit file transfer speeds are vastly faster across Ethernet
than RS232. I am thankfully free of any X.25 paths so I can't say much more
than the speed will very likely be limited by the comms line. Use long packets
and sliding windows for greatest efficiency.
	Joe D.

subject: swap dissappearing
q: Our DEC 5500 running Ultrix 4.1 with 250 meg of swap reports lots of 'missing' swap in pstat -s even though little is used. How can swap be this fragmented?
ref: Probably not fragmentation. We had the same thing: the secondary swap partition wasn't set up, so it wasn't being used. Add a line like /dev/rz2b::sw::::: to /etc/fstab, using the partition from your kernel config, and reboot. RTFM next time.
replies:
at Fox Chase we ran into what appears to be a similar problem...we're also
running images on x-terminals, with a DECstation 5000 as the host for the
x-terminals....we had configured a secondary swap area, but would constantly
run out of swap area...looking at your 'pstat -s' listing it appears you may
have the same problem...what had happened with us is that we hadn't mounted
the partition for the secondary swap area...thus virtual memory was being
utilized when trying to access the secondary swap area...if you don't have an
entry for the secondary swap area in '/etc/fstab' try adding the following
line:

		/dev/rz2b::sw:::::
		     ^^^^
		     where rz2b is the partition specified in your
		     kernel's config file...

then re-boot, this should clear your problem

subject: CURSES: use of overlay()/overwrite()
q: What is the correct way to use curses overlay() and overwrite()? I want a dialogue box that can be removed later, restoring whatever it covered, with the box doing its own refresh.
ref: Skip overlay and open a new window altogether with newwin. Then wrefresh(newwin) updates just that one, or use wnoutrefresh(newwin) and do everything with one refresh(). The windows are independent, with cursor addressing per window. Curses 101.

By making a new window you can do a wrefresh(newwin) to update just one

cursor addressing will be dependent on the window addressed.

subject: LOCALDOMAIN and $w
q: We have two equivalent mail domains, waterloo.edu and uwaterloo.ca, but sendmail sets $w to only one. If a user's LOCALDOMAIN is the other one, local mail bounces because the $=w match fails. How do I fix it?
ref: You're confusing $=w, the class w, with $w, the macro. Set the class in sendmail.cf with a line like Cwhost.waterloo.edu host.uwaterloo.ca. Don't try Cw$w.waterloo.edu, because sendmail 5.64 doesn't expand macros in class definition lines. Read the docs next time.
replies:
We have two equivalent mail domains (waterloo.edu and uwaterloo.ca), but $w is
   only set to one of these by sendmail.  If a user has LOCALDOMAIN set to the
   other one, local mail is bounced, because the match against $=w fails.

$=w matches against the *class* w, which is set via Cwxxx yyy zzz in
the .cf file.  You are confusing this with the macro w, which is
supposed to be the local hostname, set via Dwhostname in .cf.

Do the following in your sendmail.cf file:

Cwhost.waterloo.edu host.uwaterloo.ca

and things should be ok.

p.s. Please note that you can't do a

Cw$w.waterloo.edu $w.uwaterloo.ca

because sendmail 5.64 does not evaluate macros in class definition
lines.

-dave

subject: Security
q: What's wrong with using a password to protect a packet radio BBS? Phone BBSs use passwords, and if I change mine often it's hard to break, so why not packet?
ref: Because radio is a party line, genius. On a phone BBS you're alone on the line. On packet, anyone on the frequency can monitor your packets and copy your password as you send it. Changing it often doesn't help when it goes out in the clear.
replies:
The reason, of course, is that with traditional (land line) BBS systems
the communications channel is somewhat secure, barring wiretaps.  In
the radio world, you're broadcasting your password to anyone within
line of sight, who may be listening.  Even if login authentication is
performed, the network itself is not secure.

-=Paul Flaherty, N9FZX      | "Think of it as evolution in action."
->paulf@shasta.Stanford.EDU |       -- Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle

The answer to this question is fairly obvious:  when you call a phone-based
BBS, you are the only one on the line and others cannot monitor the line
and copy your password.

With packet, however, anyone on the same frequency can monitor your packets
and record your password.  Radio is like the old-fashioned telephone party
lines.

subject: Predicting Execution Times for Processors with caches
q: How do you account for unpredictable instruction timings from caches when designing hard real-time applications?
ref: Design for worst case. Disable the cache while measuring, so every access is a miss, and you get a safe overestimate of execution time. Then re-enable the cache and give the spare CPU time to aperiodic tasks. The catch is tight loops, where you waste schedulability.
replies:
We usually worry about worst-case execution time.  An overestimate of the
worst case execution time can be obtained by disabling the cache, which
guarantees that all memory accesses are cache misses.  After the timings are
made, we reenable the cache, which results in a faster program.  Any extra CPU
time can be given to aperiodic tasks.  One problem with this method is that the
number of tasks that are guaranteed to be schedulable is possibly less than it
needs to be if the worst-case times with the cache disabled is much higher
than the worst-case times with cache enabled.  This will happen mostly for
tasks with very tight loops (e.g. for (i=0;i<1000;++i) { x[i] = i;}).
Nevertheless, as long as the specified worst-case
execution time is an overestimate, predictability can be achieved.

This dilemma was partially the motivation for one VMEbus processor board I
worked on not having cache (mz7170).  We had no theoretical data to support
our decision, however.

As it turns out many of that company's customers didn't feel it was an issue
one way or the other, possibly due to their applications not having very
hard constraints.  It may be that processors of that power and/or operating
system weren't being sold into accounts of that nature, I'm honestly not
sure.

In any case for the most robust real-time design you must assume worst case
for all timings, including cache performance.

An interesting thread of discussion would be for readers with actual
applications to chip in with what their real-time constraints are.  I'm
familiar with the situations of those who have (essentially) laboratory
systems, but less so with folks who are embedding things into equipment.
These days, are they using off-the-shelf boards?  Software?

subject: SmartPort Call
q: When calling the SmartPort dispatcher at $C503 plus the byte at $C5FF, can I assume the call always lands in page $C5, to save a few bytes of code?
ref: Yes, the SmartPort entry point is in the same page as the ProDOS entry point. That ProDOS entry needs at least two bytes of code, and $CnFE and $CnFF have special meaning. But don't assume slot 5 holds a SmartPort device or that other slots don't. Think before you hardcode.
replies:
Yes, you can assume that the SmartPort entry point is in the same memory page
as the ProDOS entry point.  (My reasoning on this is that the ProDOS entry
point has to have at least two bytes of code at it, and $CnFE and $CnFF have
special meaning for ProDOS devices.)

On the other hand, you shouldn't assume that slot 5 contains a SmartPort
device, or that other slots don't contain SmartPort devices.

subject: INHIBIT flag

It sends an ACTION_INHIBIT packet to the file system.  This tells the file

subject: host/transputer link speeds?
q: What's the fastest link you can get between a PC host and a transputer board? I thought it was 300 Kbytes/sec, which is too slow for real-time video compression needing about 2 Mbytes/sec.
ref: Plain cards like the INMOS B008 max out at 300K in hardware. A single link tops out around 1.7 Mbytes/sec anyway, so skip links. Build a board with a transputer and dual-ported RAM in the PC address space. A PC/AT bus will struggle at 2MB/s, though; EISA or MCA will do it.
replies:
``Bog-standard'' PC interface cards (like the INMOS B008) do max out
at 300K for the _HARDWARE_. Generally you would need to write your
own (or modify something else) software to achieve this speed in
an application however.

Links themselves have a 1.7Mbyte max data rate and so your 2Mbyte
target would require two simultaneous links. To achieve this look
for boards which use a transputer rather than a link adaptor as
the interface device. I've seen one from Transtech which does
1Mbyte on one link through a device driver. Can't remember if it
supports multiple links. There are a few other cards out there
doing similar tricks but I forget who makes them.

As another thought, would it be possible to avoid sending
the data to the PC altogether ? Perhaps by using a JPEG TRAM
or transuter-based display board ?

David.

It is possible to build a link-interface for the AT-Bus, which easily
realizes a overall bandwith (unidirectional) of more than one MB/s.
We have build such a thing around a C011 link-adaptor and two
IDT 7204 4096x9 bit hardware Fifos. The biggest problem was, that you
have to build a 16-bit AT interface, since the 8 bit XT interface is
too slow.
With this design we realize about 1.2 MB/s transfer rate between two
of this adaptors. We have never connected it to a transputer, but i
think, that the transputer would not be the bottleneck.
Yours Stephan Wenger
stewe@opal   stewe@tub

Links wont cut it (unless you use 2 or more and that gets very messy).
So don't use links !  Build a board with a transputer and some ram dual ported
into the host PC address space.  That said you will be pushed to get 2MB
a second out of a PC/AT bus however EISA or MCA will do it.

We get close to 2MB on our EISA boards using this approach however our
product is not a general purpose design that you could adapt.

subject: Overall speed
q: The SPARC 2 is RISC with 28 MIPS and the NeXT is CISC with 15 MIPS. Since a CISC instruction does more work, is the NeXT really slower, or am I missing something?
ref: Yes, you're missing something. Benchmarks are normalized so 1 MIP equals one VAX 11/780, roughly 1700 dhrystones per second. So the claim is NeXT about 15 times a 780 and the SPARC about 28. Read the fine print in the ads, sigh.
replies:
Yes, you are.

These days benchmarks are usually "normalized" so that the amount of
real work accomplished by a 1 MIP machine is equivalent to the amount
of "real work" accomplished by a VAX 11/780.  While benchmark ratings
can of course be rigged by recoding the tests, there is *some* consistency
because of this kind of normalization.

So, the claim is that a NeXT is 15x the speed of a 780, and the
Sparcstation 2 (Sparcstation ][? ;) ) is about 28x.

Yeah, they are talking about dhrystone MIPS where 1 MIPS = ~1200 or ~1700
dhrys. I don't have the exact number. Read any IBM RS/6000 ad where they
have the SPARC 1  15 MIPS, DEC 3100 so and so mips RS/6000 1 billion MIPS
blah blah, you will find in the fine print "1 MIPS equals 1727 dhrystones
per second" or something. On a VAX 11/780 I believe that it takes about
one million instructions to do 1727 dhrys....

There you are.

subject: how to install Xenix plus PC DOS on IBM PC hard disk
q: How do I get Xenix and PC DOS to coexist on the hard disk of an IBM PC XT compatible, and how do I switch between them?
ref: Do DOS first, with its fdisk, then install Xenix, and follow the manual. To switch, run Xenix fdisk to make the DOS partition active, haltsys and reboot; from DOS, make the Xenix one active. Newer SCO Xenix lets you type dos after haltsys. Xenix on an 8088, really?
replies:
I did this a number of times with an ATT 6300.  The basic trick is to
follow the manual.  Do the DOS side first.  Use fdisk to set up your DOS
partition, then do Xenix.  The only real nastiness, as I remember, is
ambiguity in the instructions.  If you screw up or decide you want to
change sizes and have done at least part of the Xenix installation, use
the Xenix fdisk command to delete the Xenix partition.  Then, start over.
If you do not do this, msdos fdisk cannot change the partition size.

This is explained fairly coherently in the documentation.  When running
Xenix, you have two alternatives:

(a)	as root run fdisk, make the dos partition active, haltsys,
	hit any key;

(b)	insert a bootable msdos floppy, haltsys, hit any key.

From msdos, use fdisk to make the xenix partition active, use alt-ctl-del.

NO.

Recent versions of SCO Xenix allow you to haltsys, hit a key, and type
dos to reboot under MSDOS.  Since I no longer use the 8086 version and
do not have updates, I cannot tell

(1) Are you sure you want Xenix on an 8088?
(2) Most manufacturers of disk controller boards supply disk preparation
    software with which you will:
    (a) low-level format the hard disk
    (b) boot, and install MSDOS
(3) Under MSDOS, high-level format the disk and create a partition
    for MSDOS and a partition for XENIX.
(4) Select XENIX as the primary partition
(5) Boot, and install XENIX

Thereafter, the loading of the boot sector, which has been provided by
XENIX in the primary partition, will allow you to select whether to
boot MSDOS or XENIX.

I can't really give more detailed instructions than this, as the
installation procedure depends primarily on your disk formatting software.
I, fortunately, had help configuring my machine from someone very
experienced in such things; and you may look for that kind of expertise
in your local user groups.

subject: Decnet-Ultrix
q: Can I make one whole-disk "g" partition on an RZ55 under Ultrix, or does chpt force me to make a small "a" partition first?
ref: No, you don't need that workaround. The whole disk is already the c partition, so use it. The a and c partitions include a fudge factor for the disk label, and chpt is protecting you from overlaying it. Avoid overlaps with swap too.
replies:
My guess is that the other system you're talking to hasn't flushed it's arp
cache.  When DECnet-ULTRIX starts up it changes the physical address of the
Ethernet Card to aa-00-04-00-XX-YY (where XX-YY is of the relation XX *
256 + YY
= a * 1024 + n (a.n)).  If the remote system doesn't flush it's arp cache,
it will recognize the system.  Since DECnet-ULTRIX is started before IP, you
should only experience this one (the first time DECnet-ULTRIX is installed).

If the remote system BSD-based, try doing a '/etc/arp -d yourname' on
the remote
system.  This will delete the arp entry from the arp cache.

Why not just the C partition?

I do this all the time and have no problem.  Never heard of this.

No.  The whole partition is the c partition.  Use it.

Fred

Remember that the "a" and "c" partitions include a fudge factor for the
disk label.  Chpt may be "protecting" you by not letting you overlay the
disk label with some random partition.

As others have pointed out, the "c" partition is already set up to define
the entire usable disk.  Make sure you avoid either explicit or implicit
(swap area) overlaps...

subject: Borland C++ and Turbo Pascal 5
q: I have a communications library written in C using C++ 2.0, and I need to use it from a program written in Turbo Pascal 5. Several functions use the standard C library. Is that even possible?
ref: Linking directly is a mess. Try a Pascal compiler that emits standard .OBJ files, like Quick Pascal or Stony Brook, though calling conventions may bite you. Easier: if the comms job is a discrete batch, have Turbo Pascal shell out to a C++ program, passing parameters on the command line or in environment variables. Sigh, think before you link.
replies:
Ideas:

(a) check to see if Microsoft's Quick Pascal product outputs standard
.OBJ files.  If so, you should be able to link Turbo Pascal code and C++
programs together, since Quick Pascal is supposed to be fairly
compatible with TP.  Pascal versus C parameter passing conventions may
be a problem, however... don't know if Microsoft offers help on that.

(b) Stony Brook offers another Pascal compiler which is also Turbo
Pascal compatible; same ideas and caveats as (a).

(c) If the communication task is quite discrete (i.e. the Turbo Pascal
part of the program creates a bunch of data files and then needs to send
them all somewhere in a batch transfer), you could have TP shell out to
DOS to a program written solely in C++.  Parameter passing could be done
either on the command line of the "shelling out", or in environment
variables set in Turbo Pascal before the "shelling out".

subject: How to zero a file
q: What's the preferred way in perl to zero a file, and to copy a file, without using exec on shell commands?
ref: Just open the file for output with open(OUT, ">filename") and it's truncated to zero length, no exec needed. To copy, open the input, slurp it into an array and print that to the output. Mind your memory on big files, though.
replies:
What is the preferred way to zero a file in perl?  In shell scripts I
   use "> filename", so in perl I can 'exec "> filename"', but it seems
   to me that there should be a way to do this without using exec.

   In a similar vein, what is the preferred way to copy a file?  I could
   obviously just crank up 'exec "cp old new"', but again I wonder if there
   is some "better" way to do this entirely within perl.  Copying a line at
   a time, with "while () print" doesn't seem to me to be an ideal solution.

Here is a example program which should answer your questions (tested
on a Sun 4/110 running SunOS 4.0.3 and perl 3.0 patch 8).

No explicit loop: the danger is to run out of memory if copying a big
file.

#! /usr/bin/perl

open(IN,"<$ARGV[0]") || die "can't open $ARGV[0]";
open(OUT,">$ARGV[1]") || die can't open $ARGV[1]";  # create a zero length file
@in=<IN>;   #  read the whole file in the array @in (one entry perl line)
print OUT @in;

subject: AD&D: Starting First Level Characters
q: How do I get first-level AD&D characters together on their first adventure when they supposedly don't know each other, without the 'archmage summons you to his castle' cliche?
ref: Don't make them strangers. Sit down with the players beforehand and work out each character's history and how they all know each other. Or write the backstory up to the meeting point and hand it out. Meeting in a bar is phony anyway.
replies:
Why shouldn't the PCs know each other?

  An easy way to do this is to sit down with the players and decide on each PC's
past history and how all the PCs know each other, before the adventure begins.
Not only does this make your (the GM's) job easier, but it fleshes out the PCs'
backgrounds and personalities - a sure-fire way of creating a more satisfying
and enjoyable campaign for both players and the GM.

I'm about to start a campaign (GURPS, but this should appy to almost
  any system), and what I plan on doing is this: When I let my players
  make up characters, I'll tell *them* to come up with a group that
  already knows each other and has some rationale for adventuring
  together. This makes it more reasonable that they should be loyal to
  each other, and cut out the phoney meeting role playing.

DM: "You walk into a bar, you see two mean looking half-orcs at a
  table in the corner, armed to the teeth, and wearing armor. What
  do your Mage and Cleric do?"

Players: "We walk over, sit down, buy them a drink and become
  friends for life, willing to defend each other to the death,
  unless of course, we're not expecting any more player characters
  to join us, in which case we attack them!"

Keith (The Lazy DM) Hearn

I don't think it's worth it.  At best, it is a lot of solo adventuring, which
is not fun for the group as a whole.  I usually, write up a background (after
working with the player for input) that includes the story up to the point
where the characters meet.  Moreover, I do this prior to the first session,
have the stories on papers to hand out to the players.

subject: Windows V2.1 and Logitech Mouse
q: A new PS/2 Model 30 with DOS 4.0, Windows 2.1 and a Logitech Series 2 mouse works in Dosshell but under Windows the mouse gives no response and no pointer appears. How do I fix it?
ref: Windows has its own internal mouse driver and chokes on a loaded one. If config.sys has device=mouse.sys or similar, pull it out and reboot. Failing that, check the port assignment or get a fresh copy of the driver.
replies:
We have model 30's, 70's and 80's, VGA, MSW2.1, MSW386 and logitech mice,
they all work fine.

Check the port assignments or try to get a new copy of the driver, maybe
it got clobbered some how.

We had a problem similar to this at work, and it seems that windows did not
like having the mouse device driver loaded, because it had it's own internal
device drivers.  So if your config.sys file has device=mouse.sys or something
like that try removing it and rebooting and trying again.

subject: gcc?
q: What exactly is "gcc"? Is it just the C compiler on the Amiga, or is it on other machines too?
ref: The GNU C Compiler, from the Free Software Foundation. Seven years of Unix and you never heard of it? It handles ANSI and K&R C, often optimizes better than the standard compiler, and source is freely available via ftp from prep.ai.mit.edu.
replies:
The GNU C Compiler (gcc) is a publicly available C compiler provided
by the Free Software Foundation (FSF).  GCC supports both ANSI and K&R
C and provides (in some cases) better optimization that the standard C
compiler.  The source for gcc is provided as is required by the GNU
Public License (GPL).  The GPL requires full disclosure (rather than
concealment) of FSF source code and/or modifications or derivations.

If you are on the internet, you can retrieve FSF sources from
prep.ai.mit.edu via FTP.

DavidM

subject: nroff question

ref: Pipe the output through col -b, which strips the double and triple hammering nroff does for bold and italic. Something like nroff -mm yourfile.m | col -b > newfile.x. Not exactly rocket science.
replies:
Have you tried piping your nroff'ed document to col -b? If you do,
it basically strips out the bullshit you get with double and triple hammmering
of characters that nroff does with bold and italic.

newfile.x doesn't have the extra stuff.

subject: file sizes
q: After upgrading Minix 1.3 to 1.5.10, copying a 1.24 Mbyte file to a 1450 block filesystem on a 1.44Mbyte disk gives "cp : error 0". Why?
ref: A 1.44M disk has only 1440 blocks, not 1450. Also cp has a bug where it doesn't allow for partial writes, which gives "error 0". Partial writes mostly happen when writing past the end of a disk device. Count your blocks.
replies:
There are only 1440 blocks on a 1.44M disk.

There is a (probably unique) bug in cp which would cause "error 0". It
doesn't allow for partial writes.

However, I don't see how a partial write could be caused by the above
setup. In Minix, the only partial writes that I can remember occur when
writing past the end of a disk device. For these, the bug would only
cause cp to report an error one step too early.

subject: distortion in USM EF 35-135
q: Why does a straight line look curved in the viewfinder of my EF 35-135 zoom lens? Is that the lens quality or natural for lenses?
ref: Perfectly normal. Zoom lenses commonly do this, even expensive ones, since it's very hard to correct. They bend lines toward the edge at short focal lengths and toward the center at long ones. Many fixed lenses do too; only macro lenses are safe.
replies:
It is very common for zoom lenses to do this, even for quite expensive
lenses. It is very hard to correct for this kind of distortion in a zoom
lens. Most zoom lenses bends straight lenses towards to edge of the image
at short focal lengths and towards the centre of the image at long focal
lenses ("long" being 35mm for the Canon EF 20-35/2.8L lens).

Many fixed-length lenses have this kind of distortion as well. The only
lenses you can be quite sure doesn't have it are macro lenses. That's one
of the reasons why they are used for reproduction work.

subject: i-nodes disappearing in SysVr3 filesystem
q: Running inews on our System V R3 filesystem, the free i-node count suddenly drops from about 2300 to about 1, and only fsck restores it. What can we do to avoid this bug, and will making more i-nodes fix it?
ref: Yes, that's the inode bug. Fsck'ing often cuts the failures but won't eliminate them. The bug is in (s5)?ialloc and is trivial to fix, so patch it if you have source, or hassle your vendor. If he says it's hard, tell him baloney.
replies:
Inodes.

That sounds like the inode bug all right.

Fsck'ing your system frequently will cut down on the failures but will
not eliminate them. I've had an inode crunch within minutes of doing
a fsck.

If you have source code, or are handy with a disassembler, it is
fairly easy to patch the code. I can give you hints if you need them.

Of course, the right solution is to hassle your vendor. If he tells
you that this is hard to fix, tell him baloney. The bug is in
(s5)?ialloc and is trivial to fix.

subject: WB1.4
q: The major changes in WorkBench 1.4 make it sound like it should be a full revision. Could this be WB 2.0?
ref: Nope. The Amiga crew has said several times that 2.0 will be an incompatible release where they get to break everything to make it right. 1.4 looks too compatible with 1.3 to earn the name. Major version numbers are for major breakage, kid.
replies:
Nah, they haven't broken enough things to call it 2.0 :-).  Remember when
MS-DOS went from version 1 to version 2?  If the user wanted to specify

Incrementing the major version number is reserved for major changes.  It
looks like 1.4 will be too compatible with 1.3 to be called 2.0.

Nope.  The Amiga crew has said several times that 2.0 will be an
incompatible release where they joyfully get to break everything to make it
all work right. :-)

subject: turning pc off 1 year
q: I'm going out of the country for a year and want to crate my 3B1 until I return. Any hints, dangers, or recommended procedures? I worry about the clock battery.
ref: Forget the clock; worry about the disk. Grease on the spindle can harden and the drive won't spin up after a long shutdown. Make backups, clear passwords, and remove the battery jumper or let it die. In humid places, vacuum-seal it in plastic. Basic stuff.
replies:
Chris..
	I would worry more about the disk than the clock.. If you want
you can remove a jumper on the mother board that will disable the
battery, or let it run down and replace it when you get back.
The biggest problem is going to be the disk. I had a number of
20mb 7300/6300 that had 20mb disk. These ran 24hr/day for several years.
We turned these systems off for about 1month and
when I turned them back on all of the disk failed to spin up. Problem
the grease had hardened on the disk spindle. You might get away with
greasing up up the drive before you leave. Make a couple of backups
before you leave and also keep a list of passwords for the system,
or clear them out..

If your unsure about the evironment it will be in (like high humidty or
you live near an ocean) you might want to put it in a thick plastic bag.
Use a shop vac to pull all the air out of it and seal it.  Your connectors
will thank you when you return.
