subject: Wlogin for UNIX-PC
q: Is there a program for the UNIX-PC like wlogin that allows multiple logins on the console without messing up utmp/wtmp?
ref: You don't need it. Put several respawn lines in /etc/inittab running getty on the window with a CONSOLE entry in /etc/gettydefs. Each window is a separate real login with its own utmp entry. Use Shift-Suspd and Shift-Rsume to move between them. Hack less, read more.
replies:
Here's some lines from my "/etc/inittab" file -

	vid:2:respawn:/etc/getty window CONSOLE
	vi2:2:respawn:/etc/getty window CONSOLE
	vi3:2:respawn:/etc/getty window CONSOLE
	vi4:2:respawn:/etc/getty window CONSOLE

	"CONSOLE" refers to an entry in the "/etc/gettydefs" file:

CONSOLE# EXTA CLOCAL BRKINT IGNPAR ISTRIP IXON IXOFF OPOST ONLCR # CLOCAL HUPCL BRKINT ICRNL IXON OPOST ONLCR EXTA CS8 CREAD ISIG ICANON ECHO ECHOE ECHOK TAB0 #Direct (Console) login: #CONSOLE

	I use the "<SHIFT>-Suspd" and "<SHIFT>-Rsume"
	keys to move around the window list.

	Make sure that the login for the first window
	is the one you want for the "Mail" icon etc.
	To do this, click on the "Window Manager" icon
	in the upper-right of the screen and select the
	first window-id in the list after reboot.
	Then log in as yourself (or whoever).

	I run logins for myself, uucp, news and root
	in the four windows I've set up. Each is a
	separate login just like ones from the serial
	port etc., with utmp entries etc.

ref: Yes. You can define your own paper sizes, and the paper in the box fits Day-Timer binders. For import it wants a text file with one person per line, fields separated by commas or tabs. A dialog lets you skip missing fields. Export to that format.
replies:
The purpose of Address Book Plus is to print small Address Books. Since
you can define your own paper sizes, you can certainly print pages to fit
a book like a Day-Timers. The paper that comes in the box, and some of the

subject: Quirky A-Max II
q: My A-Max II works fine right when I power on the Amiga, but if it's been on 20+ minutes or more I get a cartridge start error. Turning it off and back on doesn't fix it, only letting it cool for half an hour does. Bad ROM chips, flaky cartridge?
ref: Check your 8520 CIA chips, not the cartridge, that's almost certainly it. Swap them between sockets or try the cartridge on another Amiga to isolate the fault, that's exactly how I fixed the same cartridge-not-found error, new CIAs cured it for good.
replies:
I would check your CIA chips, the 8520s. Try switching them and see what hap-
pens. Try attaching your A-Max cartridge to another Amiga and see if the
problem persists -- if not, then something's wrong with your Amiga.

I had to do all this when my A-MaxII suddenly stopped working with a ``can't
find cartridge ROMs'' error. After finding that they worked fine on another
machine, I switched the CIA chips in my machine. The problem disappeared. So
I bought a new CIA chips and now it's fine. The wierd thing was that my
external floppy drives, both the Mac compatible and the Amiga 5.25" drive
attached to the ROM cartridge, always worked just fine.

Tim.

subject: ? on Rom 03 and TWGS
q: Can I upgrade my Apple IIgs from ROM 01 to ROM 03, and should I have known about a 10 MHz upgrade for my 7 MHz Transwarp GS?

The way to upgrade to ROM 03 is to buy a new motherboard.  There is no

subject: backup program for xenix?
q: Is there a free backup program for Xenix that backs up to floppy, ideally surviving floppy errors, and is there something better than tar plus split plus cp?
ref: Why on earth tar then split then copy? Just use tar cv2 with your file or directory, and it handles multiple floppies gracefully given the media size and blocking factor. There's also a tarskip program on the net to get past bad files. Use good floppies and verify them.
replies:
Why do you want to do the tar then the split and then the copy.

What's wrong with   tar cv2 <filename.or.directory>

(Assuming 2 is the proper number in your /etc/defaults/tar file)

Passed the media size and blocking factor tar will gracefully put
everything you need out there.

There is a tarskip program on the net (a year or so ago) allowing
you to go past any bad files.

As to floppy errors, use good quality floppies, and backup often.
You could also re-read the floppies to make sure they were okay.

I do this on archiving.  I tar them off, read them back in on
another machine.  When I know the floppy is readable I remove the
originals.  If it is an important file I make two copies.

subject: EPSPRINT (Can't get it to work!)
q: When I upload the EPSPRINT library to my HP48, I get a string full of garbage instead of a library object, though other libraries load fine. What's wrong?
ref: Seen it plenty. The HP48 turns the binary into a string when the file size doesn't match the sum of its objects' sizes, so the file is corrupt, unless your KERMIT parameters were wrong. If it came from uudecode, check for stray mail headers in the source. Sigh.
replies:
I've seen this plenty of times.  This usually results when the size of the
downloaded binary file is not consistent with the sum of the sizes of the
objects that make it up.  In an effort to handle the inconsistency, the HP48
turns the binary object into a string, so instead of a library object, you get a
string containing the (corrupt) binary data.

In other words, unless you had your KERMIT parameters wrong, you probably have a
corrupt file.  If the binary is the result of a uudecoded file, then check that
there were no extra mail headers or anything in the uuencoded source.

subject: jpg/ps to tiff converter
q: Where can I find a JPEG to TIFF converter and a PostScript to TIFF converter?
ref: For JPEG, use the Independent JPEG Group's djpeg to make a PPM, then pnmtotiff from PBMPLUS. For PostScript, have Ghostscript produce a PPM, perhaps via pstoppm.ps, then PBMPLUS again. All of it is on UUNET. Archives exist for a reason, go use them.
replies:
For JPEG to TIFF, you can use the recently released JPEG
utilities from the Independent JPEG group, and the latest version of
PBMPLUS (which includes Sam Leffler's TIFF library).  The program
djpeg will decode a JPEG file and create a PPM (portable pixmap) file
that can then be converted to TIFF via the "pnmtotiff" utility in the
the PBMPLUS utility set.

	For PS to TIFF, you could use Ghostscript to create a PPM
file, and then again use PBMPLUS to convert the resulting file.  The
version of Ghostscript that I'm currently using includes a postscript
program called "pstoppm.ps" that purports to do the conversion you'd
need -- I haven't tried it myself so I don't know if there are any
pitfalls.

	All of these sources can be had from a number of archive
sites; I generally get stuff from UUNET.  The current versions and
filenames (as of 28 October) on UUNET are:

	JPEG: ~/graphics/jpeg/jpegsrc.v1.tar.Z
	PBMPLUS: ~/packages/X/R4.contrib/pbmplus05oct91.tar.Z
	Ghostscript: ~/packages/gnu/ghos

subject: (none)
q: Why does a command button in a windowing system sometimes highlight when pressed but not run its callback, especially when pressed quickly after other actions?
ref: Usually the callback hangs off the ButtonUp event. If you press near the edge and the mouse slides out before release, the widget is already unhighlighting and no callback fires. Out-of-order events from mouse motion might do it too. Hold your mouse still, nimble-fingers.
replies:
I haven't seen this in X11. What often happens is that the callback is
tied to the Button*Up* event, and the user presses a button near the edge
of the widget, accidentally (or intentionally) moves out of the widget,
and releases the button. By the time the ButtonUp event is triggered,
the mouse is already out of the widget, and the widget is in the process of
unhighlighting itself anyway.

The only other possibility I can think of is that if, again, there is mouse
motion associated closely in time with the button release, the events might
arrive out of order. I don't know offhand whether that would cause this
problem or not.

-Miles

subject: Double-Clicking and Hypercard
q: How can I detect a double-click on a button in HyperCard? It seems to treat a double-click as a single click.
ref: Put a wait in the mouseUp handler, about 10 to 15 ticks, then test the mouseClick. If true, run your double-click script, else the single-click one. Also check the clickLoc is within the rect of the button. Obvious, really.
replies:
The method I've always used  to Make HC accept double-clicks as such is to
use a wait in the mouseUp script:

on mouseUp
   wait 10 ticks     --60 ticks in a second -  adjust to your liking.
   if the mouseclick then
      --double-click script
   else
      --SIngle-click script
   end if
end mouseUp

This doesn't check if the second click was actually on the button, only if
the mouse was clicked again. Hope that is OK.

is

The following was submitted, but does not check to see if the cursor was
within the rect of the button:

on mouseUp
   wait 10 ticks     --60 ticks in a second -  adjust to your liking.
   if the mouseclick then
      --double-click script
   else
      --SIngle-click script
   end if
end mouseUp

Here is the script which will check for the mouseLoc:

on mouseUp
  wait 10 ticks     --60 ticks in a second -  adjust to your liking.
  if the mouseclick ANDB
  the clickLoc is within the rect of me then
    --double-click script
  else
    --SIngle-click script
  end if
end mouseUp

You may wish to set the "wait 10 ticks" to "wait 15 ticks", as 1/4 of a
second is an average double-click response time.  (This 'average' is based
upon 450 case studies I did.)

Have Fun!!

subject: Never Mind: Huge pointers & Global memory
q: Why didn't the compiler warn me when GlobalAlloc got only 0xc200 bytes instead of the 0x1c200 I wanted from sizeof(POINT)*NPOINTS*NANGLES?
ref: Because sizeof(POINT), NPOINTS and NANGLES are all plain ints, so the multiplication is done in int and the result is an int. No warning, since it's legal C. You only need to cast any one operand to DWORD to get a long result, not all three.
replies:
--------
The compiler didn't warn you because sizeof(POINT), NPOINTS, and NANGLES
are all denotations (i.e. actual numbers).  In C, denotations will be
automatically evaluated at the default integer size for the target
machine architecture.  Since all three arguments of the multiplication
expression are integers, the result is also an integer.  In your fix,
you converted everything to DWORDs.  Actually, to promote the result to
a long integer, you only need to convert any one of the values in the
expression to a DWORD.

Sorry to be longwinded, but you asked... :-) :-)

kevinj

subject: How do I get HyperCard to return the value of a line?
q: In HyperCard 1.2.1, how can I find text in a field, get the line it's on, and then clear that line with put?

on delFindLine findText
  find findText
  if the result is not "No match" then -- or whatever HC returns on no match
    get the foundLine
    put it              -- show you what was found
    do "delete" && it   -- delete the line that was found
  end if
end delFindLine

subject: getting UUCP expect/send scripts working
q: I'm learning UUCP on Sys V r3.0. I can call out with cu, but when I connect to a remote system the expect/send script in my Systems file seems to be ignored, according to cu -d. What am I missing?
ref: Sigh. cu doesn't use the Systems file at all, so its debug output shows Dialers, not your login script. Debug the real thing with uucico -r1 -x9 -sRemote_system, or run Uutry, which runs uucico with debugging and tails the log. You'll need read permission on Systems.
replies:
'cu' doesn't use the Systems file! The only file you must configure to
get cu to work is Devices. (I am assuming that Dialers is okay).

So, when you use 'cu' with the debug option, it is displaying the
expect/send sequence from Dialers, NOT Systems.

If you want to test a uucico link, you want to run it with the
'x' option, e.g.
		   uucico -r1 -x9 -sRemote_system

where the number with the x sets the debug level (amount of detail
reported). The most detail is reported with the x9 option.

You are on the right track in trying to use a debug option to get
uucico to work. I don't think I would try to get a link working without
using the debut option. It's just that you need the debug mode of
uucico (the -x#), rather that the debug mode of cu.

Remember, when using the debugging option, is that the failure
occurs where you have a problem. Fix the problem, and do it
again, until you finally get it to work.

Also, remember that a option such as -x9 displays a *lot* of
information which you

Cu doesn't attempt to execute the login script in the Systems file.  If you
want to debug this script, try using:
/usr/lib/uucp/Uutry -r remote_name
which is a shell script that runs uucico with debugging on and the
output redirected to a file.  You are then put into a "tail -f" of
the file so you can watch what happens.  Note that (a) you need
read permission on the Systems file or you won't see the real strings,
(b) you have to interrupt out of the tail -f, and (c) when you
interrupt out, the uucico is still running, so you either have to wait
until it fails to try the same system again or use ps to find its
process id and kill it.

subject: /etc/netgroup syntax?
q: What is the syntax of /etc/netgroup, and can long entries be broken across lines on RISC/os?
ref: With files, an entry must be on one line, since the code uses fgets. No backslash, no nested group names, and 4096 characters max. With NIS, the backslash works and nested groups are allowed. So use NIS, or several smaller groups. It's an open bug.
replies:
If you have vis.conf setup to use files to resolve netgroups, then the
following
applies

1) An entry has to be on one line. The \ character is not valid ( because
the code uses fgets to read in each line )
2) After the group name, the rest of the line can only contain
(host,user,domain) triplets. Names of other groups are not allowed.
3) The maximum length of a line is 4096 characters.

If vis.conf is set up to use NIS ( YP ) to resolve netgroups, and hence the
makedbm command is used to convert the /etc/netgroups file, then

1) the \ character is valid
2) A netgroup entry can contain the name of another group as well as
(host,user,domain) triplets.

So, either use NIS or use a number of smaller groups, and export to multiple
groups.

There is an open bug on this one( bug 8355 ).

--trevc--

subject: TRS-80 Model 1 TRS-DOS
q: My TRS-80 Model 1 with an expansion box and three floppy drives goes straight to Level II BASIC on power up instead of booting TRS-DOS. How do I get it to boot?
ref: It should hit the disk drive on power up, so it thinks there's no expansion interface. Clean the connectors with a pencil eraser, since they're tin plated and oxidize, and reseat everything. Check the EI to disk controller contact too. PRINT MEM shows if it sees the EI.
replies:
Use an eraser on the connector that goes from the expansion interface to the
cpu (keyboard).  The model I's connectors are not gold plated (they're tin
plated) so they oxidize.  When they do, then the cpu things it has no connect-
ion to the expansion interface (it happened to me a couple of times).

Try it...

Gary

Sounds like it's convinced that you don't have disk drives.  The normal
behavior is to go to the disk drives as soon as you turn it on (unless
you press <BREAK>).  A few suggestions:

	1.  Clean (with a pencil eraser) and reseat every ribbon connector
	    you see.
	2.  Type "print mem" at the BASIC prompt.  The keyboard probably has
	    16K in it and the Expansion Interface will probably have 32K.
	    If it says ~16K, it doesn't see the EI.
	3.  Let's see, you should have two power supplies not including the
	    power to the disk drives and the monitor.
	4.  The oldest Model I used a straight ribbon cable to the EI, there
	    were later ones that were "buffered" and had a small box in the
	    middle of the cable.  I believe the keyboard was labeled if it
	    needed the buffered cable

P.S.	If you must use a Model I, get LDOS.  There are others that know
	even more but would prefer that you find a different computer.

Yes.

Check the Expansion interface.

PARTICULARLY check the connections to the disk controller board.  A machine
with a working EI and disk controller attached should access the first
floppy drive upon booting up.  If it doesn't, and goes directly to BASIC,
you aren't seeing the EI and/or the disk controller (it is possible to have
an EI without the controller).

Note that Tandy did a real dumb thing with those EI units -- the contact
between the EI and disk controller is not "retained" as it is on a PC or the
like -- it's just a pressure connection.  As such, it often gets loose,
dirty, or just plain flakey.

subject: Trapping (fatal) runtime errors in TP 5.0
q: How do I trap fatal runtime errors in Turbo Pascal 5.0? I want to recover from a real math overflow.
ref: It's fairly simple. Write an error-handler procedure between {$F+} and {$F-}. At startup, save ExitProc in ExitSave and point ExitProc at your handler. The handler's last statement must restore ExitProc := ExitSave. It runs on every exit, so check the error condition first. RTFM.
replies:
Its fairly simple...you declare a procedure for error-handling somewhere
in your code.  Put a {$F+} and a {$F-} compiler directive around it
[force far call ON for the procedure, turn it back OFF afterwards]

Now, in your initialization code, make these two declarations...

ExitSave := ExitProc    [ExitProc is declared for you, ExitSave is a POINTER]
ExitProc := @MyErrorProc (or whatever)

The last statement of your error handler (refered to as MyErrorProc above)
must be   ExitProc := ExitSave

(Exiting a program is a chain procedure; this process inserts your trapper
*before* the Turbo one.  It will be called every time you exit, so you will
want to check the error condition to make sure you *need* to do anything.

Doug Oosting

ref: This gets asked every week. A filter can't count pages itself, since one line of PostScript can print thousands. It must ask the printer for its page count, print the job, and ask again; the difference is the pages. Most true Adobe printers keep that count, so check yours first.

Your filter has to get the information from the PostScript printer, IF it

subject: buttons and fields in the background

ref: Neither, it's how layers work. Bring Closer and Send Farther only work within a layer. Any card object is closer than all background objects, so your field was on the card layer above the background button. Think before you cry bug.
replies:
It sounds like the button was in the background and the field was in the
card layer. Bring Closer and Send Farther only work within a layer; in
other words, any card object will be "closer" than all background objects.

subject: UNIX Security and Monitoring
q: Is there a way in UNIX to monitor the I/O of another terminal or port, for dealing with hackers on sensitive systems?
ref: Think it through: such a tool is even more useful to the hackers. Anything that circumvents Unix's security policy, even for admins, weakens overall security. A student worker could snoop encryption keys or whole exams as they're typed. Security and monitoring are mutually exclusive.
replies:
This would be even more useful to the hackers themselves.  Think about
it.

It seems to me that security and monitoring are mutually exclusive,
especially on "sensitive systems".  Consider the following example:

You are sysadmin at a University.  The profs on your systems write their
exams on your system and encrypt them.  The student worker who does
your dumps/restores uses the monitoring tool you mention to grab the
encryption key used by his prof.  The student can then decrypt the
exam.  Or worse yet, the student can grab the entire exam as it is
typed in leaving no changed file access times.

(I'm not saying that student workers are un-trustworthy, just using this
to illustrate a point)

Generally, any tool that allows circumvention of Unix's security
policy even by administrators, only serves to weaken overall
system security.

subject: What kind of film do the astronauts use?
q: What kind of film do the astronauts use to photograph the earth from the Space Shuttle? Haze usually ruins contrast in airplane photos, yet the shuttle pictures look very saturated.
ref: Aerial films are high saturation anyway to beat haze, and even K-64 gives decent aerial results. Mostly it's physics: up there the light hasn't been diffused by the atmosphere, so it's more directional and contrasty. Not magic film, kid.
replies:
Most aerial films have a very high saturation to overcome haze and
fog... I think Kodak used to have something called SO-411 which was an
excellent example.  Another good example is a Kodak photomicrographic film
(not a special order), which is (or was) an E-4 film at 6 ASA which
offered extreme contrast and saturation.  Actually, you can get pretty
good aerial results with K-64.
  The main reason is that light up there has not been diffused by the
atmosphere and is much more directional, which seriously increases
the contrast.  When combined with relatively high-contrast film,
you get great results.
(from a former aerial photographer)

subject: problem with using system(3S) on 3b1 v3.51
q: On a 3b1, my program calls system(3S) and I get 'kw: is not an identifier' from the shell, though the command string is fine. The same code worked on HP-UX. What is happening?
ref: That message comes from sh. It parses its envp and dies if it doesn't like the variable names. The fix is to stop munging *envp. On the Unix PC, *envp sits right after *argv, so it's easy to trample. Sloppy.
replies:
That message came from sh.  Sh parses its envp, and if it doesn't like the
variable names, it complains and dies.  The fix is to stop munging *envp.
On the Unix PC, *envp is located right after *argv, for ease of munging.

subject: parallel printer with ISC 3.2 2.21
q: My parallel printer on ISC 3.2 works from WordPerfect but with lp the output is strange. As a dumb_dos printer tabs send the head to the right margin, and as dumb no CRs are sent. What does ISC expect a dumb printer to look like?
ref: The printer needs CR/LF to print text right. Translating LF to CR/LF breaks DOS text files, which get double-spaced, and corrupts graphics. I wrote a short filter to replace cat in the spooler interface script. It peeks at the file type and massages the input. Nobody's offered better.
replies:
I had a similar problem trying to configure a laser printer under ISC
2.0.2.  I needed to print three different kinds of files: 1) UNIX text
files (LF delimited)  2) DOS text files (CR/LF delimited)  3) graphics
(binary) files.  By default, the printer needs a CR/LF to print a text
file correctly, so UNIX text files wouldn't print properly.
Configuring the printer to translate LF to CR/LF made UNIX text files
print properly, but then DOS text files were double-spaced, and
graphics files were corrupted.

I ended up writing a short filter to replace "cat" in the spooler
interface script.  My filter peeks into the file to figure out which
type it is, then massages the input (or leaves it alone) accordingly.
Everything seems to work fine now.

If anyone knows of a better solution, I'd love to hear about it.
